tags.vgi.doc_md:
## loganalytics_query

KQL passthrough to an Azure Monitor / Log Analytics workspace. The `kql` text is sent verbatim; each Kusto result row comes back as one JSON `result` string. Read data rows by filtering `_row_kind IS NULL`. For incremental pulls, project `TimeGenerated`, pass `since`, and take the next cursor from the marker row's `_watermark_next` (the marker row is the one whose `_row_kind` equals `marker`).

A snapshot call reads the `timespan` window (default `P1D`); an incremental call projects `TimeGenerated`, passes `since`, and takes the next cursor from the marker row's `_watermark_next`. Aggregations (`summarize`) run server-side in the workspace and come back one JSON `result` per group. Large result sets (>~500k rows / 64MB) must be time-sliced by the caller via `timespan` or `since`. Requires an app-only `azure_graph` secret with workspace read access.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT result FROM azure.main.loganalytics_query('SigninLogs | project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName', '<workspace-guid>', since := '<prior _watermark_next>') WHERE _row_kind IS NULL

vgi.example_queries.description: Read the watermark cursor to persist for the next incremental scan
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT _watermark_next FROM azure.main.loganalytics_query('SigninLogs | project TimeGenerated', '<workspace-guid>', since := '2026-01-01T00:00:00Z') WHERE _row_kind = 'marker'

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: result
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: One Kusto result row encoded as a JSON object string, keyed by the KQL query's projected column names. NULL on the marker row.

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: _row_kind
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: NULL for business data rows; the literal 'marker' for the single trailing cursor row (present only on an incremental `since` pull).

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: _watermark_next
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: On the marker row, the clamped ISO-8601 `TimeGenerated` watermark to persist and replay via the `since` argument; NULL on data rows (and no marker row is emitted at all on a non-incremental full pull).

arguments.name: kql
arguments.description: The Kusto (KQL) query text, sent to Log Analytics verbatim — the worker never parses or rewrites it (passthrough). Required. For incremental (watermark) use, project `TimeGenerated` in the query so a cursor can be synthesized.

arguments.name: since

workers.doc_md:
## Azure Resource Graph

Whole-estate Azure inventory via Azure Resource Graph (ARG), exposed as one DuckDB table function.

- **`resourcegraph_query`** — run one KQL query across the ARM estate; returns one JSON `result` string per resource (a point-in-time snapshot, no change feed).

The KQL string is required (positional); optionally scope to specific subscriptions and tune the ARG page size. Each result row is a JSON object — extract fields with `json_extract(result, '$.name')` or the `->` / `->>` operators. An app-only `azure_graph` secret (Microsoft Entra client credentials, Reader on the target subscriptions) is required to fetch data.

workers.doc_md:
## Microsoft Entra ID Protection Risk

Incremental access to the Microsoft Entra ID Protection risk feed via Microsoft Graph, exposed as three DuckDB table functions.

- **`risky_users`** — current per-user risk state (source of truth for the verdict).
- **`risky_service_principals`** — current per-service-principal (workload identity) risk state.
- **`risk_detections`** — immutable risk detection events.

Each function returns data rows plus a single marker row (`_row_kind = 'marker'`) whose `_watermark_next` column holds the ISO-8601 instant to persist and replay as the next scan's `since`. Call with no arguments for a full sync from epoch; pass `since := '<_watermark_next>'` for an incremental sync. Reconcile `risk_detections` against `risky_users` (join `user_id` <-> `id`) for the current verdict. Requires an app-only `azure_graph` secret, the three `Identity*.Read.All` Graph permissions, and an Entra ID P2 license.

example_queries.title: risky_users_bind_probe
example_queries.description: Bind risky_users and expose its result columns (credential-free; drop LIMIT 0 and attach an azure_graph secret to sync real data)
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, user_principal_name, risk_level, risk_state FROM azure.main.risky_users() LIMIT 0;

example_queries.title: risk_detections_bind_probe
example_queries.description: Bind risk_detections and expose its result columns (credential-free; attach an azure_graph secret to sync real data)
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, user_id, risk_event_type, detected_date_time FROM azure.main.risk_detections() LIMIT 0;

example_queries.title: risky_service_principals_bind_probe
example_queries.description: Bind risky_service_principals and expose its result columns (credential-free; attach an azure_graph secret to sync real data)
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, app_id, display_name, risk_level, risk_state FROM azure.main.risky_service_principals() LIMIT 0;

example_queries.description: Users currently at risk
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, user_principal_name, risk_level FROM azure.main.risky_users() WHERE _row_kind IS NULL AND risk_state = 'atRisk'

example_queries.description: Incremental sync of risk detections from a saved watermark
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, user_id, risk_event_type FROM azure.main.risk_detections(since := '<_watermark_next>') WHERE _row_kind IS NULL

example_queries.description: Reconcile detections against the current per-user verdict (mandatory §2c join)
example_queries.sql: SELECT d.id, d.risk_event_type, u.risk_state AS current_verdict FROM azure.main.risk_detections() d JOIN azure.main.risky_users() u ON d.user_id = u.id WHERE d._row_kind IS NULL AND u._row_kind IS NULL

tags.vgi.doc_md:
## Entra ID Protection risk functions

| Function | Kind | Watermark field | Returns |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `risky_users` | State | `risk_last_updated_date_time` | current user risk + watermark |
| `risky_service_principals` | State | `risk_last_updated_date_time` | current SP risk + watermark |
| `risk_detections` | Event | `detected_date_time` | risk detection events + watermark |

All three share the same shape: read data rows with `WHERE _row_kind IS NULL`, and take the next cursor from the single marker row's `_watermark_next`. Each requires an app-only `azure_graph` secret and an Entra ID P2 license.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT d.id, d.risk_event_type, u.risk_state AS current_verdict FROM azure.main.risk_detections() d JOIN azure.main.risky_users() u ON d.user_id = u.id WHERE d._row_kind IS NULL AND u._row_kind IS NULL

workers.doc_md:
## Microsoft Entra Audit & Sign-in Logs

Incremental (lagged-watermark) access to Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) audit and sign-in logs via Microsoft Graph, exposed as two DuckDB table functions.

- **`signin_logs`** — Entra ID interactive sign-in events (`/auditLogs/signIns`); requires Entra ID P1/P2.
- **`audit_logs`** — Entra ID directory audit / activity events (`/auditLogs/directoryAudits`); available more broadly.

Each function returns events in the requested time window plus a single marker row (`_row_kind = 'marker'`) whose `_watermark_next` column holds the ISO-8601 (already lag-adjusted) high-watermark to persist and replay via the `since` argument on the next scan. Call with no arguments to backfill; pass `since := '<watermark>'` for an incremental scan. Apply idempotently (dedup-by-id) because the safety-lag overlap re-emits the window tail. An app-only `azure_graph` secret is required.

example_queries.title: signin_logs_bind_probe
example_queries.description: Bind signin_logs and expose its result columns (credential-free; drop LIMIT 0 and attach an azure_graph secret to sync real sign-in events)
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, created_date_time, app_display_name, user_principal_name, ip_address, status FROM azure.main.signin_logs() LIMIT 0;

example_queries.title: audit_logs_bind_probe
example_queries.description: Bind audit_logs and expose its result columns (credential-free; attach an azure_graph secret to sync real audit events)
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, created_date_time, app_display_name, user_principal_name, ip_address, status FROM azure.main.audit_logs() LIMIT 0;

example_queries.description: Backfill all available sign-in events
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, created_date_time, app_display_name, user_principal_name FROM azure.main.signin_logs() WHERE _row_kind IS NULL

example_queries.description: Incremental sign-in scan from a saved watermark
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, created_date_time, app_display_name FROM azure.main.signin_logs(since := '<prior _watermark_next>') WHERE _row_kind IS NULL

example_queries.description: Failed sign-ins per application (non-zero errorCode)
example_queries.sql: SELECT app_display_name, count(*) AS failures FROM azure.main.signin_logs() WHERE _row_kind IS NULL AND status <> '0' GROUP BY app_display_name ORDER BY failures DESC

example_queries.description: Read the sign-in watermark cursor to persist for the next scan
example_queries.sql: SELECT _watermark_next FROM azure.main.signin_logs() WHERE _row_kind = 'marker'

example_queries.description: Directory audit events grouped by logging service
example_queries.sql: SELECT app_display_name, count(*) AS events FROM azure.main.audit_logs() WHERE _row_kind IS NULL GROUP BY app_display_name ORDER BY events DESC

example_queries.description: List every audit feed and the table function that serves it
example_queries.sql: SELECT feed, table_function FROM azure.main.audit_feeds ORDER BY feed

example_queries.description: Find the Graph endpoint backing the sign-in feed
example_queries.sql: SELECT graph_endpoint FROM azure.main.audit_feeds WHERE table_function = 'signin_logs'

example_queries.description: Backfill all available sign-in events (data rows only)
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, created_date_time, app_display_name, user_principal_name, status FROM azure.main.signin_logs() WHERE _row_kind IS NULL

example_queries.description: Narrow the feed server-side to failed sign-ins with an additive OData $filter
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, created_date_time, app_display_name FROM azure.main.signin_logs(filter := 'status/errorCode ne 0') WHERE _row_kind IS NULL

example_queries.description: Backfill all available directory audit events (data rows only)
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, created_date_time, app_display_name, user_principal_name, status FROM azure.main.audit_logs() WHERE _row_kind IS NULL

example_queries.description: Incremental scan replaying a previously saved high-watermark cursor
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, created_date_time, app_display_name FROM azure.main.audit_logs(since := '<prior _watermark_next>') WHERE _row_kind IS NULL

example_queries.description: Replay a bounded historical window (since/until); the marker cursor here is replay-only, not the live watermark
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, created_date_time, app_display_name FROM azure.main.audit_logs(since := '2026-01-01T00:00:00Z', until := '2026-02-01T00:00:00Z') WHERE _row_kind IS NULL

example_queries.description: Read the high-watermark cursor to persist for the next scan
example_queries.sql: SELECT _watermark_next FROM azure.main.audit_logs() WHERE _row_kind = 'marker'

tags.vgi.doc_llm: The Microsoft Entra ID audit and sign-in log feed functions. Each function is an incremental feed for one Graph audit endpoint — sign-in events or directory audit events — cursored by a lagged high-watermark on createdDateTime. A scan returns events in the requested time window followed by one marker row whose _watermark_next column is the cursor to persist and replay via the `since` argument. tags.vgi.doc_md:
## Entra audit & sign-in log feeds

| Function | Graph endpoint | Returns |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `signin_logs` | `/auditLogs/signIns` | sign-in events + watermark cursor |
| `audit_logs` | `/auditLogs/directoryAudits` | directory audit events + watermark cursor |

Both share the same shape: read data rows with `WHERE _row_kind IS NULL`, and take the next cursor from the single marker row's `_watermark_next` (feed it back as `since`). Apply idempotently (dedup-by-id). Each requires an app-only `azure_graph` secret.

arguments.name: filter
arguments.description: An additional OData `$filter` expression AND-ed onto the time-window predicate to narrow the feed (e.g. `"status/errorCode ne 0"`). Empty (the default) applies no extra filter.

arguments.name: lag_minutes
arguments.description: The safety-lag in minutes subtracted from the emitted high-watermark so late-arriving, boundary-unordered events are re-captured on the next scan. Defaults to 10. This overlap is why apply must be idempotent (dedup-by-id).

arguments.name: page_size
arguments.description: The Microsoft Graph `$top` page size for each request. Graph caps sign-ins at 1000 rows per page; defaults to 1000. Pages are followed inside a single scan.

arguments.name: since
arguments.description: The already-lagged high-watermark from the prior scan (the marker row's `_watermark_next`), replayed as the lower bound (`createdDateTime ge <since>`). Empty (the default) performs a backfill from the start of retention with no lower bound.

arguments.name: until
arguments.description: Optional upper bound (`createdDateTime le <until>`) for historical replay of a bounded window. A caller-supplied `until` is a replay-only cursor and must NOT be persisted as the live ingestion watermark. Empty (the default) means no upper bound.

SELECT id, created_date_time, app_display_name FROM azure.main.signin_logs(filter := 'status/errorCode ne 0') WHERE _row_kind IS NULL

workers.summary: Barcode and QR-code decoding and generation over Apache Arrow.
workers.doc_md:
# Barcode & QR-Code Decoding and Generation for DuckDB

![ZXing logo](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wiki/zxing/zxing/zxing-logo.png)

Read and write barcodes and QR codes directly in SQL: decode QR, EAN, UPC, Code 128, Code 39, Data Matrix, PDF417, Aztec and more out of image BLOBs, and generate scannable barcode PNGs from text — all over Apache Arrow, with no external service.

## What it does and who it's for

The `barcode` extension turns DuckDB into a complete barcode and QR-code toolkit. Data engineers, retail and logistics teams, and anyone holding a column of product photos or scanned documents can pull the encoded text and symbology out of images, or mint fresh barcode/QR images for labels, tickets, and links — entirely in SQL. Decoding is hardened against hostile or oversized input: a corrupt, empty, or giant image yields `NULL` (scalars) or zero rows (tables) instead of crashing the worker, so it is safe to run across untrusted data at scale.

## How it works

Decoding and encoding are powered by [`rxing`](https://github.com/rxing-core/rxing), the maintained Rust port of the venerable [ZXing](https://github.com/zxing/zxing) ("zebra crossing") library. Input rasters (PNG, JPEG, GIF, BMP, WebP) are converted to grayscale and scanned for one or many symbols; text is encoded into a bit matrix and rendered to a PNG `BLOB`. Full API documentation for the underlying library lives at [docs.rs/rxing](https://docs.rs/rxing). The worker streams everything over Apache Arrow IPC, so results flow back into DuckDB as native columns without intermediate files.

## When to reach for it

Reach for this worker to read product or QR codes out of a column of images, to fan a single image that holds several codes into one row per symbol, or to produce scannable barcode and QR PNGs for labels, tickets, and links — without leaving SQL or standing up an external service. Text encoding and image decoding round-trip cleanly, so you can both mint and re-read codes in one query. A quick round-trip looks like:

```sql
SELECT decode_barcode(generate_qr('https://query.farm'));
SELECT generate_barcode('5901234123457', 'EAN_13');
```

example_queries.sql: SELECT barcode.main.generate_barcode('5901234123457', 'EAN_13') AS ean13_png

example_queries.sql: SELECT format FROM barcode.main.barcode_formats ORDER BY format

example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS supported_formats FROM barcode.main.barcode_formats

example_queries.sql: SELECT format FROM barcode.main.barcode_formats WHERE format LIKE 'CODE%' ORDER BY format

# barcode.main

The primary schema of the barcode worker. It groups the barcode and QR-code capabilities into three areas: **decoding** symbols out of image data, **generating** scannable barcode/QR images from text, and **reference** lookups for the supported symbologies and the worker build.

Decoding accepts raster images (PNG, JPEG, GIF, BMP, WebP) and is hardened against hostile or oversized input — unreadable data yields `NULL` or zero rows rather than an error, so it is safe to run over untrusted data at scale. Generation returns a PNG `BLOB` and raises a clear error only for an unknown symbology or an unencodable payload.

workers.title: BGP / MRT Routing-Dump Decoder
workers.tagline: Decode BGP MRT routing dumps in DuckDB with SQL — RouteViews/RIPE RIB and updates with AS-path and community helpers. A VGI worker.
workers.summary: Decode MRT routing dumps (BGP4MP updates + TABLE_DUMP_V2 RIB snapshots) into SQL rows, reusing the core INET type for prefixes and peer IPs.
workers.doc_md:
# bgp

Decode **MRT** routing dumps — the archive format RouteViews and RIPE RIS publish — directly in SQL. MRT comes in two flavors this worker reads: **BGP4MP** update streams (announcements, withdrawals, and session state changes) and **TABLE_DUMP_V2** RIB snapshots (a full routing table at one instant). Streaming them into rows turns route-leak / hijack / RIB-diff analysis into a JOIN in the engine instead of an ETL-to-Parquet step.

A source argument is a path (local / glob / `s3://` / `http(s)://`) or an inline `BLOB`; `.gz` / `.bz2` inputs auto-decompress. Prefixes, peer IPs, and next hops are DuckDB **INET** values (cast with `::INET`), so containment such as `prefix::INET <<= '203.0.113.0/24'` and prefix joins work directly. AS paths are `LIST(UINTEGER)` and BGP communities are `LIST(VARCHAR)`; scalar helpers operate on those columns. RPKI / route-origin validation is out of scope — JOIN the origin AS against your VRP table (ROV lives in vgi-netflow).

tags.vgi.doc_md:
## What this schema covers

MRT is the on-the-wire archive format route collectors such as RouteViews and RIPE RIS publish. It comes in two shapes: **BGP4MP** update streams — the announcements, withdrawals, and session-state changes a collector sees over time — and **TABLE_DUMP_V2** RIB snapshots, a full routing table frozen at one instant.

This schema streams those archives into relational rows, so route-leak, prefix-hijack, and RIB-diff analysis becomes a JOIN in the engine instead of an ETL-to-Parquet step. One kind of object streams an archive into rows; another operates on the AS-path and BGP-community values each row carries.

## Data model

Prefixes, peer IPs, and next hops are emitted in DuckDB's core **INET** physical layout, so cast them with `::INET` for containment such as `prefix::INET <<= '203.0.113.0/24'` and for joins against flow or geolocation data. AS paths surface as `UINTEGER[]` and communities as `VARCHAR[]`.

## When to reach for it

Reach for it for route-leak and prefix-hijack investigation, for diffing two RIB snapshots over time, and for origin-AS analysis. Since the catalog name matches the ATTACH name, calls qualify as `bgp.main.<name>(...)`. RPKI / route-origin validation is out of scope here — JOIN the origin AS against your own VRP table.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Scan an MRT BGP4MP update stream (a RouteViews / RIPE RIS `updates.*` archive) into one row per BGP message: a prefix announcement, a withdrawal, or an FSM state change. `src` is a path — local, a glob, an `s3://` URL, or an `http(s)://` URL — or an inline `BLOB` of MRT bytes; gzip (`.gz`) and bzip2 (`.bz2`) inputs are decompressed transparently. Each row carries the timestamp, the reporting peer (peer_ip INET, peer_asn), the message_type ('announce' / 'withdraw' / 'state_change'), the prefix (INET), AS path (`LIST(UINTEGER)`), origin ASN, next hop (INET), communities (`LIST(VARCHAR)`), and — for state changes — old_state and new_state. prefix / peer_ip / next_hop are DuckDB INET values (cast with `::INET`) so containment and prefix joins work without parsing strings. Announcements and withdrawals stay in one stream so RIB churn can be reconstructed over time. A malformed record yields a row with NULL fields and a populated `error` column unless `strict => true`. This is the update-stream counterpart of read_rib.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Scan an MRT BGP4MP update stream into rows: timestamp, peer_ip (INET), peer_asn, message_type (announce/withdraw/state_change), prefix (INET), as_path (`LIST(UINTEGER)`), origin_asn, next_hop (INET), communities (`LIST(VARCHAR)`), old_state, new_state, and an `error` capture column. `src` is a path / glob / `s3://` / `http(s)://` URL or a `BLOB`; `.gz`/`.bz2` auto-decompress. Cast INET columns with `::INET` for containment.

Each row carries the route timestamp, RIB view name, the reporting peer (peer_ip INET, peer_asn), the prefix (INET), the AS path (`LIST(UINTEGER)`), origin ASN, next hop (INET), communities (`LIST(VARCHAR)` — standard and large), MED, local pref, atomic-aggregate flag, and aggregator ASN. prefix / peer_ip / next_hop are DuckDB INET values (cast with `::INET`), so prefix containment (`prefix::INET <<= '203.0.113.0/24'`) and joins against vgi-netflow / geoip work without parsing strings. A malformed record yields a row with NULL fields and a populated `error` column unless `strict => true`. This is the RIB counterpart of read_updates.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Scan an MRT TABLE_DUMP_V2 RIB dump into rows: timestamp, view_name, peer_ip (INET), peer_asn, prefix (INET), as_path (`LIST(UINTEGER)`), origin_asn, next_hop (INET), communities (`LIST(VARCHAR)`), med, local_pref, atomic_aggregate, aggregator_asn, and an `error` capture column. `src` is a path / glob / `s3://` / `http(s)://` URL or a `BLOB`; `.gz`/`.bz2` auto-decompress. Cast INET columns with `::INET` for containment.

workers.title: BSON Decode / Extended JSON / Typed Field Codec
workers.tagline: Read and write BSON in DuckDB with SQL — decode, encode, Extended JSON, ObjectId helpers and mongodump files. A VGI worker.
workers.summary: BSON (Binary JSON) decode & encode plus Extended JSON v2, typed field extraction, and mongodump/oplog/GridFS stream splitting for SQL.
workers.doc_md:
# bson

Decode and encode **BSON** (Binary JSON, [bsonspec.org](https://bsonspec.org)) in SQL, with lossless typed handling of ObjectId, Decimal128, `UUID`-subtype Binary, and the Timestamp-vs-UTCDateTime footgun — plus correct **MongoDB Extended JSON v2** (canonical & relaxed). The value is in-engine decode of the raw BSON the live `mongo` connector never sees: **mongodump backups**, **oplog / change-stream** captures, **GridFS chunks**, and **BSON columns at rest**. The `bson_seq` / `mongodump_read` table functions fan a concatenated `.bson` stream into one row per document. Pure scalar / table compute over a `BLOB` column — no network, no state, zero egress.

**Out of scope:** any live MongoDB connection (that is the `mongo` extension's job — this is the offline/at-rest complement) and FLE / Queryable-Encryption decryption (encrypted Binary subtypes stay opaque `BLOB`).

example_queries.description: Render a BSON document as canonical (lossless) Extended JSON v2.
example_queries.sql: SELECT bson.main.to_json(bson.main.from_json('{"a":1}'))

example_queries.description: Render the same document as relaxed, human-readable Extended JSON.
example_queries.sql: SELECT bson.main.to_json(bson.main.from_json('{"a":1}'), 'relaxed')

example_queries.description: Extract a nested leaf by dotted path without decoding the whole document.
example_queries.sql: SELECT bson.main.field(bson.main.from_json('{"o":{"sku":"abc"}}'), 'o.sku')

example_queries.description: Check that a tiny empty document is structurally well-formed.
example_queries.sql: SELECT (bson.main.well_formed(from_hex('0500000000'))).ok

example_queries.description: Report the top-level BSON type name of a document.
example_queries.sql: SELECT bson.main.type_of(bson.main.from_json('{"a":1}'))

example_queries.description: Fan a concatenated BSON stream into one row per document with its byte length.
example_queries.sql: SELECT idx, octet_length(doc) AS n FROM bson.main.bson_seq(from_hex('05000000000500000000')) ORDER BY idx

example_queries.description: Canonical Extended JSON round-trips BSON byte-for-byte (the migration guarantee).
example_queries.sql: SELECT bson.main.from_json(bson.main.to_json(bson.main.from_json('{"a":1}'))) = bson.main.from_json('{"a":1}') AS roundtrips;

example_queries.description: A minimal empty document (05 00 00 00 00) is well-formed.
example_queries.sql: SELECT (bson.main.well_formed(from_hex('0500000000'))).ok AS ok;

example_queries.description: List the temporal BSON types and their Extended JSON wrappers.
example_queries.sql: SELECT type_name, type_byte, extjson_wrapper FROM bson.main.bson_types WHERE type_class = 'temporal' ORDER BY type_name

example_queries.description: Count the documents per file in a committed mongodump .bson fixture.
example_queries.sql: SELECT file, count(*) AS docs FROM bson.main.mongodump_read('test/data/users.bson') GROUP BY file ORDER BY file

example_queries.description: Decode forcing JSON mode.
example_queries.sql: SELECT bson.main.decode(bson.main.from_json('{"a":1}'), 'json') AS d

example_queries.description: List the keys of a {a:1,b:2} document.
example_queries.sql: SELECT bson.main.keys(bson.main.from_json('{"a":1,"b":2}')) AS k

example_queries.description: Type of a nested ObjectId field.
example_queries.sql: SELECT bson.main.type_of(bson.main.from_json('{"_id":{"$oid":"54759eb3c090d83494e2d804"}}'), '_id') AS t

example_queries.description: Creation time of an ObjectId.
example_queries.sql: SELECT bson.main.objectid_timestamp('54759eb3c090d83494e2d804') AS created

example_queries.description: 12-byte ObjectId from hex.
example_queries.sql: SELECT to_hex(bson.main.objectid_from_hex('54759eb3c090d83494e2d804')) AS b

example_queries.description: Relaxed Extended JSON of {a:1}.
example_queries.sql: SELECT bson.main.to_json(bson.main.from_json('{"a":1}'), 'relaxed') AS j

example_queries.description: Hex of a 12-byte ObjectId.
example_queries.sql: SELECT bson.main.objectid_hex(bson.main.objectid_from_hex('54759eb3c090d83494e2d804')) AS h

example_queries.description: Validate a tiny empty BSON document (05 00 00 00 00).
example_queries.sql: SELECT bson.main.is_valid(from_hex('0500000000')) AS ok

example_queries.description: Convert a Timestamp struct to a TIMESTAMPTZ.
example_queries.sql: SELECT bson.main.timestamp_to_ts({'t': 1416994483, 'i': 1}) AS ts

example_queries.description: Encode a JSON document to BSON and hex it.
example_queries.sql: SELECT to_hex(bson.main.from_json('{"a":1}')) AS h

example_queries.description: Extract _id as a hex ObjectId.
example_queries.sql: SELECT bson.main.field(bson.main.from_json('{"_id":{"$oid":"54759eb3c090d83494e2d804"}}'), '_id', 'objectid') AS id

example_queries.description: Read the (t, i) parts of a Timestamp.
example_queries.sql: SELECT (bson.main.timestamp_parts({'t': 1416994483, 'i': 2})).i AS inc

example_queries.description: Encode a struct to BSON and hex it.
example_queries.sql: SELECT to_hex(bson.main.encode({'a': 1, 'b': 'x'})) AS h

example_queries.description: Diagnose a truncated document.
example_queries.sql: SELECT (bson.main.well_formed(from_hex('0500000001'))).kind AS kind

## bson.main

The single schema of the `bson` worker. The catalog name matches the `ATTACH` name, so qualify calls as `bson.main.<name>`.

It covers the whole offline BSON surface, grouped into a few families: a BSON ↔ Extended JSON v2 **codec**, structural **validity** checks that stay total on hostile input, typed dotted-path **projection**, **ObjectId** and internal-**Timestamp** helpers, and **stream**-splitting table functions for mongodump / oplog / GridFS data.

The `vgi.categories` groupings show where each function fits; the codec's canonical Extended JSON round-trips byte-for-byte, making it the migration and diff surface for BSON at rest.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: A static, credential-free reference view listing all 21 BSON element types: the type name `type_of` returns, the one-byte type code (0x01–0x13, plus 0xFF minKey and 0x7F maxKey), a coarse `type_class` for browsing, the canonical Extended JSON v2 wrapper the type serializes to, and a one-line note. Use it to map a `type_of` result to its wire code, to see how a type renders in canonical Extended JSON, or to spot the footguns — Timestamp (0x11) is a replication clock, not a wall-clock time; undefined / dbPointer / symbol are deprecated. It scans instantly with no argument, so it is the cheapest way to see real data from this worker.

Handy for mapping a `type_of` result to its wire code, seeing how a value renders in canonical Extended JSON, or spotting the footguns: `timestamp` (0x11) is the replication clock (not a wall-clock time), and `undefined` / `dbPointer` / `symbol` are deprecated.

functions.name: decode
functions.comment: Decode a BSON document to its richest form (Extended JSON in v1)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Decode a BSON document to its richest self-describing form and return it as text. `decode(doc)` is the zero-decisions codec: it always yields canonical MongoDB Extended JSON v2 — the lossless column that preserves ObjectId, Decimal128, `UUID`, and the Timestamp-vs-UTCDateTime distinction — and is exactly equivalent to `to_json(doc, 'canonical')`. Prefer `to_json` when you want to choose canonical vs relaxed rendering; reach for `decode` when you just want one stable lossless column and no mode decision. The optional `mode` ('auto', 'struct', 'map', 'json') is a forward-looking hint for the output shape you would like, but because a DuckDB scalar fixes its output column type at bind time with no data sample, all four currently materialize as the same canonical Extended JSON text — the argument does not yet change the result, so omit it unless you are signalling intent. For a typed projection of a known shape, cast the JSON or use `field(doc, path, as)` per leaf. Returns NULL for a malformed blob.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Decode BSON to its richest self-describing form → canonical Extended JSON (the stable lossless column). Equivalent to `to_json(doc, 'canonical')`; prefer `to_json` when you need the canonical/relaxed choice. `mode` ∈ {auto, struct, map, json} is a forward-looking shape hint that currently always returns the same Extended JSON text.

vgi.example_queries.description: Decode forcing JSON mode.

workers.title: Calendar, Holiday & Recurrence Math
workers.tagline: Holidays, business-days & RRULE recurrence for DuckDB (Python)
workers.summary: Holiday, business-day, and recurrence calendar math for SQL
workers.doc_md:
# Calendar, Holiday & Recurrence Math in SQL

**`cal` brings public-holiday lookups, business-day arithmetic, and RFC-5545 (RRULE) recurrence expansion directly into DuckDB SQL — no ETL, no Python glue, just `SELECT`.** Ask whether a date is a holiday or a working day, name the holiday, add or count business days, or expand a recurrence rule into a series of timestamps, all as ordinary SQL expressions and table functions.

This VGI worker is for analysts, data engineers, and application developers who need correct calendar logic close to their data: payment and settlement date math, SLA and business-day deadlines, payroll and billing cycles, and scheduling and reminders. It exposes a single `cal` catalog (schema `main`) over Apache Arrow, so every function streams results back to DuckDB with native types — `DATE`, `TIMESTAMP`, and `TIMESTAMPTZ` round-trip cleanly. Coverage is global, not US-centric: hundreds of countries and their subdivisions are supported, and `'US'` is merely the default argument, not a limit.

The holiday and business-day engine is powered by the [holidays](https://github.com/vacanza/holidays) library ([docs](https://holidays.readthedocs.io/)), which models hundreds of national and subdivision calendars. Recurrence and Easter math come from [python-dateutil](https://github.com/dateutil/dateutil) ([docs](https://dateutil.readthedocs.io/)), whose `rrulestr` parser implements the [RFC-5545](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5545) recurrence grammar. For stock-exchange trading calendars (sessions, market hours, and schedules), see the companion [vgi-trading-calendar](https://github.com/Query-farm/vgi-trading-calendar) worker.

Per-row questions are answered by scalar functions you can drop straight into a projection or predicate; set-returning questions — a year's holidays, a range of working days, an expanded recurrence — are table functions. Country/subdivision are ordinary arguments that default to `'US'`; the `supported_countries` table enumerates every valid `country`/`subdiv` code. Weekend-aware `is_business_day` differs from holiday-only `is_holiday`; recurrence rules must be bounded (`COUNT`/`UNTIL`) or they never terminate.

tags.vgi.doc_md:
## Calendar, holiday & recurrence math

Holiday, business-day, and recurrence functions over Apache Arrow, exposed as ordinary DuckDB SQL.

**Key concepts**

- Scalar functions answer one question per row and slot into a projection or predicate.
- Table functions return sets of rows: a year's holidays, a range of working days, or an expanded recurrence.
- Country/subdivision are ordinary arguments; `'US'` is only a default, not a limit — coverage is global.
- `DATE`, `TIMESTAMP`, and `TIMESTAMPTZ` round-trip natively over Arrow.

**When to use it**

Reach for this schema for holiday and business-day date math (settlement, SLA, payroll, billing), calendar labels (Easter, ISO week / year-week), and RFC-5545 recurrence expansion. The `supported_countries` table enumerates the valid `country`/`subdiv` codes those functions accept.

functions.name: rrule
functions.comment: Expand an RFC-5545 recurrence rule (dateutil) into timestamps

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Expand an **RFC-5545 (iCalendar) recurrence rule** into concrete timestamps as `(seq, occurrence)` rows. Takes a `dtstart` timestamp and an RRULE string (e.g. `'FREQ=WEEKLY;COUNT=4'` or a full `'RRULE:...'`) positionally, plus optional named `count` and `until` bounds. Because an RRULE can be infinite, you **must** bound it -- either inside the rule (`COUNT=`/`UNTIL=`) or via the `count`/`until` arguments -- or it will not terminate. `seq` is the 0-based occurrence index. Parsing is via `dateutil.rrule`. Use it to materialize schedules: meetings, billing cycles, reminders, cron-like calendar events.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## rrule(dtstart, rule, count := ..., until := ...)

Expand an **RFC-5545 RRULE** into `(seq, occurrence)` timestamp rows.

Always bound the rule (`COUNT`/`UNTIL` in the string, or the `count`/`until` args) -- recurrences can be infinite. `seq` is the 0-based index. Backed by `dateutil.rrule`.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Return the **ISO-8601 week number** (1..53) for a date. Under ISO-8601, weeks start on Monday and week 1 is the week containing the first Thursday of the year, so the first few days of January can belong to week 52/53 of the *previous* ISO year (and the last days of December to week 1 of the *next*). This returns only the week component; pair it with `iso_year_week` when you need the disambiguating year. `NULL` dates pass through as `NULL`.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## iso_week

**ISO-8601 week number** (1..53) for a date.

ISO weeks start on Monday and week 1 holds the year's first Thursday, so early-January and late-December dates can land in a neighbouring ISO year's week. This returns the week number alone -- use `iso_year_week` for the `YYYY-Www` label.

vgi.example_queries.description: ISO week of a date
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT cal.main.iso_week(DATE '2026-06-22')

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Advance a date by **N business days in a country subdivision** (state/province/region), skipping weekends and that subdivision's public holidays. Pass the ISO-3166 country code plus a subdivision code (e.g. `'US','CA'`) as the third and fourth arguments. functions.name: easter
functions.comment: Western (Gregorian) Easter Sunday for a year

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Return the date of Western (Gregorian) **Easter Sunday** for a given calendar year. Easter is a *movable feast* whose date is derived from the ecclesiastical lunar calendar, so it cannot be computed with ordinary date arithmetic. Pass an integer year (e.g. `2026`) and get back a `DATE`; `NULL` years pass through as `NULL`. Useful for anchoring Easter-relative observances such as Good Friday (Easter - 2 days), Easter Monday (Easter + 1), Ascension, or Pentecost. This is the Gregorian/Western computus only -- Orthodox (Julian) Easter is not returned.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## easter

Western (Gregorian) **Easter Sunday** for a year.

Easter is a movable feast, so it needs the computus rather than plain date math. `easter(2026)` returns `DATE '2026-04-05'`.

Derive related days arithmetically: Good Friday is `easter(y) - 2`, Easter Monday is `easter(y) + 1`. Returns the Western/Gregorian date only.

vgi.example_queries.description: Easter Sunday in 2026
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT cal.main.easter(2026)

tags.vgi.title: Easter Sunday Date

functions.name: iso_year_week
functions.comment: ISO-8601 year-week label, e.g. '2026-W26'

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Return the **ISO-8601 year-week label** such as `'2026-W26'` for a date. This combines the ISO week-numbering *year* with the ISO week number, which is the correct, unambiguous way to label a week: because ISO week 1 is anchored to the first Thursday, the ISO year can differ from the calendar year for dates near the year boundary (e.g. `2027-01-01` may be labelled `'2026-W53'`). Returns a `VARCHAR`; `NULL` dates pass through. Ideal for grouping rows by week (`GROUP BY iso_year_week(ts)`).
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## iso_year_week

**ISO-8601 year-week label** like `'2026-W26'`.

Combines the ISO week-numbering year with the zero-padded week so the label is unambiguous across year boundaries (a January date can be `'2025-W52'`). Returns a string -- handy as a `GROUP BY` key for weekly rollups.

vgi.example_queries.description: ISO year-week label of a date
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT cal.main.iso_year_week(DATE '2026-06-22')

workers.doc_md:
# Causal Inference in SQL: Treatment Effects, Propensity & Doubly-Robust Estimation

![DoWhy logo](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/py-why/dowhy/main/docs/source/_static/dowhy-logo-small.png)

**Estimate the causal effect of an intervention directly in DuckDB SQL** — average treatment effect (ATE), effect on the treated (ATT), and per-subject propensity scores — from observational cohort data, with confounders adjusted for automatically. This VGI extension turns causal questions like *"did the treatment actually work, after controlling for who was likely to get it?"* into a single SQL query.

Causal inference goes beyond correlation and naive group means: a simple difference between treated and untreated subjects is biased whenever the same factors that drive treatment also drive the outcome (confounding). The `causal` catalog corrects that bias using the standard toolkit of observational causal inference — inverse probability weighting (IPW), regression adjustment (the g-formula), and doubly-robust augmented IPW (AIPW) — so analysts, data scientists, and epidemiologists can run treatment-effect, impact, and intervention analysis where their data already lives, without exporting to a notebook.

Under the hood the estimators are powered by [scikit-learn](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/) ([source](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn)) for the propensity and outcome models and [statsmodels](https://www.statsmodels.org/stable/index.html) ([source](https://github.com/statsmodels/statsmodels)) for the regression and inference machinery, with an optional doubly-robust backend via [DoWhy](https://www.pywhy.org/dowhy/) ([source](https://github.com/py-why/dowhy)). Propensities come from an L2-regularized logistic model with score clipping that keeps near-perfect separation from blowing up the weights, and standard errors come from influence functions (IPW/AIPW), OLS (regression adjustment), or a seeded bootstrap (ATT) — every estimate is deterministic and reproducible.

## Functions

Each function consumes a whole cohort as a `(SELECT ...)` relation plus named role arguments; **every column not named by a role is treated as a covariate/confounder and adjusted for**, and treatment must be binary `0/1`.

- `ate(rel, treatment, outcome)` — Average Treatment Effect `E[Y(1)-Y(0)]`, returned one row per method: IPW, regression adjustment, and doubly-robust AIPW, each with a standard error and 95% confidence interval.
- `att(rel, treatment, outcome)` — Average Treatment effect on the Treated `E[Y(1)-Y(0)|T=1]` via IPW-ATT weighting, with a bootstrap standard error.
- `propensity_scores(rel, treatment, id)` — per-row fitted propensity `e(X)=P(T=1|X)` from the logistic model, keyed by your `id` column.

Runnable, catalog-qualified demonstrations live in each object's example queries (and the schema's `vgi.example_queries`), so they are executed and coverage-checked rather than pasted inline here.

Estimates are causal only under the usual assumptions — **unconfoundedness** (no unmeasured confounders given the supplied covariates), **overlap** (`0 < e(X) < 1`), and **SUTVA**. Choosing the covariate set is your modeling decision; the worker estimates, it does not assume the assumptions hold.

example_queries.description: Average treatment effect by IPW, regression adjustment, and doubly-robust AIPW.
example_queries.sql:
WITH cohort AS (
  SELECT
    g                                                   AS id,
    (g - 30)::DOUBLE / 10.0                             AS x,
    CASE WHEN ((g * 7 + 3) % 10) < 5 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END  AS t,
    5.0 * (CASE WHEN ((g * 7 + 3) % 10) < 5 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
      + 2.0 * ((g - 30)::DOUBLE / 10.0)                 AS y
  FROM generate_series(0, 60) AS s(g)
)
SELECT method, round(estimate, 2) AS estimate FROM causal.main.ate((SELECT t, y, x FROM cohort), treatment := 't', outcome := 'y') ORDER BY method

## Causal treatment-effect estimation

Estimate the causal effect of a **binary treatment** on an outcome from observational cohort data, adjusting for measured confounders — directly in DuckDB SQL, with no export to a notebook.

### Key concepts

- **Confounding** biases a naive difference of group means whenever the factors that drive treatment also drive the outcome; adjustment corrects it.
- Estimators draw on the standard observational toolkit — inverse-probability weighting (IPW), regression adjustment (the g-formula), and doubly-robust augmented IPW (AIPW).
- Each call consumes a whole `(SELECT ...)` cohort relation plus named role arguments; every column not named by a role is treated as an adjusted-for covariate, and treatment must be binary `0/1`.

### When to use

Reach for these estimators for treatment-effect, impact, and intervention analysis where the data already lives. Estimates are causal only under unconfoundedness, overlap, and SUTVA.

Backed by scikit-learn and statsmodels, with deterministic, reproducible estimates.

# Estimator Method Reference

A small, self-contained registry of the estimator methods the `causal` worker exposes — one row per method. Use it to discover the worker's surface before calling a table function: which methods `ate` emits, which estimator is doubly-robust, and what each one estimates.

## Columns

- `method` — the estimator id (matches the `method` column emitted by `ate`).
- `function_name` — the function that produces the method (`ate`, `att`, or `propensity_scores`).
- `estimand` — the causal quantity: `ATE`, `ATT`, or the per-row propensity `e(X)`.
- `doubly_robust` — `TRUE` for AIPW (consistent if either nuisance model is correct).
- `description` — a one-line summary of the estimator.

The registry is backed by an inline `VALUES` relation, so it scans with no external data or credentials.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
# Average Treatment effect on the Treated (ATT)

Estimate `E[Y(1) - Y(0) | T = 1]`: the average treatment effect **restricted to the units that actually received treatment**, via inverse-probability-of-treatment (IPW-ATT) weighting.

**Inputs.** A `(SELECT ...)` cohort relation as the first positional argument, plus named role args `treatment` (a binary 0/1 column) and `outcome` (a numeric column). Every remaining column is a covariate/confounder and is adjusted for. An optional `random_state` (default 0) seeds the propensity fit and the bootstrap.

**Output.** A single row: `estimate` (the ATT) and `std_error` (a deterministic, seeded bootstrap standard error).

**When to use.** When the policy question is about those who were treated -- e.g. 'how much did the program help the people who enrolled?' -- rather than the whole population (which is `ate`). The ATT and ATE coincide under a homogeneous effect but diverge with effect heterogeneity.

**Edge cases / assumptions.** Controls are reweighted by `e/(1 - e)`; the propensity model is regularized and clipped, so it stays finite under near-separation. Treatment must be exactly binary `{0, 1}`. Causal only under unconfoundedness, overlap on the treated, and SUTVA. The bootstrap is seeded (`random_state`), so the SE is reproducible.

# att

Average Treatment effect on the Treated `E[Y(1) - Y(0) | T = 1]` via IPW-ATT weighting, adjusting for every covariate column.

## Usage

Pass a cohort relation as the first positional argument and name the `treatment` and `outcome` roles; every other column is an adjusted-for covariate. A complete, runnable call is attached as this function's example query.

## Notes

- Emits a single row: `(estimate, std_error)`.
- `std_error` is a deterministic, seeded bootstrap SE.
- Use `att` for the effect on the treated subpopulation; use `ate` for the whole-population effect. `treatment` must be binary 0/1.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
# Propensity Scores

Fit a logistic **propensity model** `e(X) = P(T = 1 | X)` over the cohort and emit one row per input subject: its `id`, fitted `propensity`, and observed `treatment`.

**Inputs.** A `(SELECT ...)` cohort relation as the first positional argument, plus named role args `treatment` (a binary 0/1 column) and `id` (a row identifier passed through and **excluded** from the covariates). Every other column is a covariate fed to the logistic model. An optional `random_state` (default 0) seeds the deterministic fit.

**Output.** One row per input row: `id` (`BIGINT`), `propensity` (`DOUBLE` in `(0, 1)`), and `treatment` (`INTEGER` 0/1).

**When to use.** Diagnose overlap/positivity before estimating effects, build matched or weighted cohorts, or trim units with extreme scores. The scores are the same ones `ate`/`att` use internally for IPW.

**Edge cases / behaviors.** The logistic fit is L2-regularized and scores are clipped to `[1e-6, 1 - 1e-6]`, so perfect separation does not produce 0/1 scores or infinite weights. Treatment must be exactly binary `{0, 1}`. The output is unbounded (one row per subject) and is paged through the worker's offset cursor.

# propensity_scores

Per-row fitted propensity `e(X) = P(T = 1 | X)` from a regularized logistic model.

## Usage

Pass a cohort relation as the first positional argument and name the `treatment` and `id` roles; the `id` column is passed through and every other column is a covariate. A complete, runnable call is attached as this function's example query.

## Notes

- Emits one row per input subject: `(id, propensity, treatment)`.
- The `id` column is passed through and excluded from the covariates; every other column is a covariate.
- Scores are clipped to `(0, 1)`; use them for overlap diagnostics, matching, or weighting. `treatment` must be binary 0/1.

# Average Treatment Effect (ATE)

Estimate the **average treatment effect** `E[Y(1) - Y(0)]` of a binary treatment on a numeric outcome from an observational cohort, adjusting for confounders.

**Inputs.** A `(SELECT ...)` cohort relation as the first positional argument, plus named role args `treatment` (a binary 0/1 column) and `outcome` (a numeric column). Every remaining column is treated as a covariate/confounder and is adjusted for. An optional `random_state` (default 0) seeds the deterministic propensity fit.

**Output.** Three rows, one per estimator: `ipw` (inverse-probability weighting, Hajek/self-normalized), `regression_adjustment` (g-formula via OLS), and `aipw` (doubly-robust). Each row has `estimate`, `std_error`, and a 95% Wald confidence interval (`ci_lower`, `ci_upper`).

**When to use.** Answering 'what is the overall effect of this intervention?' Comparing methods builds confidence: AIPW is doubly-robust, so it is consistent if *either* the propensity or the outcome model is correct.

**Edge cases / assumptions.** Treatment must be exactly binary `{0, 1}` or the call errors. Estimates are causal only under unconfoundedness (no unmeasured confounding given the covariates), overlap (`0 < e(X) < 1`), and SUTVA. With few rows or perfect separation the SEs widen but the regularized propensity model still returns finite estimates.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# ate

Average Treatment Effect `E[Y(1) - Y(0)]` of a binary treatment on a numeric outcome, adjusting for every covariate column in the input relation.

## Usage

Pass a cohort relation as the first positional argument and name the `treatment` and `outcome` roles; every other column is an adjusted-for covariate. A complete, runnable call is attached as this function's example query.

## Notes

- Emits one row per method: `ipw`, `regression_adjustment`, `aipw`.
- Each row carries the point estimate, its standard error, and a 95% Wald confidence interval.
- `treatment` must be binary 0/1; every non-role column is an adjusted-for covariate. Estimates are causal only under unconfoundedness, overlap, and SUTVA.

vgi.example_queries.description: Average treatment effect by IPW, regression adjustment, and AIPW.
vgi.example_queries.sql:
WITH cohort AS (
  SELECT
    g                                                   AS id,
    (g - 30)::DOUBLE / 10.0                             AS x,
    CASE WHEN ((g * 7 + 3) % 10) < 5 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END  AS t,
    5.0 * (CASE WHEN ((g * 7 + 3) % 10) < 5 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
      + 2.0 * ((g - 30)::DOUBLE / 10.0)                 AS y
  FROM generate_series(0, 60) AS s(g)
)
SELECT method, round(estimate, 2) AS estimate FROM causal.main.ate((SELECT t, y, x FROM cohort), treatment := 't', outcome := 'y') ORDER BY method

workers.doc_md:
# cbor

Decode and encode **CBOR** (RFC 8949) and **MessagePack** in SQL, plus tag-aware structural decoders for **COSE** (RFC 9052), **CWT** (RFC 8392), **COSE_Key**, and **WebAuthn / FIDO2 / CTAP2** attestation. The byte codec is commodity; the value is the in-engine security-payload decode and the bulk SQL join surface (COSE `x5t`/`x5chain` and WebAuthn `x5c` join to `vgi-x509`). Pure scalar / table compute over a `BLOB` column — no network, no state, zero egress.

**Structural decode only:** no signature/MAC verification and no decryption (a downstream verifier consumes `cose_payload` + `cose_key`).

## CBOR / MessagePack / security codec

The single schema for the `cbor` worker. The catalog name matches the `ATTACH` name, so qualify calls as `cbor.main.<fn>(...)` (or `SET search_path='cbor.main'`).

**Binary codec.** Render CBOR and MessagePack blobs to JSON or diagnostic (EDN) notation, parse them back, re-encode into canonical / core-deterministic forms, walk semantic tags, and run untrusted-input well-formedness checks that never crash a scan.

**Security payloads.** Tag-aware structural decoders explode the CBOR-based credential formats — COSE messages, CWT tokens, COSE keys, and WebAuthn authenticator data — into typed columns, and table functions fan a single CBOR Sequence or WebAuthn attestation object into rows.

**Bulk copy.** The `cbor` and `msgpack` bulk-copy formats move whole tables in and out of row files (one top-level item per row), in both directions under a single format name.

All decode is *structural only*: no signature/MAC verification and no decryption.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: A browsable lookup table of the IANA COSE registries this worker knows: the signature/encryption/MAC/KDF algorithms (RFC 9053, e.g. -7 → ES256, -8 → EdDSA, 5 → 'HMAC 256/256'), the key types (`kty`, e.g. 1 → OKP, 2 → EC2, 3 → RSA), and the elliptic curves (`crv`, e.g. 1 → P-256, 6 → Ed25519, 8 → secp256k1). Columns are `registry` ('alg' | 'kty' | 'crv'), the signed numeric `id`, and the standard `name`. It is exactly the mapping the `cose_headers`, `cose_decode`, and `cose_key` decoders apply when they turn the raw numeric COSE labels into names, so you can join a decoded id back to its name, discover which algorithms are recognized, or reverse a name to its numeric label — no CBOR blob required to get started.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## cose_registry

The IANA COSE registries the worker recognizes, as a plain browsable table.

| column | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `registry` | VARCHAR | Which registry: `alg`, `kty`, or `crv`. |
| `id` | BIGINT | The signed numeric COSE label (algorithm ids are typically negative). |
| `name` | VARCHAR | The standard IANA name (e.g. `ES256`, `EdDSA`, `EC2`, `P-256`). |

This is the same numeric-label → name mapping the `cose_headers` / `cose_decode` / `cose_key` decoders apply, so a decoded `alg` id or `kty` joins straight back to its name here.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Decode a CTAP2 / WebAuthn attestation OBJECT ({fmt, attStmt, authData}) and shred it into typed columns: fmt, aaguid, sign_count, rp_id_hash, up, uv, cred_id, alg, sig, x5c (`LIST<BLOB>`), att_stmt (JSON). Parses the embedded authenticatorData and the format-specific attStmt (packed, fido-u2f, tpm, android-key, android-safetynet, apple, none). The `x5c` certificate chain is the join key to `vgi-x509` for AAGUID / vendor trust-anchor checks. The blob argument is a per-row input column, so this works equally on a literal, on a whole enrollment column, and under a correlated LATERAL join — shredding each row's attestation beside that row's own columns. Structural only — NO signature verification. A NULL blob, or one that is not a valid attestation object, contributes no rows.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Shred a WebAuthn attestation object into a row of (fmt, aaguid, sign_count, rp_id_hash, up, uv, cred_id, alg, sig, x5c, att_stmt) — per literal, per column, or under a correlated LATERAL join. Join `x5c` to `vgi-x509`.

vgi.example_queries.description: Shred a packed CTAP2 attestation object into one typed row.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT fmt, aaguid, sign_count, alg FROM cbor.main.webauthn_attestation(from_hex(''))

functions.name: seq_decode
functions.comment: Decode a CBOR Sequence (RFC 8742) into one row per item

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Decode a CBOR Sequence (RFC 8742 — a concatenation of zero or more CBOR items) into one row per item, with columns `idx` (`BIGINT`, zero-based position) and `value` (JSON). A truncated trailing item stops the sequence cleanly, returning the items parsed so far (never panics). The blob argument is a per-row input column, so the function works equally on a literal, on a whole column, and under a correlated LATERAL join — fanning each row's sequence out beside that row's other columns. A NULL or undecodable blob contributes no rows. To load a whole *file* of CBOR rows into a table, use the `cbor` bulk-copy format instead.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Fan a CBOR Sequence (RFC 8742) into rows of `(idx BIGINT, value JSON)` — per literal, per column, or under a correlated LATERAL join.

vgi.example_queries.description: Decode the 3-item CBOR sequence 01 02 03 into rows.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT idx, value FROM cbor.main.seq_decode(from_hex('010203')) ORDER BY idx

vgi.example_queries.description: Fan every row's sequence out beside its own id, as a correlated join.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT t.id, s.idx, s.value FROM (SELECT 1 AS id, from_hex('010203') AS b) t, cbor.main.seq_decode(t.b) s ORDER BY t.id, s.idx

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: idx
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Zero-based position of the item within the CBOR sequence.

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: value
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: The decoded item rendered as JSON text.

tags.vgi.title: CBOR Sequence Decode

arguments.name: blob
arguments.description: A CBOR Sequence (RFC 8742) — zero or more concatenated CBOR items.

examples: SELECT idx, value FROM cbor.main.seq_decode(from_hex('010203')) ORDER BY idx
SELECT t.id, s.idx, s.value FROM (SELECT 1 AS id, from_hex('010203') AS b) t, cbor.main.seq_decode(t.b) s ORDER BY t.id, s.idx

functions.name: msgpack_copy

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Bulk-move whole tables in and out of MessagePack data files — the row-file counterpart to the per-blob `msgpack_decode` scalar. The file is a concatenated MessagePack items: one top-level item per row, with no container header or footer, so it appends and streams. The same format name serves both directions, and a file written by one round-trips through the other. The `FORMAT` identifier is scoped by the ATTACH alias, so it reads `<alias>.msgpack`:

```sql
COPY (<query>) TO '<path>' (FORMAT '<alias>.msgpack');
COPY <table> FROM '<path>' (FORMAT '<alias>.msgpack');
```

With the default `row_format 'map'` each item is a map keyed by column name: self-describing, so on read the columns may appear in any order, a key absent from an item reads as NULL, and extra keys are ignored. `row_format 'array'` frames each row as an array of values in column order — more compact, but positional. Column values encode exactly as the `encode` scalar does (shortest-lossless integers and floats, `BLOB` as a byte string, `TIMESTAMP` as an epoch instant, `LIST` / `STRUCT` / `MAP` as arrays and maps) and decode back onto the COPY target's exact column types. A value that cannot be represented in its target column fails the COPY with a column-qualified message; `ignore_errors true` instead skips unusable rows and tolerates a truncated trailing item. Rows are written in source order, so an ordered source query keeps its ordering in the file.

**Paths resolve on the worker.** The file is opened by the worker process, so the path is interpreted against its filesystem and working directory — not the SQL client's. That is invisible when DuckDB spawns the worker locally, but a worker in a container or on another host cannot see the caller's paths: use a location both sides agree on (a mounted volume), and prefer absolute paths. A path the worker cannot open is reported with the directory it actually looked in.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
Bulk import and export of MessagePack row files. The file is a concatenated MessagePack items — one item per row, no container header — so it appends, streams, and round-trips between the two directions. The `FORMAT` identifier is scoped by the ATTACH alias:

```sql
COPY (<query>) TO '<path>' (FORMAT '<alias>.msgpack');
COPY <table> FROM '<path>' (FORMAT '<alias>.msgpack');
```

`row_format 'map'` (the default) keys each row by column name; `row_format 'array'` is positional. On read, `ignore_errors true` skips unusable rows and tolerates a truncated tail. Writes preserve source order.

Paths are opened by the **worker** process, so they resolve against its filesystem and working directory rather than the client's — a containerized or remote worker needs a shared location, and absolute paths.

vgi.example_queries.description: Export query results to a MessagePack row file, one item per row.
vgi.example_queries.sql: COPY (SELECT 1 AS id, 'alpha' AS name) TO 'events.msgpack' (FORMAT 'cbor.msgpack')

vgi.example_queries.description: Export positionally (each row an array in column order) for a more compact file.
vgi.example_queries.sql: COPY (SELECT 1 AS id, 'alpha' AS name) TO 'events_array.msgpack' (FORMAT 'cbor.msgpack', row_format 'array')

vgi.example_queries.description: List the COPY options this format accepts, and the directions it serves.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT format_name, direction, option_name FROM vgi_copy_formats() WHERE handler = 'msgpack_copy' ORDER BY option_name

tags.vgi.result_dynamic_columns_md:
### Read direction — columns mirror the COPY target

The scan emits exactly the COPY target table's columns, in its declared order and types: DuckDB fixes them from the target and the reader projects each MessagePack item onto them, inserting no cast. There is no independent result schema, so the shape below is one worked variant — a target declared `(id INTEGER, name VARCHAR, seen TIMESTAMP)`.

| Name | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| id | INTEGER | The item's value for the `id` column — by key name under `row_format 'map'`, by position under `row_format 'array'`. |
| name | VARCHAR | The item's value for the `name` column. A nested value lands as its JSON text. |
| seen | TIMESTAMP | The item's value for the `seen` column, read from an epoch instant. A key absent from the item reads as `NULL`. |
tags.vgi.title: MessagePack Row Files (COPY FROM / TO)

arguments.description: Skip rows that cannot be projected onto the target columns, and accept a truncated trailing item, instead of failing the COPY (default false).

arguments.description: How each row is framed as one item: 'map' (default) keys it by column name; 'array' writes the values positionally in column order.

examples: COPY (SELECT 1 AS id, 'alpha' AS name) TO 'events.msgpack' (FORMAT 'cbor.msgpack')
COPY (SELECT 1 AS id, 'alpha' AS name) TO 'events_array.msgpack' (FORMAT 'cbor.msgpack', row_format 'array')

functions.comment: Return the value(s) under a CBOR semantic tag as a JSON array

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Return a JSON array of every value carried under semantic `tag` in the CBOR blob, in document order (an empty array if the tag is absent). Complements `tags`, which lists all tags; `untag` projects one. Returns NULL for a malformed blob.

functions.name: to_json
functions.comment: Render a CBOR blob as canonical JSON text (byte strings as base64url)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Decode a CBOR (RFC 8949) blob and render it as a canonical JSON string. Always succeeds on well-formed input; it is necessarily lossy on the types JSON lacks — byte strings render as base64url, non-text map keys are stringified, and semantic tags are transparent (the inner value is shown). For the lossless typed path use `decode`; for a tag- and byte-preserving human view use `diagnostic`. Returns NULL for a malformed blob.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Render a CBOR blob as JSON text. Lossy on `BLOB`/non-string keys (base64url), tags transparent. `decode` is the lossless path, `diagnostic` the debug path.

workers.title: Character Encoding Detection & Transcoding
workers.tagline: Detect text encoding & transcode to UTF-8 / fix mojibake for DuckDB (Rust)
workers.summary: Character-encoding detection and UTF-8 transcoding (mojibake repair).
workers.doc_md:
# charset — detect text encoding and transcode to UTF-8 in SQL

Detect the character encoding of raw bytes and transcode legacy or mojibake-garbled text into clean UTF-8 directly in DuckDB SQL — no Python preprocessing step and no manual `iconv` passes.

## What it does

`charset` is a [VGI](https://query.farm) worker that adds character-encoding detection and UTF-8 transcoding to DuckDB over Apache Arrow. It is built for data engineers and analysts wrangling text of unknown or mixed provenance: CSV and log dumps in legacy Windows code pages, scraped HTML, email archives, and columns that arrived double-encoded — the classic `CafÃ©`-instead-of-`Café` mojibake. Rather than shelling out to external tools, you detect, repair, and normalize encodings inline with ordinary SQL queries.

## How it works

Encoding detection is powered by Mozilla's [`chardetng`](https://github.com/hsivonen/chardetng) ([docs](https://docs.rs/chardetng)), the same heuristic Firefox applies to unlabelled legacy text. Decoding and encoding use [`encoding_rs`](https://github.com/hsivonen/encoding_rs) ([docs](https://docs.rs/encoding_rs)), the pure-Rust implementation of the [WHATWG Encoding Standard](https://encoding.spec.whatwg.org/) that Firefox ships for every web-platform codec. A byte-order-mark (BOM) check runs first; undecodable bytes within a known encoding become the U+FFFD replacement character rather than raising an error, while an unknown encoding *label* is rejected so typos surface immediately.

## When to reach for it

Reach for `charset` whenever a text column's bytes are of unknown, mixed, or legacy provenance: sniff the likely encoding and score how trustworthy that guess is, decode legacy bytes to UTF-8 either automatically or with an explicit codec label, re-encode UTF-8 back into a legacy codec for export, repair double-encoded mojibake, and check whether bytes are already clean UTF-8. Because detection is heuristic, confidence-check short or ambiguous samples before relying on a result. Empty or NULL input yields NULL everywhere.
workers.readme_sql:
LOAD vgi;
ATTACH 'charset' (TYPE vgi, LOCATION './target/release/charset-worker');
SET search_path = 'charset.main';

SELECT detect_encoding('\x63\x61\x66\xE9'::BLOB);    -- 'windows-1252'
SELECT detect_confidence('\x63\x61\x66\xE9'::BLOB);  -- 1.0
SELECT to_utf8('\x63\x61\x66\xE9'::BLOB);            -- 'café'
SELECT to_utf8_from('\x93\xFA\x96\x7B\x8C\xEA'::BLOB, 'shift_jis');  -- '日本語'
SELECT transcode('café', 'windows-1252');            -- BLOB \x63\x61\x66\xE9
SELECT fix_mojibake('CafÃ©');                         -- 'Café'
SELECT is_valid_utf8('café'::BLOB);                  -- true
SELECT * FROM supported_encodings();                 -- discovery: label

example_queries.description: Detect the character encoding of windows-1252 bytes for "café".
example_queries.sql: SELECT charset.main.detect_encoding('\x63\x61\x66\xE9'::BLOB);

example_queries.description: Auto-detect and decode windows-1252 bytes to a UTF-8 string.
example_queries.sql: SELECT charset.main.to_utf8('\x63\x61\x66\xE9'::BLOB);

example_queries.description: Decode Shift-JIS bytes to UTF-8 with an explicit codec label.
example_queries.sql: SELECT charset.main.to_utf8_from('\x93\xFA\x96\x7B'::BLOB, 'shift_jis');

example_queries.description: Encode a UTF-8 string into windows-1252 bytes for export.
example_queries.sql: SELECT charset.main.transcode('café', 'windows-1252');

example_queries.description: Repair double-encoded mojibake back to clean UTF-8.
example_queries.sql: SELECT charset.main.fix_mojibake('CafÃ©');

## charset.main

Character-encoding detection and UTF-8 transcoding over Apache Arrow. The `main` schema groups its functions into detection (identify an encoding and score confidence), decoding (turn legacy or unlabelled bytes into clean UTF-8), encoding and repair (write UTF-8 back into a legacy codec and fix double-encoded mojibake), and discovery (enumerate supported encodings). Every function is catalog-qualified as `charset.main.<fn>(...)` and operates row-wise.

### Usage

```sql
SELECT charset.main.to_utf8('\x63\x61\x66\xE9'::BLOB); -- 'café'
```

tags.vgi.doc_md:
## to_utf8_from

Decodes a `BLOB` of text bytes to a UTF-8 string using an **explicit** encoding label you supply — no auto-detection.

**Arguments:** `bytes` (the `BLOB`) and `encoding` (a codec label such as `shift_jis`, `windows-1252`, or `iso-8859-1`). Call `supported_encodings()` to see the accepted labels.

**Errors & nulls:** an unknown label raises an error (the caller named a codec that does not exist); undecodable bytes within a *known* encoding become `U+FFFD`; `NULL` input returns `NULL`.

**When to use:** prefer this over `to_utf8` whenever the source encoding is known, to avoid detection mistakes.

```sql
SELECT charset.main.to_utf8_from('\x93\xFA\x96\x7B'::BLOB, 'shift_jis');
```

It is 1.0 when the bytes decode losslessly (or carry a BOM), and is scaled down by the fraction of U+FFFD replacement characters the decode produced. Returns NULL for empty or NULL input.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## detect_confidence

Scores how trustworthy the detected encoding of a `BLOB` is, on a `[0, 1]` scale.

**How it works:** `chardetng` itself does not expose a probability, so this proxies confidence from the decode — `1.0` when the bytes decode losslessly (or carry a BOM), scaled down by the fraction of `U+FFFD` replacement characters the decode produced.

**Returns:** a `DOUBLE` in `[0, 1]`; `NULL` for empty or `NULL` input.

**Usage:** gate automated cleanup on a threshold so low-confidence guesses are flagged for review rather than silently transformed.

```sql
SELECT charset.main.detect_confidence('\x63\x61\x66\xE9'::BLOB); -- 1.0
```

tags.vgi.doc_md:
## detect_encoding

Guesses the character encoding of a `BLOB` of raw text bytes and returns its canonical label.

**How it works:** a byte-order-mark check runs first; if there is no BOM, the `chardetng` (Firefox) heuristic inspects the whole buffer.

**Returns:** a label such as `UTF-8`, `windows-1252`, or `Shift_JIS`; `NULL` for empty or `NULL` input.

**Tip:** detection is statistical, so short or ambiguous input can be mis-guessed — combine with `detect_confidence` before trusting the result.

```sql
SELECT charset.main.detect_encoding('\x63\x61\x66\xE9'::BLOB); -- windows-1252
```

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Repair the classic double-encoding mojibake where UTF-8 text was mistakenly read as Latin-1/Windows-1252 and then re-stored as UTF-8, turning garbled sequences like 'CafÃ©' back into 'Café'. It only rewrites text when doing so strictly reduces mojibake markers, otherwise it returns the input unchanged. Returns NULL for NULL input.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## fix_mojibake

Repairs the classic *mojibake* failure where UTF-8 text was mistakenly read as Latin-1/Windows-1252 and then re-stored as UTF-8, leaving garbled sequences like `CafÃ©`.

**How it works:** re-encodes the text as Windows-1252 and re-decodes it as UTF-8, accepting the result **only** when it strictly reduces the number of mojibake markers. Otherwise it returns the input unchanged, so clean text and non-mojibake garble pass through untouched.

**Returns:** a `VARCHAR`; `NULL` for `NULL` input.

```sql
SELECT charset.main.fix_mojibake('CafÃ©'); -- 'Café'
```

tags.vgi.doc_md:
## is_valid_utf8

Tests whether a `BLOB` of bytes is already well-formed UTF-8.

**Returns:** `BOOLEAN` — `true` when every byte forms a valid UTF-8 sequence, `false` otherwise. An empty `BLOB` is valid UTF-8; `NULL` input returns `NULL`.

**When to use:** as a cheap pre-check to skip decoding/transcoding for data that is already clean, or to find rows that still need repair.

```sql
SELECT charset.main.is_valid_utf8('\x63\x61\x66\xC3\xA9'::BLOB); -- true
```

Undecodable bytes within the detected encoding become the U+FFFD replacement character rather than an error. Returns NULL for empty or NULL input. Use to_utf8_from when you already know the source encoding.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## to_utf8

Auto-detects the encoding of a `BLOB` of text bytes and decodes it to a UTF-8 string in one step.

**How it works:** runs the same detection as `detect_encoding` (BOM, then `chardetng`) and decodes with `encoding_rs`. Bytes that are undecodable in the detected encoding become the `U+FFFD` replacement character rather than raising an error.

**Returns:** a `VARCHAR`; `NULL` for empty or `NULL` input.

**When to use:** the convenient default for unlabelled data. Use `to_utf8_from` instead when you already know the source codec and want to skip detection.

```sql
SELECT charset.main.to_utf8('\x63\x61\x66\xE9'::BLOB); -- 'café'
```

functions.name: transcode
functions.comment: Encode a UTF-8 string into the named encoding's bytes (BLOB) for export, e.g. transcode('café', 'windows-1252'). Unmappable chars follow encoding_rs (HTML numeric refs for legacy codecs). ERROR on unknown label; NULL for NULL input.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Encode a UTF-8 string into the bytes of a named legacy encoding (returned as a `BLOB`) so it can be exported to a system that expects that codec, e.g. transcode('café', 'windows-1252'). Characters the target encoding cannot represent are emitted as HTML numeric references per encoding_rs. Raises an error if the encoding label is unknown; returns NULL for NULL input.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## transcode

Encodes a UTF-8 string into the bytes of a named legacy encoding, returned as a `BLOB`, so it can be exported to a system that expects that codec.

**Arguments:** `text` (UTF-8 `VARCHAR`) and `to_encoding` (target codec label, e.g. `windows-1252`, `shift_jis`).

**Behaviour:** characters the target encoding cannot represent are emitted as HTML numeric references (per `encoding_rs`) rather than dropped. An unknown encoding label raises an error; `NULL` input returns `NULL`.

**When to use:** the inverse of `to_utf8`/`to_utf8_from` — producing legacy bytes for downstream systems or file exports.

```sql
SELECT charset.main.transcode('café', 'windows-1252'); -- \x63\x61\x66\xE9
```
