workers.title: Chart Rendering for SQL
workers.tagline: Render line/bar/pie/scatter charts from a query to PNG for DuckDB (Java, JFreeChart)
workers.summary: Render charts (line/bar/pie/scatter/histogram) from a query result into PNG image BLOBs via JFreeChart
workers.doc_md:
# Chart Rendering for SQL

**Turn any DuckDB query into a publication-ready chart — line, bar, pie, scatter, or histogram — rendered to a PNG image `BLOB` entirely in SQL, with no plotting notebook, BI tool, or external service.**

The `chart` extension lets you visualize query results where the data already lives. Point a chart function at a relation, name the columns to plot, and get back a single PNG ready to write to disk, embed in a report, attach to an email, or stream to a web response. It is built for data engineers, analysts, and automation pipelines that need data visualization as a first-class SQL operation — dashboards generated on a schedule, charts pasted into Markdown or HTML, and image artifacts produced straight from an ETL job, all without leaving the database.

Charts are rendered by [JFreeChart](https://www.jfree.org/jfreechart/), the mature, widely deployed Java charting library, running fully headless through `java.awt` so no display or windowing system is required. Every function follows the same table-in / table-out shape: it consumes the input relation as a table-valued first argument, accumulates the rows, draws the chart, and rasterizes it to PNG bytes. The result comes back as a single `(png BLOB)` row, so the rendered image flows through the rest of your SQL like any other value and can be saved with DuckDB's `COPY`/file functions or returned directly to a caller.

The worker covers the everyday visualization needs — trends and relationships between numeric variables, comparisons of a measure across discrete categories, and the distribution of a single column — with a shared set of optional title, width, and height controls over the rendered output.

Learn more from the [JFreeChart project homepage](https://www.jfree.org/jfreechart/), the [source code on GitHub](https://github.com/jfree/jfreechart), and the [JFreeChart API documentation](https://www.jfree.org/jfreechart/javadoc/index.html).

example_queries.description: Render a line chart from inline points.
example_queries.sql: SELECT octet_length(png) FROM chart.main.chart_line((SELECT * FROM (VALUES (1, 10), (2, 25), (3, 18)) AS t(x, y)), x := 'x', y := 'y')

example_queries.description: Render a bar chart of category counts.
example_queries.sql: SELECT octet_length(png) FROM chart.main.chart_bar((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('A', 30), ('B', 45)) AS t(category, value)), category := 'category', value := 'value')

example_queries.description: Render a pie chart of two slices.
example_queries.sql: SELECT octet_length(png) FROM chart.main.chart_pie((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('X', 65), ('Y', 35)) AS t(label, value)), label := 'label', value := 'value')

example_queries.description: Render a scatter plot of numeric x/y points.
example_queries.sql: SELECT octet_length(png) FROM chart.main.chart_scatter((SELECT * FROM (VALUES (1.0, 2.1), (2.0, 3.9)) AS t(x, y)), x := 'x', y := 'y')

example_queries.description: Render a 5-bin histogram of a numeric column.
example_queries.sql: SELECT octet_length(png) FROM chart.main.chart_histogram((SELECT * FROM (VALUES (1.0), (1.5), (2.0)) AS t(value)), value := 'value', bins := 5)

example_queries.description: List every chart type this worker offers with its category and the column arguments it takes.
example_queries.sql: SELECT chart_type, category, column_arguments FROM chart.main.chart_types() ORDER BY chart_type

example_queries.description: Find the chart types that compare a measure across discrete categories.
example_queries.sql: SELECT chart_type, summary FROM chart.main.chart_types() WHERE category = 'categorical-comparisons' ORDER BY chart_type

example_queries.description: List every chart type with its category, ordered by name.
example_queries.sql: SELECT chart_type, category FROM chart.main.chart_types() ORDER BY chart_type;

example_queries.description: Render a scatter plot of numeric x/y points and report the PNG byte size.
example_queries.sql: SELECT octet_length(png) AS bytes FROM chart.main.chart_scatter((SELECT * FROM (VALUES (1.0, 2.1), (2.0, 3.9), (3.0, 6.2)) AS t(x, y)), x := 'x', y := 'y', title := 'x vs y')

example_queries.description: Render one colored point series per cohort of height against weight.
example_queries.sql: SELECT octet_length(png) AS bytes FROM chart.main.chart_scatter((SELECT * FROM (VALUES (170.0, 65.0, 'A'), (180.0, 80.0, 'A'), (160.0, 55.0, 'B'), (175.0, 72.0, 'B')) AS t(height_cm, weight_kg, cohort)), x := 'height_cm', y := 'weight_kg', series := 'cohort', title := 'Height vs weight by cohort')

example_queries.description: Bin five values into 5 equal-width buckets and report the PNG byte size.
example_queries.sql: SELECT octet_length(png) AS bytes FROM chart.main.chart_histogram((SELECT * FROM (VALUES (1.0), (1.5), (2.0), (2.0), (3.5)) AS t(value)), value := 'value', bins := 5, title := 'Distribution')

example_queries.description: Render a 30-bucket histogram of request latency as a 900x500 PNG.
example_queries.sql: SELECT octet_length(png) AS bytes FROM chart.main.chart_histogram((SELECT * FROM (VALUES (12.0), (15.0), (15.0), (22.0), (30.0), (45.0), (9.0)) AS t(latency_ms)), value := 'latency_ms', bins := 30, title := 'Latency distribution', width := 900, height := 500)

example_queries.description: Render a pie with one slice per label and report the PNG byte size.
example_queries.sql: SELECT octet_length(png) AS bytes FROM chart.main.chart_pie((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('Chrome', 65), ('Safari', 19), ('Firefox', 16)) AS t(label, value)), label := 'label', value := 'value', title := 'Browser share')

example_queries.description: Render spend per category as a 700x700 pie (duplicate categories are summed).
example_queries.sql: SELECT octet_length(png) AS bytes FROM chart.main.chart_pie((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('Rent', 1200), ('Food', 450), ('Rent', 100), ('Travel', 300)) AS t(category, amount)), label := 'category', value := 'amount', title := 'Spend by category', width := 700, height := 700)

example_queries.description: Render a single line over numeric x/y points and report the PNG byte size.
example_queries.sql: SELECT octet_length(png) AS bytes FROM chart.main.chart_line((SELECT * FROM (VALUES (1, 10), (2, 25), (3, 18), (4, 30)) AS t(x, y)), x := 'x', y := 'y', title := 'Trend')

example_queries.description: Render one line per region (series) of revenue over months and report its PNG byte size.
example_queries.sql: SELECT octet_length(png) AS bytes FROM chart.main.chart_line((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('Jan', 100, 'East'), ('Feb', 140, 'East'), ('Jan', 80, 'West'), ('Feb', 95, 'West')) AS t(month, revenue, region)), x := 'month', y := 'revenue', series := 'region', title := 'Revenue by region')

example_queries.description: Render one bar per category and report the PNG byte size.
example_queries.sql: SELECT octet_length(png) AS bytes FROM chart.main.chart_bar((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('A', 30), ('B', 45), ('C', 12)) AS t(category, value)), category := 'category', value := 'value', title := 'Counts')

Each function takes the input relation as a table-valued first argument plus named column arguments identifying what to plot, renders the chart headless with JFreeChart, and returns a single `(png BLOB)` row. The functions cover trends and relationships between numeric variables, comparisons across discrete categories, and the distribution of a single numeric column.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## Chart functions

Render a query result to a PNG image `BLOB` via JFreeChart. Each function is a table-in / table-out function: it consumes the input relation as a table-valued first argument, reads the columns you name, and emits a single `(png BLOB)` row holding the rendered image.

The functions span the everyday visualization needs — trends and relationships between numeric variables, comparisons of a measure across discrete categories, and the shape of a single column's distribution — and share a common set of optional title, width, and height controls.

Charts render fully headless through `java.awt`, so no display is required, and the returned PNG can be written to disk, embedded in a document, or returned straight to a caller.

## chart_scatter

Render a **scatter plot** from a query result to a PNG image `BLOB`.

### Usage

Pass the relation as the table argument, name the numeric `x` and `y` columns, and optionally add a `series` column plus `title`, `width`, and `height`. See this function's example queries for complete, runnable calls.

### Notes

- Both `x` and `y` must be numeric.
- With `series`, one point series is drawn per distinct value; NULL x/y rows are ignored.

### Usage

Pass the relation as the table argument, name the numeric `value` column, and optionally set `bins` plus `title`, `width`, and `height`. See this function's example queries for complete, runnable calls.

# Cheminformatics in SQL with RDKit

![RDKit logo](https://www.rdkit.org/Images/logo.png)

**Run molecular descriptors, fingerprints, Tanimoto similarity, SMARTS substructure search and InChI/InChIKey generation directly in DuckDB SQL — computed from SMILES strings by [RDKit](https://www.rdkit.org/), the industry-standard open-source cheminformatics toolkit.**

The `chem` catalog turns DuckDB into a cheminformatics engine. Instead of exporting a column of SMILES to Python, looping through RDKit, and joining the results back, you call chemistry functions inline in a query: validate and canonicalize structures, compute physicochemical properties, generate molecular fingerprints, score structural similarity, match SMARTS patterns, and screen for drug-likeness — all on whole tables of compounds at once. It is built for chemists, computational chemists, data scientists and drug-discovery teams who already keep their compound libraries in DuckDB, Parquet or CSV and want molecular analytics without leaving SQL.

Every function is powered by [RDKit](https://github.com/rdkit/rdkit) (BSD-3-Clause), the open-source toolkit that underpins much of modern cheminformatics. RDKit is imported as an unmodified dependency and parses each SMILES (or SMARTS) string into a molecule before computing the requested property. The worker is deliberately robust: a malformed structure never raises or crashes a query — `NULL` input yields `NULL` output, and invalid (non-NULL) SMILES yields `NULL`, `false`, or no rows depending on the function. RDKit runs fully offline with no network access or model downloads, so results are deterministic and reproducible across runs. See the official [RDKit documentation](https://www.rdkit.org/docs/) for the underlying algorithms.

## What you can compute

The catalog spans the everyday cheminformatics workflow, grouped into navigation sections: structure **validity**, canonical **identity** (canonical SMILES plus InChI/InChIKey for deduplication and joins), numeric and count **descriptors** for property filtering and QSAR, circular **fingerprints** and Tanimoto **similarity** for search and clustering, SMARTS **substructure** matching for structural filters, and Lipinski **drug-likeness** screening. Everything operates on SMILES strings and runs inline over whole tables, so a column of compounds becomes a column of properties, identifiers, fingerprints or pass/fail flags in a single query.

## Getting started

Attach the catalog with `ATTACH 'chem' (TYPE vgi, LOCATION 'uv run chem_worker.py')`, then call any function inline in a query. Pass a SMILES string to get a molecular formula (`C9H8O4` for aspirin), a molecular weight (~180.16 g/mol), an InChIKey, a Tanimoto similarity score, or a Lipinski drug-likeness breakdown -- no export to Python required. New here? Browse the built-in `example_molecules()` table for ready-to-use SMILES and their pre-computed descriptors, then see each function's own example queries for ready-to-run SQL.

Source and issues: [Query-farm/vgi-chem](https://github.com/Query-farm/vgi-chem).

ATTACH 'chem' (TYPE vgi, LOCATION 'uv run chem_worker.py');

SELECT chem.tanimoto('CCO', 'CCO');                              -- 1.0
SELECT chem.substructure_match('c1ccccc1O', 'c1ccccc1');         -- true
SELECT * FROM chem.lipinski('CC(=O)OC1=CC=CC=C1C(=O)O');         -- rule-of-five rows

# chem.main

The single schema of the `chem` catalog. It groups every cheminformatics function exposed by this worker, all computed from SMILES strings via RDKit.

## Contents

Functions are organized into navigation categories: validity, identity and canonicalization, molecular descriptors, fingerprints, similarity, substructure search, and drug-likeness. Scalars return one value per SMILES row; the sole set-returning function, `lipinski`, expands one molecule into one row per rule.

## Usage

Call a function by its qualified name, `chem.main.<fn>` — or `chem.<fn>`, since `main` is the default schema. Scalars take positional arguments; `lipinski` is a set-returning table function.

## Notes

Every function is total: `NULL` in yields `NULL` out, and invalid (non-NULL) SMILES yields `NULL`/`false`/no-rows rather than raising.

## `example_molecules` (table)

A browsable registry of well-known molecules (water, ethanol, benzene, aspirin, caffeine, ibuprofen, glucose, paracetamol, nicotine, penicillin G, ...) with ready-computed descriptors, exposed as a regular table you can read without parentheses.

# `example_molecules`

A curated, browsable registry of common molecules and their descriptors, exposed as a regular table you can read without parentheses -- the zero-argument discovery entry point for the `chem` catalog.

## Columns

- `name` (`VARCHAR`, primary key), `smiles`, `formula`
- `mol_weight` (`DOUBLE`, g/mol), `logp` (`DOUBLE`), `tpsa` (`DOUBLE`, Angstrom^2)
- `h_bond_donors`, `h_bond_acceptors`, `num_rings` (`INTEGER`)
- `drug_like` (`BOOLEAN`) -- passes all four Lipinski rules

Read it directly to discover valid SMILES inputs to feed the scalar functions, or to compare descriptor ranges across common drugs.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## lipinski

A **set-returning** table function that breaks a molecule (given as SMILES) down against the **Lipinski rule of five**, emitting one row per rule with its computed value and whether the threshold is satisfied.

**Use it** for drug-likeness screening: keep compounds that pass all four rules, or inspect exactly which rule a compound violates.

Rules evaluated: molecular weight <= 500, logP <= 5, H-bond donors <= 5, H-bond acceptors <= 10.

- **Input**: one SMILES string (`VARCHAR`) as a positional table argument.
- **Output**: rows of `(rule VARCHAR, value DOUBLE, passes BOOLEAN)`.

**Edge cases**: an invalid SMILES yields **no rows** (rather than raising), so `bool_and(passes)` over an empty result behaves accordingly. Aggregate with `bool_and(passes)` to get a single drug-like flag.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# lipinski

Lipinski rule-of-five breakdown for a SMILES string, one row per rule.

## Result

Four rows -- `molecular_weight`, `logp`, `h_bond_donors`, `h_bond_acceptors` -- each with its computed `value` and a `passes` flag. Aggregate the `passes` column with `bool_and` for a single drug-like verdict, or keep the non-passing rows to see which criterion a compound violates.

## Notes

Rules: MW <= 500, logP <= 5, HBD <= 5, HBA <= 10. An invalid SMILES returns no rows.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## substructure_match

Tests whether a molecule (given as SMILES) **contains a substructure** described by a [SMARTS](https://www.daylight.com/dayhtml/doc/theory/theory.smarts.html) query pattern.

**Use it** to filter compound sets by functional group or scaffold -- e.g. find every molecule containing a benzene ring or a carboxylic acid.

- **Input**: a SMILES molecule and a SMARTS pattern (both `VARCHAR`).
- **Output**: `BOOLEAN` -- `true` if the pattern matches, `false` if not.

**Edge cases**: returns `NULL` if **either** the SMILES is invalid **or** the SMARTS pattern is invalid (a bad pattern is reported as `NULL`, never raised). `NULL` input returns `NULL`.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# substructure_match

Boolean SMARTS substructure test over a SMILES molecule.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT chem.main.substructure_match('c1ccccc1O', 'c1ccccc1');  -- true (phenol has benzene)
```

Use it in a `WHERE` predicate to keep only compounds carrying a scaffold or functional group -- e.g. the carboxylic-acid SMARTS `[CX3](=O)[OX2H1]`.

## Notes

Returns `NULL` when the SMILES or the SMARTS is invalid; otherwise `true`/`false`.

## num_h_donors

Counts the **hydrogen-bond donors** in a molecule from its SMILES, by the Lipinski definition (N-H and O-H groups).

**Use it** for drug-likeness screening; this is the Lipinski rule HBD <= 5.

- **Input**: a SMILES string (`VARCHAR`).
- **Output**: `INTEGER` H-bond donor count, or `NULL` if invalid.

**Edge cases**: uses the Lipinski (NHOH) count, which counts donor *groups*; pair with `num_h_acceptors` for the full HBD/HBA picture. `NULL`/invalid input returns `NULL`.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## mol_weight

Computes the **average molecular weight** (g/mol) of a molecule from its SMILES, using standard atomic weights (isotope-averaged).

**Use it** for stoichiometry, dosing math, molecular-property filters, or as the first Lipinski rule (MW <= 500).

- **Input**: a SMILES string (`VARCHAR`).
- **Output**: `DOUBLE` average MW in g/mol (e.g. ~180.16 for aspirin), or `NULL` if invalid.

**Edge cases**: this is the *average* (not monoisotopic) mass -- use `exact_mass` for the monoisotopic value used in mass spectrometry. `NULL`/invalid input returns `NULL`.

## num_atoms

Counts the **heavy (non-hydrogen) atoms** in a molecule from its SMILES.

**Use it** as a simple size/complexity measure for filtering fragments vs. full molecules, or as a denominator for ligand-efficiency metrics.

- **Input**: a SMILES string (`VARCHAR`).
- **Output**: `INTEGER` heavy-atom count, or `NULL` if invalid.

**Edge cases**: implicit/explicit hydrogens are **not** counted -- only heavy atoms. `NULL`/invalid input returns `NULL`.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## mol_formula

Computes the **Hill-system molecular formula** of a molecule from its SMILES (carbon first, then hydrogen, then other elements alphabetically), e.g. `C9H8O4` for aspirin.

**Use it** to report or group compounds by composition, or to feed a mass-spec / elemental-analysis pipeline.

- **Input**: a SMILES string (`VARCHAR`).
- **Output**: `VARCHAR` Hill formula, or `NULL` for invalid input.

**Edge cases**: implicit hydrogens are counted, so the formula reflects the full molecule, not just the heavy-atom skeleton. `NULL`/invalid input returns `NULL`.

## logp

Estimates **logP** -- the octanol-water partition coefficient, a lipophilicity measure -- using RDKit's Crippen `MolLogP` contribution model, from a SMILES.

**Use it** for drug-likeness and ADME filtering; logP is the third Lipinski rule (logP <= 5) and a core permeability/solubility proxy.

- **Input**: a SMILES string (`VARCHAR`).
- **Output**: `DOUBLE` Crippen logP (can be negative for very polar molecules), or `NULL` if invalid.

**Edge cases**: this is a *computed estimate* (Crippen atom contributions), not a measured value, and may differ from experimental logP. `NULL`/invalid input returns `NULL`.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT chem.main.logp('CCO');  -- small negative/near-zero (hydrophilic)
```

## Notes

An estimate from Crippen atom contributions, not an experimental measurement. Higher means more lipophilic. Returns `NULL` on invalid input.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## is_valid_smiles

Tests whether a string is a syntactically and chemically valid [SMILES](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SMILES) molecule, using RDKit's parser.

**Use it** as a cheap guard before any other `chem` function, or to filter a column of user-supplied structures.

- **Input**: a SMILES string (`VARCHAR`).
- **Output**: `BOOLEAN` -- `true` if RDKit parses it to a molecule, `false` for any non-NULL string it cannot parse.

**Edge cases**: a `NULL` input returns `NULL` (not `false`); unlike every other function here, an unparseable string returns `false` rather than `NULL`, so it is safe to use directly in a `WHERE` clause.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# is_valid_smiles

Return `true` when a string parses to a valid molecule via RDKit, `false` otherwise.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT chem.main.is_valid_smiles('CCO');   -- true (ethanol)
SELECT chem.main.is_valid_smiles('xyz');   -- false
```

## Notes

`NULL` in yields `NULL` out; any other unparseable input yields `false`, so this is the safe predicate to gate the other descriptor/identity functions.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## inchikey

Computes the **standard InChIKey** -- the fixed-length, 27-character hashed form of the InChI -- for a molecule from its SMILES.

**Use it** as a compact, collision-resistant primary key for chemical structures, ideal for indexing, joining and web search.

- **Input**: a SMILES string (`VARCHAR`).
- **Output**: `VARCHAR` InChIKey like `BSYNRYMUTXBXSQ-UHFFFAOYSA-N`, or `NULL` if invalid.

**Edge cases**: the key is derived from the standard InChI, so it inherits the same tautomer/stereo normalization. The first 14 chars encode connectivity; the next block encodes stereo/isotope/protonation. `NULL`/invalid input returns `NULL`.
tags.vgi.doc_md:

## Notes

A fixed-length, indexable structure key. The first 14 characters capture skeletal connectivity. Returns `NULL` on invalid input.

functions.name: morgan_fingerprint
functions.comment: Morgan (ECFP-like) fingerprint as a hex bit-string (defaults radius=2, nbits=2048); NULL if invalid

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## morgan_fingerprint

Builds a **Morgan (ECFP-like) circular fingerprint** for a molecule from its SMILES and returns it as a hexadecimal bit-string.

Two arities share this name:

- `morgan_fingerprint(smiles)` -- uses the fixed defaults `radius=2` and `nbits=2048`.
- `morgan_fingerprint(smiles, radius, nbits)` -- set the atom-neighborhood `radius` and the bit-vector length `nbits` explicitly.

**Use it** to vectorize molecules for similarity search, clustering, or as machine-learning features. Two molecules' fingerprints are compared with `tanimoto`.

- **Input**: a SMILES string (`VARCHAR`); the three-argument form additionally takes `radius` (`BIGINT`) and `nbits` (`BIGINT`).
- **Output**: `VARCHAR` hex-encoded bit vector, or `NULL` if invalid.

**Edge cases**: a larger `radius` captures bigger atom environments; a smaller `nbits` increases bit collisions. Only fingerprints built with identical `radius`/`nbits` are comparable. `NULL`/invalid input returns `NULL`.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# morgan_fingerprint

Morgan/ECFP circular fingerprint as a hex bit-string from a SMILES string.

## Signatures

- `morgan_fingerprint(smiles)` -- defaults `radius=2`, `nbits=2048`.
- `morgan_fingerprint(smiles, radius, nbits)` -- explicit radius and bit length.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT chem.main.morgan_fingerprint('CCO');            -- radius=2, nbits=2048
SELECT chem.main.morgan_fingerprint('CCO', 3, 1024);   -- explicit
```

## Notes

Compare two fingerprints with `tanimoto`. Only fingerprints built with the same `radius`/`nbits` are comparable. Returns `NULL` on invalid input.

## tanimoto(a, b, radius)

Explicit-radius arity of **Tanimoto similarity**: compare two molecules (from their SMILES) over Morgan fingerprints built at a caller-chosen `radius`, returning a value in [0, 1].

**Use it** when you want similarity at a specific fingerprint resolution.

functions.name: drug_like
functions.comment: True if the molecule passes all four Lipinski rule-of-five criteria, NULL if invalid

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## drug_like

A single-value **drug-likeness predicate**: `true` if the molecule (given as SMILES) passes **all four** Lipinski rule-of-five criteria, `false` if it violates any of them.

**Use it** to filter compound libraries inline -- `WHERE drug_like(smiles)` -- instead of aggregating the per-rule `lipinski` table function in a subquery. Reach for `lipinski` instead when you need to see *which* rule a compound violates.

Rules applied: molecular weight <= 500, Crippen logP <= 5, H-bond donors <= 5, H-bond acceptors <= 10.

- **Input**: a SMILES string (`VARCHAR`).
- **Output**: `BOOLEAN` -- `true` if all four rules pass, else `false`; `NULL` for `NULL` or invalid input.

**Edge cases**: this is the scalar collapse of `bool_and(passes)` over `lipinski`; `NULL`/invalid input returns `NULL` (not `false`).
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# drug_like

Boolean Lipinski rule-of-five drug-likeness flag from a SMILES string.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT chem.main.drug_like('CC(=O)OC1=CC=CC=C1C(=O)O');  -- true (aspirin)
```

Use it directly in a `WHERE` clause to keep only drug-like compounds; use the `lipinski` table function when you need the per-rule breakdown.

## Notes

Passes when MW <= 500, logP <= 5, HBD <= 5 and HBA <= 10. Returns `NULL` on invalid input.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT chem.main.drug_like('CC(=O)OC1=CC=CC=C1C(=O)O')

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## canonical_smiles

Rewrites any valid SMILES into RDKit's **canonical** SMILES -- a single, deterministic spelling for a given molecular graph.

**Use it** to deduplicate or group molecules that were written differently (`OCC` and `CCO` are the same ethanol), or to produce a stable join key.

- **Input**: a SMILES string (`VARCHAR`).
- **Output**: `VARCHAR` canonical SMILES, or `NULL` if the input does not parse.

**Edge cases**: `NULL`/invalid input returns `NULL`. Canonicalization does not neutralize charges or strip salts -- it only canonicalizes the graph as written.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# canonical_smiles

Normalize a SMILES string to RDKit's canonical form for stable comparison and deduplication.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT chem.main.canonical_smiles('OCC');   -- 'CCO'
```

Apply it over a whole SMILES column with a `DISTINCT` projection to deduplicate structures written different ways.

## Notes

Returns `NULL` on invalid input. Two strings denoting the same molecule canonicalize to the same value, making this a reliable grouping/join key.

## tpsa

Computes the **topological polar surface area (TPSA)** of a molecule, in square Angstroms, from its SMILES -- the surface area attributable to polar (N, O and attached H) atoms.

**Use it** as a predictor of membrane permeability and oral absorption; TPSA below ~140 Angstrom^2 (and ~90 for CNS penetration) is a common drug-likeness filter.

- **Output**: `DOUBLE` TPSA in Angstrom^2, or `NULL` if invalid.

**Edge cases**: TPSA is a fast 2D topological estimate (Ertl method), not a 3D surface calculation. `NULL`/invalid input returns `NULL`.

workers.summary: Source-code structure for DuckDB: tree-sitter symbols, imports, comments, strings, line counts and arbitrary tree-sitter queries.
workers.doc_md:
# Source-Code Structure Analysis for DuckDB

![tree-sitter logo](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tree-sitter/tree-sitter/master/docs/src/assets/images/tree-sitter-small.png)

Parse, search, and measure source code directly in SQL: extract symbols, imports, comments, and string literals, count physical lines and function definitions, and run arbitrary tree-sitter queries across nine programming languages — all over Apache Arrow with no language server, no checkout, and no external services.

The `code` worker turns DuckDB into a lightweight code-intelligence engine for developers, data and platform engineers, and security or research teams who need to treat large codebases as queryable data. Point it at source held in any DuckDB table or file and get structured facts back as ordinary rows and columns. Because everything is just SQL, you can join code structure against commits, issues, ownership, or CVE data and compute metrics over an entire repository in a single query.

Parsing is powered by [tree-sitter](https://tree-sitter.github.io/), the fast, incremental, error-tolerant parsing library used by editors and code-search tools such as Neovim, Zed, and GitHub. Each call builds a concrete syntax tree and runs curated per-language tree-sitter queries, so extraction stays accurate even on incomplete or malformed input (garbage in yields empty results, never a crash). Supported languages are rust, python, javascript, typescript, go, java, c, cpp, and json. See the official [tree-sitter documentation](https://tree-sitter.github.io/tree-sitter/) and the [tree-sitter source on GitHub](https://github.com/tree-sitter/tree-sitter) for grammar and query details.

## Key concepts

Everything is exposed as ordinary SQL: scalar functions take a per-row source string (and, where parsing is needed, a `language` id) and return a value or a `VARCHAR[]` array; table functions take a constant source and return a result set you can join and aggregate. Language ids are lowercase (`rust`, `python`, `go`, …) and parsing is best-effort — malformed or truncated input yields empty results rather than an error, while an unknown language or a bad tree-sitter query is reported clearly.

## When to reach for it

Use the `code` worker whenever you want to treat source as data instead of text: build codebase metrics dashboards (size, complexity, function density), audit dependencies and import graphs, mine comments and TODOs, scan string literals for secrets, URLs, or missing license headers, and run structural code search with your own tree-sitter queries. Because the answers come back as rows, you can join them against commits, ownership, issues, or CVE data and compute over an entire repository in one query.

tags.vgi.doc_md:
# Source-code structure

The single schema of the `code` worker. It exposes source-code structure to SQL over Apache Arrow, powered by [tree-sitter](https://tree-sitter.github.io/): detect a file's language, measure it, and pull structural facts out of it without a checkout, language server, or external service.

## What lives here

Scalar functions work per row and return a value or a `VARCHAR[]` you can `UNNEST`; table functions take a constant source and return joinable result sets. The work falls into a few groups — language detection and discovery, code metrics, structure and content extraction, and arbitrary tree-sitter queries.

## Languages

Parsing supports rust, python, javascript, typescript, go, java, c, cpp and json. Language ids are lowercase; malformed or truncated input yields empty results rather than an error, while an unknown language or a bad query is reported clearly.

workers.tagline: Color science — RGB/HSL/LAB, CIEDE2000 ΔE & WCAG contrast for DuckDB (Rust)
workers.summary: Color science for SQL: color-space conversions, CIEDE2000 (ΔE00) color difference, and WCAG contrast/accessibility.
workers.doc_md:
# Color Science for SQL

Bring professional color science to DuckDB — convert between color spaces, measure perceptual color difference, and check accessibility contrast directly in SQL, with no application code required.

The `color` extension is a [VGI](https://query.farm) worker that adds sRGB hex, RGB, HSL and CIELAB color tools to DuckDB over Apache Arrow. It is built for designers, data engineers, and accessibility teams who need to normalize colors, build and de-duplicate palettes, compute [CIEDE2000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_difference#CIEDE2000) (ΔE00) color differences, and audit [WCAG](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/#contrast-minimum) contrast at warehouse scale.

## How it works

Every transform is implemented directly from the canonical specifications — [sRGB / IEC 61966-2-1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SRGB) companding, the [CIELAB (D65)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CIELAB_color_space) color space, the Sharma–Wu–Dalal [CIEDE2000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_difference#CIEDE2000) ΔE formula, and the [WCAG 2.x relative-luminance and contrast](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/Understanding/contrast-minimum.html) definitions — so results match the standards exactly with zero external color dependencies. The same algorithms are available in open-source libraries such as the Rust [palette](https://github.com/Ogeon/palette) crate ([docs](https://docs.rs/palette)); here they run inside a fast, dependency-free worker. The 147 CSS named colors come from the [CSS Color Module Level 4](https://www.w3.org/TR/css-color-4/#named-colors) specification.

## Key concepts

Colors are represented as sRGB hex strings, integer RGB triples, HSL, or perceptually-uniform CIELAB. Perceptual similarity is measured with CIEDE2000 (ΔE00), where a value near 1 is roughly a just-noticeable difference. Accessibility is expressed as WCAG relative luminance (0–1) and contrast ratio (1–21), which classify into the WCAG conformance levels AAA, AA, AA Large and fail.

## When to use it

Reach for this worker whenever colors live in your data: normalizing user-entered or imported hex values, building and de-duplicating palettes, labeling arbitrary colors with their nearest name, or auditing foreground/background pairs for accessibility. Its functions are organized into four categories — conversion, color difference, accessibility, and reference.
workers.readme_sql:
LOAD vgi;
ATTACH 'color' (TYPE vgi, LOCATION './target/release/color-worker');
SET search_path = 'color.main';

SELECT to_hex(255, 0, 0);                       -- '#ff0000'
SELECT (from_hex('#ff0000')).*;                 -- (r := 255, g := 0, b := 0)
SELECT (rgb_to_hsl(255, 0, 0)).*;               -- (h := 0, s := 1, l := 0.5)
SELECT (rgb_to_lab(255, 0, 0)).*;               -- (l := 53.24, a := 80.09, b := 67.20)
SELECT ROUND(delta_e('#ff0000', '#ff4500'), 2); -- CIEDE2000 ΔE
SELECT ROUND(contrast_ratio('#000000','#ffffff'), 1);  -- 21.0
SELECT wcag_level('#000000', '#ffffff');        -- 'AAA'
SELECT is_dark('#222222');                      -- true
SELECT nearest_color_name('#ff0000');           -- 'red'
SELECT * FROM named_colors();                   -- CSS named-color table

tags.vgi.doc_md:
# color.main

Color science over Apache Arrow. Everything the `color` worker exposes lives in this single schema.

Three kinds of operation are available. **Conversions** move a color between representations — sRGB hex, RGB, HSL and CIELAB. **Color-difference** operations measure how far apart two colors look, using the perceptual CIEDE2000 (ΔE00) metric, and can map an arbitrary color to its nearest CSS name. **Accessibility** operations compute WCAG relative luminance and contrast ratios and classify conformance for text on a background.

Use this schema for color normalization, palette analysis and de-duplication, and WCAG contrast/accessibility auditing directly in SQL. The functions are grouped into four categories: conversion, color difference, accessibility, and reference.

workers.tagline: Compress and decompress blobs in DuckDB with SQL — zstd, gzip, brotli, lz4, snappy, xz, bzip2 with decompression-bomb guards. A VGI worker.
workers.summary: Multi-codec (de)compression over a DuckDB `BLOB` column — zstd, gzip, zlib, deflate, brotli, lz4, snappy, xz, lzma, bzip2 — with codec auto-detection and a decompression-bomb guard.
workers.doc_md:
# compress

**Multi-codec (de)compression over a DuckDB `BLOB` column** — `zstd`, `gzip`, `zlib`, `deflate`, `brotli`, `lz4` (frame + block), `snappy` (framed + raw), `xz`, `lzma`, `bzip2` — plus codec auto-detection by magic bytes, level control, and size/ratio introspection. Fills the one gap DuckDB core leaves open: core decompresses *files*, but there is no scalar to decode a *column* of compressed payloads at scan time. Decode a mixed-codec Kafka payload column, transcode a cold archive in place (gzip → zstd), or audit compression — all without leaving the engine.

**Security — decompression bombs.** Every decode path enforces a bounded `max_output_bytes` cap (default 256 MiB): a hostile high-ratio blob aborts that one row with a per-row error instead of OOMing the worker. Pure in-engine local CPU — no network, no state, zero egress.

tags.vgi.doc_md:
## compress.main

The single schema of the `compress` worker. The catalog name matches the `ATTACH` name, so calls are qualified with the `compress.main` prefix.

The surface is grouped into four navigable areas:

- **encode** — turn a `BLOB` into compressed bytes with a chosen codec and optional level.
- **decode** — recover the original bytes, with the codec named explicitly or auto-detected, under a decompression-bomb guard.
- **introspection** — measure compressed and decompressed size, compression ratio, and stream validity without materializing the output.
- **discovery** — identify a blob's codec and list the codecs this build supports.

Every codec — zstd, gzip, zlib, deflate, brotli, lz4, snappy, xz, lzma, and bzip2 — shares this one uniform surface over a `BLOB` column.

workers.title: Field Validation & Normalization (conform)
workers.tagline: Validate & normalize phone, email, IBAN, VAT, card, URL & postal data for DuckDB (Python)
workers.summary: Validate + normalize phone/email/IBAN/VAT/card/URL/postal fields for SQL
workers.doc_md:
# conform: Field Validation & Normalization in SQL

**Validate and normalize phone numbers, emails, IBANs, EU VAT numbers, credit-card numbers, URLs, and postal codes directly in DuckDB SQL** -- no UDF plumbing, no external service, and no network calls. The `conform` extension turns the data-cleaning steps you would normally script in Python into fast, set-based SQL functions, so you can check validity, standardize formatting, and extract field parts right where your data lives.

This catalog is built for anyone wrangling messy real-world contact, banking, and payment data: data engineers cleaning a CRM export, analysts deduplicating customer records, or pipelines that must reject malformed input before it lands. Every check is **offline, deterministic, and total** -- functions never raise on garbage (with one deliberate exception, an unknown postal-code country), returning `false` for `is_valid_*` and `NULL` for formatters and extractors. That makes the extension hermetic and safe to run over huge tables without DNS lookups or flaky I/O.

Under the hood, `conform` composes three best-in-class, battle-tested libraries. Phone parsing, validation, and E.164/national/international formatting come from [`phonenumbers`](https://github.com/daviddrysdale/python-phonenumbers) (the Python port of Google's [libphonenumber](https://github.com/google/libphonenumber)). IBAN, EU VAT, and the Luhn credit-card check come from [`python-stdnum`](https://github.com/arthurdejong/python-stdnum) ([documentation](https://arthurdejong.org/python-stdnum/)). Email syntax validation and normalization come from [`email-validator`](https://github.com/JoshData/python-email-validator). URL and postal-code handling are implemented in-process against per-country rules.

## What you get

The surface divides into three shapes -- **validity tests** that return a boolean, **normalizers/formatters** that rewrite a value into a canonical string (ideal for joining or deduplication), and **part extractors** that pull a single component (a domain, country, brand, or host) out of a well-formed value -- plus discovery tables that enumerate the phone regions and card brands the worker recognizes.

Phone and VAT functions take an optional ISO region/country argument (`'US'` and the EU-prefixed form are defaults); postal-code validation requires a country.

```sql
SELECT conform.main.normalize_email('Test@Example.COM');
SELECT conform.main.format_phone_e164('07911 123456', 'GB');
SELECT conform.main.mask_card('4111-1111-1111-1111');
```
workers.readme_sql:
INSTALL vgi FROM community; LOAD vgi;
ATTACH 'conform' (TYPE vgi, LOCATION 'uv run conform_worker.py');

SELECT conform.is_valid_email('a@b.com');                  -- true
SELECT conform.normalize_email('Test@Example.COM');        -- 'test@example.com'
SELECT conform.format_phone_e164('202-456-1111');          -- '+12024561111' (region 'US')
SELECT conform.format_phone_e164('07911 123456', 'GB');    -- '+447911123456'
SELECT conform.is_valid_iban('GB82 WEST 1234 5698 7654 32');-- true
SELECT conform.iban_country('GB82WEST12345698765432');     -- 'GB'
SELECT conform.is_valid_vat('DE136695976');                -- true
SELECT conform.card_brand('4111111111111111');             -- 'visa'
SELECT conform.mask_card('4111-1111-1111-1111');           -- '************1111'
SELECT conform.normalize_url('HTTP://Example.com:80/Path');-- 'http://example.com/Path'
SELECT conform.is_valid_postal_code('90210', 'US');        -- true

example_queries.description: Check whether a string is a syntactically valid email address.
example_queries.sql: SELECT conform.main.is_valid_email('a@b.com')

example_queries.description: Canonicalize an email address (lower-cased domain) for deduplication.
example_queries.sql: SELECT conform.main.normalize_email('Test@Example.COM')

example_queries.description: Format a US phone number into canonical E.164 storage form.
example_queries.sql: SELECT conform.main.format_phone_e164('202-456-1111')

example_queries.description: Validate an IBAN (length plus mod-97 checksum).
example_queries.sql: SELECT conform.main.is_valid_iban('GB82 WEST 1234 5698 7654 32')

example_queries.description: Detect a payment card's brand from its prefix and length.
example_queries.sql: SELECT conform.main.card_brand('4111111111111111')

example_queries.description: Mask a card number, keeping only the last four digits.
example_queries.sql: SELECT conform.main.mask_card('4111-1111-1111-1111')

example_queries.description: Format-check a US postal (ZIP) code.
example_queries.sql: SELECT conform.main.is_valid_postal_code('90210', 'US')

example_queries.description: List every recognized payment-card brand.
example_queries.sql: SELECT * FROM conform.main.card_brands() ORDER BY brand

example_queries.description: Check whether 'visa' is among the recognized card brands.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) > 0 AS has_visa FROM conform.main.card_brands WHERE brand = 'visa'

example_queries.description: Count how many card brands the worker recognizes.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS brand_count FROM conform.main.card_brands

example_queries.description: List every supported postal-code country in order.
example_queries.sql: SELECT country FROM conform.main.supported_postal_countries ORDER BY country

example_queries.description: Confirm US postal codes are supported before validating.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) > 0 AS supported FROM conform.main.supported_postal_countries WHERE country = 'US'

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Field-level validation, normalization, and extraction for the conform catalog; everything lives in this single `main` schema.

Functions come in three shapes. Validity tests return `BOOLEAN` (true/false, NULL on NULL input). Normalizers and formatters return a canonical `VARCHAR` -- a form suitable for storage, joining, or deduplication -- or NULL when the input is invalid. Part extractors pull a single component (such as a domain, country code, or card brand) out of a well-formed value. Two discovery tables enumerate the phone regions and card brands the worker recognizes.

The fields covered are email, phone, IBAN, EU VAT, credit card, URL, and postal code. All validation is offline and deterministic (no DNS or network). Phone and VAT accept an optional ISO region/country; postal-code checks require a country. Use this schema to clean, validate, and standardize contact, banking, and payment data.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# conform · main schema

Field validation, normalization, and extraction for email, phone, IBAN, EU VAT, credit-card, URL, and postal-code values, plus three discovery tables.

## What's here

The functions come in three shapes:

- **Validity tests** return `BOOLEAN` -- `true`/`false`, and `NULL` on `NULL` input.
- **Normalizers & formatters** return a canonical `VARCHAR` for storage, joining, or deduplication, or `NULL` for invalid input.
- **Part extractors** pull one component (a domain, country code, brand, or host) out of a well-formed value.

Two discovery tables enumerate the phone regions and card brands the worker recognizes.

## Conventions

All validation is **offline and deterministic** -- no DNS or network. Phone and VAT functions accept an optional ISO region/country argument; postal-code checks require a country.

tags.vgi.doc_md:
# `is_valid_card`

Check a card number against the Luhn checksum.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT conform.is_valid_card('4111 1111 1111 1111');  -- true
```

## Notes

- Luhn only -- not an authorization or existence check.
- Independent of `card_brand`.

workers.doc_md:
# CVE Lookup & Offline CVSS Scoring for DuckDB

**Query CVE / vulnerability data and compute CVSS v3.1 severity scores directly in SQL.** The `cve` extension turns DuckDB into a defensive vulnerability-management workbench: resolve advisories, search vulnerability descriptions, map products to the vulnerabilities that affect them, and score CVSS vectors offline — all without leaving your query editor.

This worker is built for security engineers, vulnerability-management and patch teams, threat researchers, and data analysts who need to enrich, triage, and report on software vulnerabilities at SQL speed. The live lookups read from the National Vulnerability Database (NVD) 2.0 REST API, which republishes and enriches the public CVE records curated by the MITRE-led CVE Program. The scoring math is a faithful, dependency-free implementation of the CVSS v3.1 base-metric equation maintained by FIRST, so a vector string always maps to the same base score and qualitative severity band that the official calculator produces.

The extension is organized in two complementary halves. **Offline CVSS scoring** runs with no network access at all: it parses a CVSS:3.1 vector string into its numeric base score and buckets any numeric score into its qualitative band (NONE, LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, or CRITICAL), fully deterministic and safe for air-gapped or high-volume pipelines. **Live NVD 2.0 lookups** stream vulnerability records from the National Vulnerability Database and accept optional `base_url` and `api_key` arguments so you can target a mirror or raise NVD rate limits with a personal key.

Reach for this worker whenever you need to attach severity to raw CVSS vectors, look up the details of a known advisory, discover vulnerabilities by keyword or by affected product, or join vulnerability data against your own asset inventory. CVEs still under analysis surface a SQL `NULL` score rather than a misleading zero.

## Learn more

- CVSS specification and scoring (FIRST): [first.org/cvss](https://www.first.org/cvss/) — [CVSS v3.1 specification document](https://www.first.org/cvss/v3-1/specification-document) and the [official CVSS v3.1 calculator](https://www.first.org/cvss/calculator/3-1).
- CVE records and program (MITRE): [cve.org](https://www.cve.org) — source data in the [CVE List repository](https://github.com/CVEProject/cvelistV5).
- This worker's source: [github.com/Query-farm/vgi-cve](https://github.com/Query-farm/vgi-cve).

## `cvss_severity_bands`

A browsable reference table of the five **CVSS v3.1 qualitative severity bands** and the inclusive base-score range each covers — the discovery counterpart to the `cvss_severity` scalar. It is fully offline and deterministic.

| severity | min_score | max_score |
|---|---|---|
| NONE | 0.0 | 0.0 |
| LOW | 0.1 | 3.9 |
| MEDIUM | 4.0 | 6.9 |
| HIGH | 7.0 | 8.9 |
| CRITICAL | 9.0 | 10.0 |

Join it against a column of scores, or read it to learn the banding before calling `cvss_severity`.

workers.summary: Disassemble PE/ELF/Mach-O binaries and shellcode into instruction rows, with section/import/string/capability triage for malware analysis.
workers.doc_md:
# Disasm — Disassembly & Malware Triage in SQL

**Disassemble PE/ELF/Mach-O binaries and raw shellcode directly in DuckDB SQL** — one instruction row per machine instruction, with section, import, string, and heuristic MITRE ATT&CK capability relations alongside. The `disasm` worker is driven by [Capstone](https://www.capstone-engine.org/) with container parsing by goblin, and is built for **fleet-scale, in-SQL triage**: disassemble and capability-tag thousands of samples and join the instruction stats and ATT&CK tags to the rest of your security tables — with no per-sample tooling and zero egress.

It pairs with `vgi-pe` (static PE/ELF/Mach-O metadata), `vgi-yara` (rule hits), and `vgi-ioc` (indicators) in a VGI security bundle. The worker is **pure static compute over the input `BLOB` — it never executes the sample**, making it safe for air-gapped / regulated malware repositories.

**How it works.** You supply a sample as inline bytes or a filesystem path; the worker sniffs the container, resolves architecture and mode, statically decodes the executable sections, and tags heuristic behaviours against MITRE ATT&CK — all as ordinary SQL relations you can filter, aggregate, and join. Nothing is ever run or emulated. See the [source repository](https://github.com/Query-farm/vgi-disasm) for the full instruction/section/import/string/capability schema and licensing.

example_queries.description: Disassemble an x64 shellcode blob and project the instruction address, mnemonic, and operands.
example_queries.sql: SELECT address, mnemonic, op_str FROM disasm.main.disassemble(from_hex('554889e5c3'), arch := 'x86', mode := 'x64')

example_queries.description: Probe a blob by its magic bytes and read back just the detected container format.
example_queries.sql: SELECT (disasm.main.format(from_hex('7f454c46'))).container AS container

example_queries.description: Count the heuristic MITRE ATT&CK capability hits on a suspicious command line.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS n FROM disasm.main.capabilities('powershell -enc ZQA='::BLOB)

example_queries.description: List every architecture the disassemble() function accepts and the mode tokens valid for each.
example_queries.sql: SELECT arch, modes FROM disasm.main.supported_targets ORDER BY arch;

example_queries.description: Extract printable strings (length ≥ 6) from a blob, ordered by file offset.
example_queries.sql: SELECT "offset", encoding, value FROM disasm.main.strings('cmd.exe /c whoami'::BLOB, min_len := 6) ORDER BY "offset";

example_queries.description: Extract ASCII strings (min length 4) from an inline blob.
example_queries.sql: SELECT value FROM disasm.main.strings('hello world embedded text'::BLOB) WHERE encoding = 'ascii' ORDER BY "offset" LIMIT 1;

example_queries.description: Count the sections of a blob (a raw blob has none); pass a real binary as inline bytes or a path to enumerate them.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS n FROM disasm.main.sections('not a binary'::BLOB);

example_queries.description: A raw (non-container) blob has no sections.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS n FROM disasm.main.sections('not a binary');

example_queries.description: Count the imported symbols of a blob (a raw blob has none); pass a real binary as inline bytes or a path to list them.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS n FROM disasm.main.imports('not a binary'::BLOB);

example_queries.description: A raw (non-container) blob has no imports.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS n FROM disasm.main.imports('not a binary');

example_queries.description: Disassemble x64 shellcode at an explicit base (0x1000); list its return sites.
example_queries.sql: SELECT address, mnemonic, op_str FROM disasm.main.disassemble(from_hex('554889e5c3'), arch := 'x86', mode := 'x64', base := 4096) WHERE list_contains(groups, 'ret');

example_queries.description: Count decoded instructions in a raw x64 nop sled.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS n FROM disasm.main.disassemble(from_hex('90909090'), arch := 'x86', mode := 'x64');

example_queries.description: Surface ATT&CK-tagged capability indicators (rule, technique id, evidence) for a suspicious command line.
example_queries.sql: SELECT rule, attack_id, evidence FROM disasm.main.capabilities('powershell.exe -EncodedCommand ZQA='::BLOB);

example_queries.description: A PowerShell -EncodedCommand string flags T1059.001.
example_queries.sql: SELECT attack_id FROM disasm.main.capabilities('powershell.exe -EncodedCommand ZQA='::BLOB) WHERE attack_id = 'T1059.001' LIMIT 1;

example_queries.description: Resolve a blob's entry point; a raw blob yields NULL fields.
example_queries.sql: SELECT (disasm.main.entrypoint('not a binary'::BLOB)).arch AS arch;

## The `disasm` worker

A static binary-analysis toolkit exposed as SQL. It turns an opaque executable — a PE, ELF, or Mach-O file, or a raw shellcode blob, supplied inline as a `BLOB` or as a filesystem path — into queryable relations.

### Key concepts

- **Static only.** Every decode is a pure parse; the sample is *never* executed or emulated.
- **Bounded & panic-free.** Malformed or hostile input yields empty or diagnostic output, never a crash.
- **Triage-oriented.** Beyond raw machine instructions you get container layout, imported symbols, printable strings, and heuristic MITRE ATT&CK capability tags.

### When to use it

Reach for this schema to disassemble shellcode or binaries, inspect a container's structure and entry point, or run first-pass malware triage entirely inside DuckDB.

functions.name: disassemble
functions.comment: Disassemble a binary or shellcode blob into one row per machine instruction (address, size, bytes, mnemonic, op_str, groups)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Disassemble the executable sections of a PE/ELF/Mach-O binary — or a raw shellcode blob — into one row per machine instruction via Capstone. Arch/mode auto-detect from the container, or pass arch (x86, arm, arm64, mips, ppc, sysz, riscv) and mode (x16, x32, x64, arm, thumb, big, little) explicitly (required for raw blobs). base seeds the address column and makes branch targets print absolute; section selects auto (every executable section), all (the whole blob as raw bytes), or a section name. Each row carries address, size, bytes, mnemonic, op_str, and a normalized groups `LIST<VARCHAR>` (call/jump/ret/int/privileged/branch_relative/fpu/sse/vm). Output is address-ordered and bounded; undecodable bytes become '.byte' rows so the sweep never stalls. The input is statically decoded, never executed.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Disassemble a binary or shellcode into instruction rows (`address`, `size`, `bytes`, `mnemonic`, `op_str`, `groups`) via [Capstone](https://www.capstone-engine.org/). Arch/mode auto-detect from a PE/ELF/Mach-O container, or pass `arch` / `mode` explicitly (required for raw shellcode). v1 uses a **linear sweep** from the start of each selected section — simple and deterministic, but it can mis-decode data interleaved in code; undecodable bytes become `.byte` rows and the sweep resumes, so it never stalls. Supported arches: x86 (16/32/64), arm, arm64, mips, ppc, sysz, riscv.

workers.doc_md:
# docgen: DOCX Mail Merge and Document Generation in SQL

**Turn DuckDB query results into finished Word documents and PDFs — generate invoices, contracts, statements, and letters straight from SQL with mail-merge templates, no application code required.**

`docgen` is a VGI worker that does the inverse of text-extraction tools such as vgi-tika and vgi-pdf: rather than pulling text and structure *out* of documents, it pushes your SQL row data *into* DOCX (Microsoft Word) templates to produce filled, ready-to-send documents. Each rendered document is returned to DuckDB as a `BLOB`, so you can write it to a file, store it in a table, or stream it onward. It is built for anyone who needs to automate document production at query time — billing and finance teams generating invoices and account statements, operations teams producing contracts and form letters, and developers building reporting or notification pipelines directly on their data warehouse.

Rendering is powered by [docxtpl](https://github.com/elapouya/python-docx-template) ([documentation](https://docxtpl.readthedocs.io/)), which layers the [Jinja2](https://jinja.palletsprojects.com/) templating engine over [python-docx](https://github.com/python-openxml/python-docx) ([documentation](https://python-docx.readthedocs.io/)). You design a normal `.docx` template in Word using `{{ field }}` placeholders and `{% for %}` loops, and every field or column from your query becomes a template variable. Multi-document output is stitched together with [docxcompose](https://pypi.org/project/docxcompose/), and optional DOCX-to-PDF conversion is handled by a headless [LibreOffice](https://www.libreoffice.org/) when it is available on the host (PDF is always optional and never a hard dependency).

The catalog exposes two functions. The scalar `docgen_render(template, data[, pdf])` renders one document per row: pass a template — either a `VARCHAR` path (resolved directly, then under `$VGI_DOCGEN_TEMPLATES`) or inline `.docx` `BLOB` bytes — and a `STRUCT` of fields that become the Jinja2 variables, with an optional `pdf` flag. The table function `docgen_merge(relation, template := ..., [pdf := true])` consumes an entire relation and concatenates one render per input row into a single combined document, ideal for batch statement runs or multi-page contract packs.

The `sample_templates` discovery table lists every template the worker ships along with its absolute path and the placeholder fields it expects, so an agent can produce a real document without supplying a file of its own.

Untrusted bytes are magic-checked before rendering, and bad input degrades cleanly to NULL (scalar) or a visible error (merge).

example_queries.description: Render one document per row, filling the template with a STRUCT of fields.

example_queries.sql: SELECT docgen.main.docgen_render('not a docx'::BLOB, {customer: 'Ada'}) AS doc

example_queries.description: Request PDF output (pdf=true) via headless LibreOffice; NULL when LibreOffice is absent.
example_queries.sql: SELECT docgen.main.docgen_render('invoice.docx', {total: '99.50'}, true) AS doc

example_queries.description: Merge a whole relation into one document; an empty input relation yields zero rows.
example_queries.sql: SELECT doc FROM docgen.main.docgen_merge((SELECT 'Ada' AS customer WHERE false), template := 'invoice.docx')

example_queries.sql: SELECT name, path, fields FROM docgen.main.sample_templates ORDER BY name

example_queries.sql: SELECT octet_length(doc) > 0 AS ok FROM docgen.main.docgen_merge((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('Ada', '99.50'), ('Grace', '42.00')) AS t(customer, total)), template := '/home/ec2-user/vgi-fleet-20261106/repos/vgi-docgen/vgi_docgen/data/sample_invoice.docx')

example_queries.sql: SELECT octet_length(docgen.main.docgen_render('/home/ec2-user/vgi-fleet-20261106/repos/vgi-docgen/vgi_docgen/data/sample_invoice.docx', {customer: 'Ada', total: '99.50'})) > 0 AS ok

## DOCX mail merge in SQL

Turn query results into finished Word documents. This schema mail-merges row data into `.docx` templates and returns each rendered file as a `BLOB`, so documents are produced at query time with no application code.

### Key concepts

- **Templates** are ordinary Word files with `{{ field }}` placeholders and `{% for %}` loops, powered by Jinja2 over python-docx.
- **Data** comes straight from your columns: every field or column becomes a template variable at render time.
- **Output** is a document `BLOB` — DOCX by default, or PDF when a headless LibreOffice is available on the host.

### When to use it

functions.name: docgen_merge
functions.comment: Mail-merge: render a DOCX 'template' once per input row and concatenate into ONE merged document (page break between rows), returned as a single BLOB. With pdf:=true, convert via headless LibreOffice. Every relation column is a template variable.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Mail-merge a **whole input relation into a SINGLE merged DOCX (or PDF) document**, returned as a one-row, one-column `BLOB`.

## What it does

`docgen_merge` is the "many rows -> one document" path. It consumes an entire input relation (passed positionally as a `(SELECT ...)` subquery), renders the named `template` once per row, and concatenates the results into one `.docx`, with a page break between rows. Every column of the relation is exposed to the template as a Jinja2 variable (`{{ column }}`). Because it is a buffering (Sink+Source) function, it sinks every input batch first and renders+merges once at finalize.

## When to use it

Use it to assemble one combined document from many rows -- a single PDF of all monthly statements, one Word file containing every contract. When you instead want a *separate* document per row, use the `docgen_render` scalar.

## Inputs and output

- `data` -- the input relation, a positional `(SELECT ...)` subquery; every column becomes a template variable.
- `template` -- named `VARCHAR` arg: path to a `.docx` template, resolved under `$VGI_DOCGEN_TEMPLATES`.
- `pdf` -- named `BOOLEAN` arg; `true` converts the merged document to PDF via headless LibreOffice.
- Returns a single `doc` `BLOB` row.

## Edge cases

An **empty input relation yields zero output rows** (no document). A missing/typo'd template name or an unavailable LibreOffice surfaces as a clean DuckDB error (the merge path fails loudly rather than emitting a silently empty file); the worker stays alive and serving afterwards.

# Merge Rows into One Document

Mail-merge a whole relation into a **single merged DOCX/PDF** `BLOB` -- one template render per input row, concatenated with a page break.

## Usage

Pass the input relation as the positional `(...)` subquery argument and the template as the named `template := '...'` argument; add `pdf := true` to convert the merged result via headless LibreOffice. The single `doc` column carries the combined document. Ready-to-run queries are in this function's example queries.

## Notes

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Mail-merge **one DOCX (Microsoft Word) document per input row** from a template, returning each rendered file as a `BLOB`.

## What it does

The first argument is the template, accepted as **either** a `VARCHAR` path (resolved directly, then under `$VGI_DOCGEN_TEMPLATES`) **or** a `BLOB` of raw `.docx` bytes. The second argument is an arbitrary `STRUCT` of row data: every field becomes a Jinja2 variable in the template (`{{ field }}`), and nested lists/structs drive `{% for %}` loops and tables. An optional third boolean (`pdf`) converts the result to PDF via a headless LibreOffice when one is on PATH.

## When to use it

Use this scalar to produce a separate filled document for each row -- one invoice per customer, one letter per recipient, one statement per account. When you instead want a *single* document concatenating every row, use the `docgen_merge` table function.

## Inputs and output

- `template` -- `VARCHAR` path or `BLOB` `.docx` bytes.
- `data` -- `STRUCT`; fields become template variables.
- `pdf` (optional) -- `BOOLEAN`; `true` requests PDF output.
- Returns a `BLOB`: the rendered `.docx` (or PDF).

## Edge cases

Hostile or missing input degrades to `NULL`, never a crash: a `NULL` template or `NULL` data, a non-DOCX blob, a missing template file, a malformed template, a Jinja render error, and a requested-but-unavailable PDF conversion all yield `NULL`.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# Render Document from Template

Mail-merge **one DOCX document per row** from a template, returning each rendered file as a `BLOB`.

## Usage

Call `docgen_render(template, data)` in any projection: the first argument is a template file path or inline `.docx` bytes, and the second is a `STRUCT` of the row's fields (`{customer: name, total: amt}`). Pass a third `true` argument to request PDF output via headless LibreOffice. Ready-to-run queries are in this function's example queries.

## Notes

- The template is a `VARCHAR` path (resolved under `$VGI_DOCGEN_TEMPLATES`) or inline `.docx` `BLOB` bytes.
- Every field of the `STRUCT` data argument becomes a Jinja2 variable (`{{ field }}`); nested lists drive `{% for %}` loops.
- Missing/hostile input (NULL, non-DOCX blob, bad placeholder, missing template, unavailable LibreOffice) degrades to `NULL` rather than crashing.

vgi.example_queries.description: Request PDF output (pdf=true) via headless LibreOffice; NULL when LibreOffice is absent.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT docgen.main.docgen_render('invoice.docx', {total: '99.50'}, true) AS doc

vgi.example_queries.description: Render from inline template BLOB bytes; non-DOCX bytes yield a clean NULL.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT docgen.main.docgen_render('not a docx'::BLOB, {customer: 'Ada'}) AS doc

# Elasticsearch & OpenSearch for DuckDB

![Elasticsearch logo](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f4/Elasticsearch_logo.svg/250px-Elasticsearch_logo.svg.png)

Query [Elasticsearch](https://www.elastic.co) and [OpenSearch](https://opensearch.org) indices as live SQL tables over Apache Arrow — full-text search, the query DSL, and consistent deep pagination, straight from DuckDB SQL with no application code.

This VGI worker turns any Elasticsearch or OpenSearch cluster into queryable tables inside DuckDB. It is built for data engineers, analysts, and anyone who needs to read, filter, join, and export search-engine data without standing up a separate ETL pipeline or learning a client library. Point it at a cluster endpoint and an index (or an index pattern such as `logs-*`) and select the fields you want; the worker handles authentication, mapping introspection, pagination, and the translation of SQL filters into Elasticsearch query DSL for you. It works with both the commercial Elasticsearch distribution from Elastic and the Apache-2.0 licensed OpenSearch fork.

Under the hood the worker speaks the native Elasticsearch/OpenSearch REST API and JSON [query DSL](https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/query-dsl.html) directly over HTTP. Large result sets are streamed using a [Point-In-Time (PIT)](https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/point-in-time-api.html) snapshot combined with a `search_after` cursor, and that cursor is carried as externalized scan state — so a scan resumes cleanly across batch boundaries with no duplicated and no dropped documents, even across millions of hits. The `flavor` option selects the correct PIT dialect for OpenSearch versus Elasticsearch. See the [Elasticsearch documentation](https://www.elastic.co/docs) and the [OpenSearch documentation](https://opensearch.org/docs/latest/) for cluster-side details.

Reads support projection pushdown (only the requested fields are fetched via `_source` filtering), predicate pushdown (`term`, `terms`, `range`, and `exists` filters are compiled into the query DSL), a raw query-DSL escape hatch for anything more advanced, explicit `sort`, and basic-auth or API-key credentials. Every row carries the document `_id` and relevance `_score` alongside one typed column per source field. Typical use cases include exploring and aggregating log or product indices, joining search hits against local DuckDB tables or Parquet files, and exporting filtered subsets — for example projecting `name` and `price` from a `products` index, keeping only rows where `price` exceeds a threshold, and ordering by price. See the `es_search` function's examples for ready-to-run queries, and browse the `es_type_mapping` view to see how each Elasticsearch field type becomes a DuckDB column type.

# elasticsearch.main

Elasticsearch and OpenSearch search over Apache Arrow. This schema turns a live cluster index into a SQL table you can read, filter, join, and export directly from DuckDB.

## Capabilities

- **Consistent deep pagination** using a Point-In-Time snapshot plus a `search_after` cursor carried as externalized scan state, so a scan resumes cleanly across batch boundaries with no duplicated or dropped documents.
- **Projection and predicate pushdown**: only requested fields are fetched via `_source` filtering, and `term`/`terms`/`range`/`exists` filters compile into the query DSL, with a raw query-DSL escape hatch for anything more advanced.
- **Both dialects and authentication**: the OpenSearch and Elasticsearch PIT dialects, plus basic-auth and API-key credentials.

## When to use it

Reach for this schema to explore or aggregate log and product indices, join search hits against local DuckDB tables or Parquet files, or export filtered subsets — without writing application code.

The result always begins with two meta columns, then adds one column per indexed source field (from the explicit `fields` spec, or the introspected index mapping when `fields` is omitted). The per-field DuckDB type follows the `es_type_mapping` reference view.

## Always-present meta columns

| Name | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `_id` | VARCHAR | The Elasticsearch/OpenSearch document `_id`. Always present. |
| `_score` | DOUBLE | The relevance score for the hit; NULL when sorting suppresses scoring. Always present. |

## Source columns (example: `fields => 'name:keyword,price:double,created:date,meta:object'`)

| Name | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | VARCHAR | An ES `keyword`/`text` field. |
| `price` | DOUBLE | An ES `double`/`float` field. |
| `created` | TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE | An ES `date`/`date_nanos` field, parsed to a UTC microsecond timestamp. |
| `meta` | VARCHAR | An ES `object`/`nested`/`geo_*` field, surfaced as raw JSON text. |

workers.doc_md:
# Local Text Embeddings & Semantic Search in SQL

![fastembed logo](https://qdrant.tech/images/logo_with_text.png)

**Turn text into vector embeddings directly in DuckDB SQL** — generate fixed-length `FLOAT[]` embedding vectors and score them with cosine similarity for semantic search, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and nearest-neighbor ranking, all without leaving your query and without sending a single byte to an external API.

The **embed** extension brings sentence-transformer text embeddings to SQL for data engineers, RAG builders, and search teams who want vector search inside the database instead of a separate embedding service. Embeddings are computed **entirely in-process and offline** — there is no torch dependency, no GPU requirement, and no network call after the one-time model download — so the same query runs identically on a laptop, in CI, and in production.

Under the hood it is powered by [fastembed](https://github.com/qdrant/fastembed) from [Qdrant](https://qdrant.tech) (Apache-2.0), which runs quantized sentence-transformer models through [ONNX Runtime](https://onnxruntime.ai) ([source](https://github.com/microsoft/onnxruntime)). The default model is [`BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5`](https://huggingface.co/BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5) (384-dimensional, MIT licensed), downloaded on first use and cached locally; larger `bge` models and `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` are also supported. Vectors are returned over Apache Arrow as native DuckDB `FLOAT[]` lists, ready to index and rank with the [DuckDB VSS extension](https://duckdb.org/docs/extensions/vss.html).

## How it works

There are two embedding modes. *Symmetric* embedding maps any text to a vector for text-to-text comparison (dedup, clustering, classification). *Asymmetric* retrieval follows the query/passage convention these models are trained on: a short search query and a longer document are embedded with slightly different instruction prefixes so they land in the same space, which improves recall over plain symmetric embedding. Ranking is then just cosine similarity between vectors -- pure arithmetic, no model load. Model discovery and dimension lookups let you size a vector column or VSS index ahead of time.

```sql
-- A sentence is more similar to itself than to an unrelated one
SELECT embed.similarity(embed.embed('cat'), embed.embed('kitten')) AS score;
```

NULL or empty input text yields a NULL vector, and the model is loaded once and amortized across every row in a scan.

## embed.main schema

The single schema of the embed worker. It groups the local text-embedding and vector-similarity surface into a few concepts: symmetric text-to-text embedding, the asymmetric query/passage convention used for retrieval, a pure-arithmetic cosine-similarity score, and model-discovery/dimension helpers for sizing vector columns and indexes.

Everything runs in-process via fastembed/ONNX (no torch, no network after the one-time model download). Use it to build semantic search and RAG pipelines that store and rank vectors with DuckDB VSS, all in SQL.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# embed.main

Local text-embedding and cosine-similarity functions over Apache Arrow, for semantic search and RAG with DuckDB.

## Overview

This schema holds the worker's scalar embedding and similarity helpers plus a model-discovery table. Embeddings are generated locally with fastembed on ONNX Runtime; the default model is `BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5` (384-dim). Symmetric embedding is for text-to-text comparison; the query/passage pair is for asymmetric retrieval.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT embed.similarity(embed.embed('cat'), embed.embed('kitten')) AS score;
```

## Notes

- Use the query/passage pair for retrieval; use plain symmetric embedding for text-to-text comparison.
- NULL or empty text yields a NULL vector.

## supported_models()

List every embedding model the worker can use, one `(model, dim)` pair per row. Takes no arguments.

**When to use.** Use it to discover the valid values for the second argument of `embed(text, model)` (and for `embedding_dim(model)`) and to see each model's output dimension before you size a vector column or VSS index.

functions.name: similarity
functions.comment: Cosine similarity of two FLOAT[] vectors, in [-1, 1] (pure arithmetic, no model). NULL/empty/length-mismatch -> NULL.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## similarity(a, b)

Compute the **cosine similarity** of two `FLOAT[]` vectors, a value in `[-1, 1]` where 1 means identical direction. This is pure arithmetic -- it loads no model and does no I/O -- so it is cheap to call over large joins.

**When to use.** Use it to rank or threshold embedding pairs: `ORDER BY similarity(embed_query(q), embed_passage(doc)) DESC` for retrieval, or a `WHERE similarity(...) > 0.8` cutoff for dedup/near-duplicate detection.

**Input/output.** Inputs: two `FLOAT[]` vectors (typically from `embed*`). Output: one `DOUBLE` per row. NULL, empty, or length-mismatched vector pairs yield NULL rather than an error.

**Edge cases.** A zero vector has undefined direction and yields NULL; vectors must be the same length to be comparable.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# similarity(a, b)

Cosine similarity of two `FLOAT[]` vectors, in `[-1, 1]` (pure arithmetic, no model).

## Usage

Feed two `FLOAT[]` vectors (typically from the `embed*` functions) to `similarity(a, b)` to get a `DOUBLE` in `[-1, 1]`; order retrieval candidates by it descending, or threshold it (e.g. `> 0.8`) for near-duplicate detection. Runnable, catalog-qualified examples are attached as example queries.

## Notes

- 1.0 = identical direction, 0 = orthogonal, -1 = opposite.
- NULL / empty / length-mismatch returns NULL.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT embed.main.similarity(embed.main.embed('dog'), embed.main.embed('puppy')) > embed.main.similarity(embed.main.embed('dog'), embed.main.embed('airplane')) AS related_wins

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## embedding_dim(model)

Return the output dimension (the `FLOAT[]` length) a model produces, **without** loading the model or embedding anything. Pass `''` or NULL to get the default model's dimension.

**When to use.** Use it to size a vector column or index ahead of time (e.g. an `ARRAY[FLOAT, N]` / VSS HNSW index), or to validate that a chosen model matches an existing index width before re-embedding a corpus.

**Input/output.** Input: a `VARCHAR` model name (`''`/NULL = default). Output: `INTEGER` dimension, or NULL for an unknown model name (it does not raise).

**Edge cases.** Unknown model names return NULL rather than erroring, so a dirty model column won't abort a scan.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# embedding_dim(model)

Output dimension (vector length) for a model name -- `''`/NULL = the default model. No model is loaded.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT embed.embedding_dim('BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5');  -- 384
SELECT embed.embedding_dim('');                        -- default model dim
```

## Notes

- Unknown model name -> NULL (no error).
- Use to size a vector column / VSS index before embedding.

functions.comment: Embed a search query with the default model, applying the model's recommended query instruction prefix (for bge: 'Represent this sentence for searching relevant passages: '). NULL/empty -> NULL.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## embed_query(text)

Embed a *search query* for retrieval, applying the default model's recommended query instruction prefix (for bge: `Represent this sentence for searching relevant passages: `). This is the query side of asymmetric retrieval.

**When to use.** Use `embed_query` for the short user query and `embed_passage` for the corpus documents, then rank passages by `similarity(embed_query(q), embed_passage(doc))`. The prefix nudges the query vector toward the passages that answer it, improving recall over a plain symmetric `embed`.

**Input/output.** Input: one `VARCHAR` query per row. Output: one `FLOAT[]` per row (NULL/empty -> NULL), same dimension as `embed`.

**Edge cases.** Pair only with `embed_passage` (not `embed`) so query and passage live in the same trained retrieval space.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# embed_query(text)

Embed a search query for retrieval, applying the model's query instruction prefix (the query side of asymmetric retrieval).

## Usage

Embed the short user query with `embed_query(text)` and the corpus documents with `embed_passage(text)`, then rank documents by `similarity(embed_passage(body), embed_query(q))` descending. Runnable, catalog-qualified retrieval examples are attached as example queries.

## Notes

- Pair with `embed_passage` for the documents, not plain `embed`.
- NULL or empty input returns NULL.

functions.name: embed_passage
functions.comment: Embed a document/passage with the default model. For bge retrieval models passages get NO instruction prefix (queries do); this mirrors that. NULL/empty -> NULL.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## embed_passage(text)

Embed a *document/passage* for retrieval. For bge-style retrieval models, passages get **no** instruction prefix (only queries do), and this function mirrors that convention exactly.

**When to use.** Use `embed_passage` for the corpus side of asymmetric retrieval and `embed_query` for the user query, then rank with `similarity(embed_query(q), embed_passage(doc))`. Pre-compute passage vectors once and store them (e.g. in a DuckDB VSS HNSW index).

**Input/output.** Input: one `VARCHAR` passage per row. Output: one `FLOAT[]` per row (NULL/empty -> NULL), same dimension as `embed`.

**Edge cases.** Numerically this equals plain `embed` for bge (passages have no prefix); it exists as a named counterpart to `embed_query` so retrieval pipelines read symmetrically.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# embed_passage(text)

Embed a document/passage for retrieval (the corpus side of asymmetric retrieval -- no query prefix).

## Usage

Materialize passage vectors once with `embed_passage(body)` into a stored column (e.g. a DuckDB VSS HNSW index over the resulting `FLOAT[]`), then at query time score them against `embed_query(q)`. Runnable, catalog-qualified examples are attached as example queries.

## Notes

- Pair with `embed_query` for the query side.
- For bge, passages get no instruction prefix (by design).
- NULL or empty input returns NULL.
