functions.name: copy_to_fixed
functions.comment: Write the COPY source out to a fixed-width / flat-file / COBOL-copybook file (the COPY-TO counterpart of write_fixed)

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Write a query or table out to a fixed-width / flat-file / COBOL-copybook file — the COPY-TO counterpart of write_fixed. It is invoked as a COPY statement (not called directly):

```sql
COPY (<query>|<table>) TO '<path>' (FORMAT 'fixed.fixed_out', spec '<layout>');
```

The writer uses a DISTINCT format name 'fixed.fixed_out' (catalog-qualified by the ATTACH name) because the VGI SDK advertises FROM and TO as separate formats. Each input column is matched to a layout field BY NAME, encoded to record bytes per the `spec` option (a Perl/Python `unpack` template, a JSON field list, or a COBOL copybook; auto-detected unless `format` is given), framed per `framing`, and written to `<path>` (overwritten if it exists). Options are named: `spec` (required), `format`, `encoding` ('ascii'/'ebcdic'), `framing` ('newline'/'fixed'/'rdw'/'rdw_blocked'), plus `endpoint`/`region`/`url_style`/`use_ssl` for `s3://` destinations. NOTE: CREATE SECRET credentials are NOT forwarded on the COPY-TO path — use named S3 overrides, ambient credentials, or write_fixed for secret-backed cloud writes.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
Write a relation to a fixed-width file:

```sql
COPY (<query>|<table>) TO '<path>' (FORMAT 'fixed.fixed_out', spec '<layout>');
```

Input columns map to layout fields by name. Named options: `spec` (required), `format`, `encoding`, `framing`, and S3 overrides. The COPY-TO counterpart of `write_fixed`.
tags.vgi.result_dynamic_columns_md:
`copy_to_fixed` is invoked through `COPY (<query>|<table>) TO '<path>' (FORMAT 'fixed.fixed_out', …)`, not as a table function, so it returns **no result set of its own**. The COPY source rows are encoded to fixed-width records and written to `<path>` (overwritten if it exists); each input column is matched to a layout field **by name** before encoding. DuckDB reports only a single value — the number of rows written:

| Name | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `Count` | BIGINT | The number of source rows written to the file, reported by DuckDB as the `COPY … TO` statement's result. |
tags.vgi.title: Write Fixed-Width File (COPY TO)

functions.name: write_multi
functions.comment: Write a relation's UNION column to a multi-record-type file (inverse of read_multi)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Write a relation whose single UNION column holds heterogeneous records back out to a multi-record-type fixed-width / flat file — the inverse of read_multi. The `data` relation (passed as a subquery, e.g. `(FROM read_multi(...))` or a `(SELECT ...)`) must have exactly ONE column: a sparse UNION whose variant names are the discriminator tags of the `spec` (the exact shape read_multi emits). For each row the active variant gives its record type and its `STRUCT` field values; the matching variant layout encodes those fields, the discriminator field is stamped with the tag, the records are framed per the named `framing =>` argument ('newline' the default, 'fixed', 'rdw', or 'rdw_blocked'), encoded under named `encoding =>` ('ascii' the default, or 'ebcdic'/CP037), optionally compressed via `compression =>`, and streamed to `path` (overwritten if it exists). The `spec` is the SAME multi-record JSON as read_multi: a `discriminator` ({offset,width}) plus a `records` map of tag → JSON field list. `encoding`, `framing`, and `compression` are NAMED arguments. Use it to emit header/detail/trailer or other heterogeneous mainframe flat files from SQL. Returns exactly one summary row: `rows_written BIGINT` and `bytes_written BIGINT`.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Write a relation's single UNION column out to a heterogeneous multi-record-type fixed-width file — the inverse of read_multi. The relation is a subquery with one UNION column whose variant names are the spec's discriminator tags. The `spec` is the same multi-record JSON (`discriminator` + `records`). Each row's active variant is encoded with its layout and the discriminator stamped with the tag. Optional NAMED args: `encoding =>` ('ascii'/'ebcdic'), `framing =>` ('newline'/'fixed'/'rdw'/'rdw_blocked'), `compression =>`. Returns one row `(rows_written BIGINT, bytes_written BIGINT)`.

vgi.example_queries.description: Round-trip a heterogeneous flat file: read it into a UNION column and write it back out to a new multi-record file, reporting the counts.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT rows_written, bytes_written FROM fixed.main.write_multi((FROM fixed.main.read_multi('data/multi.dat', '{"discriminator":{"offset":0,"width":1},"records":{"H":[{"type":"filler","width":1},{"name":"co","type":"str","width":20}],"D":[{"type":"filler","width":1},{"name":"sku","type":"str","width":10},{"name":"qty","type":"int","digits":5}],"T":[{"type":"filler","width":1},{"name":"cnt","type":"int","digits":6}]}}')), 'data/_example_multi_out.dat', '{"discriminator":{"offset":0,"width":1},"records":{"H":[{"type":"filler","width":1},{"name":"co","type":"str","width":20}],"D":[{"type":"filler","width":1},{"name":"sku","type":"str","width":10},{"name":"qty","type":"int","digits":5}],"T":[{"type":"filler","width":1},{"name":"cnt","type":"int","digits":6}]}}')

vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Number of records written to the file across all record types.

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: bytes_written
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Total number of bytes written to the file, including record framing and any compression.

arguments.name: data
arguments.description: The input relation to write out, supplied as a subquery (e.g. `(FROM read_multi(...))`). It must have exactly ONE column: a UNION whose variant names are the discriminator tags of `spec`.

arguments.name: path
arguments.description: Path of the multi-record file to create; it is overwritten if it already exists. May also be an 's3://bucket/key' URL (AWS S3, or R2/MinIO/GCS-HMAC via a `CREATE SECRET (TYPE s3, …, ENDPOINT …)`) — credentials come from the matching DuckDB secret, scoped to the URL. Writing to 'http(s)://' is not supported.

arguments.name: spec
arguments.description: The multi-record JSON layout (the same spec read_multi uses): a `discriminator` ({offset, width}) plus a `records` map of record-type tag → JSON field list. The UNION column's variant names must match these tags.

arguments.name: encoding
arguments.description: Byte encoding to write: 'ascii' (the default) or 'ebcdic' (CP037). The discriminator tag is transcoded to this encoding.

arguments.name: framing
arguments.description: How to delimit records in the output: 'newline' (the default), 'fixed', 'rdw', or 'rdw_blocked'.

arguments.name: compression
arguments.description: Compress the output: 'auto' (the default — gzip if the path ends '.gz', zstd if '.zst', else raw), 'none', 'gzip', or 'zstd'. The whole file is compressed.

arguments.name: endpoint
arguments.description: Custom S3 endpoint for an `s3://` path (e.g. MinIO/R2 'host:9000'); a scheme is inferred from `use_ssl` when omitted. Overrides any endpoint from a CREATE SECRET.

arguments.name: region
arguments.description: AWS region for an `s3://` path. Overrides the region from a CREATE SECRET.

arguments.name: url_style
arguments.description: S3 addressing for an `s3://` path: 'path' (path-style, e.g. MinIO) or 'vhost' (the default). Overrides a CREATE SECRET's URL_STYLE.

arguments.name: use_ssl
arguments.description: Whether to use TLS for an `s3://` path's custom endpoint (default true). Set false for a plain-HTTP endpoint such as a local MinIO.

tags.vgi.title: Write Fixed-Width File

arguments.name: data
arguments.description: The input relation to write out, supplied as a subquery (e.g. `(FROM tbl)`). Each row's columns are matched by name to the layout fields.

arguments.name: path
arguments.description: Path of the fixed-width file to create; it is overwritten if it already exists. May also be an 's3://bucket/key' URL (AWS S3, or R2/MinIO/GCS-HMAC via a `CREATE SECRET (TYPE s3, …, ENDPOINT …)`) — credentials come from the matching DuckDB secret, scoped to the URL. Writing to 'http(s)://' is not supported.

arguments.name: spec
arguments.description: The record layout to encode each row with: a Perl/Python `unpack` template, a JSON field list, or a COBOL copybook. Format is auto-detected unless `format` is given.

arguments.name: format
arguments.description: Force how `spec` is interpreted: 'template', 'json', or 'copybook'. Omit to auto-detect.

arguments.name: encoding
arguments.description: Byte encoding to write: 'ascii' (the default) or 'ebcdic' (CP037).

arguments.name: framing
arguments.description: How to delimit records in the output: 'newline' (the default), 'fixed', 'rdw', or 'rdw_blocked'.

arguments.name: compression
arguments.description: Compress the output: 'auto' (the default — gzip if the path ends '.gz', zstd if '.zst', else raw), 'none', 'gzip', or 'zstd'. The whole file is compressed.

arguments.name: endpoint
arguments.description: Custom S3 endpoint for an `s3://` path (e.g. MinIO/R2 'host:9000'); a scheme is inferred from `use_ssl` when omitted. Overrides any endpoint from a CREATE SECRET.

arguments.name: region
arguments.description: AWS region for an `s3://` path. Overrides the region from a CREATE SECRET.

arguments.name: url_style
arguments.description: S3 addressing for an `s3://` path: 'path' (path-style, e.g. MinIO) or 'vhost' (the default). Overrides a CREATE SECRET's URL_STYLE.

arguments.name: use_ssl
arguments.description: Whether to use TLS for an `s3://` path's custom endpoint (default true). Set false for a plain-HTTP endpoint such as a local MinIO.

examples: SELECT rows_written, bytes_written FROM fixed.main.write_fixed((FROM (VALUES ('ALICE', 5), ('BOB', 999)) AS v(name, qty)), 'data/_example_write.dat', 'name:A10 qty:9(5)')
SELECT rows_written FROM fixed.main.write_fixed((FROM (VALUES ('ALICE', 5), ('BOB', 999)) AS v(name, qty)), 'data/_example_write.dat', 'name:A10 qty:9(5)', framing => 'fixed')

functions.name: read_multi
functions.comment: Read a heterogeneous (multi-record-type) flat file into a UNION column

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Scan a heterogeneous fixed-width / flat file whose records have DIFFERENT layouts — e.g. a header, many detail rows, and a trailer — selected by a 'record type' discriminator field. The `spec` is a JSON object: a `discriminator` ({offset, width} of the bytes that identify each record's type) and a `records` map of tag → field list (each field list uses the same JSON field syntax as `read_fixed`'s JSON spec, so every field type / group / OCCURS works per record type). Each record is framed per `framing =>` ('newline' the default, 'fixed', 'rdw', or 'rdw_blocked'), its discriminator bytes pick the matching variant, and it is decoded with that variant's layout. The result is a single column `record` of type UNION — one `STRUCT` variant per record type, the variant names being the discriminator tags. Use `union_tag(record)` to get a row's record type and `union_extract(record, 'D')` to pull out a given variant's `STRUCT`. An unmatched discriminator value is an error unless the spec gives a `default` tag. `path` may glob and may be a cloud URL. `framing`, `encoding`, `compression`, and `record_length` are NAMED arguments.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Scan a heterogeneous flat file whose records have different layouts selected by a discriminator field. The JSON `spec` declares a `discriminator` ({offset,width}) and a `records` map of tag → JSON field list; the result is one UNION column `record` with a `STRUCT` variant per record type. Use `union_tag(record)` / `union_extract(record, 'TAG')`. Named args: `framing =>`, `encoding =>`, `compression =>`, `record_length =>`.

vgi.example_queries.description: Read a header/detail/trailer flat file into a UNION column and project the detail rows' sku and qty.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT union_extract(record, 'D').sku AS sku, union_extract(record, 'D').qty AS qty FROM fixed.main.read_multi('data/multi.dat', '{"discriminator":{"offset":0,"width":1},"records":{"H":[{"type":"filler","width":1},{"name":"co","type":"str","width":20}],"D":[{"type":"filler","width":1},{"name":"sku","type":"str","width":10},{"name":"qty","type":"int","digits":5}],"T":[{"type":"filler","width":1},{"name":"cnt","type":"int","digits":6}]}}') WHERE union_tag(record) = 'D' ORDER BY sku

vgi.example_queries.description: Count records of each type in a heterogeneous multi-record file.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT union_tag(record) AS record_type, count(*) AS n FROM fixed.main.read_multi('data/multi.dat', '{"discriminator":{"offset":0,"width":1},"records":{"H":[{"type":"filler","width":1},{"name":"co","type":"str","width":20}],"D":[{"type":"filler","width":1},{"name":"sku","type":"str","width":10},{"name":"qty","type":"int","digits":5}],"T":[{"type":"filler","width":1},{"name":"cnt","type":"int","digits":6}]}}') GROUP BY record_type ORDER BY record_type

tags.vgi.result_dynamic_columns_md:
The result is always a **single** column, `record`, whose UNION variants are determined by the multi-record `spec` argument — one `STRUCT` variant per record type, named by that record type's discriminator tag. Read a row's record type with `union_tag(record)` and pull a variant's `STRUCT` with `union_extract(record, '<tag>')`.

For example, the header/detail/trailer spec used in the examples below (record types `H`, `D`, `T`) yields:

| Name | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `record` | UNION(H STRUCT(co VARCHAR), D STRUCT(sku VARCHAR, qty BIGINT), T STRUCT(cnt BIGINT)) | A sparse UNION with one `STRUCT` variant per record type in the spec — here `H` (header), `D` (detail), and `T` (trailer). |
tags.vgi.title: Read Multi-Record-Type File

arguments.name: path
arguments.description: Path(s) to the file(s) to read: a single path or a list of paths. May glob (e.g. 'data/*.dat') or be a cloud URL ('s3://bucket/key' or 'https://host/file'). Credentials come from the matching DuckDB secret, scoped per path.

arguments.name: spec
arguments.description: The multi-record JSON layout: a `discriminator` ({offset, width}) plus a `records` map of record-type tag → JSON field list (the same field syntax as read_fixed's JSON spec). An optional `default` tag handles unmatched values. Determines the UNION variants of the output `record` column.

arguments.name: encoding
arguments.description: Byte encoding of the file: 'ascii' (the default) or 'ebcdic' (CP037). The discriminator bytes are transcoded out of EBCDIC before matching.

arguments.name: framing
arguments.description: How records are delimited: 'newline' (the default), 'fixed' (back-to-back equal-length records — every record type padded to a common length), 'rdw', or 'rdw_blocked'.

arguments.name: record_length
arguments.description: Per-record length in BYTES for 'fixed' framing; ignored otherwise. Defaults to the longest record type's layout length.

arguments.name: compression
arguments.description: Input compression: 'auto' (default — detect gzip/zstd from magic bytes), 'none', 'gzip', or 'zstd'. Decompression happens before framing/decoding.

arguments.name: max_decompressed_bytes
arguments.description: Safety cap on total DECOMPRESSED bytes per file (default 16 GiB). Only applies to gzip/zstd input.

arguments.name: endpoint
arguments.description: Custom S3 endpoint for an `s3://` path (e.g. MinIO/R2 'host:9000'); a scheme is inferred from `use_ssl` when omitted. Overrides any endpoint from a CREATE SECRET.

arguments.name: region
arguments.description: AWS region for an `s3://` path. Overrides the region from a CREATE SECRET.

arguments.name: url_style
arguments.description: S3 addressing for an `s3://` path: 'path' (path-style, e.g. MinIO) or 'vhost' (the default). Overrides a CREATE SECRET's URL_STYLE.

arguments.name: use_ssl
arguments.description: Whether to use TLS for an `s3://` path's custom endpoint (default true). Set false for a plain-HTTP endpoint such as a local MinIO.

examples: SELECT union_extract(record, 'D').sku AS sku, union_extract(record, 'D').qty AS qty FROM fixed.main.read_multi('data/multi.dat', '{"discriminator":{"offset":0,"width":1},"records":{"H":[{"type":"filler","width":1},{"name":"co","type":"str","width":20}],"D":[{"type":"filler","width":1},{"name":"sku","type":"str","width":10},{"name":"qty","type":"int","digits":5}],"T":[{"type":"filler","width":1},{"name":"cnt","type":"int","digits":6}]}}') WHERE union_tag(record) = 'D' ORDER BY sku

SELECT union_tag(record) AS record_type, count(*) AS n FROM fixed.main.read_multi('data/multi.dat', '{"discriminator":{"offset":0,"width":1},"records":{"H":[{"type":"filler","width":1},{"name":"co","type":"str","width":20}],"D":[{"type":"filler","width":1},{"name":"sku","type":"str","width":10},{"name":"qty","type":"int","digits":5}],"T":[{"type":"filler","width":1},{"name":"cnt","type":"int","digits":6}]}}') GROUP BY record_type ORDER BY record_type

functions.name: read_fixed
functions.comment: Read a fixed-width file (template / JSON / copybook spec) into rows

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Scan a fixed-width / flat-file data file into typed rows. `path` may be a glob (e.g. '/data/*.dat'); matching files are read in sorted order and their rows concatenated. Each record is framed per the named `framing =>` argument ('newline' the default, 'fixed', 'rdw', or 'rdw_blocked') and decoded into a row of typed columns according to the layout `spec` — a Perl/Python `unpack` template, a JSON field list, or a COBOL copybook (format auto-detected unless you pass `format =>` 'template' / 'json' / 'copybook'). In a template spec, prefix each field with a name to set its column name, e.g. `'name:A10 qty:9(5)'`; unnamed fields become positional `field_1`, `field_2`, …. The named `encoding =>` argument is 'ascii' (default) or 'ebcdic' (CP037). The named `record_length =>` argument is the per-record length in BYTES; it is only used for 'fixed' framing (back-to-back records of equal length) and defaults to the length implied by the `spec`; it is ignored for the other framings. `format`, `encoding`, `framing`, and `record_length` are all NAMED arguments. The returned column set is dynamic: it is determined by the spec, with OCCURS becoming `LIST` columns and groups / REDEFINES becoming `STRUCT` columns. Use it to ingest mainframe or legacy flat-file data into SQL. This is the file-scanning counterpart of unpack_fixed and the inverse of write_fixed.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Scan a fixed-width file into rows, decoding each record per the layout `spec` (template, JSON, or COBOL copybook). `path` may glob (e.g. `read_fixed('/data/*.dat', 'A10 N')`), reading matching files in sorted order. Optional NAMED args: `format =>`, `encoding =>` ('ascii'/'ebcdic'), `framing =>` ('newline'/'fixed'/'rdw'/'rdw_blocked'), and `record_length =>` (per-record length in bytes, used only for `fixed` framing). The returned columns are dynamic — they depend on the spec, with OCCURS → `LIST` and group/REDEFINES → `STRUCT`.

vgi.example_queries.description: Profile a newline-delimited fixed-width feed of 7-digit ids: count the rows and report the id range.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS records, min(id) AS min_id, max(id) AS max_id FROM fixed.main.read_fixed('data/large.dat', 'id:9(7)')

vgi.example_queries.description: Glob several account files (10-char name, 5-digit qty) and total the quantity across every record.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT sum(qty) AS total_qty FROM fixed.main.read_fixed('data/acct*.dat', 'name:A10 qty:9(5)')

tags.vgi.result_dynamic_columns_md:
The returned columns are **dynamic** — determined by the layout `spec`, one column per top-level field. Column names come from the field names in the spec — name your fields (e.g. `name:A10 qty:9(5)`); **unnamed** template fields become positional `field_1`, `field_2`, …. Column types follow the field kind: text/hex → `VARCHAR`, integer → `BIGINT`, float/double → `REAL`/`DOUBLE`, COMP-3 / zoned / implied-point decimal → `DECIMAL(p,s)`, `?` boolean → `BOOLEAN`, OCCURS / repeat → `LIST` of the element type, and group / REDEFINES → `STRUCT` of the child fields.

For the spec `name:A10 qty:9(5)` the result columns are:

| Name | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | `VARCHAR` | The 10-byte text field decoded from bytes 0–9. |
| `qty` | `BIGINT` | The 5-digit zoned integer decoded from bytes 10–14. |

For the single-field spec `id:9(7)` the result is one column:

| Name | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `id` | `BIGINT` | The 7-digit zoned integer decoded from bytes 0–6. |
tags.vgi.title: Read Fixed-Width File

arguments.name: path
arguments.description: Path(s) to the fixed-width file(s) to read: a single path, or a list of paths to read several files in one call (their rows are concatenated in order). A path may be a glob (e.g. 'data/*.dat') to scan matching files in sorted order, or a cloud URL: 's3://bucket/key' (AWS S3, or R2/MinIO/GCS-HMAC via a `CREATE SECRET (TYPE s3, …, ENDPOINT …)`) or 'https://host/file'. Credentials come from the matching DuckDB secret, resolved per path scope — so a list spanning several buckets picks the right secret for each.

arguments.name: spec
arguments.description: The record layout to decode each row with: a Perl/Python `unpack` template, a JSON field list, or a COBOL copybook. Determines the output column names and types; format is auto-detected unless `format` is given.

arguments.name: format
arguments.description: Force how `spec` is interpreted: 'template', 'json', or 'copybook'. Omit to auto-detect.

arguments.name: encoding
arguments.description: Byte encoding of the file: 'ascii' (the default) or 'ebcdic' (CP037).

arguments.name: framing
arguments.description: How records are delimited in the file: 'newline' (the default), 'fixed' (back-to-back records of equal length), 'rdw', or 'rdw_blocked'.

arguments.name: record_length
arguments.description: The length of each record in BYTES. Used only for 'fixed' framing (back-to-back equal-length records); ignored for the other framings. Defaults to the length implied by the layout `spec`.

arguments.name: compression
arguments.description: Input compression: 'auto' (the default — detect gzip/zstd from the file's magic bytes, else read raw), 'none', 'gzip', or 'zstd'. Applies to local and cloud paths alike; decompression happens before framing/decoding.

arguments.name: max_decompressed_bytes
arguments.description: Safety cap on total DECOMPRESSED bytes per file (a decompression-bomb backstop; default 16 GiB). Only applies to gzip/zstd input — uncompressed files are unbounded. Raise it to read a legitimately huge compressed file.

arguments.name: endpoint
arguments.description: Custom S3 endpoint for an `s3://` path (e.g. MinIO/R2 'host:9000'); a scheme is inferred from `use_ssl` when omitted. Overrides any endpoint from a CREATE SECRET.

arguments.name: region
arguments.description: AWS region for an `s3://` path. Overrides the region from a CREATE SECRET.

arguments.name: url_style
arguments.description: S3 addressing for an `s3://` path: 'path' (path-style, e.g. MinIO) or 'vhost' (the default). Overrides a CREATE SECRET's URL_STYLE.

arguments.name: use_ssl
arguments.description: Whether to use TLS for an `s3://` path's custom endpoint (default true). Set false for a plain-HTTP endpoint such as a local MinIO.

examples: SELECT count(*) AS records, min(id) AS min_id, max(id) AS max_id FROM fixed.main.read_fixed('data/large.dat', 'id:9(7)')
SELECT sum(qty) AS total_qty FROM fixed.main.read_fixed('data/acct*.dat', 'name:A10 qty:9(5)')

functions.name: describe_multi
functions.comment: Describe a multi-record spec (each record type's fields) without reading data

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Introspect a multi-record `spec` without reading any data: returns one row per (record type, field), describing how every variant's layout resolves. The leading `record_type` column is the discriminator tag; the remaining columns mirror describe_fixed — `path` (dotted field path), `depth`, `kind` (codec label), `sql_type` (the DuckDB type the field maps to), `byte_offset` and `width`, `occurs` (OCCURS maximum, else NULL), and `depending_on` (the OCCURS … DEPENDING ON controller, else NULL). The `spec` is the same multi-record JSON object as read_multi (a `discriminator` plus a `records` map of tag → field list). Use it to debug a multi-record layout or document each record type before running read_multi / unpack_multi.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Describe how a multi-record `spec` resolves — one row per (record type, field) with its dotted path, codec kind, DuckDB type, byte offset, width, and OCCURS info. Reads no data. The multi-record counterpart of describe_fixed.

vgi.example_queries.description: Resolve a header/detail multi-record spec and show each record type's fields with their DuckDB types and byte offsets.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT record_type, path, sql_type, byte_offset FROM fixed.main.describe_multi('{"discriminator":{"offset":0,"width":1},"records":{"H":[{"name":"co","type":"str","width":20}],"D":[{"name":"sku","type":"str","width":10},{"name":"qty","type":"int","digits":5}]}}') ORDER BY record_type, byte_offset

vgi.example_queries.description: Count how many fields each record type declares in a multi-record layout.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT record_type, count(*) AS field_count FROM fixed.main.describe_multi('{"discriminator":{"offset":0,"width":1},"records":{"H":[{"name":"co","type":"str","width":20}],"D":[{"name":"sku","type":"str","width":10},{"name":"qty","type":"int","digits":5}]}}') GROUP BY record_type ORDER BY record_type

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: record_type
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: The discriminator tag of the record type this field belongs to.

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: path
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Dotted field path within that record type, e.g. `item.sku`.

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: depth
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Nesting level of the field (0 at the top level).

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: kind
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Codec label describing how the bytes are decoded, e.g. `text`, `int32 LE`, `comp-3`.

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: sql_type
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: The DuckDB column type this field maps to, e.g. `VARCHAR`, `DECIMAL(9,2)`, `STRUCT`.

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: byte_offset
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Static byte position of the field within its record type.

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: width
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Per-occurrence field width in bytes.

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: occurs
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: OCCURS maximum for a repeating field, else NULL.

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: depending_on
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: The controlling field name for an `OCCURS … DEPENDING ON` table, else NULL.

arguments.name: spec
arguments.description: The multi-record JSON layout to describe: a `discriminator` ({offset, width}) plus a `records` map of record-type tag → JSON field list (same as read_multi).

examples: SELECT record_type, path, sql_type, byte_offset FROM fixed.main.describe_multi('{"discriminator":{"offset":0,"width":1},"records":{"H":[{"name":"co","type":"str","width":20}],"D":[{"name":"sku","type":"str","width":10},{"name":"qty","type":"int","digits":5}]}}') ORDER BY record_type, byte_offset

functions.name: describe_fixed
functions.comment: Describe a fixed-width layout spec (fields, types, offsets) without reading data

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Introspect a fixed-width layout `spec` without reading any data: returns one row per field (group items and their children included) describing how the spec resolves. Columns: `path` (dotted field path, e.g. `item.sku`), `depth` (nesting level), `kind` (codec label, e.g. `text`, `int32 LE`, `comp-3`), `sql_type` (the DuckDB column type the field maps to, e.g. `VARCHAR`, `DECIMAL(9,2)`, `STRUCT`, `BIGINT[]`), `byte_offset` and `width` (static byte position and per-occurrence width), `occurs` (declared repeat / OCCURS maximum, else NULL), and `depending_on` (the controlling field for `OCCURS … DEPENDING ON`, else NULL). `spec` is a Perl/Python `unpack` template, a JSON field list, or a COBOL copybook (auto-detected unless you pass `format =>` 'template'/'json'/'copybook'). Use it to debug a spec, document a layout, or check field offsets before running `read_fixed`. For a variable-length layout (OCCURS DEPENDING ON) the reported offsets are the static positions before the table.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Describe how a fixed-width layout `spec` resolves — one row per field with its dotted path, codec kind, DuckDB type, byte offset, width, OCCURS count, and DEPENDING ON controller. Reads no data. `format =>` forces template/json/copybook.

vgi.example_queries.description: Introspect a two-field template layout: show each field's DuckDB type, byte offset, and width.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT path, sql_type, byte_offset, width FROM fixed.main.describe_fixed('name:A10 qty:9(5)') ORDER BY byte_offset

vgi.example_queries.description: Resolve a COBOL copybook (forcing the copybook format) and list only the repeating OCCURS fields.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT path, sql_type, occurs FROM fixed.main.describe_fixed('01 REC. 05 SKU PIC X(8). 05 QTY PIC 9(3) OCCURS 4.', format => 'copybook') WHERE occurs IS NOT NULL

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: path
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Dotted field path within the record, e.g. `item.sku`; group items and their children are each a row.

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: depth
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Nesting level of the field (0 at the top level, deeper for group children).

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: kind
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Codec label describing how the bytes are decoded, e.g. `text`, `int32 LE`, `comp-3`, `zoned`.

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: sql_type
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: The DuckDB column type this field maps to, e.g. `VARCHAR`, `DECIMAL(9,2)`, `STRUCT`, `BIGINT[]`.

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: byte_offset
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Static byte position of the field within the record (before any OCCURS DEPENDING ON table).

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: width
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Per-occurrence field width in bytes.

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: occurs
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Declared repeat / OCCURS maximum for a repeating field, else NULL.

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: depending_on
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: The controlling field name for an `OCCURS … DEPENDING ON` table, else NULL.

arguments.name: spec

arguments.name: format
arguments.description: Force how `spec` is interpreted: 'template', 'json', or 'copybook'. Omit to auto-detect.

SELECT path, sql_type, occurs FROM fixed.main.describe_fixed('01 REC. 05 SKU PIC X(8). 05 QTY PIC 9(3) OCCURS 4.', format => 'copybook') WHERE occurs IS NOT NULL

functions.name: copy_fixed
functions.comment: Read a fixed-width / flat-file / COBOL-copybook file into the COPY target table (the COPY-FROM counterpart of read_fixed)

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Load a fixed-width / flat-file / COBOL-copybook file straight into a DuckDB table — the COPY-FROM counterpart of read_fixed. It is invoked as a COPY statement (not called directly):

```sql
COPY <table> FROM '<path>' (FORMAT 'fixed.fixed', spec '<layout>');
```

The format name is catalog-qualified by the ATTACH name (e.g. 'fixed.fixed'). Each record is decoded per the `spec` option (a Perl/Python `unpack` template, a JSON field list, or a COBOL copybook; auto-detected unless `format` is given) and the decoded columns are assigned to the COPY target table's columns BY POSITION and cast to each target column's type, so the spec must produce the same number of columns in the same order. Options are named: `spec` (required), `format`, `encoding` ('ascii'/'ebcdic'), `framing` ('newline'/'fixed'/'rdw'/'rdw_blocked'), `record_length` (bytes, 'fixed' framing only), plus `endpoint`/`region`/`url_style`/`use_ssl` for `s3://` sources. `path` may be local, `s3://`, or `http(s)://`. Use it to ingest mainframe or legacy flat-file data into an existing table without a read_fixed call.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
Load a fixed-width file into a table:

```sql
COPY <table> FROM '<path>' (FORMAT 'fixed.fixed', spec '<layout>');
```

Decoded columns map to the target table's columns by position (cast to each type). Named options: `spec` (required), `format`, `encoding`, `framing`, `record_length`, and S3 overrides. The COPY-FROM counterpart of `read_fixed`.
tags.vgi.result_dynamic_columns_md:
`copy_fixed` is invoked through `COPY <table> FROM '<path>' (FORMAT 'fixed.fixed', …)`, not as a table function, so it returns **no result set of its own**. The rows decoded from the file are inserted into the COPY **target table**, and DuckDB reports the number of rows loaded as the statement's `Count`. The materialized columns are therefore the target table's own columns — each decoded field is mapped to a target column **by position** and cast to that column's type, so the `spec` must produce the same number of columns, in the same order, as the table.

For a target table `accounts(name VARCHAR, qty INTEGER)` loaded with the spec `name:A10 qty:9(5)`, the loaded columns are:

| Name | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|

The `spec` is the same multi-record JSON object (a `discriminator` of {offset, width} plus a `records` map of record-type tag → JSON field list); the record's discriminator bytes pick the variant to decode it with. workers.summary: Offline reverse geocoding: lat/lon -> place, country, admin regions, timezone, plus haversine distance
workers.doc_md:
# Offline Reverse Geocoding in SQL

**Turn latitude/longitude coordinates into the nearest city, country, admin regions and IANA timezone -- entirely offline, with no API keys, no rate limits and no network calls -- directly in DuckDB.**

`geocode` is a VGI worker that brings fast, hermetic **reverse geocoding** to SQL. Point it at any column of `(lat, lon)` coordinates and it enriches each row with the nearest known place name, its ISO-3166 country code, first- and second-level administrative regions (state/region, county/district), and the local IANA timezone. Because every lookup runs against bundled spatial databases rather than a hosted geocoding API, it works on air-gapped hosts, scales to millions of rows without per-request billing, and returns deterministic results. It is built for data engineers, analysts and GIS practitioners who need to attach human-readable geography and time zones to coordinate data sets -- IoT and GPS traces, telemetry, event logs, store/asset locations -- without leaving the database.

Under the hood, place lookups are powered by [`reverse_geocoder`](https://github.com/thampiman/reverse-geocoder) ([PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/reverse_geocoder/)), which queries a [GeoNames](https://www.geonames.org/) cities KD-tree to find the nearest populated place in sub-millisecond time. Timezone resolution uses [`timezonefinder`](https://github.com/jannikmi/timezonefinder) ([documentation](https://timezonefinder.readthedocs.io/)), which maps a point to its [IANA time-zone](https://www.iana.org/time-zones) polygon offline. Distances are computed with the great-circle [haversine formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haversine_formula). Every function is total and NULL-safe: a NULL or out-of-range coordinate yields `NULL` rather than an error, so the functions are safe to drop into large batch queries.

## What you can do

The worker groups its capabilities into three areas:

- **Place lookup** -- resolve a coordinate to the nearest city, its ISO-3166 country, and first- and second-level administrative regions (state/region and county/district), either one attribute at a time or as a single combined `STRUCT` record for the whole place.
- **Timezone** -- map a coordinate to its IANA timezone name (e.g. `America/New_York`) for localizing timestamps.
- **Distance** -- measure the great-circle (haversine) distance in kilometers between two coordinates.

Every operation is a per-row scalar you can use inline in any projection or predicate, so enriching a whole coordinate column -- or filtering it by proximity -- is a single `SELECT` with no joins, staging tables, or API round-trips.

Backed by GeoNames cities (`reverse_geocoder`, LGPL-3.0, used as an unmodified dependency) and offline IANA timezone polygons (`timezonefinder`, MIT).
workers.readme_sql:
INSTALL vgi FROM community; LOAD vgi;
ATTACH 'geocode' (TYPE vgi, LOCATION 'uv run geocode_worker.py');

SELECT geocode.nearest_city(40.7128, -74.0060);          -- 'New York City'
SELECT geocode.country_code(48.8566, 2.3522);            -- 'FR'
SELECT geocode.admin1(35.6762, 139.6503);                -- 'Tokyo'
SELECT geocode.admin2(34.0522, -118.2437);               -- county / district
SELECT geocode.timezone(40.7128, -74.0060);              -- 'America/New_York'
SELECT geocode.reverse_geocode(40.7128, -74.0060);       -- STRUCT(...)
SELECT geocode.reverse_geocode(40.7128, -74.0060).city;  -- 'New York City'
SELECT geocode.distance_km(40.7128, -74.0060, 51.5074, -0.1278);  -- ~5570 km

example_queries.description: Enrich a set of coordinates with nearest city and ISO-3166 country code.
example_queries.sql: SELECT lat, lon, geocode.main.nearest_city(lat, lon) AS city, geocode.main.country_code(lat, lon) AS country FROM (VALUES (40.7128, -74.0060), (48.8566, 2.3522), (35.6762, 139.6503)) AS t(lat, lon)

example_queries.description: Count coordinates per country by reverse-geocoding to a country code.
example_queries.sql: SELECT geocode.main.country_code(lat, lon) AS country, count(*) AS n FROM (VALUES (40.7, -74.0), (34.0, -118.2), (48.8, 2.35)) AS t(lat, lon) GROUP BY country ORDER BY n DESC

example_queries.description: Keep only points within 1000 km of Paris using the haversine distance.
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, round(geocode.main.distance_km(lat, lon, 48.8566, 2.3522)) AS km_to_paris FROM (VALUES ('London', 51.5074, -0.1278), ('New York', 40.7128, -74.0060)) AS t(name, lat, lon) WHERE geocode.main.distance_km(lat, lon, 48.8566, 2.3522) < 1000

example_queries.description: Pull the first-level admin region straight out of the reverse_geocode STRUCT.
example_queries.sql: SELECT geocode.main.reverse_geocode(40.7128, -74.0060).admin1 AS state

example_queries.description: Resolve the IANA timezone name for a coordinate to localize timestamps.
example_queries.sql: SELECT geocode.main.timezone(40.7128, -74.0060) AS tz

example_queries.description: Full nearest-place STRUCT for the New York City coordinates.
example_queries.sql: SELECT geocode.main.reverse_geocode(40.7128, -74.0060) AS place

example_queries.description: Pluck the city field from the nearest-place STRUCT (Tokyo).
example_queries.sql: SELECT geocode.main.reverse_geocode(35.6762, 139.6503).city AS city

example_queries.description: Nearest city to the New York City coordinates.
example_queries.sql: SELECT geocode.main.nearest_city(40.7128, -74.0060) AS city

example_queries.description: ISO-3166 country code for Paris coordinates.
example_queries.sql: SELECT geocode.main.country_code(48.8566, 2.3522) AS cc;

example_queries.description: First-level admin region (state) for Tokyo.
example_queries.sql: SELECT geocode.main.admin1(35.6762, 139.6503) AS region;

example_queries.description: Great-circle distance from New York to London (km).
example_queries.sql: SELECT geocode.main.distance_km(40.7128, -74.0060, 51.5074, -0.1278) AS km;

example_queries.sql: SELECT geocode.main.country_code(48.8566, 2.3522) AS country

tags.vgi.doc_md:
## Reverse-geocoding scalars

Per-row scalar functions over Apache Arrow that turn a `(lat, lon)` coordinate into human-readable geography: the nearest city, its ISO-3166 country code, the first- and second-level administrative regions, and a single combined nearest-place record. All take coordinates positionally.

## Timezone and distance

The schema also resolves a coordinate to its IANA timezone name (for localizing timestamps) and computes the great-circle (haversine) distance in kilometers between two points.

## Semantics

Every function returns `NULL` for a `NULL` or out-of-range input, never an error, so it is safe to drop into large batch queries. Lookups are backed by GeoNames cities and offline IANA timezone polygons -- no API keys or network required.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Return the **IANA timezone name** (e.g. `America/New_York`, `Europe/Paris`, `Asia/Tokyo`) for a latitude/longitude, computed **offline** from bundled IANA timezone polygons (`timezonefinder`).

## When to use
Use it to localize timestamps, derive local time, or bucket coordinate data by timezone -- the returned string drops straight into DuckDB's `timezone(name, ts)` / `AT TIME ZONE`.

## Inputs / outputs
- `lat` `DOUBLE` in `[-90, 90]`, `lon` `DOUBLE` in `[-180, 180]`.
- Returns the IANA tz name as `VARCHAR`, or `NULL`.

## Behavior & edge cases
- Uses true timezone *polygons*, not a nearest-place lookup, so it is exact at borders on land.
- Points outside every tz polygon return `NULL`; some uninhabited ocean cells resolve to a valid `Etc/GMT±N` name instead.
- `NULL` or out-of-range coordinates return `NULL` (never an error).

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Resolve a latitude/longitude to the **full nearest-place record** in a single call, returning a `STRUCT(city, admin1, admin2, country_code, place_lat, place_lon)` computed **entirely offline**.

## When to use
Prefer this over the single-field helpers (`nearest_city`, `country_code`, `admin1`, `admin2`) when you need several attributes at once -- it does the KD-tree lookup once and lets you pluck fields with dot access.

## Inputs / outputs
- `lat` `DOUBLE` in `[-90, 90]`, `lon` `DOUBLE` in `[-180, 180]`.
- Returns a `STRUCT` with `city`, `admin1`, `admin2` (`VARCHAR`), `country_code` (`VARCHAR`), and `place_lat`/`place_lon` (`DOUBLE`, the coordinates of the matched GeoNames place).

## Behavior & edge cases
- For a `NULL` or out-of-range coordinate the **entire struct is `NULL`**.
- Individual fields may be `NULL` (notably `admin2`) even for a valid match.
- Access fields with `reverse_geocode(lat, lon).city`, etc.

# reverse_geocode

Full nearest-place record for `(lat, lon)` as a `STRUCT`, computed offline.

## Columns (struct fields)

| field | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `city` | VARCHAR | Nearest city / place name. |
| `admin1` | VARCHAR | First-level admin region (state / region). |
| `admin2` | VARCHAR | Second-level admin region (county / district). |
| `country_code` | VARCHAR | ISO-3166 alpha-2 country code. |
| `place_lat` | DOUBLE | Latitude of the matched place. |
| `place_lon` | DOUBLE | Longitude of the matched place. |

## Usage

```sql
SELECT geocode.main.reverse_geocode(40.7128, -74.0060);        -- STRUCT(...)
SELECT geocode.main.reverse_geocode(35.6762, 139.6503).city;   -- 'Tokyo'
```

## Notes

Whole struct is `NULL` for `NULL`/out-of-range inputs; `admin2` is often `NULL`.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Return the name of the nearest known populated place (city/town) to a given latitude/longitude, **entirely offline** using a GeoNames cities KD-tree.

## When to use
Reach for this when you have raw coordinate columns (GPS pings, device telemetry, store/asset locations) and want a human-readable place label to group, filter, or display by.

## Inputs / outputs
- `lat` `DOUBLE` in `[-90, 90]`, `lon` `DOUBLE` in `[-180, 180]`.
- Returns a `VARCHAR` city name, or `NULL`.

## Behavior & edge cases
- This is a *nearest-land-place* lookup: the index has no notion of water, so a point in the ocean resolves to the closest coastal city.
- A `NULL` coordinate or one out of range yields `NULL` (never an error).
- City labels track the bundled GeoNames snapshot and can drift slightly between releases.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Compute the **great-circle (haversine) distance in kilometers** between two `(lat, lon)` points on a spherical Earth. Pure arithmetic -- no index, no lookup, no network.

## When to use
Use it for proximity filtering ('within N km of'), nearest-of ranking, trip length, or any straight-line distance between coordinate pairs in SQL.

## Inputs / outputs
- Four `DOUBLE` arguments: `lat1, lon1, lat2, lon2`, each in the usual lat `[-90, 90]` / lon `[-180, 180]` ranges.
- Returns the distance as a `DOUBLE` in kilometers, or `NULL`.

## Behavior & edge cases
- Uses a mean Earth radius (~6371 km); it is a sphere approximation, not a geodesic on the WGS-84 ellipsoid, so expect sub-percent error.
- If **any** of the four coordinates is `NULL` or out of range the result is `NULL` (never an error).
- Distance is symmetric and zero for identical points.

# Google APIs for SQL

![Google logo](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2f/Google_2015_logo.svg/250px-Google_2015_logo.svg.png)

**Query the entire Google REST API surface directly from DuckDB SQL** — read Google Sheets ranges, list Google Drive files, pull Google Calendar events, search YouTube videos, and reach any other Google API as ordinary SQL table functions, no glue code required.

This extension turns Google's APIs into a relational data source. It is built on the official [google-api-python-client](https://github.com/googleapis/google-api-python-client) library and Google's [API Discovery Service](https://developers.google.com/discovery), so any service Google publishes a discovery document for is reachable — not just a hand-picked few. Curated READ adapters give first-class, typed columns for the high-demand surfaces (Sheets, Drive, Calendar, YouTube), while a generic escape hatch covers everything else. Authentication is service-account-first (or an API key for public data), resolved securely through the VGI secret provider — credentials are never inlined in SQL. See the [client library documentation](https://googleapis.github.io/google-api-python-client/docs/) for the full API catalog and auth model.

It is built for data engineers and analysts who want spreadsheet data, file metadata, calendar schedules, and video statistics in their warehouse without standing up a separate ETL service. Three kinds of access work together: **curated data adapters** provide typed columns for the high-demand surfaces (Sheets, Drive, Calendar, YouTube), **generic API access** reaches any other Google REST method by name and returns its JSON response as rows, and **API discovery** lets you introspect which APIs and methods are reachable — all from inside SQL.

A typical query loads a spreadsheet range straight into SQL by naming a spreadsheet ID and an A1 range; the per-function example queries show the exact call shapes for Sheets, Drive, Calendar, YouTube, and the generic hatch. Pagination (Google's `nextPageToken`) is handled automatically and a `count` argument caps total rows. The connector is **READ-only**; data, quotas, billing and compliance with Google's Terms of Service remain the responsibility of the operator whose credentials are used.

example_queries.description: Discover the Sheets API's reachable versions via the Discovery Service.
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, version, title FROM google.main.google_apis() WHERE name LIKE '%sheets%' ORDER BY name LIMIT 5

example_queries.description: Browse the Drive v3 methods you can invoke through google_call.
example_queries.sql: SELECT method, http_method FROM google.main.google_methods('drive', 'v3') ORDER BY method LIMIT 5

example_queries.description: Read a header sheet range, projecting a named column from each row.
example_queries.sql: SELECT row_number, record ->> '$.name' AS name FROM google.main.google_sheet('1AbC...', 'Sheet1!A1:Z', header := true) WHERE row_number <= 100 ORDER BY row_number

example_queries.description: List up to 100 PDF files in Google Drive by MIME type.
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, name FROM google.main.google_drive(query := "mimeType='application/pdf'", count := 100)

example_queries.description: Search YouTube for 'duckdb' videos and project their view counts.
example_queries.sql: SELECT video_id, title, view_count FROM google.main.google_youtube('duckdb', count := 25)

example_queries.description: Find the Sheets APIs in the directory and their versions.
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, version, title FROM google.main.google_api_directory WHERE name LIKE '%sheets%' ORDER BY name, version

example_queries.description: List the preferred version of every reachable Google API.
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, version FROM google.main.google_api_directory WHERE preferred ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: List Drive v3 methods reachable via google_call
example_queries.sql: SELECT method, http_method FROM google.main.google_methods('drive', 'v3')

example_queries.description: List the user-created Gmail label names via the generic hatch
example_queries.sql: SELECT result ->> '$.name' AS label FROM google.main.google_call('gmail', 'v1', 'users.labels.list', '{"userId":"me"}') WHERE result ->> '$.type' = 'user' ORDER BY label

example_queries.description: List up to 50 events on the primary calendar
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, summary, start_time FROM google.main.google_calendar(calendar_id := 'primary', count := 50)

example_queries.description: Find the Sheets API and its versions
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, version, title FROM google.main.google_apis() WHERE name LIKE '%sheets%'

example_queries.description: Discover which Google Sheets APIs are reachable via the public Discovery Service.
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, version, title FROM google.main.google_apis() WHERE name LIKE '%sheets%' ORDER BY name, version LIMIT 5;

## Google API table functions

The `main` schema exposes Google's REST surface as SQL table functions, grouped into three kinds of access.

- **Curated data adapters** give first-class, typed columns for the high-demand surfaces — Sheets ranges, Drive file metadata, Calendar events, and YouTube video statistics.

functions.name: google_sheet
functions.comment: Read a Google Sheets range as rows (values, optional header)

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## google_sheet

Read a rectangular range from a Google Sheet as SQL rows. Pass the **spreadsheet ID** (the long token in the sheet's URL) and an **A1 range** such as `Sheet1!A1:Z`. With `header := true` the first row is treated as column names and surfaced as a JSON `record` per row; otherwise rows come back as a `values` text array.

**When to use:** pull tabular data maintained in Sheets (config, lookups, hand-curated lists) directly into SQL for joins and aggregation. Auth is **service-account-first** (or an API key for a publicly shared sheet) resolved via the VGI secret provider — never inline.

**Inputs:** `spreadsheet_id`, `range`, `header` (default false), `count` (row cap). **Outputs:** `row_number`, `values`, `record`. Empty trailing cells may be omitted by the API, so rows can be ragged; `count` bounds the scan.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# google_sheet

Reads a Google Sheets A1 range into rows. Pass the spreadsheet ID (the long token in the sheet URL) and an A1 range such as `Sheet1!A1:Z`; the attached example queries show the exact call shape.

## Notes

- With the `header` argument true, columns are named from the first row and surfaced in the JSON `record` column; otherwise `record` is NULL and cells live in the `values` array.
- Requires a `google_service_account` secret (or `google_api_key` for a publicly shared sheet); the worker is READ-only.
- The API may omit empty trailing cells, so rows can vary in width.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT row_number, record ->> '$.name' AS name FROM google.main.google_sheet('1AbC...', 'Sheet1!A1:Z', header := true) WHERE row_number <= 100 ORDER BY row_number

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: record
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: With the header argument true, a JSON-encoded object of header to cell for this row (read with the json extension's ->> operator); else NULL.

List the callable methods of a single Google API, one row per method, by reading that API's **discovery document**. Provide the discovery `api` name (e.g. `drive`) and `version` (e.g. `v3`). ## google_drive

List or search Google Drive files and return their metadata as SQL rows. The optional `query` argument uses Drive's native **`q` query syntax** (e.g. `mimeType='application/pdf'`, `name contains 'report'`, `modifiedTime > '2024-01-01'`). Results page automatically; `count` caps the total and `order_by` (e.g. `modifiedTime desc`) sorts them. Pass `drive_id` to search within a Shared Drive.

**When to use:** inventory files, find documents by type/name/date, or join Drive metadata against other tables. This returns **metadata only**, not file contents. Auth is service-account-first via the VGI secret provider.

**Inputs:** `query`, `count`, `page_size`, `order_by`, `drive_id`. **Outputs:** id, name, mime_type, timestamps, size, links, parents, owner, and trashed/starred flags.

functions.name: google_call
functions.comment: Call any Google API method; returns JSON rows (generic escape hatch)

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## google_call

The generic escape hatch: invoke **any** Google REST API method (beyond the curated adapters) and get its JSON response as SQL rows. Provide the discovery `api` name (e.g. `gmail`), the `version` (e.g. `v1`), the dotted `method` path (e.g. `users.messages.list`), and a `params_json` JSON object of method parameters.

Row shaping is automatic: if the response has exactly one list-valued field (e.g. `files`, `items`, `messages`), **each element becomes a row**; otherwise the whole response is a single JSON row. `nextPageToken` is followed transparently and `count` caps total rows.

**When to use:** reach a Google surface that has no dedicated adapter here. Discover what to pass with `google_apis()` and `google_methods(api, version)`. Auth is service-account-first via the VGI secret provider; parse the JSON with the DuckDB `json` extension (`result ->> '$.field'`). Parameters are validated at bind time, so malformed `params_json` is a clean error.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# google_call

Calls any Google API method and returns JSON rows. The attached example queries show how to project fields out of the JSON `result` column.

## Notes

- A single list field in the response is expanded to one row per element; otherwise the whole response is one row.
- `nextPageToken` is followed automatically; `count` bounds the scan.
- Use `google_apis()` / `google_methods()` to discover api/version/method, and the `json` extension to read the `result` column.

vgi.example_queries.description: List the user-created Gmail label names via the generic hatch
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT result ->> '$.name' AS label FROM google.main.google_call('gmail', 'v1', 'users.labels.list', '{"userId":"me"}') WHERE result ->> '$.type' = 'user' ORDER BY label

## google_youtube

Search YouTube for videos matching a query and return each hit with its engagement statistics as SQL rows. The first positional argument is the **search query**; `order_by` controls ranking (`relevance`, `date`, `viewCount`, `rating`) and `count` caps the results. Each row carries the video's title, channel, publish time, duration, and view/like/comment counts.

**When to use:** analyze video reach, find recent uploads on a topic, or rank content by views/likes. Auth is by **API key** (`google_api_key`) via the VGI secret provider — YouTube Data API is public. Statistics columns can be NULL when a video hides them.

**Inputs:** `query`, `count`, `page_size`, `order_by`. **Outputs:** video_id, title, description, channel, published_at, view/like/comment counts, duration, and the watch URL.

## google_calendar

List events from a Google Calendar as SQL rows. Defaults to the `primary` calendar; pass `calendar_id` (an address or ID) to target another. Bound the window with `time_min` / `time_max` (a date or RFC-3339 timestamp) and free-text filter with `query`. With `single_events := true` (the default) recurring events are expanded into individual instances; set it false to see the recurring master.

**When to use:** pull schedule data into SQL to count meetings, find events in a date range, or join calendar activity with other data. All-day events have NULL `start_time`/`end_time` and `all_day = true`. Auth is service-account-first via the VGI secret provider.

**Inputs:** `calendar_id`, `time_min`, `time_max`, `query`, `count`, `page_size`, `single_events`. **Outputs:** id, summary, description, location, status, start/end timestamps, all_day, organizer, creator, and an HTML link.

workers.title: Grammar, Style & Spelling Checker
workers.tagline: Grammar/style/spell check & auto-correct for DuckDB (Java, LanguageTool)
workers.summary: Grammar, style, and spelling checking + auto-correction (LanguageTool)
workers.doc_md:
# Grammar, Style & Spelling Checking in SQL

![LanguageTool logo](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/45/LanguageTool_Logo.svg/250px-LanguageTool_Logo.svg.png)

**Proofread, spell-check, and auto-correct natural-language text directly in DuckDB SQL** — grammar checking, style suggestions, typo detection, and one-call rewriting, powered by [LanguageTool](https://languagetool.org) and served to DuckDB over Apache Arrow.

This VGI worker turns the open-source LanguageTool proofreading engine into a set of SQL functions, so you can clean up and quality-check text without leaving your database or calling an external API. It is built for data engineers, analysts, and anyone running text-heavy pipelines: validating user-generated content, normalizing product descriptions and support tickets, flagging typos in scraped or imported data, scoring writing quality, or batch-correcting columns of free text. Everything runs locally in the worker process — your text is never sent to a third-party service.

Under the hood the worker embeds [LanguageTool](https://languagetool.org), the same multilingual grammar and style checker used by millions of writers. Each query runs against a cached `JLanguageTool` engine that applies LanguageTool's rule set (grammar, punctuation, style, and spelling rules) to your text and returns structured results. The English language pack (`en-US`, `en-GB`, `en-CA`, and other English variants) is shipped in the JAR; every function accepts an optional `language` argument that defaults to `en-US`. For implementation details and the rule catalog, see the [LanguageTool developer documentation](https://dev.languagetool.org) and the [LanguageTool source on GitHub](https://github.com/languagetool-org/languagetool).

**Key concepts.** An *issue* is a single problem LanguageTool flags — a grammar, punctuation, style, or spelling rule that fired over a span of your text — carrying the rule that matched, a human-readable category and message, the offending span, and an ordered list of suggested replacements (best first). A *language* is a dialect/locale code (this worker ships the English family: `en-US`, `en-GB`, `en-CA`, ...) that decides which spellings and rules apply; it defaults to `en-US`.

**When to reach for it.** Use this worker whenever a SQL pipeline needs to find, quantify, gate on, or repair writing problems in a text column without leaving the database or shipping data to an external proofreading API: validating user-generated content, scoring writing quality, flagging typos in scraped data, or batch-cleaning free-text columns. The functions group into checking (surface or count issues, or test whether text is clean), correction (rewrite text by applying the top suggested fix), and reference (discover the supported language codes).

example_queries.description: Surface each grammar/spelling issue in a sentence with its rule, category, and suggested fixes.
example_queries.sql: SELECT rule_id, category, message, suggestions FROM grammar.main.grammar_check('She go to school every day.') ORDER BY "offset"

example_queries.description: Count the writing issues in a piece of text (default en-US).
example_queries.sql: SELECT grammar.main.grammar_count('I has two dog.') AS issue_count

example_queries.description: Test whether text is free of writing issues.
example_queries.sql: SELECT grammar.main.is_grammatical('The quick brown fox jumps.') AS clean

example_queries.description: Auto-correct text by applying the top suggested fix for each issue.
example_queries.sql: SELECT grammar.main.correct('She go to school evry day.') AS corrected

example_queries.description: List the supported English language codes to pass as the language argument.
example_queries.sql: SELECT code, name FROM grammar.main.grammar_languages WHERE code LIKE 'en-%' ORDER BY code

example_queries.description: List every supported language code with its human-readable name, alphabetically.
example_queries.sql: SELECT code, name FROM grammar.main.grammar_languages ORDER BY code

example_queries.description: Filter to the English variants accepted by the language argument.
example_queries.sql: SELECT code FROM grammar.main.grammar_languages WHERE code LIKE 'en-%' ORDER BY code

example_queries.description: Count how many language codes this worker accepts.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS supported_languages FROM grammar.main.grammar_languages

example_queries.description: List every supported language code with its human-readable name, alphabetically.
example_queries.sql: SELECT code, name FROM grammar.main.grammar_languages() ORDER BY code

example_queries.description: Filter to the English variants accepted by the language argument.
example_queries.sql: SELECT code FROM grammar.main.grammar_languages() WHERE code LIKE 'en-%' ORDER BY code

example_queries.description: Count how many language codes this worker accepts.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS supported_languages FROM grammar.main.grammar_languages()

example_queries.description: List each grammar/spelling issue in a sentence with its rule, category, flagged text, and suggested fixes, in reading order.
example_queries.sql: SELECT rule_id, category, message, bad_text, suggestions FROM grammar.main.grammar_check('She go to school every day.') ORDER BY "offset"

example_queries.description: Show the single best suggested replacement for every fixable issue, checking a specific language variant.
example_queries.sql: SELECT rule_id, message, suggestions[1] AS top_fix FROM grammar.main.grammar_check('I has a apple.', language := 'en-US') WHERE length(suggestions) > 0

example_queries.description: Aggregate how many issues fall into each LanguageTool category for a passage.
example_queries.sql: SELECT category, count(*) AS issues FROM grammar.main.grammar_check('Their going too the store, its there problem.') GROUP BY category ORDER BY issues DESC

example_queries.description: List every grammar/spelling issue in a sentence, one row each.
example_queries.sql: SELECT rule_id, category, message FROM grammar.main.grammar_check('She go to school every day.');

example_queries.description: Test whether a sentence is free of issues in the default language (returns true).

## grammar.main

The single schema for this worker: grammar, style, and spelling checking plus auto-correction over Apache Arrow, powered by LanguageTool. Its functions fall into three groups — checking (surface or quantify writing issues, or test whether text is clean), correction (rewrite text by applying the top suggested fix), and reference (discover the supported language codes).

Every text-checking function takes an optional `language` argument that defaults to `en-US` and controls which dialect's spellings and rules apply. This worker ships the English family (`en-US`, `en-GB`, `en-CA`, ...); query the reference function to enumerate the exact codes before passing one.

vgi.example_queries.description: Surface each grammar/spelling issue in a sentence with its rule, category, and suggested fixes.

vgi.example_queries.description: Count the writing issues in a piece of text (default en-US).

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT grammar.main.is_grammatical('The quick brown fox jumps.') AS clean
vgi.example_queries.description: Test whether text is free of writing issues.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT grammar.main.correct('She go to school evry day.') AS corrected
vgi.example_queries.description: Auto-correct text by applying the top suggested fix for each issue.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Run LanguageTool over a piece of text and return one row per grammar, style, or spelling issue it finds, each with the rule that fired, its category, an explanatory message, the character offset/length of the flagged span, the flagged substring, and an ordered list of suggested replacements (best first). Accepts an optional `language` argument (default `en-US`). tags.vgi.doc_md:
## grammar_check(text [, language])

Returns one row per grammar/style/spelling issue LanguageTool reports for `text`, with suggested replacements. Each row carries the rule that fired, its category, an explanatory message, the `offset`/`length` of the flagged span, the flagged `bad_text`, and an ordered `suggestions` array (best first). Accepts an optional `language` (default `en-US`).

`NULL` or empty text returns no rows; an unknown language fails the query.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT rule_id, category, message, bad_text, suggestions FROM grammar.main.grammar_check('She go to school every day.') ORDER BY "offset"
vgi.example_queries.description: List each grammar/spelling issue in a sentence with its rule, category, flagged text, and suggested fixes, in reading order.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT rule_id, message, suggestions[1] AS top_fix FROM grammar.main.grammar_check('I has a apple.', language := 'en-US') WHERE length(suggestions) > 0
vgi.example_queries.description: Show the single best suggested replacement for every fixable issue, checking a specific language variant.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT category, count(*) AS issues FROM grammar.main.grammar_check('Their going too the store, its there problem.') GROUP BY category ORDER BY issues DESC
vgi.example_queries.description: Aggregate how many issues fall into each LanguageTool category for a passage.

workers.tagline: Parse HL7 v2 clinical messages for DuckDB (Java)
workers.summary: HL7 v2.x clinical message parsing (pure-Java, no HAPI)
workers.doc_md:
# HL7 v2.x Clinical Message Parsing in SQL

![HL7 International logo](https://brandguide.hl7.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/5/2025/07/HL7-V2Primary-Logo600px.png)

Parse, validate, and query **HL7 v2.x** pipe-delimited clinical messages directly in DuckDB SQL — turn raw ADT, ORU, and ORM feeds into queryable rows over Apache Arrow, with no ETL pipeline and no heavyweight HL7 library to install.

This extension is built for healthcare data engineers, interoperability and integration teams, and anyone who needs to ingest HL7 v2 messages from EHR/EMR systems, interface engines, or message archives and analyze them with plain SQL. HL7 v2 is the most widely deployed healthcare messaging standard in the world, and its segment/field/component/subcomponent layout is notoriously fiddly to parse by hand. Reach for it whenever a clinical feed arrives as raw pipe-delimited text and you want to JOIN, filter, and aggregate its fields the same way you would any other table — rather than pre-processing the messages in an external language first.

The core concepts mirror the HL7 v2 grammar. A **message** is a sequence of carriage-return–separated **segments** (MSH, EVN, PID, PV1, OBX, ...), each of which is a list of **fields**; a field can carry repetitions and decomposes further into **components** and **subcomponents**. Individual elements are addressed by an **HL7 location** path such as `PID-5.1` (component 1 of field 5 of the PID segment) or `MSH-9`, optionally with a segment repetition like `DG1[2]-3`. Indices are 1-based per HL7 convention.

Under the hood the parser is a compact, pure-Java (pure-JDK) implementation — there is **no HAPI dependency**, keeping the worker MIT-licensed and dependency-light. It is fully **MSH-driven**: the field separator (MSH-1) and encoding characters (MSH-2: component, repetition, escape, and subcomponent delimiters) are read from each message rather than assumed, so non-standard delimiters are handled correctly. Malformed input never crashes the worker — it simply parses as invalid and yields no rows, so the functions are safe to run across dirty, mixed-quality feeds.

The format and message grammar follow the official **HL7 v2** standard published by [Health Level Seven International](https://www.hl7.org); see the [HL7 v2 product brief and documentation](https://www.hl7.org/implement/standards/product_brief.cfm?product_id=185) for the canonical segment, field, and message-type definitions. Source code, examples, and issues live in the [Query-farm/vgi-hl7 repository](https://github.com/Query-farm/vgi-hl7).

example_queries.description: Split an admit message into its segments, in message order.
example_queries.sql: SELECT seq, segment, field_count FROM hl7.main.hl7_segments(E'MSH|^~\\&|SENDING_APP|SENDING_FAC|RECV_APP|RECV_FAC|20240101120000||ADT^A01|MSG00001|P|2.5\rEVN|A01|20240101120000\rPID|1||10001^^^HOSP^MR||Doe^John||19800101|M\rPV1|1|I') ORDER BY seq

example_queries.description: Explode the PID segment into long-format field rows.
example_queries.sql: SELECT segment, field, repetition, value FROM hl7.main.hl7_fields(E'MSH|^~\\&|SENDING_APP|SENDING_FAC|RECV_APP|RECV_FAC|20240101120000||ADT^A01|MSG00001|P|2.5\rEVN|A01|20240101120000\rPID|1||10001^^^HOSP^MR||Doe^John||19800101|M\rPV1|1|I') WHERE segment = 'PID' ORDER BY field, repetition

example_queries.description: Extract the patient family name (component 1 of PID-5) by location.
example_queries.sql: SELECT hl7.main.hl7_get(E'MSH|^~\\&|SENDING_APP|SENDING_FAC|RECV_APP|RECV_FAC|20240101120000||ADT^A01|MSG00001|P|2.5\rEVN|A01|20240101120000\rPID|1||10001^^^HOSP^MR||Doe^John||19800101|M\rPV1|1|I', 'PID-5.1') AS family_name

example_queries.description: Read the message type (MSH-9) for routing a mixed feed.

tags.vgi.doc_md:
## HL7 v2.x parsing functions

Clinical-message parsing over Apache Arrow. The functions in this schema fall into three capability areas that mirror how you work with an HL7 v2 feed.

**Parsing** turns a raw message into rows: one row per segment, or a long-format explosion with one row per field value (repetitions expanded), so you can query a message set-wise instead of by hand.

**Extraction** pulls out individual values addressed by an HL7 location path (such as `PID-5.1` or `MSH-9`), including the common MSH header accessors for message type, version, and control id.

**Validation** tests whether text is a well-formed HL7 v2 message, which is handy for filtering dirty feeds before parsing. The parser is pure-JDK and MSH-driven — the field separator and encoding characters are read from each message rather than assumed.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: A curated, browsable registry of ready-to-use example HL7 v2 messages, one per row. tags.vgi.doc_md:
## example_messages

A small, built-in catalog of sample **HL7 v2** messages you can query without supplying any input. It exists so you can see a well-formed message and the message types this worker understands before calling the parsing functions, which all require a message argument.

Each row describes one sample: a slug `name`, the HL7 `message_type` (e.g. `ADT^A01`, `ORU^R01`), the `trigger_event` code, a precomputed `segment_count`, a short `description`, and the raw CR-delimited `message` text itself. Browse it, sort by `segment_count`, or copy a `message` literal into `hl7_segments`, `hl7_fields`, or `hl7_get` to experiment.

The view is defined over an inline `VALUES` list, so it scans instantly with no network access and no credentials.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT name, message_type, trigger_event, segment_count FROM hl7.main.example_messages ORDER BY segment_count DESC, name;
vgi.example_queries.description: List the built-in sample messages, richest first, showing their type, trigger event, and segment count.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Splits an HL7 v2.x message into its constituent segments, returning one row per segment in message order. Each row carries the 1-based ordinal (`seq`), the 3-letter segment id (`segment`, e.g. `MSH`, `PID`, `PV1`), the number of fields in the segment (`field_count`, using HL7 numbering so `MSH-1` counts), and the raw segment text (`raw`).

Use it as the first step when ingesting a feed: enumerate what segments a message contains before drilling into fields with `hl7_fields` or `hl7_get`. The `message` argument is polymorphic — a `VARCHAR` carrying the message text or a `BLOB` carrying its bytes. NULL or malformed input (no leading MSH) yields no rows; the worker never throws.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## hl7_segments

Returns one row per segment of an HL7 v2.x message, in order. Handy for discovering a message's structure before extracting fields.

Pass the message inline as a `VARCHAR`/`BLOB`. Malformed or NULL input simply produces no rows. The returned columns are listed in this function's result schema.

functions.name: hl7_fields
functions.comment: Explode an HL7 v2.x message into long format: one row per field value (repetitions expanded), keyed by segment, segment occurrence, field, and repetition. Component structure is preserved in the raw value text.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Explodes an HL7 v2.x message into long (tidy) format: one row per field value, with repeating fields expanded into separate rows. Each row is keyed by `segment` (3-letter id), `segment_rep` (0-based occurrence of that segment within the message, to disambiguate repeated OBX/DG1/etc.), `field` (1-based HL7 field number), and `repetition` (0-based index of the repeated value); `value` holds the raw field text with its component/subcomponent structure preserved.

Use it to unpivot an entire message for set-based SQL (filtering, grouping, joining) instead of addressing one location at a time with `hl7_get`. Note the MSH quirk: MSH-1 (the field separator) and MSH-2 (the encoding characters, which literally contain `~`) are emitted as single verbatim values and are not re-split on the repetition separator. The `message` argument is a `VARCHAR` text or `BLOB` bytes; NULL or malformed input yields no rows.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## hl7_fields

Unpivots a whole HL7 v2.x message into long format — one row per field value with repetitions expanded — so you can query it with ordinary SQL.

Component/subcomponent structure stays intact in `value`; decompose it further with `hl7_get` or by splitting on the encoding characters. MSH-1/MSH-2 are kept verbatim. The returned columns are listed in this function's result schema.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT field, value FROM hl7.main.hl7_fields(E'MSH|^~\\&|SENDING_APP|SENDING_FAC|RECV_APP|RECV_FAC|20240101120000||ADT^A01|MSG00001|P|2.5\rEVN|A01|20240101120000\rPID|1||10001^^^HOSP^MR||Doe^John||19800101|M\rPV1|1|I') WHERE segment = 'PID';
vgi.example_queries.description: List every field of the PID (patient identification) segment as long-format rows.

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: segment
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: 3-letter segment identifier (e.g. MSH, PID).

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: segment_rep
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: 0-based occurrence index of this segment within the message.

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: field
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: 1-based HL7 field number within the segment.

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: repetition
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: 0-based repetition index of the field value.

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: value
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Raw field-value text (component/subcomponent structure preserved).

functions.name: is_valid_hl7
functions.comment: True when the input parses as a well-formed HL7 v2.x message (begins with an MSH segment defining the field separator and encoding characters).

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Tests whether text parses as a well-formed HL7 v2.x message: it must begin with an `MSH` segment that defines the field separator (MSH-1) and the encoding characters (MSH-2). Returns true for a valid message, false for malformed text (never an error), and NULL for a NULL input.

Use it as a cheap gate before parsing — e.g. filter a staging table to rows that are actually HL7 v2 before calling `hl7_segments`, `hl7_fields`, or `hl7_get`. The `message` argument is a `VARCHAR` text or a `BLOB` of bytes.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## is_valid_hl7

Boolean predicate: does this text look like an HL7 v2.x message (leading MSH with separators and encoding chars)?

Designed to be safe on dirty input — malformed text returns `false` rather than raising, and NULL maps to NULL. Pair it with a `WHERE` clause to skip non-HL7 rows before parsing.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT hl7.main.is_valid_hl7(E'MSH|^~\\&|SENDING_APP|SENDING_FAC|RECV_APP|RECV_FAC|20240101120000||ADT^A01|MSG00001|P|2.5\rEVN|A01|20240101120000\rPID|1||10001^^^HOSP^MR||Doe^John||19800101|M\rPV1|1|I');
vgi.example_queries.description: Check that a well-formed ADT^A01 message validates.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT hl7.main.is_valid_hl7('not an hl7 message');
vgi.example_queries.description: Malformed text validates as false (never errors).

arguments.name: message
arguments.description: The candidate HL7 text to test, supplied inline as the message itself (either its text or its raw bytes), never a file path. Evaluated per row; returns true for a well-formed HL7 v2.x message, false for malformed text, and NULL for NULL input.

functions.name: hl7_version
functions.comment: The HL7 version ID from MSH-12 (e.g. '2.5').

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Reads the HL7 version ID from field MSH-12, e.g. `2.3`, `2.5`, or `2.7`. This tells you which release of the HL7 v2.x standard the message claims to conform to, which affects field semantics across versions.

Use it to branch parsing logic or to audit which versions a feed is sending. Returns the raw MSH-12 text, or NULL when the message is malformed or the field is absent; NULL input yields NULL. The `message` argument is a `VARCHAR` text or `BLOB` bytes.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## hl7_version

Returns MSH-12, the HL7 v2.x version id (e.g. `2.5`).

Useful for version-aware handling and feed audits. Malformed or absent input maps to NULL rather than erroring.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT hl7.main.hl7_version(E'MSH|^~\\&|SENDING_APP|SENDING_FAC|RECV_APP|RECV_FAC|20240101120000||ADT^A01|MSG00001|P|2.5\rEVN|A01|20240101120000\rPID|1||10001^^^HOSP^MR||Doe^John||19800101|M\rPV1|1|I');
vgi.example_queries.description: Read the HL7 version (MSH-12) from a message.
