Minimum-cost flow over a capacitated, costed network.

Supplies must sum to zero. Returns one row per arc with positive flow.

**Reference:** [OR-Tools documentation](https://developers.google.com/optimization/flow/mincostflow)

functions.name: solve_cpsat
functions.comment: Solve an arbitrary CP-SAT constraint-programming model expressed as a versioned JSON document (variables, constraints, objective). Returns one row per variable plus solve metadata. The general escape hatch for constraints highs/LP cannot express.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## `solve_cpsat`

Solve an **arbitrary CP-SAT constraint-programming model** handed in as a **versioned JSON document** -- the general escape hatch for everything the per-domain builders and the `highs` LP/MIP extension cannot express (global constraints like `all_different`, `no_overlap`, `cumulative`, `circuit`, reification, intervals).

**The model.** A JSON object with `version` (must be 1), `variables` (each `int` / `bool` / `interval` with a unique `name`), `constraints`, and an optional `objective`. All numeric domains are **integers** -- a fractional bound / coefficient / constant is rejected with a clear error (scale floats to integers first). The full grammar is in the README (section A).

**Outputs.** One row per variable: `var`, `value`, plus the solve metadata (`status`, `objective`, `best_bound`, `wall_time`, `num_branches`) repeated on every row so a single SELECT is self-describing. Interval variables expand to `<name>.start` / `.size` / `.end` (and `.presence` for optional intervals).

**The empty-vs-infeasible contract.** A model with no solution still returns **exactly one row** carrying `status` in {`INFEASIBLE`, `MODEL_INVALID`, `UNKNOWN`} with NULL `var`/`value`; a solve is never an empty result set. Test `WHERE status='INFEASIBLE'`, never `count(*)=0`.

**Determinism.** Single-threaded by default (`num_workers := 0`) with a fixed `random_seed`, so the objective and assignment are reproducible.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# solve_cpsat

Solve a hand-built **CP-SAT** model expressed as a versioned JSON document.

See the README (section A) for the full JSON dialect: `variables` (int / bool / interval), `constraints` (linear, all_different, element, table, no_overlap, cumulative, circuit, reservoir, mult/div/abs/min/max equality, bool_or/and/xor, implication, with optional `enforce` reification), and an optional `objective`.

All numeric domains are integers. A no-solution model returns a single status row.

**Reference:** [OR-Tools documentation](https://developers.google.com/optimization/cp/cp_solver)

vgi.example_queries.description: 0/1 knapsack as a CP-SAT model: maximize value within a weight budget (optimum 40).
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT var, value, status, objective FROM ortools.main.solve_cpsat(model := '{"version":1,"variables":[{"kind":"bool","name":"a"},{"kind":"bool","name":"b"},{"kind":"bool","name":"c"}],"constraints":[{"type":"linear","expr":{"sum":[{"coef":5,"var":"a"},{"coef":10,"var":"b"},{"coef":15,"var":"c"}]},"op":"<=","rhs":20}],"objective":{"sense":"maximize","terms":[{"coef":10,"var":"a"},{"coef":20,"var":"b"},{"coef":30,"var":"c"}]}}') ORDER BY var

vgi.example_queries.description: Single-machine no-overlap schedule minimizing makespan (optimum 10).
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT objective, status FROM ortools.main.solve_cpsat(model := '{"version":1,"variables":[{"kind":"int","name":"s0","lb":0,"ub":20},{"kind":"int","name":"e0","lb":0,"ub":20},{"kind":"int","name":"s1","lb":0,"ub":20},{"kind":"int","name":"e1","lb":0,"ub":20},{"kind":"int","name":"s2","lb":0,"ub":20},{"kind":"int","name":"e2","lb":0,"ub":20},{"kind":"interval","name":"i0","start":{"var":"s0"},"size":{"const":3},"end":{"var":"e0"}},{"kind":"interval","name":"i1","start":{"var":"s1"},"size":{"const":5},"end":{"var":"e1"}},{"kind":"interval","name":"i2","start":{"var":"s2"},"size":{"const":2},"end":{"var":"e2"}},{"kind":"int","name":"makespan","lb":0,"ub":20}],"constraints":[{"type":"no_overlap","intervals":["i0","i1","i2"]},{"type":"max_equality","target":{"var":"makespan"},"exprs":[{"var":"e0"},{"var":"e1"},{"var":"e2"}]}],"objective":{"sense":"minimize","terms":[{"coef":1,"var":"makespan"}]}}', time_limit_s := 5.0) LIMIT 1

vgi.executable_examples.description: 0/1 knapsack as a CP-SAT model: maximize value within a weight budget (optimum 40).
vgi.executable_examples.sql: SELECT var, value, status, objective FROM ortools.main.solve_cpsat(model := '{"version":1,"variables":[{"kind":"bool","name":"a"},{"kind":"bool","name":"b"},{"kind":"bool","name":"c"}],"constraints":[{"type":"linear","expr":{"sum":[{"coef":5,"var":"a"},{"coef":10,"var":"b"},{"coef":15,"var":"c"}]},"op":"<=","rhs":20}],"objective":{"sense":"maximize","terms":[{"coef":10,"var":"a"},{"coef":20,"var":"b"},{"coef":30,"var":"c"}]}}') ORDER BY var

functions.name: solve_vrp
functions.comment: Vehicle routing problem: route a fleet from a depot to serve stops at minimum total distance, with optional capacity dimensions, time windows, service/travel time, pickup-delivery pairs, droppable stops, and route balancing. OR-Tools routing library.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## `solve_vrp`

Route a **fleet of vehicles** from a depot to serve a set of stops at **minimum total distance**, with the full routing surface: multi-dimension **capacity** (`demand` + `vehicle_capacity`), **time windows** (`time_windows` + `service_time` / `travel_time`), **pickup-delivery** pairs (same vehicle + precedence), droppable stops (`allow_dropping` + `drop_penalty`), route balancing (`span_cost_coefficient`), and the OR-Tools `first_solution_strategy` / `local_search_metaheuristic`.

**Inputs.** `distance` (sparse `[from, to, meters]` or dense `n x n`); `demand` = `[node, d0, d1, ...]` (the number of demand columns sets the number of capacity dimensions and therefore the `load_0` .. `load_k` output columns); `num_vehicles`; `vehicle_capacity`; `depot`. Advanced shapes -- per-vehicle / per-dimension capacities, per-vehicle `[start, end]` depots -- go through `settings_json`.

**Outputs.** One row per stop: `route_id` (vehicle), `seq`, `node`, `arrival`, `departure`, `load_0` .. `load_k`, `is_dropped`, `status`. A dropped node appears as a single row with `is_dropped = true` and NULL `route_id`. An unsolved instance returns one status row.

**Determinism.** Governed by the fixed `first_solution_strategy` / `local_search_metaheuristic`. The output `load_*` column count is fixed at bind time from the `demand` argument, so pass `demand` as a literal or a session VARIABLE that is set before the query binds.

Capacitated, time-windowed vehicle routing.

**Reference:** [OR-Tools documentation](https://developers.google.com/optimization/routing/cvrp)

tags.vgi.result_dynamic_columns_md:
The number of `load_d` columns is fixed at bind time from the `demand` argument (one per capacity dimension), so the output schema varies by call. For `k+1` capacity dimensions the columns are:

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| route_id | INTEGER | Vehicle index (NULL on a dropped-node row). |
| seq | INTEGER | 0-based stop order on the vehicle. |
| node | BIGINT | Node id (depot at seq 0 and last). |
| arrival | BIGINT | Cumulative time/distance at arrival. |
| departure | BIGINT | Arrival + service time. |
| load_0 | BIGINT | Cumulative load for capacity dimension 0. |
| load_k | BIGINT | Cumulative load for capacity dimension k (one load_d column per dimension). |
| is_dropped | BOOLEAN | True on the row emitted for a dropped node. |
| status | VARCHAR | OPTIMAL / FEASIBLE / INFEASIBLE / UNKNOWN / MODEL_INVALID. |

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## `solve_jobshop`

Schedule the tasks of several **jobs** onto shared **machines** to minimize the **makespan** (the time the last task finishes). Within a job, tasks run in `task` order; each machine runs one task at a time.

**Inputs.** `tasks` = `[job, task, machine, duration]` integer rows. Optional `horizon` (defaults to the sum of durations), `time_limit_s`, `random_seed`.

**Outputs.** One row per task with its `start` / `end`, the optimal `makespan` (repeated on every row), and `status`. An infeasible / unsolved instance returns a single status row.

functions.name: solve_assignment
functions.comment: Linear sum assignment: match workers to tasks over sparse [worker, task, cost] arcs, minimizing (or maximizing) total cost. Backed by OR-Tools SimpleLinearSumAssignment.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## `solve_assignment`

Solve a **linear sum assignment**: match each worker to at most one task (and each task to at most one worker) so the **total arc cost is minimized** (or maximized).

**Inputs.** `cost` is a sparse `LIST<LIST<BIGINT>>` of `[worker, task, cost]` integer triples (build it with `array_agg([w, t, c])`); a pair that is absent is a disallowed assignment. `maximize := true` negates costs internally. All costs must be integers.

**Outputs.** One row per matched worker: `worker`, `task`, `cost`, `status`. When no perfect matching of every worker exists the result is **exactly one row** with `status = 'INFEASIBLE'` and NULL `task`/`cost` -- never an empty set.

**Edge cases.** A non-integer cost raises a clear error (scale to integers first).

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## `solve_rcpsp`

Solve a **resource-constrained project scheduling problem**: schedule tasks (each with a duration and a per-resource demand) subject to finish-to-start **precedences** and renewable **resource capacities**, minimizing the makespan.

**Inputs.** `tasks` = `[task, duration, r0_demand, r1_demand, ...]` (one demand column per resource, in `resources` order); `precedences` = `[pred, succ]`; `resources` = `[resource, capacity]`. **Outputs.** One row per task with `start` / `end`, the optimal `makespan`, and `status`.

workers.title: PDF Structure & Rendering
workers.tagline: PDF tables, word boxes, form fields & page render for DuckDB (Python, pdfplumber)
workers.summary: Extract PDF structure (tables, word boxes, geometry, forms, metadata) and render pages to PNG.
workers.doc_md:
# PDF Structure & Rendering for DuckDB

Query the **structure, layout, and coordinates of PDF documents directly in SQL** -- pull tabular data, per-word geometry, page dimensions, form submissions, and document properties, check whether a file is encrypted, and rasterize any page to an image, all streamed to DuckDB over Apache Arrow. Where a plain-text extractor flattens a document to a string, this worker preserves *where* every word, cell, and box sits on the page.

## Who it is for

Built for data engineers, analysts, and document-mining pipelines that need to pull structured data out of reports, invoices, statements, and scanned forms without leaving SQL. Reach for it whenever the *position* of content matters -- reconstructing tabular layouts, locating text by coordinate, auditing filled-in forms, or generating page thumbnails -- and reach for a plain-text extraction worker instead when you only need the raw prose.

## Key concepts

- **Path or bytes.** Inputs are accepted as either a `VARCHAR` filesystem path the worker opens, or a `BLOB` of raw bytes travelling over Arrow -- so a document already living in a DuckDB column works as directly as a file on disk.
- **PDF points.** All geometry is reported in PDF points (1 pt = 1/72 inch) with the origin at the top-left corner of the page.
- **Long-format output.** Set-returning functions expand one document into many tidy rows, ready to pivot, filter, and join with ordinary SQL.

## Backed by permissive libraries only

Table detection and word geometry come from [pdfplumber](https://github.com/jsvine/pdfplumber) ([docs](https://github.com/jsvine/pdfplumber#readme)); high-fidelity page rasterization is powered by [pypdfium2](https://github.com/pypdfium2-team/pypdfium2) ([docs](https://pypdfium2.readthedocs.io/)), Google's Chromium PDFium engine; document properties, encryption detection, and AcroForm reading use [pikepdf](https://github.com/pikepdf/pikepdf) ([docs](https://pikepdf.readthedocs.io/)); and rendered bitmaps are encoded to PNG with [Pillow](https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow) ([docs](https://pillow.readthedocs.io/)). Deliberately **never PyMuPDF** -- only permissively licensed dependencies.

tags.vgi.doc_md:
# PDF Structure -- `main`

The `main` schema groups every PDF structure, layout, and rendering capability this worker exposes, all served to DuckDB over Apache Arrow. It reads a document's *structure and coordinates* -- not its plain text -- so you always know where content sits on the page.

## What you can do here

- **Structure** -- count pages and read per-page geometry (width, height, rotation).
- **Content** -- pull detected table cells in long format, per-word bounding boxes, and filled-in form-field values.
- **Metadata** -- read the document information dictionary and check encryption status.
- **Rendering** -- rasterize a single page to a PNG image at a chosen resolution.

## Conventions

Inputs are accepted as either a `VARCHAR` filesystem path or a `BLOB` of raw bytes, and all coordinates are expressed in PDF points (1/72 inch) measured from the top-left corner. The set-returning functions take DuckDB `name := value` keyword arguments; the per-row question-answering functions are ordinary scalars used inline in any projection.

# functions

A **browsable discovery view** listing every object this worker exposes, one row per object: `name`, `kind` (`scalar`, `table function`, or `view`), `category` (Structure/Content/Metadata/Rendering/Discovery), and a one-line `summary`. It is a plain view -- read it as `pdf.main.functions` with no arguments.

Use it as the entry point when you do not yet know what the worker offers: read this view first to pick the right object, then call that object with a PDF path or bytes. Filter by `category` to narrow to a capability area, or by `kind` to separate per-row scalars from set-returning table functions.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# List Worker Objects

A static registry view of every object this worker exposes -- the browsable entry point for discovering the surface before calling anything.

## Example

Reading `pdf.main.functions` returns one row per object with its `name`, `kind`, `category`, and `summary`; keep rows whose `category` equals `Content` to see the table-cell, word-box, and form-field extractors. Ready-to-run SQL lives in the example queries.

## Columns

| column | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | VARCHAR | Object name (call it as `pdf.main.<name>`). |
| `kind` | VARCHAR | `scalar`, `table function`, or `view`. |
| `category` | VARCHAR | Structure, Content, Metadata, Rendering, or Discovery. |
| `summary` | VARCHAR | One-line description of what the object returns. |

## Notes

The view is static and offline -- it needs no PDF, file, or network access, so it always answers instantly.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
# words

Table function returning **one row per word** in a PDF, with each word's text and its bounding box: `page` (1-based), `text`, and the box edges `x0`/`top`/`x1`/`bottom` in PDF points (origin at the top-left). Call by keyword: `words(pdf := '...')`, with the optional `page := N` filter to restrict to one page. `pdf` is a `VARCHAR` path or a `BLOB`.

Use it to locate text by coordinate, reconstruct reading order (`ORDER BY top, x0`), find where a keyword appears on a page, or build a spatial layout index.

**Edge cases:** a scanned/image-only page yields no words; a NULL `pdf` raises a clean argument error; an unreadable PDF raises a clean DuckDB error. Output streams in bounded slices, so pages with thousands of words page safely over every transport.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# Extract PDF Word Boxes

Returns every word in a PDF together with its bounding box, one row per word.

## Example

Calling `pdf.main.words(pdf := 'invoice.pdf')` returns one row per word -- its `text` and the box edges `x0`, `top`, `x1`, `bottom` (PDF points, origin top-left). Order by `top` then `x0` to recover reading order, or pass `page := 1` to restrict to the first page. Ready-to-run SQL lives in the example queries.

## Columns

| column | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `page` | INTEGER | 1-based page number the word is on. |
| `text` | VARCHAR | The word's text. |
| `x0` | DOUBLE | Left edge, in PDF points from the left. |
| `top` | DOUBLE | Top edge, in PDF points from the top. |
| `x1` | DOUBLE | Right edge, in PDF points from the left. |
| `bottom` | DOUBLE | Bottom edge, in PDF points from the top. |

## Notes

Coordinates are in PDF points with the origin at the top-left. Image-only (scanned) pages produce no words -- this reads the text layer, it does not OCR. Call by keyword (`pdf := ...`, optional `page := N`).

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
# tables

Table function that detects tables in a PDF and returns them in **long (tidy) format -- one row per cell**: `page` (1-based), `table_index` (0-based ordinal of the table on the page), `row` and `col` (0-based indices within the table), and `value` (the cell text, NULL when empty). Call by keyword: `tables(pdf := '...')`, with the optional `page := N` filter. `pdf` is a `VARCHAR` path or a `BLOB`.

Use it to mine numeric/tabular data out of reports and statements. Pivot back to a grid with conditional aggregation on `row`/`col`, or filter a single table with `table_index`.

**Gotcha:** `row` is a SQL keyword -- quote it as `"row"`. **Edge cases:** a page with no detectable table contributes no rows; a NULL `pdf` raises a clean argument error; an unreadable PDF raises a clean DuckDB error. Output streams in bounded slices.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# Extract PDF Table Cells

Detects tables in a PDF and returns their cells in long (one-row-per-cell) format.

## Example

Calling `pdf.main.tables(pdf := 'report.pdf')` yields one row per cell, with `page`, `table_index`, `row`, `col`, and `value`. Order by `page, table_index, "row", col` to read cells in layout order, and pivot back to a grid with conditional aggregation over `row`/`col`. Ready-to-run SQL lives in the example queries.

## Columns

| column | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `page` | INTEGER | 1-based page number the cell is on. |
| `table_index` | INTEGER | 0-based table ordinal within the page. |
| `row` | INTEGER | 0-based row index in the table (SQL keyword: quote as `"row"`). |
| `col` | INTEGER | 0-based column index within the table. |
| `value` | VARCHAR | Cell text (NULL for an empty/missing cell). |

## Notes

The `row` column is a SQL keyword -- quote it as `"row"`. Pages without a detectable table produce no rows. Call by keyword (`pdf := ...`, optional `page := N`).

vgi.example_queries.description: Count the detected table cells on page 1
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS cells FROM pdf.main.tables(pdf := 'test/sql/data/table.pdf', page := 1)

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
# pages

Table function returning **one row per page** of a PDF with its physical geometry: `page` (1-based), `width` and `height` in PDF points (1 pt = 1/72 inch), and `rotation` in degrees. Call by keyword: `pages(pdf := '...')`, where `pdf` is a `VARCHAR` path or a `BLOB` of raw bytes.

Use it to learn how many pages a document has and each page's size/orientation -- e.g. to detect landscape vs portrait pages, find oversized pages, or drive per-page rendering.

**Edge cases:** a NULL `pdf` is rejected with a clean argument error; an unreadable/encrypted PDF surfaces a clean DuckDB error (not a crash). Output streams in bounded slices so even very large documents page safely over every transport.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# List PDF Page Geometry

Returns the geometry of every page in a PDF, one row per page: the 1-based page number and each page's width, height, and rotation.

## Example

Calling `pdf.main.pages(pdf := 'report.pdf')` yields one row per page; a US-Letter portrait page reports a width of `612` and a height of `792` (points) with a rotation of `0`. Restrict to landscape pages by keeping rows where `width` exceeds `height`. Ready-to-run SQL lives in the example queries.

## Columns

| column | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `page` | INTEGER | 1-based page number. |
| `width` | DOUBLE | Page width in PDF points. |
| `height` | DOUBLE | Page height in PDF points. |
| `rotation` | INTEGER | Page rotation in degrees (0/90/180/270). |

## Notes

Dimensions are in PDF points (1/72 inch). Call the function by keyword (`pdf := ...`). A NULL `pdf` raises an argument error; an unreadable document raises a clean error.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
# pdf_metadata

Return the PDF's **document information dictionary** as a `MAP(VARCHAR, VARCHAR)` -- keys such as `Title`, `Author`, `Subject`, `Creator`, `Producer`, `CreationDate`, and `ModDate`. The `pdf` argument is a `VARCHAR` path or a `BLOB`.

Index a single field with `pdf_metadata(...)['Title']`, or expand the whole map with `UNNEST(map_entries(...))`. Use it to catalog documents, sort by author, or extract titles.

**Edge cases:** keys present depend on the producer (any subset may be missing); a NULL input or an unreadable PDF returns NULL. Never raises.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# Read PDF Document Metadata

Extracts the document information dictionary (Title, Author, Producer, dates, ...) as a `MAP(VARCHAR, VARCHAR)`.

## Example

Index a single field with `pdf.main.pdf_metadata('report.pdf')['Title']`, or expand the whole map with `map_entries(...)` to list every key/value pair. Typical keys are `Title`, `Author`, `Subject`, `Creator`, `Producer`, `CreationDate`, and `ModDate`. Ready-to-run SQL lives in the example queries.

## Notes

Available keys vary by the tool that produced the PDF. Returns `NULL` for a NULL input or an unreadable document.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT pdf.main.pdf_metadata('test/sql/data/meta.pdf')['Title'] AS title

vgi.example_queries.description: Author from PDF bytes' metadata (NULL for non-PDF bytes)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT pdf.main.pdf_metadata('not-a-pdf'::BLOB)['Author'] AS author

# form_fields

Return the values of an **AcroForm** (fillable PDF form) as a `MAP(VARCHAR, VARCHAR)` mapping each field's fully-qualified name to its current value. The `pdf` argument is a `VARCHAR` path or a `BLOB`.

Use it to read submitted form data -- applications, invoices, government forms -- straight into SQL, then pivot fields into columns with `['field_name']` lookups.

**Edge cases:** a document with no AcroForm yields an empty map; checkbox/radio values are the export value strings; a NULL input or unreadable PDF returns NULL. Never raises.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# Extract PDF Form Fields

Reads filled-in AcroForm field values from a fillable PDF, returning a `MAP(VARCHAR, VARCHAR)` of field name to value.

## Notes

A PDF without a form returns an empty map. Returns `NULL` for a NULL input or an unreadable document.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
# is_encrypted

Return `TRUE` if the PDF is **encrypted** (password/permissions protected), `FALSE` if it is plain, or `NULL` if the bytes are not a readable PDF at all. The `pdf` argument is a `VARCHAR` path or a `BLOB` of bytes.

Use it to triage a batch of documents before processing -- encrypted files cannot be parsed for words/tables/metadata without a password.

**Key behavior:** an encrypted file that has no user password still returns `TRUE`. Encryption is a *successful* answer, not an error, so the function never attempts to brute-force a password and never hangs. NULL input yields NULL.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# Detect PDF Encryption

Reports whether a PDF is encrypted, returning a `BOOLEAN`.

## Example

Calling `pdf.main.is_encrypted('secret.pdf')` returns `true` for a password/permissions protected document and `false` for a plain one. Use it to triage a batch of uploads before parsing, since encrypted files cannot be read for words, tables, or metadata without a password. Ready-to-run SQL lives in the example queries.

## Notes

`TRUE` means the document is password/permissions protected. `NULL` means the input was not a readable PDF. Detection is purely structural -- no password guessing is performed.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT pdf.main.is_encrypted('test/sql/data/form.pdf') AS encrypted

vgi.example_queries.description: Whether a PDF held as bytes is encrypted (NULL for non-PDF bytes)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT pdf.main.is_encrypted('not-a-pdf'::BLOB) AS encrypted

**Key behavior:** an encrypted file that has no user password still returns `TRUE`. Encryption is a *successful* answer, not an error, so the function never attempts to brute-force a password and never hangs. NULL input yields NULL.

# Detect PDF Encryption

Reports whether a PDF is encrypted, returning a `BOOLEAN`.

## Example

Calling `pdf.main.is_encrypted('secret.pdf')` returns `true` for a password/permissions protected document and `false` for a plain one. Use it to triage a batch of uploads before parsing, since encrypted files cannot be read for words, tables, or metadata without a password. Ready-to-run SQL lives in the example queries.

## Notes

`TRUE` means the document is password/permissions protected. `NULL` means the input was not a readable PDF. Detection is purely structural -- no password guessing is performed.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
# render_page

Rasterize **one (1-based) page** of a PDF to a **PNG image** returned as a `BLOB`. Signature `render_page(pdf, page[, dpi])`: `pdf` is a `VARCHAR` path or a `BLOB`, `page` is the 1-based page number, and the optional `dpi` sets the resolution (default 150, capped at 300).

Use it to thumbnail PDFs, preview a page, or feed a page image to a vision model.

**Bounds & edge cases:** the output bitmap area is capped (an enormous page renders at reduced scale rather than exhausting memory); a NULL input, NULL page, out-of-range page, or unreadable PDF returns NULL. Never raises and never OOMs.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# Render PDF Page to Image

Rasterizes a single PDF page to a PNG image, returned as a `BLOB`.

## Example

Calling `pdf.main.render_page('report.pdf', 1)` renders the first page at the default 150 DPI and hands back the raw PNG bytes; pass a third argument to override the resolution, as in `pdf.main.render_page('report.pdf', 1, 72)` for a lighter 72-DPI thumbnail. The `page` argument is 1-based and `dpi` is clamped to 300. The input `pdf` is a `VARCHAR` filesystem path or a `BLOB` of raw bytes. Ready-to-run SQL lives in the example queries.

## Notes

The rendered bitmap area is capped to avoid runaway memory use. Returns `NULL` for a NULL input, an out-of-range page, or an unreadable document.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT octet_length(pdf.main.render_page('test/sql/data/multipage.pdf', 1)) AS png_bytes

workers.tagline: Static PE/ELF/Mach-O analysis — sections, entropy & imports for DuckDB (Python, LIEF)
workers.summary: Defensive malware-triage worker: static, read-only analysis of PE/ELF/Mach-O executables as SQL functions (the binary is never executed)
workers.doc_md:
# Executable Binary Analysis in SQL (PE / ELF / Mach-O)

![LIEF logo](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/lief-project/LIEF/main/doc/sphinx/_static/logo_blue.png)

**Static, read-only malware triage and binary forensics over Apache Arrow** — parse Windows PE, Linux ELF, and macOS Mach-O executables and query their format, architecture, entropy, imports, exports, sections, and strings directly from DuckDB SQL.

The `pe` catalog turns static binary analysis into ordinary SQL. It is built for malware analysts, incident responders, threat hunters, reverse engineers, and anyone running build-provenance or binary-corpus checks at scale. Instead of shelling out to a pile of command-line tools and stitching their output together, you `ATTACH` this worker and `SELECT` the facts you need — across thousands of samples — with the full power of joins, filters, and aggregation. Every input is treated as untrusted and possibly hostile: the worker only **reads and describes** the bytes. It NEVER executes the sample and never resolves an external reference, and malformed, truncated, or non-binary input degrades cleanly to `NULL` (scalars) or no rows (table functions) rather than crashing or hanging.

Cross-format parsing is powered by [LIEF](https://lief.re) (Library to Instrument Executable Formats), a permissive Apache-2.0 library that reads PE, ELF, and Mach-O through one consistent API. See the [LIEF source on GitHub](https://github.com/lief-project/LIEF) and the [LIEF documentation](https://lief.re/doc/stable/index.html) for format details. The worker wraps LIEF in total, crash-proof extractors and exposes them as Arrow-native DuckDB functions; bounds on input size, string counts, and row counts keep even adversarial "bomb" inputs from exhausting memory.

The catalog exposes two shapes of query. **Per-binary facts** answer a single question about a sample — its container format and CPU architecture, its entry point, whether it is code-signed, its build timestamp and import-hash fingerprint, and its whole-file entropy — so they slot directly into a projection or a filter and scale across an entire corpus. **Set-returning functions** expand one binary into many rows — its per-section layout with entropy, its imported and exported symbols, and its printable strings — for row-level IOC hunting, filtering, and joining. Every function accepts the binary as either a filesystem path it opens or raw bytes passed inline, so you can analyze files on disk or blobs already living in a table, and each pairs its narrative with runnable, tested example queries. Static analysis only — the binary is never executed.
workers.readme_sql:
INSTALL vgi FROM community; LOAD vgi;
ATTACH 'pe' (TYPE vgi, LOCATION 'uv run pe_worker.py');

SELECT pe.binary_format('sample.exe');            -- 'PE' | 'ELF' | 'MachO' | NULL
SELECT pe.machine('sample.exe');                  -- 'X86_64', 'ARM64', ...
SELECT pe.is_signed('sample.exe');                -- Authenticode / Mach-O code signature
SELECT pe.imphash('sample.exe');                  -- PE import hash (clustering)
SELECT pe.overall_entropy('sample.exe');          -- 0-8; high => packed/encrypted

SELECT * FROM pe.sections('sample.exe') ORDER BY name;   -- per-section entropy + flags
SELECT * FROM pe.imports('sample.exe');                  -- imported symbols
SELECT * FROM pe.exports('sample.so');                   -- exported symbols
SELECT * FROM pe.strings('sample.exe', min_len := 8);    -- printable strings

example_queries.description: Browse the worker's analysis catalog before owning a binary.
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, kind, formats FROM pe.main.analyses ORDER BY kind, name

example_queries.description: Detect the executable container format of a sample.
example_queries.sql: SELECT pe.main.binary_format('test/sql/data/hello.exe')

example_queries.description: Read the target CPU architecture of a sample.
example_queries.sql: SELECT pe.main.machine('test/sql/data/hello.exe')

example_queries.description: Compute whole-file entropy as a packing/encryption signal.
example_queries.sql: SELECT pe.main.overall_entropy('test/sql/data/hello.exe')

example_queries.description: Fingerprint a PE by its import hash for clustering.
example_queries.sql: SELECT pe.main.imphash('test/sql/data/hello.exe')

example_queries.description: Rank a sample's sections by per-section entropy.
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, entropy FROM pe.main.sections('test/sql/data/hello.exe') ORDER BY entropy DESC

example_queries.description: List the first imported symbols of a sample.
example_queries.sql: SELECT library, function FROM pe.main.imports('test/sql/data/hello.exe') LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: Extract long printable strings for IOC hunting.
example_queries.sql: SELECT seq, value FROM pe.main.strings('test/sql/data/hello.exe', min_len := 8) LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: List the scalar analyses (one value per binary) in category order.
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, category, result FROM pe.main.analyses WHERE kind = 'scalar' ORDER BY category, name

example_queries.description: Which analyses are PE-only?
example_queries.sql: SELECT name FROM pe.main.analyses WHERE formats = 'PE only' ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Count analyses by kind.
example_queries.sql: SELECT kind, count(*) AS n FROM pe.main.analyses GROUP BY kind ORDER BY kind

example_queries.description: Top sections by entropy (a packing signal)
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, virtual_size, raw_size, entropy FROM pe.main.sections('test/sql/data/hello.exe') ORDER BY entropy DESC LIMIT 5

example_queries.description: List the sections of a PE with their per-section entropy.
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, entropy FROM pe.main.sections('test/sql/data/hello.exe') ORDER BY entropy DESC LIMIT 5;

example_queries.description: Flag high-entropy sections (a packing/encryption signal).
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, entropy FROM pe.main.sections('test/sql/data/hello.exe') WHERE entropy > 6;

example_queries.description: Count the imported symbols of a PE.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS imports FROM pe.main.imports('test/sql/data/hello.exe');

example_queries.description: List exported symbols of a Mach-O binary.
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, address FROM pe.main.exports('test/sql/data/hello_macho') ORDER BY name;

example_queries.description: Extract long printable strings from a binary.
example_queries.sql: SELECT seq, value FROM pe.main.strings('test/sql/data/hello.exe', min_len := 8) ORDER BY seq LIMIT 5;

example_queries.description: Printable strings of a binary file
example_queries.sql: SELECT seq, value FROM pe.main.strings('test/sql/data/hello.exe') ORDER BY seq LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: How many strings are at least 8 chars long
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS long_strings FROM pe.main.strings('test/sql/data/hello.exe', min_len := 8)

example_queries.description: Extract printable strings from raw BLOB bytes (no file needed)
example_queries.sql: SELECT seq, value FROM pe.main.strings('demo payload: printable ASCII recovered straight from a BLOB'::BLOB, min_len := 5) ORDER BY seq

example_queries.description: Imported symbols of a binary file
example_queries.sql: SELECT library, function FROM pe.main.imports('test/sql/data/hello.exe') ORDER BY library, function LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: Overall entropy of binary bytes
example_queries.sql: SELECT pe.main.overall_entropy((SELECT content FROM read_blob('test/sql/data/hello.exe')))

example_queries.description: Detect the executable format of bytes
example_queries.sql: SELECT pe.main.binary_format((SELECT content FROM read_blob('test/sql/data/hello.exe')))

example_queries.description: PE compile timestamp of a binary file
example_queries.sql: SELECT pe.main.compile_timestamp('test/sql/data/hello.exe')

example_queries.description: PE compile timestamp of binary bytes
example_queries.sql: SELECT pe.main.compile_timestamp((SELECT content FROM read_blob('test/sql/data/hello.exe')))

example_queries.description: Entry-point address of a binary file
example_queries.sql: SELECT pe.main.entry_point('test/sql/data/hello.exe')

example_queries.description: Entry-point address of binary bytes
example_queries.sql: SELECT pe.main.entry_point((SELECT content FROM read_blob('test/sql/data/hello.exe')))

example_queries.description: Architecture of binary bytes
example_queries.sql: SELECT pe.main.machine((SELECT content FROM read_blob('test/sql/data/hello.exe')))

example_queries.description: Import hash of PE bytes
example_queries.sql: SELECT pe.main.imphash((SELECT content FROM read_blob('test/sql/data/hello.exe')))

example_queries.description: Whether a binary file is code-signed
example_queries.sql: SELECT pe.main.is_signed('test/sql/data/hello.exe')

example_queries.description: Whether binary bytes are code-signed
example_queries.sql: SELECT pe.main.is_signed((SELECT content FROM read_blob('test/sql/data/hello.exe')))

example_queries.description: Section count of a binary file
example_queries.sql: SELECT pe.main.section_count('test/sql/data/hello.exe')

example_queries.description: Section count of binary bytes
example_queries.sql: SELECT pe.main.section_count((SELECT content FROM read_blob('test/sql/data/hello.exe')))

## main

Static analysis of PE/ELF/Mach-O binaries over Apache Arrow.

This schema groups the worker's functions into navigation categories covering format and architecture detection, structural layout, entropy and packing signals, signing and build provenance, imported/exported symbols, and printable-string extraction. Per-binary scalar facts fold into projections and filters; set-returning functions expand a single sample into rows for hunting and joining.

Every function accepts a `VARCHAR` path or a `BLOB` and degrades to NULL / no rows on hostile input. Static (read-only) — the binary is never executed.

tables.comment: Browsable registry of every analysis (scalar/table) this worker exposes (discovery table).

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Browse the worker's own **analysis catalog** — one row per function this worker exposes, so you can discover its capabilities without supplying a binary first. Columns: `name` (the function to call), `kind` (`scalar` for one value per binary, `table` for many rows per binary), `category` (its navigation slug), `formats` (which of PE / ELF / Mach-O it applies to), and `result` (what it returns). This is a static registry: scanning it reads no file and touches no network.

Use it as the entry point for planning: filter by `kind` to find scalars that fold into a projection, by `formats` to see what is PE-only (e.g. `imphash`, `compile_timestamp`), or by `category` to enumerate a family (e.g. all `signing` analyses). Then call the named function on an actual binary path or `BLOB`.

| `result` | VARCHAR | What the analysis returns. |

functions.name: sections
functions.comment: Per-section (name, virtual_size, raw_size, entropy, flags) of a binary (VARCHAR path)

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Enumerate the **sections** of a binary, one row per section, with size and **per-section Shannon entropy** — the workhorse table for layout-level triage. Columns: `name`, `virtual_size`, `raw_size`, `entropy` (0–8), `characteristics` (PE flags; empty for ELF/Mach-O). Accepts a `VARCHAR` path or a `BLOB`; unparseable or non-binary input yields **no rows** (never an error).

Use it to find *where* in a file suspicious data lives: a high-entropy (`> ~7`) `.text`/code section, an executable+writable section, or a section whose raw size dwarfs its virtual size all point to packing, embedded payloads, or self-modifying code. Cross-reference with `pe.entry_point(...)` to confirm the entry point lands in a sane section. Static read-only; the binary is never executed.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## sections

One row per section of the binary, with sizes and per-section entropy.

### Returns

| column | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | VARCHAR | Section name (e.g. `.text`, `.data`, `__TEXT`). |
| `virtual_size` | BIGINT | Size in bytes when mapped into memory. |
| `raw_size` | BIGINT | Size in bytes on disk. |
| `entropy` | DOUBLE | Per-section Shannon entropy (0-8); high (>~7) suggests packing/encryption. |
| `characteristics` | VARCHAR | Comma-joined section flags (PE only; empty for ELF/Mach-O). |

### Notes

`characteristics` is populated for PE only. High `entropy` (`> ~7`) localizes packing/encryption to a specific section; a large `raw_size`-vs-`virtual_size` gap or an entry point outside an executable section are further packing signals. Unparseable input returns no rows.

vgi.example_queries.description: Top sections by entropy (a packing signal)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT name, virtual_size, raw_size, entropy FROM pe.main.sections('test/sql/data/hello.exe') ORDER BY entropy DESC LIMIT 5

vgi.executable_examples.description: List the sections of a PE with their per-section entropy.
vgi.executable_examples.sql: SELECT name, entropy FROM pe.main.sections('test/sql/data/hello.exe') ORDER BY entropy DESC LIMIT 5

vgi.executable_examples.description: Flag high-entropy sections (a packing/encryption signal).
vgi.executable_examples.sql: SELECT name, entropy FROM pe.main.sections('test/sql/data/hello.exe') WHERE entropy > 6

vgi.executable_examples.description: Count the imported symbols of a PE.
vgi.executable_examples.sql: SELECT count(*) AS imports FROM pe.main.imports('test/sql/data/hello.exe')

vgi.executable_examples.description: List exported symbols of a Mach-O binary.
vgi.executable_examples.sql: SELECT name, address FROM pe.main.exports('test/sql/data/hello_macho') ORDER BY name

vgi.executable_examples.description: Extract long printable strings from a binary.
vgi.executable_examples.sql: SELECT seq, value FROM pe.main.strings('test/sql/data/hello.exe', min_len := 8) ORDER BY seq LIMIT 5

functions.name: strings

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Extract **printable strings** from a binary, one row per string, as `(seq, value)` in file order. It recovers both ASCII and UTF-16LE runs at least `min_len` characters long (`min_len` defaults to 5 and is passed as the named argument `min_len :=`). Accepts a `VARCHAR` path or a `BLOB`; output is capped for safety against string-bomb input, and unparseable input yields no rows.

Strings are the fastest way to surface human-readable indicators inside an opaque binary: URLs, IP addresses, file paths, registry keys, command lines, mutex names, embedded error messages, and crypto constants. Filter `value` with SQL `LIKE`/regex to hunt for IOCs across a corpus. Raise `min_len` to cut noise from packed samples. Static read-only; the binary is never executed.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## strings

One row per printable string (ASCII + UTF-16LE) of length `>= min_len`.

### Arguments

- `binary` — a `VARCHAR` path or a `BLOB`.
- `min_len` (named, default 5) — minimum string length to report.

### Returns

| column | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `seq` | BIGINT | 1-based ordinal of the string in file order. |
| `value` | VARCHAR | Printable ASCII/UTF-16 string (length >= `min_len`). |

### Notes

Output is bounded against string-bomb inputs. Use `WHERE value LIKE '%http%'` (and friends) to hunt URLs, paths, registry keys, and other IOCs; raise `min_len` to reduce noise on packed samples.

vgi.example_queries.description: Printable strings of a binary file
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT seq, value FROM pe.main.strings('test/sql/data/hello.exe') ORDER BY seq LIMIT 10

vgi.example_queries.description: How many strings are at least 8 chars long
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS long_strings FROM pe.main.strings('test/sql/data/hello.exe', min_len := 8)

vgi.example_queries.description: Extract printable strings from raw BLOB bytes (no file needed)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT seq, value FROM pe.main.strings('demo payload: printable ASCII recovered straight from a BLOB'::BLOB, min_len := 5) ORDER BY seq

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: seq
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: 1-based ordinal of the string in file order.

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: value
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Printable ASCII/UTF-16 string (length >= `min_len`).

functions.name: imports
functions.comment: Imported symbols (library, function) of a binary (VARCHAR path)

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Enumerate the **imported symbols** of a binary, one row per import, as `(library, function)`. For PE the `library` is the DLL (e.g. `KERNEL32.dll`) and `function` the imported API, or `ordinal#N` when imported by ordinal; for ELF/Mach-O `library` is empty and `function` is the symbol. Accepts a `VARCHAR` path or a `BLOB`; unparseable input yields no rows.

The import table is one of the richest behavioral fingerprints of a binary: which APIs it pulls in (networking, crypto, process injection, registry, file I/O) sketches what it *can* do without running it, and the normalized import set underlies `pe.imphash(...)` clustering. Watch for tiny import tables (a packer that resolves APIs at runtime) and for suspicious API combinations. Static read-only.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## imports

One row per imported symbol, as `(library, function)`.

### Returns

| column | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `library` | VARCHAR | Imported library/DLL name (empty for ELF/Mach-O). |
| `function` | VARCHAR | Imported symbol name, or `ordinal#N` when imported by ordinal. |

### Notes

PE rows carry the DLL in `library` (functions imported by ordinal appear as `ordinal#N`); ELF/Mach-O leave `library` empty. A suspiciously small import table often means runtime API resolution (a packing/evasion signal). Feeds `pe.imphash(...)`.

vgi.example_queries.description: Imported symbols of a binary file
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT library, function FROM pe.main.imports('test/sql/data/hello.exe') ORDER BY library, function LIMIT 10

vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Imported library/DLL name (empty for ELF/Mach-O).

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: function
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Imported symbol name, or `ordinal#N` when imported by ordinal.

functions.name: exports
functions.comment: Exported symbols (name, address) of a binary (VARCHAR path)

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Enumerate the **exported symbols** of a binary, one row per export, as `(name, address)` where `address` is the symbol's address/value (0 when unavailable). Exports are typical of shared libraries (DLLs, `.so`, `.dylib`) and plugin-style modules. Accepts a `VARCHAR` path or a `BLOB`; unparseable input or a binary with no exports yields no rows.

Use it to understand a module's public API surface, to spot a DLL whose exports mimic a legitimate system library (a side-loading / proxying tactic), or to match named exports against known-bad indicators. Static read-only; the binary is never executed.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## exports

One row per exported symbol, as `(name, address)`.

### Returns

| column | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | VARCHAR | Exported symbol name. |
| `address` | UBIGINT | Symbol address/value (0 when unavailable). |

### Notes

Most relevant for shared libraries / plugins; executables often export nothing (no rows). `address` is `0` when the value is unavailable. Exports that impersonate a known system library are a DLL side-loading signal.

vgi.example_queries.description: Exported symbols of a shared binary
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT name, address FROM pe.main.exports('test/sql/data/hello_macho') ORDER BY name

functions.name: exports
functions.comment: Exported symbols (name, address) of a binary (BLOB bytes)

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Enumerate the **exported symbols** of a binary, one row per export, as `(name, address)` where `address` is the symbol's address/value (0 when unavailable). Exports are typical of shared libraries (DLLs, `.so`, `.dylib`) and plugin-style modules. Accepts a `VARCHAR` path or a `BLOB`; unparseable input or a binary with no exports yields no rows.

Use it to understand a module's public API surface, to spot a DLL whose exports mimic a legitimate system library (a side-loading / proxying tactic), or to match named exports against known-bad indicators. Static read-only; the binary is never executed.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## exports

One row per exported symbol, as `(name, address)`.

### Returns

| column | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | VARCHAR | Exported symbol name. |
| `address` | UBIGINT | Symbol address/value (0 when unavailable). |

### Notes

Most relevant for shared libraries / plugins; executables often export nothing (no rows). `address` is `0` when the value is unavailable. Exports that impersonate a known system library are a DLL side-loading signal.

vgi.example_queries.description: Exported symbols of a shared binary
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT name, address FROM pe.main.exports('test/sql/data/hello_macho') ORDER BY name

functions.name: overall_entropy
functions.comment: Shannon entropy (bits/byte, 0-8) of a binary (VARCHAR path); high => packed/encrypted

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Return the **Shannon entropy** of the entire file as a `DOUBLE` in bits-per-byte on a `0.0`–`8.0` scale. It is computed over the raw file bytes (independent of the section layout), so it works even when LIEF can't fully resolve the structure — but it still returns `NULL` for NULL or non-binary input so a random text blob isn't given a misleading number.

High whole-file entropy (typically `> ~7.0`) is the single strongest cheap signal of **packing, compression, or encryption**: most native code sits around `5.5`–`6.5`, while packed/encrypted payloads push toward `8.0`. Use it as a first-pass triage filter, then drill into per-section entropy via `pe.sections(...)`. Static read-only.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## overall_entropy

Whole-file Shannon entropy as a `DOUBLE`, in bits/byte on a `0`–`8` scale.

### Interpreting the value

| range | typical meaning |
|---|---|
| ~5.5–6.5 | ordinary native code/data |
| > ~7.0 | likely packed, compressed, or encrypted |

Computed over raw bytes (independent of section layout). Returns `NULL` for non-binary input. For where the high entropy lives, see per-section entropy in `pe.sections(...)`.

vgi.example_queries.description: Overall entropy of a binary file
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT pe.main.overall_entropy('test/sql/data/hello.exe')

vgi.example_queries.description: Overall entropy of binary bytes
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT pe.main.overall_entropy((SELECT content FROM read_blob('test/sql/data/hello.exe')))

tags.vgi.title: Whole-File Shannon Entropy

functions.name: binary_format
functions.comment: Executable format ('PE'/'ELF'/'MachO') of a binary (VARCHAR path), or NULL

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Detect the **container format** of an executable image and return it as a short string: `PE` (Windows portable executable), `ELF` (Linux/Unix), or `MachO` (macOS). Pass the binary as either a `VARCHAR` filesystem path the worker opens or a `BLOB` of raw bytes. Returns `NULL` when the input is NULL, empty, truncated, or not a recognizable executable, so it is safe to run across a mixed corpus.

Use this first when triaging an unknown sample: the format decides which downstream signals are meaningful (e.g. `imphash` and `compile_timestamp` are PE-only). The binary is parsed statically and **never executed**.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## binary_format

Returns the executable container format of a binary as `PE`, `ELF`, or `MachO`.

Call it with a single argument — a `VARCHAR` filesystem path the worker opens, or a `BLOB` of raw bytes — and it returns the container-format string (for example `PE` for a Windows executable). Returns `NULL` for NULL, empty, or unrecognizable input — never an error. Typically the first step in a triage pipeline because the format gates which other functions apply. Ready-to-run example queries are attached to this function.

vgi.example_queries.description: Detect the executable format of a file
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT pe.main.binary_format('test/sql/data/hello.exe')

vgi.example_queries.description: Detect the executable format of bytes
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT pe.main.binary_format((SELECT content FROM read_blob('test/sql/data/hello.exe')))

tags.vgi.title: Detect Executable Format

functions.name: compile_timestamp
functions.comment: PE build timestamp (TimeDateStamp) of a binary (VARCHAR path); NULL for ELF/Mach-O

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Return the PE **build timestamp** (the COFF header `TimeDateStamp`) as a `TIMESTAMP`. This is **PE-only**: ELF and Mach-O have no equivalent header field and return `NULL`, as does any unparseable input. The raw field is a Unix epoch in seconds; the worker scales it to microsecond-precision Arrow timestamp.

Use it for build-provenance and timeline analysis — bucketing samples by build date, spotting implausible values (the field is attacker-controllable, so a zero, far-future, or suspiciously round timestamp is itself a signal), and correlating related builds. Treat the value as a *claim*, not ground truth.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## compile_timestamp

The PE COFF `TimeDateStamp` as a `TIMESTAMP` (PE only).

### Usage

```sql
SELECT pe.compile_timestamp('sample.exe');
```

Returns `NULL` for ELF, Mach-O, and unparseable input. The field is stored as a Unix epoch (seconds) and is **attacker-controllable** — implausible values (zero, far future, round numbers) are a triage signal, not an error.

vgi.example_queries.description: PE compile timestamp of a binary file
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT pe.main.compile_timestamp('test/sql/data/hello.exe')

vgi.example_queries.description: PE compile timestamp of binary bytes
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT pe.main.compile_timestamp((SELECT content FROM read_blob('test/sql/data/hello.exe')))

tags.vgi.title: PE Build Timestamp

functions.name: entry_point
functions.comment: Entry-point virtual address of a binary (VARCHAR path), or NULL

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Return the **entry-point address** of an executable as an unsigned 64-bit integer — the virtual address at which execution would begin (the PE `AddressOfEntryPoint` rebased to the image base, the ELF/Mach-O entry address). Returns `NULL` for unparseable input. The worker only reports the address; it never transfers control there.

Use it to fingerprint a build, to spot an entry point that lands outside the expected code section (a classic packer/injection tell when correlated with `sections` and `overall_entropy`), or as a join key when clustering related samples.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## entry_point

The virtual address where execution begins, as a `UBIGINT`.

### Usage

```sql
SELECT pe.entry_point('sample.exe');   -- e.g. 5392
```

Returns `NULL` when the binary cannot be parsed. Compare against the address ranges from `pe.sections(...)` to check that the entry point falls inside an executable section — an entry point in a high-entropy or writable section is a common packing/injection signal.

vgi.example_queries.description: Entry-point address of a binary file
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT pe.main.entry_point('test/sql/data/hello.exe')

vgi.example_queries.description: Entry-point address of binary bytes
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT pe.main.entry_point((SELECT content FROM read_blob('test/sql/data/hello.exe')))

tags.vgi.title: Entry-Point Address

functions.name: machine
functions.comment: Architecture of a binary (VARCHAR path), e.g. 'X86_64'/'ARM64', or NULL

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Return the **target CPU architecture** of a binary as a normalized string, e.g. `X86_64`, `I386`, `ARM64`, `ARM`. It reads LIEF's *abstract* architecture so the answer is comparable across PE, ELF, and Mach-O rather than each format's raw machine code. Returns `NULL` for unparseable input.

Use it to filter or partition a corpus by architecture (e.g. find all ARM64 samples), to sanity-check that a sample matches the platform it claims, or to route a sample to the right disassembler. Static read-only; the binary is never executed.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## machine

The target CPU architecture as a normalized string (`X86_64`, `I386`, `ARM64`, `ARM`, …).

### Usage

```sql
SELECT pe.machine('sample.exe');   -- 'X86_64'
```

Uses LIEF's abstract architecture so PE / ELF / Mach-O report on a common scale. Returns `NULL` for input that cannot be parsed.

functions.name: imphash
functions.comment: PE import hash (for clustering) of a binary (VARCHAR path); NULL for ELF/Mach-O

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Return the **imphash** (import hash) of a PE: the MD5 over the normalized, ordered list of imported library/function names. It is **PE-only** — ELF and Mach-O, and any unparseable input, return `NULL`. Two PEs built from the same source/toolchain with the same import table share an imphash even if their bytes differ, which makes it a classic **clustering / family-attribution** key for malware triage.

Use it to `GROUP BY` related samples, to pivot from one known-bad sample to others, or to match against threat-intel imphash blocklists. Caveat: packers and import obfuscation can collapse or mangle the import table, so an imphash is a strong-but-not-definitive link. Static read-only; the binary is never executed.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## imphash

The PE import hash — MD5 of the normalized import table — as a hex string (PE only).

Call it with one argument (a `VARCHAR` path or a `BLOB`) to get the sample's 32-character hex import hash, or `NULL` for ELF, Mach-O, and unparseable input. Because two PEs built from the same toolchain and import table share an imphash, it is a classic clustering / family-attribution key: group a corpus by this value to bucket related samples. Packing or import obfuscation weakens the signal, so treat a match as a strong hint rather than proof. Ready-to-run example queries are attached to this function.

vgi.example_queries.description: Import hash of a PE file
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT pe.main.imphash('test/sql/data/hello.exe')

vgi.example_queries.description: Import hash of PE bytes
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT pe.main.imphash((SELECT content FROM read_blob('test/sql/data/hello.exe')))

tags.vgi.title: PE Import Hash (imphash)

functions.name: is_signed
functions.comment: True if a binary (VARCHAR path) carries a code signature (PE Authenticode / Mach-O)

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Return whether a binary carries an embedded **code signature**: `true`/`false`, or `NULL` for unparseable input. The check is format-aware — PE Authenticode signatures, Mach-O embedded code signatures — and ELF, which has no native embedded-signature concept, always reports `false`. A `false` result is a *successful* answer (the file simply isn't signed), not a parse failure.

Use it as a quick trust signal during triage: unsigned system-looking binaries, or binaries that masquerade as signed vendors but report `false`, are worth a closer look. Note: this reports the *presence* of a signature, not whether the signature is valid or trusted. Static read-only check; the binary is never executed.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## is_signed

Boolean: does the binary carry an embedded code signature?

### Behavior by format

| format | meaning |
|---|---|
| PE | has an Authenticode signature |
| Mach-O | has an embedded code signature |
| ELF | always `false` (no native embedded signature) |

Returns `NULL` only for input that cannot be parsed. This reports *presence*, not cryptographic *validity* — verify the chain separately if trust matters.

vgi.example_queries.description: Whether a binary file is code-signed
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT pe.main.is_signed('test/sql/data/hello.exe')

vgi.example_queries.description: Whether binary bytes are code-signed
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT pe.main.is_signed((SELECT content FROM read_blob('test/sql/data/hello.exe')))

tags.vgi.title: Binary Is Code-Signed

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Return the **number of sections** in a binary as an integer (PE sections, ELF sections, Mach-O sections across segments). Returns `NULL` for unparseable input.

Returns `NULL` for input that cannot be parsed. This is the scalar summary of `pe.sections(...)`; very low or very high counts are mild packing/obfuscation signals.

workers.doc_md:
# perf — Decode Linux `perf.data` Profiles in SQL

**Load a fleet of Linux `perf.data` captures and analyze them relationally in DuckDB.** `perf script` and `perf report` are interactive, single-file CLIs; this worker turns the binary `perf.data` format into ordinary SQL tables so SRE and observability teams can run **CI performance-regression gates** and bulk profile analysis — diffing captures, ranking hot instruction pointers, and joining samples to the modules they fell in — without leaving SQL.

Attach the worker, then point `search_path` at its schema:

```sql
ATTACH 'perf' (TYPE vgi, LOCATION '/path/to/perf-worker');
SET search_path = 'perf.main';
```

You then call a decode function with a `perf.data` path (or the raw capture bytes) and analyze the rows in ordinary SQL. The marquee move is an address-range join of each sample's raw `ip` to the memory mapping it fell in, ranking the hottest modules — that query, and others, are shipped ready-to-run in this worker's example queries and per-function documentation. Browse the `perf.main.functions` reference table to see every function and the columns it returns before you have a capture in hand.

**What you get.** Each decode function takes one source argument — a path to a `perf.data` file, or the raw capture bytes already loaded into a column — and streams the decoded records out as ordinary typed rows. The profiling samples (with their raw call chains), the process address-space mappings, the recorded event attributes, the process/thread names, and the capture-wide host metadata are each a separate function. Ranges, IDs, and timestamps come through as real integer columns so they join and aggregate directly in SQL.

**Raw IPs, by design.** Instruction pointers and call-chain frames are emitted **unsymbolicated**. The `mmaps` records — with their `build_id`s — are what make a raw `ip` interpretable: range-join `samples.ip BETWEEN m.addr AND m.addr + m.len` to find the backing DSO, then feed `build_id` + the IP to **`vgi-symbols`** for native symbolication, mirroring the pprof / minidump → symbols loop. Collapsed-stack text files throw the mmap + build-id information away; the binary `perf.data` path keeps it.

**Scope.** v1 decodes the **binary** `perf.data` record structure only. The folded/collapsed-stack text path is intentionally out of scope (DuckDB's `read_csv` already covers it), as is symbolication (→ vgi-symbols) and `perf.data` *writing*. `perf.data` varies by kernel and perf build; any `HEADER_*` feature section a capture omits comes back as NULL columns rather than failing the query.

## perf — main

The single schema for the `perf` worker: the decode functions that turn a Linux profiling capture into typed SQL rows. They are grouped into three areas:

- **Profile samples** — the per-event rows with their raw, unsymbolicated call chains.
- **Address space** — the process memory mappings and build-ids that make a raw instruction pointer interpretable.
- **Capture context** — process/thread names, the sampled event attributes, and the capture-wide host metadata.

Every decode function takes a `perf.data` path or the raw capture bytes.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Decode the memory-mapping records (PERF_RECORD_MMAP / MMAP2) of a Linux perf.data capture into rows — which shared object / DSO backs each range of a process's address space. `src` is a `VARCHAR` path or a `BLOB` of perf.data bytes. Columns: `pid`, `tid`, `addr` (start address), `len` (length in bytes — the mapping covers [addr, addr+len)), `pgoff` (offset into the file), `filename` (e.g. '/usr/lib/libc.so.6', '[vdso]'), and `build_id` (the DSO build-id as lowercase hex, from an inline MMAP2 build-id record or the HEADER_BUILD_ID feature section; NULL when unknown). These are what make a sample `ip` interpretable: join `samples.ip BETWEEN m.addr AND m.addr + m.len` to find which DSO an IP fell in, and feed `build_id` + the IP to vgi-symbols for native symbolication. Collapsed-stack text files throw this information away; the binary perf.data keeps it.

IPs are unsymbolicated — join to `mmaps` + vgi-symbols to resolve. Rank raw IPs by frequency to find the hottest addresses in a capture.

workers.doc_md:
# PII Detection & Redaction in SQL

![Microsoft Presidio logo](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/microsoft/presidio/main/docs/assets/dps-icon.svg)

**Find, redact, and anonymize personally-identifiable information (PII) in free text directly from DuckDB SQL** — person names, email addresses, phone numbers, credit-card numbers, US SSNs, locations, URLs, IP addresses and more — powered by [Microsoft Presidio](https://microsoft.github.io/presidio/).

This extension brings privacy scrubbing, data-loss-prevention (DLP) checks, and PII auditing to your data warehouse without exporting a single row to an external service. It is built for data engineers, privacy and security teams, and analysts who need to sanitize logs, user-generated content, support transcripts, and other text columns before sharing, training, or archiving them. Every function runs in-process over Apache Arrow, so detection happens right next to your data and PII never leaves your environment.

Detection is powered by [Microsoft Presidio](https://github.com/microsoft/presidio) (its analyzer and anonymizer engines) backed by a [spaCy](https://spacy.io/) named-entity-recognition pipeline using the pinned `en_core_web_sm` model from the [spaCy models](https://github.com/explosion/spacy-models) collection. Presidio combines this NLP model with pattern recognizers and checksum validation (for example, Luhn validation of credit-card numbers) to flag a broad catalog of entity types, each with a confidence score and character offsets you can inspect or threshold.

## What you can do

Two complementary capabilities are grouped in the `main` schema. *Detection* answers whether text holds sensitive data, which categories it holds, and exactly where each value sits (with a confidence score you can threshold). *Redaction* rewrites the text so the sensitive values are gone -- either labelled by the kind of value that was there, or masked so even the shape is hidden. Detection powers filtering, alerting, and auditing; redaction powers safe sharing, export, and archival. Every operation accepts an optional ISO language argument (defaulting to English) and treats NULL or blank input gracefully.

```sql
SELECT pii.main.redact('Call John Smith at john@example.com');
-- 'Call <PERSON> at <EMAIL_ADDRESS>'
```

Learn more from the [Presidio documentation](https://microsoft.github.io/presidio/), the [Presidio source repository](https://github.com/microsoft/presidio), and the [spaCy NLP library](https://github.com/explosion/spaCy).

example_queries.description: Flag whether text contains any PII (a boolean predicate for filtering).
example_queries.sql: SELECT pii.main.has_pii('Call John Smith at john@example.com')

example_queries.description: Replace each PII entity with a <TYPE> tag naming its kind.
example_queries.sql: SELECT pii.main.redact('Call John Smith at john@example.com')

example_queries.description: Mask each PII entity's characters with '*'.
example_queries.sql: SELECT pii.main.anonymize('Call John Smith at john@example.com')

example_queries.description: List the distinct PII entity types present in text.
example_queries.sql: SELECT pii.main.pii_types('Call John Smith at john@example.com')

example_queries.description: Enumerate every detected PII entity with its offsets and confidence.
example_queries.sql: SELECT entity_type, text, start, end_pos, score FROM pii.main.detect_pii('Call John Smith at john@example.com') ORDER BY start

example_queries.description: Discover which entity types the analyzer can detect.
example_queries.sql: SELECT entity_type FROM pii.main.supported_entities() ORDER BY entity_type

example_queries.description: Count how many PII entity types the analyzer recognises.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS n FROM pii.main.entity_types

example_queries.description: Check whether the analyzer recognises credit-card numbers.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) > 0 AS detects_cards FROM pii.main.entity_types WHERE entity_type = 'CREDIT_CARD'

example_queries.description: Keep only high-confidence detections via score_threshold.
example_queries.sql: SELECT entity_type, text FROM pii.main.detect_pii('Email john@example.com', score_threshold := 0.8)

example_queries.description: Detect whether text contains any PII.
example_queries.sql: SELECT pii.main.has_pii('Call John Smith at john@example.com') AS has_pii;

example_queries.description: Tag-redact each PII entity with its <TYPE> label.
example_queries.sql: SELECT pii.main.redact('Call John Smith at john@example.com') AS redacted;

example_queries.description: Mask each PII entity's characters with '*'.
example_queries.sql: SELECT pii.main.anonymize('Call John Smith at john@example.com') AS masked;

example_queries.description: List the distinct PII entity types present in text.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## main

The main schema groups every PII capability in the pii catalog. Reach for it whenever you need to find, scrub, or audit personally-identifiable information in a text column. Two kinds of work live here.

- **Detection** tells you about the PII in a value without changing it: whether any is present (a boolean predicate for filtering), which distinct entity types occur (as a sorted array), the full per-occurrence detail (one row per entity with its type, character offsets, and confidence score you can threshold), and which entity types the analyzer is able to recognise at all.
- **Redaction** rewrites the text so the sensitive values are removed -- either replaced by a tag naming the kind of value that was there, or masked character-for-character so even the shape is hidden.

The per-row operations are scalars usable inline in any projection or predicate; the per-occurrence and discovery operations are table functions. Every operation takes an optional ISO language argument (defaulting to English). Detection is powered by Microsoft Presidio with a spaCy NLP model; NULL or blank input is handled gracefully (NULL or no rows). Detection tags a broad set of entity types (PERSON, EMAIL_ADDRESS, PHONE_NUMBER, CREDIT_CARD, US_SSN, LOCATION, URL, IP_ADDRESS, and more), each with a confidence score you can raise via the `score_threshold` argument to trade recall for precision.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# main

PII detection and redaction over free text, exposed as DuckDB scalar and table functions.

## Detection vs. redaction

The schema offers two complementary kinds of operation. **Detection** inspects text without changing it -- flag whether any PII is present, summarise which entity types occur, enumerate each occurrence with its character offsets and confidence score, and introspect which entity types the analyzer can recognise. **Redaction** rewrites text so the sensitive values are removed -- either tagged by the kind of value or masked so even its shape is hidden.

## Notes

Per-row operations are scalars (usable inline in any projection or predicate) and take an optional trailing `language`; the per-occurrence and discovery operations are table functions that accept named arguments (`language :=`, `score_threshold :=`). Raise `score_threshold` on the table functions to keep only high-confidence detections, and pass `language` to scan non-English text. Powered by [Microsoft Presidio](https://microsoft.github.io/presidio/).

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## detect_pii

A table function that returns **one row per detected PII entity** in the input text, with the matched substring, its character offsets, the entity type, and the detection confidence. Use it when you need the full, per-occurrence detail -- e.g. to highlight spans, build a redaction map, or audit exactly what was found and where.

- **Arguments:** `text` (positional `VARCHAR`); optional named `language := 'en'` and `score_threshold := 0.5` (minimum confidence in `[0, 1]`).
- **Returns:** rows of `(entity_type, text, start, end_pos, score)`. `end_pos` is exclusive (named with a `_pos` suffix because `end` is a SQL keyword).
- **Edge cases:** `NULL`, empty, or whitespace-only text yields **no rows**; raising `score_threshold` drops low-confidence guesses.

For a per-row boolean or a list of types, use the `has_pii` / `pii_types` scalars instead. Backed by Microsoft Presidio.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# detect_pii

Expand text into one row per detected PII entity, with offsets and confidence.

## Signature

`detect_pii(text[, language := 'en'][, score_threshold := 0.5])` — the single positional `text` argument is required; `language` and `score_threshold` are optional named arguments.

## Result columns

Each row is `(entity_type, text, start, end_pos, score)`: the entity type, the matched substring, its inclusive start and exclusive end character offsets, and the detection confidence in `[0, 1]`.

## Notes

`end_pos` is the exclusive end offset (the column is named `end_pos` because `end` is a SQL keyword). NULL/blank text returns no rows. Raise `score_threshold` to keep only high-confidence detections. See this function's example queries for runnable demonstrations.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## redact

Return the input text with every detected PII span replaced by a tag naming its entity type, e.g. `<PERSON>` or `<EMAIL_ADDRESS>`. Use it when you want a human-readable, *self-documenting* scrub that preserves which kind of value was removed (useful for audit, debugging, and downstream classification).

- **Input:** a `VARCHAR` of free text; an optional second argument is the ISO language code (defaults to `'en'`).
- **Output:** `VARCHAR` -- the same text with each entity replaced by `<TYPE>`.
- **Example:** `'Call John Smith at john@example.com'` -> `'Call <PERSON> at <EMAIL_ADDRESS>'`.
- **Edge cases:** `NULL`, empty, or whitespace-only input returns `NULL`; text with no PII is returned unchanged.

Contrast with `anonymize`, which masks characters (`****`) instead of labelling them. Backed by Microsoft Presidio (analyzer + anonymizer).
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# redact

Replace each PII entity in text with a tag that names its type, leaving the surrounding text intact.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT pii.main.redact('Call John Smith at john@example.com');
-- 'Call <PERSON> at <EMAIL_ADDRESS>'
```

## Notes

Use `redact` when you want to know *what kind* of value was removed; use `anonymize` when you want the value's shape hidden behind a `*` mask. Accepts an explicit language as the second argument. NULL/blank input yields NULL.

- Returns `true` as soon as any entity (a person name, email, phone number, credit card, US SSN, location, URL, IP address, ...) is detected, otherwise `false`.
- Pass an explicit ISO language as the optional second argument (`has_pii(text, 'en')`) to scan non-English text.
- `NULL`, empty, or whitespace-only input yields `NULL` rather than `false`.

See this function's example queries for a runnable demonstration.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## anonymize

Return the input text with every detected PII span overwritten character-for-character by a `*` mask, so the value is hidden but its length/position is preserved. Use it for display or export where the *shape* of the data can remain but the value must not.

- **Input:** a `VARCHAR` of free text; an optional second argument is the ISO language code (defaults to `'en'`).
- **Output:** `VARCHAR` -- the same text with each entity replaced by `*` characters.
- **Example:** `'Call John Smith at john@example.com'` -> `'Call **** at ****************'`.
- **Edge cases:** `NULL`, empty, or whitespace-only input returns `NULL`; text with no PII is returned unchanged.

Contrast with `redact`, which labels each entity with a `<TYPE>` tag. Backed by Microsoft Presidio (analyzer + anonymizer).
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# anonymize

Mask each PII entity in text with `*` characters, hiding the value while keeping the rest of the text readable.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT pii.main.anonymize('Call John Smith at john@example.com');
-- 'Call **** at ****************'
```

## Notes

Choose `anonymize` over `redact` when the type label `<PERSON>` would itself leak structure you want hidden. Accepts an explicit language as the second argument. NULL/blank input yields NULL.

workers.title: Excel Spreadsheet Read & Write
workers.tagline: Rich Excel read (formulas/types) and write query to .xlsx for DuckDB (Java, Apache POI)
workers.summary: Read and write Microsoft Excel spreadsheets (.xls / .xlsx) as DuckDB SQL functions, backed by Apache POI.
workers.doc_md:
# Excel Spreadsheet Read & Write in SQL

![Apache POI logo](https://poi.apache.org/images/project-header.png)

**Query Microsoft Excel workbooks (`.xls` and `.xlsx`) directly from DuckDB SQL — read every cell with its value, type, and formula, and export any query result to a downloadable `.xlsx` file — powered by [Apache POI](https://poi.apache.org/).**

This extension turns spreadsheets into first-class SQL data sources. It is built for data engineers, analysts, and application developers who need to ingest Excel files, inspect workbook structure, or hand results back to spreadsheet users — without leaving SQL or writing glue code in Python or a BI tool. Both the legacy binary `.xls` format (OLE2 / HSSF) and the modern Office Open XML `.xlsx` format (OOXML / XSSF) are supported, and inputs may be supplied either as a file path or as raw `BLOB` bytes already loaded into DuckDB.

Under the hood the worker embeds [Apache POI](https://github.com/apache/poi), the mature, battle-tested Java library for reading and writing Microsoft Office file formats. POI parses the workbook, evaluates formulas, and preserves cell typing (numbers, dates, booleans, strings, and errors), while the worker streams the results back to DuckDB over Apache Arrow. Untrusted spreadsheets are opened behind zip-bomb and decompression-ratio defenses, and external workbook links are never resolved, so importing arbitrary `.xlsx` files stays safe. See the [Apache POI spreadsheet documentation](https://poi.apache.org/components/spreadsheet/) and the [HSSF/XSSF quick guide](https://poi.apache.org/components/spreadsheet/quick-guide.html) for format details.

## Key concepts

- **Rich, cell-level reads.** A workbook is surfaced not as opaque rows but cell by cell, each with its worksheet, position, A1 reference, evaluated value, data type, and (for formula cells) the underlying formula text — so numbers, dates, booleans, strings, errors, and computed values are all preserved and distinguishable.
- **Structure before data.** You can inspect a workbook's worksheet directory — names and dimensions — cheaply, without materializing every cell, then drill into a single sheet.
- **Path or bytes.** Reader inputs may be a filesystem path the worker opens, or raw `BLOB` bytes already loaded into DuckDB, so the same function works on files on disk and on content that arrived over the wire.
- **Round-tripping to Excel.** Any query result can be serialized back into a downloadable `.xlsx` workbook, and raw bytes can be sniffed to confirm their format.

## When to use it

Reach for this worker when you need to ingest spreadsheet exports into an analytical pipeline, audit the sheets and formulas inside a workbook, validate untrusted uploads by content rather than file extension, or hand polished Excel deliverables back to spreadsheet users — all without leaving SQL or writing glue code in Python or a BI tool.

# Excel functions

Read and write Microsoft Excel workbooks (`.xls` and `.xlsx`) directly in SQL over Apache Arrow, powered by [Apache POI](https://poi.apache.org/).

The functions in this schema cover three areas:

- **Reading** — stream a workbook's non-blank cells as rows (with type, A1 reference, evaluated value, and formula text), and list its worksheet directory with per-sheet dimensions.
- **Writing** — serialize any SQL relation into a downloadable `.xlsx` workbook returned as a `BLOB`.
- **Detection** — sniff raw bytes to classify them as `.xlsx`, `.xls`, or neither, without trusting a file name.

Reader inputs are polymorphic: pass a filesystem path the worker opens, or a raw `BLOB` of workbook bytes already loaded into DuckDB. Formula cells are evaluated, cell typing is preserved, and a corrupt or non-spreadsheet input yields no rows (or `NULL`) rather than failing the query.
