workers.title: SAML Decode, Signature Verification & Attack Detection
workers.tagline: Parse and verify SAML in DuckDB with SQL — XML-DSig / C14N signature validation and golden-SAML / XML-signature-wrapping detection. A VGI worker.
workers.summary: SAML 2.0 decode + XML-DSig / exclusive-C14N signature verification + XSW / Golden-SAML detection, in SQL.
workers.doc_md:
# SAML — Decode, Signature Verification & Attack Detection in SQL

**Shred and security-check SAML 2.0 single-sign-on messages directly in DuckDB.** The `saml` worker base64-decodes (and, for the HTTP-Redirect binding, raw-DEFLATE inflates) a column of `SAMLResponse` blobs, decodes them into typed rows — subject, issuer, audience, the `Conditions` validity window, `AuthnContext`, and attribute statements — and, more importantly, runs the **XML-DSig** structural check the one-off tools only do one message at a time: exclusive XML canonicalization (`xml-exc-c14n#`), per-`Reference` digest verification, and signature math (RSA / ECDSA / EdDSA) against the **embedded** certificate.

The defensible value is **bulk security compute**: running **XML Signature Wrapping (XSW)** and **Golden-SAML** detection across millions of historical SAML messages in a forensic lake — in SQL, joinable against your IdP cert inventory and login telemetry. The worker flags the structural invariants every XSW1-XSW8 attack violates (multiple assertions, a signature that covers a different element than the consumer reads, duplicate/dangling reference IDs, an unsigned assertion inside a signed response, comment-splitting NameIDs, digest mismatches), and surfaces the signer certificate SHA-256 fingerprint so a left join against your known-good IdP certs surfaces the Golden-SAML smoking gun (a cryptographically perfect signature from a key you do not trust).

**Trust stays with you.** `sig_valid = true` means the embedded cert signed these bytes — never that the cert is authorized. The worker holds no private keys, no trust store, makes no network calls, and decrypts nothing; an `EncryptedAssertion` is counted and flagged, not opened. All decode and canonicalization is local CPU on bytes you already hold, so it is safe for air-gapped / regulated forensic data.

**Hardened against hostile input.** Every blob is attacker-controlled, so the XML loader rejects DTDs and entities unparsed (defeating XXE and billion-laughs/exponential-entity-expansion), bounds document size and inflate ratio (DEFLATE-bomb guard), and never panics — a hostile message returns an error verdict, it does not crash the scan. A well-formedness triage verdict reports the reason, and its dtd-present / entity-blocked kinds double as XXE and billion-laughs signals.

**When to reach for it.** Use it whenever you already hold a column of raw or encoded SAML messages and need to shred, verify, or threat-hunt over them at warehouse scale rather than one message at a time in a browser plugin. The signer certificate SHA-256 fingerprint left-joins against your IdP cert inventory, and decoded NameIDs can be scrubbed before sharing extracts when the source data is sensitive.

example_queries.description: Identify a SAML message by its root element.
example_queries.sql: SELECT saml.main.message_type('<samlp:Response xmlns:samlp="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:protocol"/>') AS kind

example_queries.description: Triage why a blob is not a usable SAML message.
example_queries.sql: SELECT (saml.main.well_formed('not a saml message')).kind AS kind

example_queries.description: Decode an assertion and read its issuer.
example_queries.sql: SELECT (saml.main.decode('<saml:Assertion xmlns:saml="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:assertion" ID="_a"><saml:Issuer>https://idp.example.com</saml:Issuer></saml:Assertion>')).issuer AS issuer

example_queries.description: Base64-decode a SAMLResponse POST field to text.
example_queries.sql: SELECT saml.main.b64decode('PHNhbWw+')::VARCHAR AS decoded

example_queries.description: Count the structural anomaly flags on a message.
example_queries.sql: SELECT len(saml.main.anomalies('<saml:Assertion xmlns:saml="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:assertion"/>')) AS n

example_queries.description: Recover the XML from a URL-encoded, base64-wrapped transport parameter.
example_queries.sql: SELECT saml.main.unwrap('PHNhbWxwOlJlc3BvbnNlIHhtbG5zOnNhbWxwPSJ1cm46b2FzaXM6bmFtZXM6dGM6U0FNTDoyLjA6cHJvdG9jb2wiLz4%3D');

example_queries.description: Base64-decode then raw-DEFLATE-inflate a redirect-binding SAMLRequest to its XML text.
example_queries.sql: SELECT saml.main.inflate(saml.main.b64decode('sylOzM0psHIsLcnIC0otLE0tLlGoyM3JK7YCS9gqlRblWeUnFmcWW+Ul5qYWW5UkWwU7+vpYGekZWBUU5ZfkJ+fnKCl4utgqxRcZKunbAQA='));

example_queries.description: Surface signature-wrapping / structural red flags (here, multiple-assertions) for a message.
example_queries.sql: SELECT saml.main.anomalies('<samlp:Response xmlns:samlp="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:protocol" xmlns:saml="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:assertion"><saml:Assertion ID="_a1"/><saml:Assertion ID="_a2"/></samlp:Response>');

example_queries.description: Explode a multi-valued attribute to long form (one row per value).
example_queries.sql: SELECT a.name, a.value FROM UNNEST(saml.main.attributes('<saml:Assertion xmlns:saml="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:assertion"><saml:AttributeStatement><saml:Attribute Name="role"><saml:AttributeValue>admin</saml:AttributeValue><saml:AttributeValue>user</saml:AttributeValue></saml:Attribute></saml:AttributeStatement></saml:Assertion>')) AS _(a) ORDER BY a.value;

example_queries.description: Flag the multiple-assertions XSW indicator on a two-assertion Response.
example_queries.sql: SELECT list_contains(saml.main.anomalies('<samlp:Response xmlns:samlp="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:protocol" xmlns:saml="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:assertion" ID="_r"><saml:Assertion ID="_a1"/><saml:Assertion ID="_a2"/></samlp:Response>'), 'multiple-assertions') AS has_multi;

example_queries.description: Explode a multi-valued attribute into one row per value.
example_queries.sql: SELECT a.value AS value FROM UNNEST(saml.main.attributes('<saml:Assertion xmlns:saml="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:assertion"><saml:AttributeStatement><saml:Attribute Name="role"><saml:AttributeValue>admin</saml:AttributeValue><saml:AttributeValue>user</saml:AttributeValue></saml:Attribute></saml:AttributeStatement></saml:Assertion>')) AS _(a) ORDER BY a.value;

example_queries.description: Decode a SAML assertion to its subject + core fields.
example_queries.sql: SELECT (saml.main.decode('<saml:Assertion xmlns:saml="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:assertion" ID="_a"><saml:Issuer>https://idp.example.com</saml:Issuer><saml:Subject><saml:NameID>alice@example.com</saml:NameID></saml:Subject></saml:Assertion>')).subject;

example_queries.description: Enumerate assertions and their parents to reveal wrapping.
example_queries.sql: SELECT a.idx, a.id, a.parent FROM UNNEST(saml.main.assertions('<samlp:Response xmlns:samlp="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:protocol" xmlns:saml="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:assertion"><saml:Assertion ID="_a1"/></samlp:Response>')) AS _(a) ORDER BY a.idx;

example_queries.description: Read the AuthnContext class (e.g. detect MFA downgrade).
example_queries.sql: SELECT (saml.main.authn('<saml:Assertion xmlns:saml="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:assertion"><saml:AuthnStatement><saml:AuthnContext><saml:AuthnContextClassRef>urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:ac:classes:PasswordProtectedTransport</saml:AuthnContextClassRef></saml:AuthnContext></saml:AuthnStatement></saml:Assertion>')).class_ref;

example_queries.description: Decode a base64 SAMLResponse form field to raw bytes.
example_queries.sql: SELECT saml.main.b64decode('PHNhbWw+');

example_queries.description: Enumerate every signature and its scope to spot wrapping.
example_queries.sql: SELECT s.idx, s.scope, s.sig_valid FROM UNNEST(saml.main.signatures('<samlp:Response xmlns:samlp="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:protocol" xmlns:saml="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:assertion" xmlns:ds="http://www.w3.org/2000/09/xmldsig#"><ds:Signature><ds:SignedInfo><ds:Reference URI="#_a1"/></ds:SignedInfo></ds:Signature><saml:Assertion ID="_a1"/></samlp:Response>')) AS _(s) ORDER BY s.idx;

example_queries.description: Read the assertion validity window for an own-skew expiry check.
example_queries.sql: SELECT (saml.main.conditions('<saml:Assertion xmlns:saml="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:assertion"><saml:Conditions NotBefore="2026-01-01T00:00:00Z" NotOnOrAfter="2026-01-01T01:00:00Z"/></saml:Assertion>')).not_on_or_after;

example_queries.description: Check whether a SAML message's embedded signature is internally valid (false here — the assertion is unsigned).
example_queries.sql: SELECT (saml.main.signature('<saml:Assertion xmlns:saml="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:assertion" ID="_a"><saml:Issuer>https://idp.example.com</saml:Issuer></saml:Assertion>')).sig_valid;

example_queries.description: Identify the kind of a SAML message from its root element.
example_queries.sql: SELECT saml.main.message_type('<samlp:Response xmlns:samlp="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:protocol"/>');

example_queries.description: Classify why a blob is not a usable SAML message (kind = 'not-saml' here).
example_queries.sql: SELECT (saml.main.well_formed('not a saml message')).kind;

tags.vgi.doc_md:
SAML 2.0 forensic decoding and XML-DSig verification, in-database.

## What it does

Turns an opaque SAML message — a base64 / DEFLATE / URL-encoded blob or raw XML — into typed, queryable rows, and independently re-verifies its cryptographic signature so you can trust (or distrust) what an identity provider asserted, without leaving SQL. Each capability is a separate function that takes one content-sniffed message argument (raw XML, base64, base64+DEFLATE, or a URL-encoded wrapper).

## Key concepts

- **Signature verification is real, not implied.** The outermost XML-DSig signature is re-checked here — SignedInfo is re-canonicalized with exclusive C14N, per-Reference digests are recomputed, and SignatureValue is verified (RSA / ECDSA / EdDSA) against the certificate embedded in the message itself. A validity result reports whether that embedded key signed these exact bytes; it never asserts the key is trusted, so Golden-SAML detection is a downstream JOIN of the signer certificate SHA-256 fingerprint against your own IdP cert inventory. No key store, no network egress.
- **Attack detection.** Structural red flags for XML Signature Wrapping (XSW) and Golden-SAML — multiple assertions, a signature that covers a different element than the consumer reads, duplicate/dangling reference IDs, digest mismatches, comment-splitting NameIDs — surface tampering a naive parser misses.
- **Hostile-input safety.** Every entry point is total and panic-free, with DTD / entity expansion disabled (defeating XXE and billion-laughs) and decompression bomb-bounded.

## When to use

Reach for this schema to audit or bulk-scan SAML responses and assertions offline: confirming who signed a message, reading its subject / issuer / audience / validity window / AuthnContext / attribute statements, checking whether its signature holds, and flagging attack fingerprints — over millions of historical messages, joinable against your cert inventory and login telemetry.

functions.name: inflate
functions.comment: Raw-DEFLATE-inflate bytes to text (HTTP-Redirect binding), bounded against decompression bombs; NULL on failure

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Inflate raw-DEFLATE (and zlib-wrapped) bytes to text — the HTTP-Redirect binding compresses the XML with raw DEFLATE before base64. The inflate is bounded by a 64 MiB cap so a DEFLATE bomb (tiny payload, gigabytes inflated) is rejected rather than exhausting memory. Returns NULL when the bytes do not inflate or exceed the cap.

functions.name: anomalies
functions.comment: Flag XSW (XML Signature Wrapping) / Golden-SAML / structural anomalies as a LIST<VARCHAR>; empty list = no structural red flag found (not a safety guarantee)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Return the structural anomaly flags for a SAML message as a `LIST(VARCHAR)`. These are the invariants every XML Signature Wrapping (XSW1-XSW8) attack violates plus the XXE-class text-extraction tells: multiple-assertions, signature-covers-other-element, reference-uri-id-mismatch, unsigned-assertion-in-signed-response, signature-placement-anomaly, detached-signature, nameid-comment-splitting, digest-mismatch, c14n-inclusive-on-moved-assertion, and encrypted-assertion-present. An EMPTY list is not a safety guarantee — Golden SAML (a forgery with a stolen but valid IdP key) leaves no structural trace, so combine this with a trust-table JOIN on signer_cert_sha256.
tags.vgi.doc_md: List XSW / structural red flags for a SAML message (e.g. `multiple-assertions`, `signature-covers-other-element`, `digest-mismatch`); empty != safe.

functions.name: decode
functions.comment: Decode a SAML message (raw XML / base64 / base64+DEFLATE / URL-encoded) to a STRUCT of core fields: subject, issuer, audience, conditions window, authn_context, status, ids, counts, and signed. Never errors on bad input — returns null fields + signed=false (see well_formed).

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Decode a SAML 2.0 Response or Assertion to a struct of its core fields — response_id / assertion_id, issuer, subject (+ NameID format and SP qualifier), SubjectConfirmation recipient / in_response_to, the Conditions NotBefore / NotOnOrAfter window, audience(s), AuthnInstant / SessionIndex / AuthnContext class, Status, Destination, IssueInstant, Version, the assertion/encrypted counts, and whether a top-level Signature is present. The input is content-sniffed: it accepts raw XML, base64 (HTTP-POST binding), base64+raw-DEFLATE (HTTP-Redirect binding), or a URL-encoded wrapper. It never errors on malformed input — a bad blob yields a struct with null fields and signed=false (call well_formed for the reason). Timestamps are `TIMESTAMPTZ` (UTC); the worker surfaces the window but does not decide 'expired'.

functions.name: signature
functions.comment: Verify the outermost XML-DSig signature: STRUCT(signed, c14n_ok, digest_ok, sig_valid, algo, c14n_method, digest_method, signer_cert BLOB, signer_cert_sha256, signer_subject, signer_issuer, references LIST<STRUCT>). sig_valid is math against the EMBEDDED cert — trust is your JOIN.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Run the XML-DSig structural check on a SAML message's outermost signature using exclusive XML canonicalization, and return a struct: signed (is there a signature), digest_ok (do the per-Reference digests match the referenced nodes — i.e. does the signature cover the bytes you think it does), c14n_ok (does SignedInfo canonicalize under a recognized exclusive-C14N method), sig_valid (does SignatureValue verify against the EMBEDDED KeyInfo cert — RSA/ECDSA/EdDSA math), algo (RS256/ES256/EdDSA/…), the c14n/digest method URIs, the signer_cert (DER `BLOB`), signer_cert_sha256 (the join key to your IdP trust table), signer_subject / signer_issuer, and the references list. Crucially, sig_valid=true means only that the embedded cert signed these bytes — NOT that the key is trusted. Detecting Golden SAML (a forgery with a stolen-but-valid IdP key) is a downstream LEFT JOIN of signer_cert_sha256 against your known-good cert inventory.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Structurally verify a SAML signature (exclusive C14N + digest + embedded-cert math) → `(signed, c14n_ok, digest_ok, sig_valid, algo, signer_cert_sha256, …)`. Trust is your JOIN.

workers.title: Scholarly Literature Search
workers.tagline: Scholarly search across OpenAlex/arXiv/Crossref for DuckDB (Python)
workers.summary: Scholarly-literature search across OpenAlex, arXiv, and Crossref, unified for SQL and RAG
workers.doc_md:
# Scholarly Literature Search in SQL

**Search academic papers, preprints, and citations directly from DuckDB/SQL** across [OpenAlex](https://docs.openalex.org), [arXiv](https://arxiv.org), and [Crossref](https://www.crossref.org) — three free, ToS-clean scholarly APIs unified behind one pluggable query surface, with no API key required.

The `scholar` catalog turns the world's open scholarly-metadata graph into ordinary SQL tables. It is built for researchers, data engineers, librarians, and anyone wiring up retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipelines who would rather write a query than glue together three different REST clients. Every search returns the **same unified result schema** — `title`, `authors`, `abstract`, `doi`, `year`, `published`, `venue`, `citations_count`, `url`, `source`, and a JSON `extra` column — so a query never has to know or care which provider produced a given row. Switch providers with a single named argument and the rest of your SQL stays identical.

Under the hood the worker talks plain HTTP to each provider's public API: the [OpenAlex API](https://docs.openalex.org) (the open catalog of ~250M scholarly works, used by default), the [arXiv API](https://info.arxiv.org/help/api/index.html) for physics, math, and CS preprints, and the [Crossref REST API](https://www.crossref.org/documentation/retrieve-metadata/rest-api/) for DOI-registered publications. Results are fetched page by page and streamed back to DuckDB as Arrow, so large result sets never have to be buffered in full. Pagination cursors round-trip through the worker, retries back off on rate limits, and a provider error surfaces as a clean SQL error rather than crashing the attach.

## Table functions

- `scholar_search(query, provider := 'openalex', count := 10, page_size := 0)` — full-text search scholarly works and stream up to `count` rows in the unified schema. Pass `provider := 'arxiv'` or `provider := 'crossref'` to target a different source.
- `scholar_providers()` — list every provider `scholar_search` can target (also queryable as the table `scholar.main.scholar_providers`), with its keyless and default flags.

## Getting started

Install and load the signed `vgi` community extension, `ATTACH` this worker at a `LOCATION` such as `uv run scholar_worker.py`, and then call the two table functions directly. Ready-to-run, copy-paste queries live in this schema's example queries and in each function's own examples, so they are executed and coverage-checked rather than duplicated inline here.

Typical uses: find papers by topic, resolve and enrich DOIs, gather citation counts, assemble a literature-review corpus, or feed a RAG index — all without leaving SQL. **No API key is required** for any provider; set `VGI_SCHOLAR_MAILTO` to your contact e-mail to join OpenAlex's and Crossref's faster "polite pool".

Powered by [OpenAlex](https://docs.openalex.org) ([source](https://github.com/ourresearch/openalex-guts)), [arXiv](https://arxiv.org) ([API docs](https://info.arxiv.org/help/api/index.html)), and [Crossref](https://www.crossref.org) ([REST API docs](https://github.com/CrossRef/rest-api-doc)).

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## scholar_providers (table)

The fixed set of scholarly-search providers that `scholar_search` can target, one row per provider. This is the table form of the `scholar_providers()` function: because it takes no arguments and always returns the same rows, you can read it as a plain table — `scholar.main.scholar_providers`, no parentheses — rather than calling it as a function. Use it to discover the valid values for `scholar_search`'s `provider :=` argument, to find the default provider, or to confirm a provider is keyless before running a search.

Columns: `provider` (the name to pass as `provider := '...'`; unique per row and the table's primary key), `requires_key` (true if the provider needs an API key — all current providers are keyless, so false), and `default` (true for the single provider used when `scholar_search` omits `provider`). Reading this table makes no network calls.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# scholar_providers (table)

Every scholarly-search provider available to `scholar_search`, one row each. This is the table form of the parameterless `scholar_providers()` function.

Read it with no parentheses, e.g. `scholar.main.scholar_providers`, to enumerate the valid `provider :=` values, filter on the `"default"` flag to see which provider is used when a search omits `provider`, or count the `requires_key` column to confirm a provider is keyless. Runnable examples are attached as this table's example queries.

## Columns

- `provider` (`VARCHAR`, primary key) — name to pass as `provider := '...'`.
- `requires_key` (`BOOLEAN`) — whether the provider needs an API key (all v1 providers are keyless).
- `default` (`BOOLEAN`) — whether this is the default provider; exactly one row is true.

## Notes

Reading this table needs no network access, so it is a reliable capability/health probe.

## scholar_search

Search scholarly / academic literature and stream up to `count` matching works as rows in a single **unified schema**, regardless of which provider answered. Use this whenever an agent needs to find papers by topic, resolve DOIs, gather citation counts, assemble a literature review, or build a corpus for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG).

### Inputs
- `query` (positional, `VARCHAR`) — free-text search string, e.g. `'retrieval augmented generation'`.
- `provider :=` (`VARCHAR`, default `'openalex'`) — one of `'openalex'`, `'arxiv'`, `'crossref'`. Call `scholar_providers()` to enumerate the valid values.
- `count :=` (`INTEGER`, default 10, 1–1000) — maximum rows to return; the function pages the provider until this budget is met or results are exhausted.
- `page_size :=` (`INTEGER`, default 0, 0–200) — rows fetched per provider request; 0 picks an automatic page size.

### Output
One row per work in the unified schema (`title`, `authors`, `abstract`, `doi`, `year`, `published`, `venue`, `citations_count`, `url`, `source`, `extra`). `authors` is a `LIST<VARCHAR>`, `published` is a UTC `TIMESTAMPTZ`, and `extra` is provider-specific JSON.

### Behavior & edge cases
- No API key is required for any provider; set `VGI_SCHOLAR_MAILTO` to join the OpenAlex / Crossref polite pool.
- An unknown `provider` is rejected at bind time with a clean DuckDB error.
- Provider/network failures surface as a DuckDB error rather than crashing the worker.
- Fields a provider does not supply (e.g. missing `doi` or `abstract`) come back as NULL.
- Requires outbound network access to the provider's public API to return rows.

workers.doc_md:
# Unified Web Search in SQL

Query the live web directly from DuckDB SQL through one pluggable provider surface that unifies **Brave Search**, **Tavily**, **Exa**, **SearXNG**, and **DuckDuckGo** behind a single result schema -- built for RAG, retrieval, and agent grounding.

This extension turns web search into a first-class SQL data source. Instead of wiring a different HTTP client and JSON shape for every search API, you call one table function and get back the same unified rows -- `title`, `url`, `snippet`, `rank`, `source`, `published`, `score`, and an `extra` JSON column for provider-specific fields -- no matter which provider served the query. It is designed for developers building retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipelines, search-driven analytics, and AI agents that need fresh, citable web results inside the database, with the ability to swap or A/B providers without rewriting a single query.

Under the hood the worker is a thin, dependency-light connector: every provider is reached over plain HTTP with the [httpx](https://www.python-httpx.org/) client ([source](https://github.com/encode/httpx)) -- no heavyweight provider SDKs are bundled. Each backend is a small adapter that maps the upstream JSON into the shared result shape, with a per-call timeout plus bounded retry/backoff on rate-limit and server errors so a flaky provider never crashes the engine. Because it is an egress connector, results and quotas come from your own upstream subscription: API keys are supplied through the VGI secret provider (one secret type per keyed provider) and are **never** passed inline in SQL, while DuckDuckGo works key-free.

The function surface is intentionally small. The table function `web_search(query, provider := ..., count := ..., page := ...)` runs one search against the chosen provider and streams the ranked, unified rows with 0-based page pagination. The scalar `web_answer(query, provider)` returns a single synthesized one-line answer (via Tavily or the free DuckDuckGo Instant Answer API) or NULL when none is available. The table function `search_providers()` lists every provider and whether each currently has a key or base URL configured. Runnable, catalog-qualified queries for each function live in that object's examples.

### Providers & documentation

- **Brave Search** -- [API docs](https://brave.com/search/api/), [developer dashboard](https://api-dashboard.search.brave.com/app/documentation/web-search/get-started)
- **Tavily** -- [site](https://tavily.com/), [docs](https://docs.tavily.com/)
- **Exa** -- [site](https://exa.ai/), [docs](https://docs.exa.ai/)
- **SearXNG** (self-hosted, base_url required) -- [source](https://github.com/searxng/searxng), [docs](https://docs.searxng.org/)
- **DuckDuckGo** (free, key-free) -- [duckduckgo.com](https://duckduckgo.com/)

Opt-in SerpApi/Serper SERP backends are also available when explicitly enabled. Built and maintained by [Query.Farm](https://query.farm).

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Run one web search against a pluggable provider and stream a unified, ranked result set as a table.

`web_search(query, provider := ..., count := ..., page := ...)` returns rows with a fixed shape -- `title`, `url`, `snippet`, `rank`, `source`, `published`, `score`, `extra` (JSON) -- no matter which backend served them (Brave, Tavily, Exa, SearXNG, DuckDuckGo, or the opt-in SerpApi/Serper scrapers).

**Use it for RAG / retrieval** when you need live web results to ground a prompt. It is a table function, so named arguments apply: `provider` selects the backend (defaults to the configured default), `count` caps results (1-50, default 10), and `page` is a 0-based page index for pagination (page N skips N*count results) -- note it is `page`, not `offset` (`offset` is a DuckDB reserved word).

**Inputs:** `query` (positional), `provider`/`count`/`page` (named). **Output:** the unified result schema above; `published`/`score`/`extra` are `NULL` when a provider does not expose them. **Edge cases:** keyed providers (`brave`/`tavily`/`exa`/serp*) need a key from the VGI secret provider and return no rows when unconfigured; `ddg` works for free; a bad/disabled provider name fails cleanly at bind; provider/network errors surface as a single DuckDB error, never a worker crash.

# web_search

The unified **web-search table function**: one search against a pluggable provider, streamed as a single ranked result schema. Runnable, catalog-qualified queries live in this object's examples; the arguments and result columns are described below.

## Arguments

- `query` -- the search string (positional).
- `provider :=` -- backend name (`brave`, `tavily`, `exa`, `searxng`, `ddg`, or opt-in `serpapi`/`serper`); defaults to the configured default provider.
- `count :=` -- number of results, 1-50 (default 10).
- `page :=` -- 0-based page index for pagination (default 0). It is `page`, not `offset`.

## Notes

- Returns the same columns for every provider; `published`/`score`/`extra` are `NULL` when the provider omits them.
- Keyed providers read their key from the VGI secret provider (never from SQL) and return no rows until configured; `ddg` is free.
- Provider/network failures surface as a clean DuckDB error and never crash the worker.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Return a single synthesized one-line answer for a natural-language question, as a scalar `VARCHAR`.

`web_answer(query, provider)` asks a provider that exposes a *zero-click* / synthesized answer -- `tavily` (with an API key) or `ddg` (DuckDuckGo Instant Answer, free, no key) -- and returns the answer text, or `NULL` when the provider has no answer for the query, is unknown/disabled, or has no key. It NEVER raises: a provider failure degrades to `NULL` so it is safe to use inside a larger scan.

**Use it when** you want a quick factual snippet to ground a prompt and do not need ranked result rows; for the full list of results use `web_search` instead.

**Inputs:** `query` (the question, one per row) and `provider` (a positional constant: `'tavily'` or `'ddg'`). **Output:** one `VARCHAR` per input row (the answer or `NULL`). **Edge cases:** queries with no instant answer return `NULL`; the `tavily` key is read from the VGI secret provider, never from SQL; a `NULL` input query yields `NULL`.

# web_answer

A scalar that returns a **synthesized one-line answer** for a question, or `NULL` when none is available.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT search.main.web_answer('python programming language', 'ddg');
SELECT search.main.web_answer('who maintains duckdb', 'tavily');
```

The second argument is the provider name, a positional constant (scalars are positional-only in VGI/DuckDB). Use `'ddg'` for a free DuckDuckGo Instant Answer or `'tavily'` for a keyed, richer synthesis.

## Notes

- Returns `NULL` -- never an error -- when the provider has no answer, is unknown/disabled, or is missing its key, so it is safe inside a wider query.
- The Tavily key comes from the VGI secret provider; keys are never passed in SQL.
- For ranked result rows (title/url/snippet/...) use the `web_search` table function.

workers.doc_md:
# Secret Scanner — Detect Leaked API Keys, Tokens & Credentials in SQL

![Gitleaks logo](https://gitleaks.io/logo.png)

Find leaked secrets in text and source code directly from SQL: scan strings for AWS, GCP, and Azure cloud keys, GitHub, GitLab, Slack, and Stripe tokens, RSA/SSH private keys, JWTs, and high-entropy credentials — powered by the embedded [gitleaks](https://github.com/gitleaks/gitleaks) detection engine and delivered over Apache Arrow to DuckDB.

This extension is built for security, DevSecOps, and data engineers who need fast, in-database secret detection and credential-leak scanning without shipping sensitive data to an external service. Point it at a column of commit messages, log lines, config blobs, support tickets, or any free text, and it flags rows that contain leaked secrets so you can audit, redact, and remediate at the speed of a SQL query. Detection is **pure and fully offline** — it makes no network calls and **never verifies** whether a credential is live, so every finding is a *candidate* leak that is safe to surface in untrusted pipelines.

Under the hood the worker runs the [gitleaks](https://github.com/gitleaks/gitleaks) secret-scanning engine with its default ruleset of 200+ regular-expression detectors, embedded straight into the binary so there is nothing to download or configure. For generic and entropy-gated rules it layers a Shannon-entropy heuristic to score how random a candidate string looks, and it assigns each hit a `confidence` value so structurally-distinctive matches (a real-looking AWS access key) rank above noisy generic ones. Crucially, the **raw credential never leaves the process**: every reported match is redacted to a fixed-width mask that also hides the secret's true length. See the gitleaks [documentation](https://gitleaks.io) and the [default ruleset](https://github.com/gitleaks/gitleaks/blob/master/config/gitleaks.toml) for the full detector catalog.

The extension exposes two scalar/table functions plus a browsable `secret_detectors` registry view. Use the scalar **`secret_contains(text)` → `BOOLEAN`** as a cheap predicate — ideal in a `WHERE` clause to keep only the rows worth a deeper look. Then call the table function **`secret_scan(text)`** to enumerate findings: it emits one row per detected secret with `rule_id`, `description`, `match_redacted`, `start_offset` (a byte offset), `entropy`, and `confidence` (in `[0,1]`). `NULL` or empty input yields no findings, so the functions compose cleanly across large columns. For whole-repository or git-history scanning, reach for the gitleaks CLI; this worker scans the text you pass it.

example_queries.description: Predicate: does this string hold any detectable secret? (Returns TRUE for the AWS-style key.)
example_queries.sql: SELECT secretscan.main.secret_contains('aws_secret = AKIAZ3MZ7EXAMPLE4Q2T') AS leaked;

example_queries.description: Enumerate each finding with its rule, redacted match, and confidence.
example_queries.sql: SELECT rule_id, match_redacted, confidence FROM secretscan.main.secret_scan('aws_secret = AKIAZ3MZ7EXAMPLE4Q2T');

example_queries.description: Browse the detector registry, highest-confidence first.
example_queries.sql: SELECT rule_id, provider, confidence FROM secretscan.main.secret_detectors ORDER BY confidence DESC, rule_id;

example_queries.description: Browse every detector this worker recognises, highest-confidence first.
example_queries.sql: SELECT rule_id, provider, category, confidence FROM secretscan.main.secret_detectors ORDER BY confidence DESC, rule_id;

example_queries.description: List only the high-confidence structural detectors (confidence >= 0.9).
example_queries.sql: SELECT rule_id, provider FROM secretscan.main.secret_detectors WHERE confidence >= 0.9 ORDER BY rule_id;

example_queries.description: Count the recognised detectors grouped by the provider family they cover.
example_queries.sql: SELECT category, count(*) AS detectors FROM secretscan.main.secret_detectors GROUP BY category ORDER BY detectors DESC, category;

## secretscan.main

Offline secret-detection functions over text and source code, backed by the embedded [gitleaks](https://github.com/gitleaks/gitleaks) ruleset plus Shannon-entropy heuristics.

### Functions

- **`secret_contains(text)` → `BOOLEAN`** — a cheap predicate that returns `TRUE` when the text holds at least one detectable secret. Ideal in a `WHERE` clause to filter rows worth a deeper scan.
- **`secret_scan(text)` → rows** — a table function emitting one row per finding (`rule_id`, `description`, `match_redacted`, `start_offset`, `entropy`, `confidence`).

### Notes

Detection is **pure and offline** (no network) and **never verifies** whether a secret is live — findings are *candidate* leaks. Output is always the **redacted** match; the raw credential never leaves the process.

## Recognised Secret Detectors

A browsable, zero-argument view listing the marquee [gitleaks](https://github.com/gitleaks/gitleaks) detector rules this worker flags — a map of the detection surface for when you want to know *what* is detected before scanning any text.

### Columns

- **`rule_id`** — the gitleaks rule id (matches `secret_scan.rule_id`).
- **`provider`** — the provider or credential family (AWS, GitHub, Slack, ...).
- **`category`** — a broad grouping (Cloud Keys, VCS Tokens, Chat Tokens, Payment Keys, Private Keys, Tokens, Entropy).
- **`confidence`** — the heuristic confidence in `[0,1]` a match of this rule earns (structural rules `0.95`; generic/entropy rules scale with entropy).
- **`description`** — a one-line summary of what the detector matches.

### Notes

The registry is a curated, representative slice of the full 200+-rule default ruleset, not an exhaustive list. It is a static VALUES list, so it returns instantly with no network access. Pick a `rule_id` here, then scan text with `secret_contains` / `secret_scan` and join the findings back on `rule_id`.

workers.doc_md:
# Sigma Detection Rules in SQL

![Sigma logo](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SigmaHQ/sigma/master/images/Sigma_0.3.png)

Run [Sigma](https://sigmahq.io) detection rules — the open, vendor-neutral standard for **detection-as-code** — directly over your log and event tables in SQL, powered by [pySigma](https://github.com/SigmaHQ/pySigma).

This extension brings SIEM-style threat detection and threat hunting into DuckDB. If you have events as rows (Windows Security logs, EDR telemetry, cloud audit trails, web/proxy logs, or any JSON records), you can take a Sigma rule and ask, per row, "does this event match?" — without exporting data to a separate SIEM. It is built for detection engineers, threat hunters, incident responders, and data engineers who want to test, triage, and measure detection coverage where the data already lives. It is a defensive security tool and part of Query Farm's cyber analytics cluster alongside YARA, IOC, CVE, PE, and X.509 workers.

Under the hood, each rule's YAML is parsed and compiled once by pySigma — the reference Sigma implementation maintained by [SigmaHQ](https://github.com/SigmaHQ/sigma) — into a boolean condition tree, then evaluated against every row. Compilation is cached by rule text, so a constant rule scanned across a whole log column compiles a single time and only the per-row match runs hot, keeping column scans cheap. The evaluator honors Sigma field modifiers (contains, startswith, endswith, regex, and the rest), wildcard string matching, numeric, boolean and null values, and the full selector grammar (`1 of selection_*`, `all of them`, and friends). Rules and their metadata, including [MITRE ATT&CK](https://attack.mitre.org) tags, are read straight from the rule text.

The workflow is deliberately simple: keep your events as rows, express detection logic as Sigma YAML, and evaluate one against the other as an ordinary SQL predicate. Because a constant rule compiles once and only the boolean match runs per row, applying a detection across a whole log column stays cheap enough to run interactively. Beyond matching, the catalog also lets you validate a rule library before you trust it, and introspect a rule's header metadata and referenced fields for triage, index planning, and coverage analysis — so a single attached worker covers the detect / validate / plan loop of detection engineering.

A typical hunt applies a matcher predicate per row over a log table (for example in a `WHERE` clause against `to_json(row)`), while separate helpers validate that a rule library compiles and introspect rule metadata and referenced fields for planning. A browsable discovery table lists the field modifiers the evaluator supports.

Learn more from the [Sigma documentation](https://sigmahq.io/docs/), the [pySigma reference docs](https://sigmahq-pysigma.readthedocs.io), and the [pySigma source repository](https://github.com/SigmaHQ/pySigma).
workers.readme_sql:
INSTALL vgi FROM community; LOAD vgi;
ATTACH 'sigma' (TYPE vgi, LOCATION 'uv run sigma_worker.py');

-- The headline: which log rows match a rule?
SELECT *
FROM windows_security_log AS t
WHERE sigma.sigma_match(
    to_json(t),
    'title: Failed Network Logon
logsource: {product: windows, service: security}
detection:
  selection:
    EventID: 4625
    LogonType: 3
  condition: selection');

example_queries.description: Does a failed-network-logon event match a brute-force detection rule?
example_queries.sql: SELECT sigma.main.sigma_match('{"EventID": 4625, "LogonType": 3}', '{title: Failed Network Logon, logsource: {service: security}, detection: {selection: {EventID: 4625, LogonType: 3}, condition: selection}}') AS matched

example_queries.description: Validate that a process-creation rule parses and compiles.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sigma.main.sigma_check('{title: Process Create, logsource: {service: security}, detection: {sel: {EventID: 1}, condition: sel}}') AS valid

example_queries.description: Read a rule's title and severity level from its header metadata.
example_queries.sql: SELECT title, level FROM sigma.main.sigma_rule_info('{title: Failed Logon, level: high, logsource: {service: security}, detection: {sel: {EventID: 4625}, condition: sel}}')

example_queries.description: List the event fields a rule keys on, for index and coverage planning.
example_queries.sql: SELECT field FROM sigma.main.sigma_match_fields('{title: Failed Network Logon, logsource: {service: security}, detection: {sel: {EventID: 4625, LogonType: 3}, condition: sel}}') ORDER BY field

example_queries.description: Browse the field modifiers the evaluator supports.
example_queries.sql: SELECT modifier, kind FROM sigma.main.supported_modifiers ORDER BY modifier

example_queries.description: Show only the affix modifiers (contains / startswith / endswith).
example_queries.sql: SELECT modifier, description FROM sigma.main.supported_modifiers WHERE kind = 'affix' ORDER BY modifier

example_queries.description: Is the regular-expression modifier supported?
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) > 0 AS has_regex FROM sigma.main.supported_modifiers WHERE modifier = 're'

example_queries.description: Read a rule's title and severity level from its header.
example_queries.sql: SELECT title, level FROM sigma.main.sigma_rule_info('{title: T, level: high, logsource: {service: security}, detection: {sel: {EventID: 1}, condition: sel}}')

example_queries.description: Expand a rule's MITRE ATT&CK tags into one row per tag.
example_queries.sql: SELECT UNNEST(tags) AS tag FROM sigma.main.sigma_rule_info('{title: T, tags: [attack.t1110], logsource: {service: security}, detection: {sel: {EventID: 1}, condition: sel}}')

example_queries.description: List the distinct event fields a rule keys on (-> EventID, LogonType).
example_queries.sql: SELECT field FROM sigma.main.sigma_match_fields('{title: Failed Network Logon, logsource: {service: security}, detection: {sel: {EventID: 4625, LogonType: 3}, condition: sel}}')

example_queries.description: A failed-logon event matches a rule requiring EventID 4625.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sigma.main.sigma_match('{"EventID": 4625, "LogonType": 3}', '{title: Failed Network Logon, logsource: {service: security}, detection: {selection: {EventID: 4625}, condition: selection}}')

example_queries.description: Hunt per row over an inline log table, keeping only matching events.
example_queries.sql: SELECT event FROM (VALUES ('{"EventID": 4625, "LogonType": 3}'), ('{"EventID": 1}')) AS logs(event) WHERE sigma.main.sigma_match(event, '{title: Failed Network Logon, logsource: {service: security}, detection: {selection: {EventID: 4625, LogonType: 3}, condition: selection}}')

example_queries.description: An unrelated process-creation event does not match the same rule.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sigma.main.sigma_match('{"EventID": 1}', '{title: Failed Network Logon, logsource: {service: security}, detection: {selection: {EventID: 4625, LogonType: 3}, condition: selection}}') AS matched;

example_queries.description: Apply the matcher per row over an inline log table -- the headline hunting pattern.
example_queries.sql: SELECT event, sigma.main.sigma_match(event, '{title: Failed Network Logon, logsource: {service: security}, detection: {selection: {EventID: 4625, LogonType: 3}, condition: selection}}') AS matched FROM (VALUES ('{"EventID": 4625, "LogonType": 3}'), ('{"EventID": 1}')) AS logs(event) ORDER BY matched;

example_queries.description: A well-formed rule with a logsource and condition validates as true.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sigma.main.sigma_check('{title: Failed Logon, logsource: {service: security}, detection: {selection: {EventID: 4625}, condition: selection}}')

example_queries.description: A rule that is not valid Sigma YAML returns false rather than raising.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sigma.main.sigma_check('not a valid rule')

## sigma.main

The single schema of the `sigma` catalog, bringing SIEM-style 'detection-as-code' into SQL. Use it to compile a [Sigma](https://sigmahq.io) rule once and test it against an entire log/event table, all without leaving the database.

**What it's for.** The schema spans the everyday loop of detection engineering: match events against a rule to hunt for a known threat, validate that a rule library parses and compiles before you trust it, and introspect a rule's header metadata and the fields it keys on for triage, index planning, and MITRE ATT&CK coverage analysis. Matching is the hot path and the usual entry point; validation and introspection support it around the edges.

**Notes.** Every rule must include a non-empty `logsource:` block. Rules compile once per distinct text (cached), then evaluate per row, so a constant rule over a column is cheap. Events are supplied as JSON object strings (e.g. from `to_json(row)`).

# sigma.main

Sigma detection-rule evaluation for SQL, powered by [pySigma](https://github.com/SigmaHQ/pySigma).

## What it covers

This schema turns Sigma 'detection-as-code' into ordinary SQL. It supports the everyday detection-engineering loop directly over your log tables:

- **Detect** — test log/event rows against a rule to hunt for a known threat.
- **Validate** — confirm a rule library parses and compiles before you rely on it.
- **Plan** — introspect a rule's header metadata and the fields it references for triage, index planning, and coverage analysis.

List the schema to browse the individual functions; each ships its own documentation and runnable examples. A browsable discovery table lists the Sigma field modifiers the evaluator understands, so you can review them before authoring a rule.

## Typical use

Apply a matcher predicate per row over a log table (typically in a `WHERE` clause against `to_json(row)`), and use the validation and introspection helpers to check a rule library and plan coverage. Every attached example query is fully catalog-qualified and runnable.

Every example rule carries a non-empty `logsource:` block, which pySigma requires.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: A ready-to-scan **discovery table** of every Sigma field modifier this worker's evaluator understands, so you can check what a rule may use before authoring or trusting it. Browse the view directly (no arguments): the `modifier` column holds the keyword written after a pipe in a rule field (e.g. `CommandLine|contains`), with the `plain` row standing for the default modifier-free comparison; `kind` groups them into `equality`, `affix`, `startswith`/`endswith` style, `regex`, and the `all` `combiner`; and `description` explains the matching semantics. A rule that uses any modifier absent from this table is rejected by `sigma_check` and raises from `sigma_match`, so this is the authoritative capability list. # supported_modifiers (view)

Every Sigma field modifier the evaluator implements, as a plain browsable table.

The `modifier` column is the keyword written after a pipe on a rule field (`CommandLine|contains`, `Image|endswith`); the `plain` row is the default modifier-free comparison. The `kind` column groups modifiers into `equality`, `affix`, `regex`, and `combiner` families, and `description` explains the matching semantics. A rule using any modifier not listed here is rejected by `sigma_check` and raises from `sigma_match`, so this view is the authoritative capability list. The rows are generated from the evaluator's own registry, so they stay in lockstep with behaviour: filter by `kind` to review a family, or probe for a specific `modifier` before authoring a rule that uses it.

## sigma_rule_info(rule_yaml)

Parses a [Sigma](https://sigmahq.io) rule (YAML) and returns a single row of its header metadata: `title`, `id`, `level`, `status`, `description`, logsource `product`/`service`, and the rule's `tags` (a `VARCHAR[]`, typically MITRE ATT&CK references like `attack.t1110`).

**When to use it.** Triage and catalog rules without evaluating them against events -- e.g. build an inventory of a rule repository, filter by severity `level`, group by logsource `product`, or expand `tags` with `UNNEST` to map coverage against MITRE ATT&CK.

**Inputs.** `rule_yaml` -- a complete Sigma rule (positional). Like every rule here it needs a non-empty `logsource:` block.

**Output & edge cases.** A table function returning exactly one row. A NULL rule yields **no rows**; a malformed rule raises a clear parse error (this is an introspection helper run against a known rule, not a per-row scan). Header fields absent from the rule come back NULL.

# sigma_rule_info

Returns one row of header metadata for a Sigma rule -- the human-facing fields you would show in a rule catalog or triage view.

## Usage

Pass a rule and project the header columns you need (`title`, `level`, ...), or expand the `tags` list with `UNNEST` to map MITRE ATT&CK coverage. Fully runnable, catalog-qualified queries are attached as example queries.

## Notes

- One row per rule; a NULL rule yields no rows.
- A malformed rule raises a clear parse error.
- The `tags` column is a `VARCHAR[]` (use `UNNEST` to expand it).

## sigma_match_fields(rule_yaml)

Returns one row per distinct event field that a [Sigma](https://sigmahq.io) rule keys on (e.g. `EventID`, `LogonType`, `Image`). It answers 'what columns does this rule actually look at?' without evaluating the rule against any data.

**When to use it.** Plan indexes and storage coverage: discover which log fields must be present and indexed for a rule to be evaluable, audit a fleet of rules for a common field set, or detect rules that reference fields your pipeline does not collect.

**Inputs.** `rule_yaml` -- a complete Sigma rule (positional), with a non-empty `logsource:` block.

**Output & edge cases.** A table function emitting one `field` row per referenced field. A NULL rule yields **no rows**; a malformed rule raises a clear parse error. Bare-keyword conditions (which match anywhere in the event rather than a named field) contribute no field rows.

## sigma_match(event_json, rule_yaml)

Tests whether a single log/event row, supplied as a JSON object string, matches a [Sigma](https://sigmahq.io) detection rule supplied as YAML. This is the headline function of the catalog: it turns 'detection-as-code' into a SQL predicate so you can hunt for a known threat across an entire log table.

**When to use it.** Apply it per row over a log column to find matching events, typically in a `WHERE` clause: `WHERE sigma.sigma_match(to_json(t), :rule)`. The rule is parsed and compiled exactly once per distinct rule string (the engine is `lru_cache`-d), so scanning one constant rule across millions of rows compiles a single time and then evaluates the boolean condition tree per row.

**Inputs.** `event_json` — the event as a JSON object string (e.g. from `to_json(row)`); `rule_yaml` — a complete Sigma rule, which must include a non-empty `logsource:` block and a `detection:` section with a `condition`.

**Output & edge cases.** Returns `BOOLEAN`. A NULL input row yields NULL. A malformed *event* JSON yields `false` (one bad log row is a non-match, never a crash), but a malformed or unsupported *rule* raises a clear error so you never silently mis-evaluate. Supported leaf forms include field/value comparisons (equals, contains, startswith, endswith, regex, wildcards) and bare keyword searches; selector forms like `1 of selection_*` and `all of them` are expanded by pySigma and work for free.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# sigma_match

Returns `true` when a JSON event matches a Sigma detection rule. It is the core matcher for SIEM-style threat detection directly in SQL.

## Usage

Apply it per row over a log column -- typically in a `WHERE` clause against `to_json(row)` -- to keep only the events a rule matches. Fully runnable, catalog-qualified queries are attached as example queries.

## Arguments

| name | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `event_json` | VARCHAR | The event as a JSON object string. |
| `rule_yaml` | VARCHAR | A Sigma rule (YAML) with a non-empty `logsource:`. |

## Notes

- A malformed *event* returns `false`; a malformed *rule* raises a clear error.
- NULL in, NULL out.
- The rule compiles once per distinct string, then evaluates per row, so a constant rule over a whole column is cheap.

vgi.example_queries.description: A failed-logon event matches a rule requiring EventID 4625.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT sigma.main.sigma_match('{"EventID": 4625, "LogonType": 3}', '{title: Failed Network Logon, logsource: {service: security}, detection: {selection: {EventID: 4625}, condition: selection}}')

vgi.example_queries.description: Hunt per row over an inline log table, keeping only matching events.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT event FROM (VALUES ('{"EventID": 4625, "LogonType": 3}'), ('{"EventID": 1}')) AS logs(event) WHERE sigma.main.sigma_match(event, '{title: Failed Network Logon, logsource: {service: security}, detection: {selection: {EventID: 4625, LogonType: 3}, condition: selection}}')

vgi.executable_examples.description: A failed-logon event (EventID 4625, network logon type 3) matches a brute-force detection rule.
vgi.executable_examples.sql: SELECT sigma.main.sigma_match('{"EventID": 4625, "LogonType": 3}', '{title: Failed Network Logon, logsource: {service: security}, detection: {selection: {EventID: 4625, LogonType: 3}, condition: selection}}') AS matched

vgi.executable_examples.description: An unrelated process-creation event does not match the same rule.
vgi.executable_examples.sql: SELECT sigma.main.sigma_match('{"EventID": 1}', '{title: Failed Network Logon, logsource: {service: security}, detection: {selection: {EventID: 4625, LogonType: 3}, condition: selection}}') AS matched

vgi.executable_examples.description: Apply the matcher per row over an inline log table -- the headline hunting pattern.
vgi.executable_examples.sql: SELECT event, sigma.main.sigma_match(event, '{title: Failed Network Logon, logsource: {service: security}, detection: {selection: {EventID: 4625, LogonType: 3}, condition: selection}}') AS matched FROM (VALUES ('{"EventID": 4625, "LogonType": 3}'), ('{"EventID": 1}')) AS logs(event) ORDER BY matched

## sigma_check(rule_yaml)

Returns `true` when a [Sigma](https://sigmahq.io) rule (YAML) parses and compiles successfully using only features this worker supports, and `false` otherwise. Unlike `sigma_match`, it **never raises** -- it is the safe, boolean-returning gate you run before trusting a rule.

**When to use it.** Validate rules in bulk -- e.g. lint a column of candidate rules, filter a detection-rule repository down to the ones this engine can actually evaluate, or guard a pipeline with `WHERE sigma.sigma_check(rule_text)` before feeding rules to `sigma_match`.

**Inputs.** `rule_yaml` -- a complete Sigma rule. Remember that pySigma requires a non-empty `logsource:` block; a rule missing it (or with `logsource: {}`) is invalid and returns `false`.

**Output & edge cases.** Returns `BOOLEAN`; NULL in, NULL out. It returns `false` for malformed YAML, a missing `logsource:`, a missing `condition`, or any unsupported modifier. Because it swallows errors into `false`, use `sigma_rule_info` if you need the specific parse error surfaced.

# sigma_check

A non-raising validator: returns `true` when a Sigma rule parses and compiles with only supported features, `false` otherwise.

## Usage

Run it over a column of candidate rules to keep (or reject) the ones this engine can evaluate before feeding them to `sigma_match`. Fully runnable, catalog-qualified queries are attached as example queries.

## Notes

- A rule **must** have a non-empty `logsource:` block, or it is invalid.
- Never raises -- malformed or unsupported rules simply return `false`.
- NULL in, NULL out.

workers.title: Source Map Decoder & Position Resolver
workers.tagline: Resolve JavaScript source maps in DuckDB with SQL — decode v3 mappings and de-minify stack frames in bulk. A VGI worker.
workers.summary: Decode JavaScript Source Map v3 (.map) files and resolve minified positions back to original source locations.
workers.doc_md:
# sourcemap

Decode **JavaScript Source Map v3** (`.map`) files and resolve minified `(line, col)` positions back to original `source:line:col:name`, directly in DuckDB SQL. Nothing else in DuckDB reads source maps — `read_json` gives you the wrapper object but not the decoded Base64-VLQ `mappings` grammar. This worker performs that decode and exposes both the raw mapping rows and resolved original positions, so a column of production RUM / error-tracking frames can be de-minified in bulk with a single JOIN.

The heavy lifting (Base64-VLQ decode, index maps via `sections`, inline `sourcesContent`, the nearest-preceding lookup) is done by the Sentry `sourcemap` crate; this worker is a thin Arrow adapter over it. A map is supplied as a **path** to a `.map` file, the raw map **JSON text** (e.g. from `read_text(...)`), or map `BLOB` bytes — so data-URI inline maps decode via the text/bytes mode.

## Semantics

- All line/column numbers are **0-indexed** (Source Map v3); browser stack frames are usually 1-indexed, so subtract one before resolving.
- Position resolution is **nearest-preceding** (the greatest mapping `<=` the requested position), so an exact `(line, col)` match isn't required.
- Per-row resolution is **tolerant**: a NULL, malformed, or empty map — or a position with no match — yields NULL rather than failing the query, so one bad frame never aborts a scan.

## When to use

Reach for it whenever you have minified positions (deployed bundle line/column) and the corresponding source map, and you want the original file, line, column, and symbol name back — one frame at a time or a whole error table at once.

example_queries.description: Decode a source map into its full token (mapping) table.
example_queries.sql: SELECT gen_line, gen_col, source FROM sourcemap.main.tokens('{"version":3,"file":"o.js","sources":["index.js"],"names":[],"mappings":"AAAA"}')

example_queries.description: Resolve a minified (line, col) position to its original source location.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sourcemap.main.lookup('{"version":3,"file":"o.js","sources":["index.js"],"names":[],"mappings":"AAAA"}', 0, 0)

example_queries.description: List the original source files a map references.
example_queries.sql: SELECT src_id, source, has_content FROM sourcemap.main.sources('{"version":3,"file":"o.js","sources":["index.js"],"names":[],"mappings":"AAAA"}')

example_queries.description: Read a map's version and mapping counts.
example_queries.sql: SELECT version, n_sources, n_mappings FROM sourcemap.main.meta('{"version":3,"file":"o.js","sources":["index.js"],"names":[],"mappings":"AAAA"}')

example_queries.description: Preview the decoded token rows of the built-in sample map.
example_queries.sql: SELECT gen_line, gen_col, source FROM sourcemap.main.example_tokens

example_queries.description: Count how many decoded mappings the sample map contains.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS n FROM sourcemap.main.example_tokens

example_queries.description: Resolve a column of frames against one inline map, joining back by id.
example_queries.sql: SELECT r.id, r.source, r.src_line FROM sourcemap.main.lookup_all((SELECT * FROM (VALUES (1, 0, 0)) AS f(id, line, col)), map := '{"version":3,"file":"o.js","sources":["index.js"],"names":[],"mappings":"AAAA"}', id := 'id') AS r

example_queries.description: Fetch the embedded original source text for source 0.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sourcemap.main.source_content('{"version":3,"sources":["a.js"],"sourcesContent":["const x = 1;"],"names":[],"mappings":"AAAA"}', 0);

example_queries.description: Resolve a generated line/column back to its original location.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sourcemap.main.lookup('{"version":3,"sources":["index.js"],"names":[],"mappings":"AAAA"}', 0, 0);

agent_tasks: I have a source map as JSON text: {"version":3,"sources":["a.js"],"names":[],"mappings":"AAAA,CAAC"}. How many decoded mappings (tokens) does it contain? Return one column named n.

Using the source map JSON {"version":3,"sources":["index.js"],"names":[],"mappings":"AAAA"}, resolve the minified position at generated line 0, column 0 and return the original source file as a single column named source.
How many original source files does this source map reference? Map JSON: {"version":3,"sources":["a.js","b.js"],"names":[],"mappings":"AAAA"}. Return one column named n_sources.

I have one minified error frame with id 1 at generated line 0, column 0. Resolve it against the map {"version":3,"sources":["index.js"],"names":[],"mappings":"AAAA"} and return the id and the resolved original source, as columns id and source.

A source map can embed its original files inline via sourcesContent. For the map JSON {"version":3,"sources":["a.js"],"sourcesContent":["const x = 1;"],"names":[],"mappings":"AAAA"}, return the embedded original source text for source id 0 as a single column named content.

For the source map {"version":3,"sources":["a.js","b.js"],"sourcesContent":["const x=1;",null],"names":[],"mappings":"AAAA"}, how many of its original source files embed inline text? Return the count as a single column named n.
This worker ships a browsable example view of decoded source-map tokens. How many token (mapping) rows does that built-in example contain? Return the count as a single column named n.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Resolve a whole column of minified (line, col) error frames against ONE source map, returning the original (source, src_line, src_col, name) for each — with the input id column passed through so the result joins back to the originating row. The input relation is supplied as a subquery (e.g. `(SELECT id, line, col FROM frames)`); the single map is the named `map :=` argument (a .map path, raw JSON text, or `BLOB`). Name the id/line/col columns with `id :=` / `line :=` / `col :=` (defaults 'id', 'line', 'col'). Positions are 0-indexed; resolution is nearest-preceding. A malformed map, NULL position, or no-match yields NULL resolution columns for that row (the id still passes through). This is the bulk de-minify entry point for RUM / error-tracking frames.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Bulk-resolve a column of minified `(line, col)` frames against one map, with `id` passthrough: `lookup_all((SELECT id, line, col FROM frames), map := …, id := 'id')`. Emits `(id, source, src_line, src_col, name)`.

tags.vgi.result_dynamic_columns_md:
The first output column is the **passthrough id** — it takes the exact name and type of the input `id` column (whatever you named via `id :=`), so results join back to the originating row. It is followed by four fixed resolution columns. For an input relation whose id column is a `BIGINT` named `id`, the result columns are:

| Name | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `id` | BIGINT | Passthrough of the input id column (same name and type as the input). |
| `source` | VARCHAR | Original source file, or NULL when the frame does not resolve. |
| `src_line` | BIGINT | 0-indexed original line, or NULL when unresolved. |
| `src_col` | BIGINT | 0-indexed original column, or NULL when unresolved. |
| `name` | VARCHAR | Original symbol name, or NULL if the mapping carries none. |

workers.title: Regression & Statistical Inference
workers.tagline: Regression with inference (p-values/CIs) & hypothesis tests for DuckDB (Python, statsmodels)
workers.summary: statsmodels-powered regression and inference for DuckDB/SQL: OLS/Logit/GLM fits, model statistics, and t-test/ADF hypothesis tests
workers.doc_md:
# statsmodels: Regression & Statistical Inference in SQL

![statsmodels logo](https://www.statsmodels.org/stable/_images/statsmodels-logo-v2-horizontal.svg)

Run regression with full statistical inference and classic hypothesis tests directly in DuckDB SQL: fit OLS, logistic, and generalized linear models and get coefficient tables complete with standard errors, t/z-statistics, p-values, and 95% confidence intervals — no Python notebook required.

This extension brings the proven statistics of the [statsmodels](https://www.statsmodels.org/stable/index.html) library ([source on GitHub](https://github.com/statsmodels/statsmodels)) to anyone who already speaks SQL. It is built for data analysts, data scientists, and engineers who want trustworthy estimation and inference — effect sizes, significance, model fit, and stationarity checks — without exporting data to a separate stats environment. Every function takes a whole input relation as a `(SELECT ...)` subquery, so you model the result of any DuckDB query: joins, filters, window functions, and aggregates all flow straight into the fit.

Under the hood each call buffers the input relation, builds the design matrices from a [Patsy](https://patsy.readthedocs.io/en/latest/) ([source on GitHub](https://github.com/pydata/patsy)) `formula` (for the regressions) or from named column roles (for the tests), then runs the corresponding statsmodels routine once and returns the results as an ordinary SQL table you can join, filter, and persist. The familiar R-style formula syntax (`y ~ x1 + x2 + C(group)`) makes specifying interactions, transformations, and categorical encodings concise and readable.

The capabilities group into three areas. **Regression** estimates how predictors drive an outcome — linear for continuous responses, logistic for binary events, and generalized linear models for counts and other exponential-family outcomes — always returning coefficients with standard errors, t- or z-statistics, p-values, and 95% confidence intervals. **Model fit** reports whole-model diagnostics such as R-squared, adjusted R-squared, the F-test, AIC/BIC, and log-likelihood so you can judge how well a linear model explains the data. **Hypothesis tests** compare two group means and check a time series for a unit root (stationarity). Together they let you ask, in SQL alone, which predictors matter and by how much, whether an effect is significant, how well a model fits, and whether a series is stationary.

example_queries.description: Fit y ~ x by OLS and read each term's coefficient and p-value.
example_queries.sql: SELECT term, round(coef, 3) AS coef, round(p_value, 6) AS p_value FROM statsmodels.main.ols((SELECT * FROM (VALUES (1,5.1),(2,7.9),(3,11.2),(4,13.8)) AS t(x, y)), formula := 'y ~ x') ORDER BY term

example_queries.description: Report the R-squared goodness-of-fit for an OLS model of y on x.
example_queries.sql: SELECT round(value, 4) AS r_squared FROM statsmodels.main.model_stats((SELECT * FROM (VALUES (1,5.1),(2,7.9),(3,11.2),(4,13.8)) AS t(x, y)), formula := 'y ~ x') WHERE statistic = 'r_squared'

example_queries.description: Fit a Poisson GLM of count y on x and read the log-rate coefficient on x.
example_queries.sql: SELECT term, round(coef, 3) AS coef FROM statsmodels.main.glm((SELECT * FROM (VALUES (1,1),(2,2),(3,2),(4,4),(5,5),(6,7),(7,9),(8,12)) AS t(x, y)), formula := 'y ~ x', family := 'poisson') WHERE term = 'x'

example_queries.description: Two-sample t-test of v across groups; read the p-value and mean difference.
example_queries.sql: SELECT round(p_value, 6) AS p_value, round(mean_diff, 2) AS mean_diff FROM statsmodels.main.ttest((SELECT * FROM (VALUES (10,'a'),(11,'a'),(20,'b'),(22,'b')) AS t(v, g)), "column" := 'v', "group" := 'g')

example_queries.description: List every GLM family with its link function and the outcome it suits.
example_queries.sql: SELECT family, link, typical_outcome FROM statsmodels.main.glm_families ORDER BY family

example_queries.description: Which GLM family should you use for count outcomes?
example_queries.sql: SELECT family, example_use FROM statsmodels.main.glm_families WHERE typical_outcome = 'Non-negative integer counts'

example_queries.description: Fit y ~ x by OLS and read each term's coefficient and p-value
example_queries.sql: SELECT term, round(coef, 3) AS coef, round(p_value, 6) AS p_value FROM statsmodels.main.ols((SELECT * FROM (VALUES (1,5.1),(2,7.9),(3,11.2),(4,13.8),(5,17.1),(6,19.9),(7,23.2),(8,25.8)) AS t(x, y)), formula := 'y ~ x') ORDER BY term

example_queries.description: Logistic fit of binary y on x; read the x log-odds coefficient and odds ratio
example_queries.sql: SELECT term, round(coef, 3) AS coef, round(odds_ratio, 3) AS odds_ratio FROM statsmodels.main.logit((SELECT * FROM (VALUES (1,0),(2,0),(3,0),(4,1),(5,0),(6,1),(7,0),(8,1),(9,1),(10,1),(11,1),(12,1)) AS t(x, y)), formula := 'y ~ x') WHERE term = 'x'

example_queries.description: Two-sample t-test of v across groups; read the p-value and mean difference
example_queries.sql: SELECT round(p_value, 6) AS p_value, round(mean_diff, 2) AS mean_diff FROM statsmodels.main.ttest((SELECT * FROM (VALUES (10,'a'),(11,'a'),(9,'a'),(12,'a'),(10,'a'),(20,'b'),(22,'b'),(19,'b'),(21,'b'),(20,'b')) AS t(v, g)), "column" := 'v', "group" := 'g')

example_queries.description: Read the R-squared goodness-of-fit for an OLS model of y on x
example_queries.sql: SELECT round(value, 4) AS r_squared FROM statsmodels.main.model_stats((SELECT * FROM (VALUES (1,5.1),(2,7.9),(3,11.2),(4,13.8),(5,17.1),(6,19.9),(7,23.2),(8,25.8)) AS t(x, y)), formula := 'y ~ x') WHERE statistic = 'r_squared'

## Regression & inference over SQL relations

This schema fits statistical models and runs classic hypothesis tests directly over DuckDB relations, powered by [statsmodels](https://www.statsmodels.org/). Every function takes a whole input relation as a `(SELECT ...)` subquery plus either a Patsy formula (`y ~ x1 + x2`) or named column roles, buffers the rows, runs the routine once, and returns a coefficient or statistic table you can join, filter, and persist.

It covers three areas:

- **Regression** — linear, logistic, and generalized linear fits that return a coefficient table with standard errors, t/z-statistics, p-values, and 95% confidence intervals.
- **Model fit** — whole-model diagnostics for a linear fit, such as R-squared, the F-test, and AIC/BIC.
- **Hypothesis tests** — compare two group means, and test a time series for a unit root (stationarity).

Reach for it to estimate effects, judge model fit, compare two groups, or check a series for stationarity — all without leaving SQL.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
# glm_families

A small browsable reference view listing the **GLM error families** the `glm` function accepts as its `family` argument. Each row pairs a family name with its default link function, the kind of outcome it models, and a concrete example use.

**Use it** to discover valid `family` values before calling `glm`: the `family` column is exactly what you pass as `glm(<relation>, formula := '...', family := '<family>')`. Four families are available: `gaussian` (identity link, equals OLS), `binomial` (logit link, for binary/proportion outcomes), `poisson` (log link, for counts), and `gamma` (inverse link, for positive right-skewed responses). The view is a fixed in-memory table, so it scans instantly with no arguments.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## GLM error families

A reference view of the four error families the [statsmodels](https://www.statsmodels.org/) GLM fit supports, exposed so you can browse valid `family` values before calling `glm`.

Each row gives the `family` name (what you pass as `glm(..., family := '<family>')`), its default `link` function, the `typical_outcome` it models, and an `example_use`. The families are `gaussian` (identity link, equivalent to OLS), `binomial` (logit link, binary or proportion outcomes), `poisson` (log link, count outcomes), and `gamma` (inverse link, positive right-skewed outcomes).

It is a fixed four-row table, so it always scans instantly.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
# ols

Fit an **ordinary least squares** linear regression over a whole SQL relation and return its coefficient table with full statistical inference. The first positional argument is the data, passed as a `(SELECT ...)` subquery; the model is given as a Patsy `formula` named argument such as `'y ~ x1 + x2'`. Every column of the relation is available to the formula by name.

**Use it** to estimate how continuous predictors drive a continuous outcome and to judge which terms matter: each row is one model term (predictors plus the `Intercept`) with its coefficient, standard error, t-statistic, two-sided p-value, and 95% confidence interval. For whole-model fit quality (R-squared, F-test, AIC/BIC) use `model_stats` with the same formula.

**Edge cases:** a malformed formula, a missing or non-numeric column, empty input, or a singular (rank-deficient) design raises a clean `StatsError` rather than crashing.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## OLS regression

Ordinary least squares regression over a SQL relation, powered by [statsmodels](https://www.statsmodels.org/). Pass the data as a `(SELECT ...)` subquery and the model as a Patsy `formula`.

Returns one row per model term (`Intercept` and each predictor) with the estimated coefficient, standard error, t-value, p-value, and 95% confidence bounds.

Call it as `ols(<relation>, formula := 'y ~ x')`; a ready-to-run version is in this function's example queries. See `model_stats` for whole-model fit statistics on the same formula.

# logit

Fit a **binary logistic regression** over a whole SQL relation and return its coefficient table on the log-odds scale, with full inference and a convenience odds ratio per term. Pass the data as a `(SELECT ...)` subquery and a Patsy `formula` named argument; the response on the left of the formula must be binary (two distinct values, e.g. 0/1).

**Use it** when the outcome is a yes/no event and you want to know how each predictor shifts the odds: each row is one model term with its log-odds coefficient, standard error, Wald z-statistic, p-value, 95% confidence interval, and `odds_ratio` (= `exp(coef)`; >1 raises the odds, <1 lowers them).

**Edge cases:** a non-binary response, perfect separation, a singular design, a bad formula, a missing/non-numeric column, or empty input raises a clean `StatsError`.

functions.comment: Two-sample (pooled-variance) t-test of 'column' across the two levels of 'group'; emits one row (statistic, p_value, df, mean_diff). 'column' and 'group' are SQL keywords -- double-quote both arg names in SQL.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
# ttest

Run a **two-sample (pooled-variance) t-test** comparing the mean of a numeric column across the two levels of a grouping column. Pass the data as a `(SELECT ...)` subquery, the value column as `column`, and the grouping column as `group`. Because `column` and `group` are SQL reserved words, **double-quote both argument names** at the call site: `"column" := 'v', "group" := 'g'`.

**Use it** to answer 'do these two groups differ in mean?'. The result is a single row: the t-statistic, the two-sided p-value for equal means, the degrees of freedom, and `mean_diff` (mean of the first group minus the second). A small p-value is evidence the group means differ.

**Edge cases:** a grouping column that does not have exactly two levels, a missing/non-numeric value column, or empty input raises a clean `StatsError`.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## Two-sample t-test

Pooled-variance two-sample t-test over a SQL relation, powered by [statsmodels](https://www.statsmodels.org/). Compares the mean of a value column across the two levels of a grouping column.

Note that `column` and `group` are SQL keywords, so both argument names must be double-quoted in SQL.

Returns a single row: the t-statistic, the two-sided p-value, the degrees of freedom, and the difference in group means.

Call it as `ttest(<relation>, "column" := 'value', "group" := 'arm')` with both argument names double-quoted; a ready-to-run version is in this function's example queries.

# model_stats

Fit the same **OLS** model as `ols` but return the **whole-model fit statistics** instead of the per-term coefficient table. Pass the data as a `(SELECT ...)` subquery and a Patsy `formula` named argument.

**Use it** to judge how well a linear model explains the data: the result is one `(statistic, value)` row per metric, covering `r_squared`, `adj_r_squared`, `f_statistic`, `f_pvalue`, `aic`, `bic`, `log_likelihood`, `nobs`, `df_model`, and `df_resid`. ## OLS model fit statistics

Whole-model goodness-of-fit metrics for an OLS regression, powered by [statsmodels](https://www.statsmodels.org/). Same inputs as `ols` (a `(SELECT ...)` relation and a Patsy `formula`), but the output describes the model as a whole rather than each term.

# glm

Fit a **generalized linear model** over a whole SQL relation with a selectable error `family`, returning a coefficient table on the link scale with full inference. Pass the data as a `(SELECT ...)` subquery, a Patsy `formula`, and `family := 'gaussian' | 'binomial' | 'poisson' | 'gamma'` (default `gaussian`).

**Use it** for outcomes that aren't plain continuous Gaussian: `poisson` for counts (log link), `binomial` for binary/proportion outcomes (logit link), `gamma` for positive skewed responses, and `gaussian` to reproduce OLS. Each row is one model term with its coefficient, standard error, Wald z-statistic, p-value, and 95% confidence interval.

**Edge cases:** an unknown family name, a family/data mismatch, a singular design, a bad formula, a missing/non-numeric column, or empty input raises a clean `StatsError`.

functions.name: adfuller
functions.comment: Augmented Dickey-Fuller unit-root (stationarity) test over an already-ordered series; emits one row (statistic, p_value, used_lag, n_obs). Pass an ORDER BY'd relation so rows are in time order. Small p_value => reject unit root => stationary.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
# adfuller

Run the **Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) unit-root test** to decide whether a time series is stationary. Pass the series as a `(SELECT ...)` subquery and the series column as `column`. Because `column` is a SQL reserved word, **double-quote the argument name**: `"column" := 'v'`.

**Ordering matters:** SQL has no inherent row order, so the input must already be time-ordered — pass `(SELECT v FROM series ORDER BY t)`. The function treats the rows in the order it receives them.

**Use it** for stationarity checks before ARIMA / regression on time series. The result is a single row: the test `statistic`, the MacKinnon `p_value` (small => reject the unit-root null => the series is stationary), the number of lags chosen by AIC (`used_lag`), and the observation count after lagging/differencing (`n_obs`).

**Edge cases:** a missing/non-numeric column, empty input, or a series too short for the chosen lag raises a clean `StatsError`.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## Augmented Dickey-Fuller test

Stationarity (unit-root) test for a time series over a SQL relation, powered by [statsmodels](https://www.statsmodels.org/).

The input must be time-ordered — pass an `ORDER BY`'d subquery, since SQL rows have no inherent order. `column` is a SQL keyword, so the argument name must be double-quoted.

Returns a single row: the test statistic, the MacKinnon p-value (small means the series is stationary), the lag count chosen by AIC, and the effective observation count.

Call it as `adfuller(<ordered-relation>, "column" := 'v')` with the argument name double-quoted and the rows already time-ordered; a ready-to-run version is in this function's example queries.
