LOAD vgi;
ATTACH 'units' (TYPE vgi, LOCATION './target/release/units-worker');
SET search_path = 'units.main';

SELECT convert(1, 'mi', 'km');        -- 1.609344
SELECT convert(0, 'C', 'F');          -- 32.0
SELECT convert(1, 'GiB', 'byte');     -- 1073741824.0
SELECT dimension('mi');               -- 'length'
SELECT compatible('mi', 'kg');        -- false
SELECT to_base(1, 'km');              -- 1000.0   (SI base unit of the dimension)
SELECT (parse_quantity('5 km')).*;    -- (value := 5.0, unit := 'km')
SELECT * FROM supported_units();      -- discovery: unit, dimension, base_unit

tags.vgi.doc_md:
# Units — main schema

The single namespace for the `units` worker, bringing runtime, string-driven physical-unit conversion and dimensional analysis to SQL.

Its capabilities are organized into a few areas:

- **Conversion** — convert and normalize numeric quantities between units of the same dimension, including reduction to the SI base unit.
- **Analysis** — look up a unit's physical dimension and test whether two units are compatible for conversion.
- **Parsing** — turn free-text quantity strings such as `5 km` into a structured value and unit.
- **Discovery** — browse the catalog of every recognized unit string, its dimension, and its SI base unit.

Reach for this schema whenever a query must reconcile mixed-unit measurements, confirm that two quantities are comparable, or normalize values to a common base before aggregating.

workers.doc_md:
# useragent — HTTP User-Agent Parsing & Bot Detection in SQL

Turn raw HTTP `User-Agent` header strings into structured **browser**, **operating-system**, and **device** facts — and flag **bots, crawlers, and spiders** — directly in DuckDB SQL over Apache Arrow.

The `useragent` extension brings production-grade User-Agent parsing to your SQL workflow. It is built for web-analytics teams, log-pipeline engineers, and anyone who needs to segment HTTP traffic by client, platform, or device without leaving the database. Point it at a column of raw `User-Agent` headers and get clean, normalized browser / OS / device attributes plus a reliable bot signal — no hand-written UDFs, no external services, and no row-by-row API round-trips.

Parsing is powered by the community-maintained [uap-core](https://github.com/ua-parser/uap-core) regex database — the same ruleset behind the cross-language ua-parser project — executed through the Rust [`uaparser`](https://docs.rs/uaparser/latest/uaparser/) crate. The full uap-core `regexes.yaml` ruleset is embedded into the worker at compile time and compiled exactly once per process, so the binary is fully self-contained and matching stays fast across millions of rows. Results stream back to DuckDB over Apache Arrow. Unidentified families normalize to SQL `NULL` (never the literal `'Other'`), and crawlers are recognized via uap-core's `Spider` device classification.

The function surface is small and composable: single-field accessors pull one attribute (browser, operating system, or device) at a time, a boolean predicate flags automated traffic, and a one-shot parser returns every field together as a `STRUCT` when you need several at once. Every accessor takes a single `ua VARCHAR` argument and returns `NULL` for empty or unrecognizable input, so it drops straight into web-analytics enrichment, traffic segmentation by platform/device, and bot filtering. Reach for this worker whenever you have a column of raw User-Agent headers to enrich, segment, or filter in SQL.

## Learn more

- Source code: [ua-parser/uap-core](https://github.com/ua-parser/uap-core)
- Specification: [uap-core spec](https://github.com/ua-parser/uap-core/blob/master/docs/specification.md)
- Rust parser docs: [uaparser on docs.rs](https://docs.rs/uaparser/latest/uaparser/)

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## ua_parse

Parses an HTTP `User-Agent` string into a **single `STRUCT`** containing every component at once, in one pass over the input.

**Returned struct fields:**

- `browser` (`VARCHAR`) — client family
- `browser_version` (`VARCHAR`) — dotted client version
- `os` (`VARCHAR`) — operating-system family
- `os_version` (`VARCHAR`) — dotted OS version
- `device` (`VARCHAR`) — device family/model
- `brand` (`VARCHAR`) — device brand/manufacturer
- `is_bot` (`BOOLEAN`) — spider/crawler flag

**When to use:** prefer `ua_parse` over calling the individual `ua_*` accessors when you need several fields, since it parses the string only once. Project with `(ua_parse(ua)).*` or pick fields like `(ua_parse(ua)).os`.

**Edge cases:** `NULL`, empty, or unparseable input yields a `NULL` struct row. For bots, `device` and `brand` are suppressed to `NULL` while `is_bot` is `TRUE`. Unidentified individual fields are `NULL` rather than `'Other'`.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# Parse all fields

`ua_parse(ua)` returns a `STRUCT` with every parsed User-Agent field in one pass. Project all fields with `(ua_parse(ua)).*`, or pick individual fields like `(ua_parse(ua)).browser`.

## Struct shape

`STRUCT(browser, browser_version, os, os_version, device, brand, is_bot)`

## Notes

- More efficient than calling each `ua_*` accessor separately.
- `NULL`/unparseable input yields a `NULL` row.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## ua_is_bot

Returns a `BOOLEAN` that is `TRUE` when an HTTP `User-Agent` string identifies a **spider / crawler / bot** (for example Googlebot, Bingbot, or other automated agents) and `FALSE` for ordinary human browsers.

**When to use:** filter automated traffic out of web-analytics aggregates, route bot requests differently, or compute a human-vs-bot split. A typical pattern is `WHERE NOT ua_is_bot(ua)` to keep only real visitors.

**Input:** one `ua VARCHAR` column or literal.
**Output:** `TRUE`/`FALSE`, or `NULL` when the input is `NULL`.

**How it works:** detection is driven by the embedded uap-core regex database, which classifies crawlers under the device family `Spider`. Unrecognized agents are treated as non-bots (`FALSE`).
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# Bot detection

`ua_is_bot(ua)` returns `TRUE` for spiders/crawlers and `FALSE` for ordinary browsers. A common pattern is `WHERE NOT ua_is_bot(ua)` to keep only human traffic.

## Notes

- `NULL` input yields `NULL`.
- Backed by uap-core's `Spider` device family.

workers.doc_md:
# Vision: Image Classification (ImageNet) in SQL

![ONNX Runtime](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/microsoft/onnxruntime/main/docs/images/ONNX_Runtime_logo_dark.png)

**Run deep-learning image classification directly in DuckDB SQL** — point a query at a column of image blobs (or image file paths) and get back ImageNet-1k labels, no Python notebook, model server, or ML pipeline required. The `vision` catalog turns computer-vision inference into ordinary SQL functions you can `SELECT`, filter, `JOIN`, and aggregate.

This extension is for data engineers, analysts, and application developers who want to tag, filter, search, or group images by what they depict without leaving the database. Classic use cases include auto-labeling a column of photo blobs, finding every row whose image looks like a cat or a car, ranking an image's most probable subjects, and enriching a media table with predicted categories — all expressed as the SQL you already write. Because the model runs out-of-process behind VGI, untrusted inputs are safe: a malformed, empty, or oversized image yields SQL `NULL` (scalar) or no rows (table function), never a worker crash.

Under the hood, inference is powered by [ONNX Runtime](https://onnxruntime.ai), Microsoft's high-performance, cross-platform inference engine for ONNX models ([source on GitHub](https://github.com/microsoft/onnxruntime), [documentation](https://onnxruntime.ai/docs/)). The classifier is a permissively-licensed MobileNetV2 model trained on the [ImageNet](https://www.image-net.org) 1000-class dataset (Apache-2.0 weights served via ONNX Runtime's MIT license) — deliberately chosen to be safe for a commercial marketplace, unlike copyleft alternatives. The model and its 1000 labels are downloaded once on first use and cached locally, so subsequent queries pay only inference cost.

## Functions

- **`top_label(image)` / `top_label(path)`** — scalar: the single #1 predicted ImageNet label per row. Ideal as a per-row enrichment column over a table of image blobs.
- **`classify(image[, top_k])` / `classify(path[, top_k])`** — table function returning the top-k `(label, confidence)` predictions, confidence descending (default top-5).
- **`image_classes()`** — table function listing the model's full `(idx, label)` label set (all 1000 ImageNet classes); also exposed as the parenthesis-free view `vision.main.image_classes` for discovery and joins.

## Notes

Every image argument is accepted either as a `BLOB` column or via a filesystem-path overload. Untrusted or malformed images yield SQL `NULL` (scalar) or no rows (table), never a crash, making the functions safe to apply across an entire column of user-supplied data.

| function | kind | returns |

| `top_label(image\|path)` | scalar | the #1 predicted label |

## `image_classes` (table)

A scan-backed table listing **every ImageNet-1k class** the model can predict (1000 rows), queried without parentheses (`vision.main.image_classes`) — the same data the `image_classes()` table function returns.

### Columns

| column | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `idx` | INTEGER | 0-based class index into the model output |
| `label` | VARCHAR | ImageNet class label |

### Notes

Useful to validate or join against predicted labels from `top_label` / `classify`.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Explode one image into its **top-k ImageNet `(label, confidence)` predictions**, one row per prediction, ordered confidence-descending. Use it when you want ranked candidate labels with probabilities — not just the single best label (`top_label`) — e.g. to show the model's top guesses, threshold on confidence, or pick among close alternatives.

It is a *source* table function: pass the image **positionally**. Overloads resolve by argument type and arity — `classify(image)` / `classify(image, top_k)` over a `BLOB`, and `classify(path)` / `classify(path, top_k)` over a `VARCHAR` filesystem path; `top_k` defaults to 5. A table-function argument cannot be a `(SELECT ...)` subquery (DuckDB rejects it), so pass a `BLOB` column/literal or a path string directly. A NULL/malformed/over-large/unreadable image emits **no rows** rather than crashing. Returns columns `label VARCHAR` and `confidence DOUBLE` (softmax probability in [0, 1]).
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## `classify`

Table function returning the **top-k `(label, confidence)`** ImageNet predictions for an image, confidence-descending.

### Overloads

- `classify(image BLOB[, top_k INTEGER])`
- `classify(path VARCHAR[, top_k INTEGER])` — read the image off disk first.

`top_k` defaults to 5.

### Returns

| column | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `label` | VARCHAR | predicted ImageNet class label |
| `confidence` | DOUBLE | softmax probability in [0, 1] |

### Notes

functions.name: classify
functions.comment: Top-k ImageNet predictions (label, confidence) for an image BLOB

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Explode one image into its **top-k ImageNet `(label, confidence)` predictions**, one row per prediction, ordered confidence-descending. Use it when you want ranked candidate labels with probabilities — not just the single best label (`top_label`) — e.g. to show the model's top guesses, threshold on confidence, or pick among close alternatives.

It is a *source* table function: pass the image **positionally**. Overloads resolve by argument type and arity — `classify(image)` / `classify(image, top_k)` over a `BLOB`, and `classify(path)` / `classify(path, top_k)` over a `VARCHAR` filesystem path; `top_k` defaults to 5. A table-function argument cannot be a `(SELECT ...)` subquery (DuckDB rejects it), so pass a `BLOB` column/literal or a path string directly. A NULL/malformed/over-large/unreadable image emits **no rows** rather than crashing. Returns columns `label VARCHAR` and `confidence DOUBLE` (softmax probability in [0, 1]).
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## `classify`

Table function returning the **top-k `(label, confidence)`** ImageNet predictions for an image, confidence-descending.

### Overloads

- `classify(image BLOB[, top_k INTEGER])`
- `classify(path VARCHAR[, top_k INTEGER])` — read the image off disk first.

`top_k` defaults to 5.

### Returns

| column | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `label` | VARCHAR | predicted ImageNet class label |
| `confidence` | DOUBLE | softmax probability in [0, 1] |

### Notes

A NULL/malformed image yields **no rows**. A table-function argument cannot be a `(SELECT ...)` subquery — pass a `BLOB` column/literal or a path string.

functions.name: classify
functions.comment: Top-5 ImageNet predictions for an image file path

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Explode one image into its **top-k ImageNet `(label, confidence)` predictions**, one row per prediction, ordered confidence-descending. Use it when you want ranked candidate labels with probabilities — not just the single best label (`top_label`) — e.g. to show the model's top guesses, threshold on confidence, or pick among close alternatives.

It is a *source* table function: pass the image **positionally**. Overloads resolve by argument type and arity — `classify(image)` / `classify(image, top_k)` over a `BLOB`, and `classify(path)` / `classify(path, top_k)` over a `VARCHAR` filesystem path; `top_k` defaults to 5. A table-function argument cannot be a `(SELECT ...)` subquery (DuckDB rejects it), so pass a `BLOB` column/literal or a path string directly. A NULL/malformed/over-large/unreadable image emits **no rows** rather than crashing. Returns columns `label VARCHAR` and `confidence DOUBLE` (softmax probability in [0, 1]).
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## `classify`

Table function returning the **top-k `(label, confidence)`** ImageNet predictions for an image, confidence-descending.

### Overloads

- `classify(image BLOB[, top_k INTEGER])`
- `classify(path VARCHAR[, top_k INTEGER])` — read the image off disk first.

`top_k` defaults to 5.

### Returns

| column | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `label` | VARCHAR | predicted ImageNet class label |
| `confidence` | DOUBLE | softmax probability in [0, 1] |

### Notes

A NULL/malformed image yields **no rows**. A table-function argument cannot be a `(SELECT ...)` subquery — pass a `BLOB` column/literal or a path string.

functions.name: classify
functions.comment: Top-k ImageNet predictions for an image file path

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Explode one image into its **top-k ImageNet `(label, confidence)` predictions**, one row per prediction, ordered confidence-descending. Use it when you want ranked candidate labels with probabilities — not just the single best label (`top_label`) — e.g. to show the model's top guesses, threshold on confidence, or pick among close alternatives.

It is a *source* table function: pass the image **positionally**. Overloads resolve by argument type and arity — `classify(image)` / `classify(image, top_k)` over a `BLOB`, and `classify(path)` / `classify(path, top_k)` over a `VARCHAR` filesystem path; `top_k` defaults to 5. A table-function argument cannot be a `(SELECT ...)` subquery (DuckDB rejects it), so pass a `BLOB` column/literal or a path string directly. A NULL/malformed/over-large/unreadable image emits **no rows** rather than crashing. Returns columns `label VARCHAR` and `confidence DOUBLE` (softmax probability in [0, 1]).
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## `classify`

Table function returning the **top-k `(label, confidence)`** ImageNet predictions for an image, confidence-descending.

### Overloads

- `classify(image BLOB[, top_k INTEGER])`
- `classify(path VARCHAR[, top_k INTEGER])` — read the image off disk first.

`top_k` defaults to 5.

### Returns

| column | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `label` | VARCHAR | predicted ImageNet class label |
| `confidence` | DOUBLE | softmax probability in [0, 1] |

### Notes

A NULL/malformed image yields **no rows**. A table-function argument cannot be a `(SELECT ...)` subquery — pass a `BLOB` column/literal or a path string.

functions.name: top_label
functions.comment: The #1 predicted ImageNet label for an image BLOB (NULL if not an image)

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Return the single most likely ImageNet-1k class label for an image, as a scalar — one image per row in, one `VARCHAR` label out — so it composes anywhere in a `SELECT` projection or a `WHERE`/`GROUP BY` predicate. Use it to tag a column of images, filter rows to a subject (`WHERE top_label(img) = 'tabby'`), or bucket images by what they depict.

Two arity-1 overloads share the name and resolve by input type: a `BLOB` overload (`top_label(image)`) over raw image bytes, and a `VARCHAR` overload (`top_label(path)`) that reads the image off a filesystem path. Inputs are untrusted: a NULL, malformed, empty, over-large, or unreadable image yields SQL `NULL` rather than raising. For the top-k predictions with confidences, use `classify` instead.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## `top_label`

Scalar function returning the **#1 predicted ImageNet label** for an image.

### Overloads

- `top_label(image BLOB) -> VARCHAR` — classify raw image bytes.
- `top_label(path VARCHAR) -> VARCHAR` — read the image at a filesystem path, then classify.

### Returns

A single ImageNet class label (e.g. `tabby`, `envelope`), or `NULL` for a NULL/malformed/unreadable image.

### Notes

Use in projections or predicates. For ranked `(label, confidence)` predictions, use the `classify` table function.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Return the single most likely ImageNet-1k class label for an image, as a scalar — one image per row in, one `VARCHAR` label out — so it composes anywhere in a `SELECT` projection or a `WHERE`/`GROUP BY` predicate. Use it to tag a column of images, filter rows to a subject (`WHERE top_label(img) = 'tabby'`), or bucket images by what they depict.

Two arity-1 overloads share the name and resolve by input type: a `BLOB` overload (`top_label(image)`) over raw image bytes, and a `VARCHAR` overload (`top_label(path)`) that reads the image off a filesystem path. Inputs are untrusted: a NULL, malformed, empty, over-large, or unreadable image yields SQL `NULL` rather than raising. For the top-k predictions with confidences, use `classify` instead.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## `top_label`

Scalar function returning the **#1 predicted ImageNet label** for an image.

### Overloads

- `top_label(image BLOB) -> VARCHAR` — classify raw image bytes.
- `top_label(path VARCHAR) -> VARCHAR` — read the image at a filesystem path, then classify.

### Returns

A single ImageNet class label (e.g. `tabby`, `envelope`), or `NULL` for a NULL/malformed/unreadable image.

### Notes

Use in projections or predicates. For ranked `(label, confidence)` predictions, use the `classify` table function.

workers.doc_md:
# Wikipedia & MediaWiki Search in SQL

![MediaWiki logo](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dd/MediaWiki-2020-logo.svg/250px-MediaWiki-2020-logo.svg.png)

Run Wikipedia full-text search and page-summary retrieval directly from DuckDB SQL — powered by the free, official MediaWiki API, with no API key, no scraping, and no setup.

This VGI extension turns any DuckDB session into a live Wikipedia and MediaWiki client. It is built for engineers and data teams who want to ground large language models with encyclopedic facts, enrich rows with authoritative context, or run ad-hoc knowledge lookups without leaving SQL. Because it speaks plain MediaWiki, it works against English Wikipedia by default, any of the 300+ Wikipedia language editions via a single `lang` argument, and any third-party MediaWiki wiki via `api_url`. It is a thin, polite **egress connector**: queries leave the engine for the wiki, results come back as Arrow rows, and the worker process never crashes on a missing page or a flaky network.

Under the hood the extension calls the [MediaWiki Action API](https://www.mediawiki.org/wiki/API:Main_page) for ranked search and the [MediaWiki REST API](https://www.mediawiki.org/wiki/API:REST_API) page-summary endpoint for rich lead extracts and thumbnails — the same free, open interfaces that power [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/) itself. The networked client sends a descriptive User-Agent, applies per-call timeouts, and retries with backoff on rate limits and server errors, so it stays well-behaved against the public Wikimedia endpoints. The software is open source and mirrors the upstream [MediaWiki source on GitHub](https://github.com/wikimedia/mediawiki); see the [MediaWiki search API documentation](https://www.mediawiki.org/wiki/API:Search) for the underlying query semantics.

**SQL use cases and function surface.** Use `wiki_search(query, lang := 'en', count := 10, max_pages := 1, api_url := '')` — a table function — to run full-text search and get ranked rows of article title, plain-text snippet, page id, word count and canonical URL, ideal for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) candidate selection. Use the `wiki_page(title)` / `wiki_page(title, lang)` scalar to fetch a single page's plain-text summary extract inline in a `SELECT` (returns NULL on a missing page rather than erroring). Use `wiki_page_summary(title, lang := 'en', api_url := '')` — a table function — for the rich single-row summary including the extract, canonical URL, thumbnail and page id. Pair it with vgi-embed and vgi-rerank to build knowledge-grounding pipelines entirely in SQL.

Retrieved article **content is CC-BY-SA** — attribution and share-alike are the caller's responsibility; the `url` column is provided so you can link back and attribute.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Fetch the **rich, multi-column page summary** of a single Wikipedia (or any MediaWiki) article as a one-row table.

Call it as a table function: `wiki.main.wiki_page_summary(title, lang := 'en', api_url := '')`. Being a table function, `lang` and `api_url` are `name :=` named arguments: `lang` picks the language wiki and `api_url` targets a non-Wikimedia wiki's api.php.

Use it when you need more than just the extract text -- the canonical URL (for attribution / linking back), a thumbnail image, and the page id -- e.g. when enriching rows for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), knowledge cards, or fact lookup. For just the extract text as a scalar over a whole column of titles, use the `wiki_page` scalar instead.

**Returns** one row with columns `title` (resolved), `extract` (plain-text summary), `url`, `thumbnail_url` (may be NULL), and `pageid`.

**Edge cases:** an empty title is rejected at bind time. A missing page yields **zero rows** (not an error). A transport failure surfaces as a clean DuckDB error. Retrieved text is **CC-BY-SA**: attribution and share-alike are the caller's responsibility.

# wiki_page_summary

Returns a single Wikipedia / MediaWiki page's **rich summary** as a one-row table -- the multi-column companion to the `wiki_page` scalar -- over the free MediaWiki REST summary endpoint.

## Usage

Call it as a table function in `FROM`: the page title is the one positional argument, and `lang` and `api_url` are `name :=` named options. See the runnable examples in this function's `example_queries` metadata.

The page title is positional; the language wiki and a custom MediaWiki endpoint are named options. See the per-argument docs (`vgi_function_arguments`) for the exact names and defaults.

## Notes

- A missing page returns zero rows; it is not an error.
- `thumbnail_url` may be NULL when the page has no lead image.
- For just the extract over many titles, use the `wiki_page` scalar.
- Retrieved text is **CC-BY-SA** -- attribution and share-alike are your responsibility.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Run a **full-text search** over Wikipedia (or any MediaWiki) and stream back ranked article results, one row per hit.

Call it as a table function: `wiki.main.wiki_search(query, lang := 'en', count := 10, max_pages := 1, api_url := '')`. Because it is a table function, the options are `name :=` named arguments: `lang` picks the language wiki, `count` is results per API page (1-50), `max_pages` bounds how many continuation (`sroffset`) pages to follow (1-20), and `api_url` targets a non-Wikimedia wiki's api.php.

Use it for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), candidate-document retrieval, fact lookup, and turning a topic into a ranked set of article titles and snippets you can then feed to `wiki_page` / `wiki_page_summary` or to vgi-embed / vgi-rerank.

**Returns** the unified search schema: `title`, `snippet` (HTML stripped to plain text), `pageid`, `wordcount`, `url`, `lang`, and `extra` (a JSON `VARCHAR` of timestamp/size, NULL when absent).

**Edge cases:** an empty query is rejected at bind time. Paging is sequential (each page's `sroffset` comes from the previous response) and pinned to a single scan worker so results are emitted exactly once. A transport failure surfaces as a clean DuckDB error. Retrieved text is **CC-BY-SA**: attribution and share-alike are the caller's responsibility.

# wiki_search

Full-text search over Wikipedia / any MediaWiki, returning ranked results as a table, over the free MediaWiki Action API (`action=query&list=search`).

## Usage

Call it as a table function in `FROM`: the search query is the one positional argument, and `lang`, `count`, `max_pages`, and `api_url` are `name :=` named options. Raise `max_pages` to follow more `sroffset` continuation pages. See the runnable examples in this function's `example_queries` metadata.

The query is positional; the language wiki, page size, continuation depth, and a custom MediaWiki endpoint are named options. See the per-argument docs (`vgi_function_arguments`) for the exact names, defaults, and ranges.

## Notes

- Snippets are HTML-stripped to plain text; `extra` is a JSON string (use the `json` extension's `->>`).
- Paging is sequential and emitted exactly once (pinned to one scan worker).
- Retrieved text is **CC-BY-SA** -- attribution and share-alike are your responsibility.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Fetch the plain-text **lead-paragraph summary extract** of a Wikipedia (or any MediaWiki) article as a single `VARCHAR`.

Call it as `wiki.main.wiki_page(title)` for English, or `wiki.main.wiki_page(title, lang)` to target another language wiki (e.g. `'de'`, `'fr'`). Because VGI scalars are positional-only, `lang` is a positional argument, not a `lang :=` named argument.

Use it to enrich an existing column of titles with encyclopedic context for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), fact lookup, or knowledge grounding -- it is set-based, so it resolves a whole column of titles in one scan.

**Input:** an article title column (`VARCHAR`). **Output:** the summary extract `VARCHAR`.

**Edge cases:** a missing page, a blank title, or a NULL input yields NULL for that row -- a single bad title never aborts the scan. A transport-level failure surfaces as a clean DuckDB error rather than crashing the worker. For the richer multi-column shape (title, extract, url, thumbnail_url, pageid) use the `wiki_page_summary` table function instead. Retrieved article text is **CC-BY-SA**: attribution and share-alike are the caller's responsibility.

# wiki_page

Returns the plain-text summary **extract** (lead paragraphs) of a Wikipedia / MediaWiki page as a scalar `VARCHAR`, over the free MediaWiki REST summary endpoint (with an Action-API `prop=extracts` fallback).

## Usage

Call `wiki.main.wiki_page(title)` for English or `wiki.main.wiki_page(title, lang)` for another language edition. Scalars are positional-only, so the language is a positional argument (no `lang :=`). Because it is set-based, referencing a title column resolves the whole column in one scan. See the runnable examples in this function's `example_queries` metadata.

## Notes

- A missing page, blank title, or NULL input returns NULL (the scan is never aborted by one bad row).
- Transport failures raise a clean DuckDB error; the worker never crashes.
- Need the URL, thumbnail, or page id too? Use the `wiki_page_summary` table function.
- Retrieved text is **CC-BY-SA** -- attribution and share-alike are your responsibility.

workers.title: X12 / EDIFACT EDI Parser
workers.tagline: Parse X12 and EDIFACT EDI in DuckDB with SQL — 837/835/834/270/271 and more, public segment syntax. A VGI worker.
workers.summary: Parse ANSI ASC X12 EDI and UN/EDIFACT interchanges into queryable segment / element / envelope / shaped rows. Public syntax only; parsing is 100% local.
workers.doc_md:
# x12 — ANSI ASC X12 / UN-EDIFACT EDI in SQL

**Query raw EDI interchanges directly from DuckDB** — files (`.edi` / `.x12` / `.835` / `.837`, which may glob), inline `VARCHAR` content, or a `BLOB`. No staging, no external service.

**What it does.** It sniffs each interchange's own delimiters from the fixed-width ISA header, walks the ISA/GS/ST nesting, and hands back rows you can filter, join, and aggregate in SQL. Structural counts and control numbers are validated, so you can tell a complete interchange from a truncated one.

**Pick your level of shaping.** Work at the *raw* level — one row per segment, or one row per element with composite components and repetitions split out — for full-fidelity inspection; at the *interchange-summary* level — one row per transaction with its ISA/GS/ST control metadata and the SE/GE/IEA structural validity flags — for envelope checks; or at the *shaped* level — flat relational projections of the common healthcare and B2B transaction sets, keyed by public segment ID and element position. Inline delimiter- and type-sniffing scalars let you route or triage content before a full parse, and UN/EDIFACT (UNA/UNB/UNH, release-character un-escaping) is handled alongside X12.

**When to reach for it.** Ad-hoc inspection and structural validation of inbound/outbound EDI, extracting claim / remittance / eligibility / purchase-order fields into tables, or classifying files by transaction type before loading.

**Data residency.** Parsing is 100% local with no outbound calls — a feature for PHI/PII workloads. Ships **public X12 syntax only**: it embeds no copyrighted ASC X12 TR3 implementation-guide content, so human-readable code-value translation needs your own licensed X12 reference.

example_queries.description: Pull the elements of every CLM (claim) segment from a folder of 837 claim files.
example_queries.sql: SELECT source_path, segment_index, element_index, value FROM x12.main.segments_elements('/data/claims/*.837') WHERE segment_id = 'CLM';

example_queries.description: Flag interchanges whose SE segment count fails to validate across an inbound folder.
example_queries.sql: SELECT source_path, interchange_ctrl, transaction_type, se_count_ok FROM x12.main.envelope('/data/inbound/*.edi') WHERE se_count_ok IS DISTINCT FROM TRUE;

example_queries.description: Extract claim id, total paid, and payer from a folder of 835 remittance files.
example_queries.sql: SELECT clp_claim_id, clp_total_paid, payer_name FROM x12.main.read_835('/data/era/*.835');

example_queries.description: Classify inbound files by transaction set type for routing.
example_queries.sql: SELECT filename, x12.main.transaction_type(content) AS tx_type FROM read_text('/data/inbound/*.edi');

example_queries.description: Count exploded EDIFACT elements per message type across an orders folder.
example_queries.sql: SELECT transaction_type, count(*) AS n_elements FROM x12.main.edifact_segments('/data/orders/*.edi') GROUP BY transaction_type;

example_queries.description: List the shaped X12 transaction sets and their read_* function.
example_queries.sql: SELECT transaction_set, shaped_function FROM x12.main.transaction_sets WHERE family = 'X12' ORDER BY transaction_set;

example_queries.description: Find which shaped function parses 835 remittance advice.
example_queries.sql: SELECT shaped_function, summary FROM x12.main.transaction_sets WHERE transaction_set = '835';

example_queries.description: List every shaped transaction set and its read_* function.
example_queries.sql: SELECT transaction_set, shaped_function FROM x12.main.transaction_sets ORDER BY transaction_set;

tags.vgi.doc_md:
## The `main` schema

The single schema for the `x12` worker. It groups every parsing surface for ANSI ASC X12 and UN/EDIFACT interchanges, so you attach one worker and reach the raw, envelope, and shaped views from the same place.

**Choose a function by how much shaping you want:**

- *Raw* — segment- and element-level explosion for full-fidelity inspection, with composite components and repetitions split out.
- *Interchange summary* — one row per transaction carrying the ISA/GS/ST control metadata and the SE/GE/IEA structural validity flags, for envelope-level completeness checks.
- *Shaped* — flat relational projections of the common healthcare and B2B transaction sets, keyed by public segment ID and element position, for direct column access.

Inline delimiter- and type-sniffing scalars let you route or triage content before committing to a full parse, and the UN/EDIFACT family (UNA/UNB/UNH, release-character un-escaping) is handled alongside X12.

Every function accepts the same overloaded input: a file path (which may glob), inline `VARCHAR` content, or a `BLOB` — auto-detected by the interchange's `ISA`/`UNA`/`UNB` magic prefix.

Start from the browsable `transaction_sets` reference view to see which shaped `read_*` view covers each transaction set.

vgi.example_queries.description: Pull the elements of every CLM (claim) segment from a folder of 837 claim files.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT source_path, segment_index, element_index, value FROM x12.main.segments_elements('/data/claims/*.837') WHERE segment_id = 'CLM';

vgi.example_queries.description: Flag interchanges whose SE segment count fails to validate across an inbound folder.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT source_path, interchange_ctrl, transaction_type, se_count_ok FROM x12.main.envelope('/data/inbound/*.edi') WHERE se_count_ok IS DISTINCT FROM TRUE;

vgi.example_queries.description: Extract claim id, total paid, and payer from a folder of 835 remittance files.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT clp_claim_id, clp_total_paid, payer_name FROM x12.main.read_835('/data/era/*.835');

vgi.example_queries.description: Classify inbound files by transaction set type for routing.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT filename, x12.main.transaction_type(content) AS tx_type FROM read_text('/data/inbound/*.edi');

vgi.example_queries.description: Count exploded EDIFACT elements per message type across an orders folder.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT transaction_type, count(*) AS n_elements FROM x12.main.edifact_segments('/data/orders/*.edi') GROUP BY transaction_type;

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Shaped, relational view of X12 transaction set 997 (read_997) — a 997 functional acknowledgment. The single `input` argument takes a file path or glob (e.g. '/data/*.997'), or inline `VARCHAR`/`BLOB` content (auto-detected by the ISA/UNA/UNB prefix). Every row carries the five envelope keys (interchange_ctrl, group_ctrl, transaction_ctrl, transaction_type, source_path), then this set's positional columns — for example ak2_transaction_control, ak5_status, ak9_status, ak3_segment_id. Columns are named by the PUBLIC segment ID and element position only (e.g. ak5_status = AK501); raw codes are surfaced verbatim, so code-value translation needs your own licensed X12 reference. Each AK2 parent starts a logical row group; repeating children fan out to one row each sharing the parent's keys, so re-aggregate with GROUP BY on the parent id. Structural / positional only — no TR3 loop or code-set rules.

functions.name: envelope
functions.comment: One row per ST transaction: ISA/GS/ST envelope metadata + structural validity flags

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Summarize ANSI ASC X12 EDI file(s) as one row per ST transaction set — the routing / triage view. The single `input` argument is a file path/glob or inline content (auto-detected by the ISA/UNA/UNB magic prefix). Columns expose the ISA interchange header (control number, sender/receiver qualifiers + IDs, date/time, version, P/T usage indicator), the GS functional group header (functional id, app sender/receiver, date, GS08 version), the ST header (control number, transaction type, impl reference), the actual ST..SE segment_count, and the structural validity flags se_count_ok / ge_count_ok / iea_count_ok / se_ctrl_match / ge_ctrl_match / iea_ctrl_match (NULL when the matching trailer is absent — e.g. a truncated interchange). This is structural validation only (segment counts + control-number matching) — no loop or code-set rules.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Shaped, relational view of X12 transaction set 270 (read_270) — a 270 eligibility / benefit inquiry. workers.title: X.509 Certificate & TLS Inspection
workers.tagline: Parse X.509 certificates & inspect TLS endpoints for DuckDB (Go)
workers.summary: Parse X.509 certificates and inspect TLS endpoints
workers.doc_md:
# X.509 Certificate & TLS Inspection for DuckDB

**Parse X.509 certificates and inspect live TLS endpoints directly in SQL** — read subjects, issuers, validity windows, SHA-256 fingerprints, and subject alternative names (SANs) from PEM or DER certificates, and pull the certificate chain a TLS server presents, all without leaving DuckDB.

This is a defensive security and compliance toolkit for anyone who works with certificates at scale: SREs auditing certificate expiry across a fleet, security engineers triaging TLS configurations, and compliance teams reporting on certificate authorities, key algorithms, and signature algorithms. Instead of shelling out to `openssl` and parsing text by hand, you query certificates and endpoints as ordinary SQL columns and rows, then filter, join, and aggregate them like any other DuckDB data.

It is powered entirely by the Go standard library's battle-tested [`crypto/x509`](https://pkg.go.dev/crypto/x509) and [`crypto/tls`](https://pkg.go.dev/crypto/tls) packages — no third-party parsing code and no external services. The worker speaks the VGI protocol over Arrow, so DuckDB attaches it as a catalog and certificate parsing runs in-process at native speed. Certificate inputs are accepted as **PEM text** (`VARCHAR`) or **DER bytes** (`BLOB`); the format is sniffed from the content at runtime, so one query works for both.

## When to reach for it

Reach for this worker whenever certificates or TLS endpoints show up in your data and you want to treat them as structured columns rather than opaque blobs: auditing expiry windows across a fleet, pinning or comparing SHA-256 fingerprints, checking key and signature algorithms against a policy, expanding a certificate into a row per attribute for ad-hoc inspection, or pulling the chain a live server presents to confirm what it actually serves. Offline certificate parsing runs entirely in-process; live endpoint inspection **opens a network connection, so use it against AUTHORIZED endpoints only.**

## Typical uses

A few patterns recur. To flag soon-to-expire certificates, apply `cert_not_after` to a column of PEM or DER certificates and keep the rows whose expiry falls inside your renewal window, reporting each certificate's `cert_subject` alongside. To audit cryptographic hygiene across a fleet, group a certificate table by `cert_key_algorithm` and `cert_signature_algorithm` and count the weak ones. To confirm what a server actually serves, call the `tls_inspect` table function on an **authorized** `host:port` and read back the presented chain. Browse the `cert_fields` registry view to discover every attribute the worker can read and the scalar that returns each; ready-to-run, fully qualified statements live in the `x509.main` schema's example queries.

Learn more about the underlying library in the [Go `crypto/x509` documentation](https://pkg.go.dev/crypto/x509) and the [Go source on GitHub](https://github.com/golang/go/tree/master/src/crypto/x509). Source for this worker lives at [github.com/Query-farm/vgi-x509](https://github.com/Query-farm/vgi-x509).

tags.vgi.doc_md:
## x509.main

Defensive **X.509 certificate** parsing and **TLS endpoint** inspection, exposed as DuckDB SQL functions over Apache Arrow.

### Two ways to work

Scalar functions take one certificate and return a single field (subject, issuer, serial, key and signature algorithms, SHA-256 fingerprint, validity window, CA flag, or subject alternative names) — ideal for filtering, joining, and aggregating certificate columns. Table functions expand a certificate or endpoint into rows: one dumps every attribute of a certificate for ad-hoc inspection, the other connects to a live TLS endpoint (**AUTHORIZED endpoints only**) and returns the presented chain.

### Usage

Certificate inputs accept **PEM text** (`VARCHAR`) or **DER bytes** (`BLOB`); the content is sniffed at runtime. NULL certificate input yields NULL (scalars) or zero rows.

functions.name: tls_inspect
functions.comment: Connect to a TLS host:port and return the presented certificate chain (AUTHORIZED endpoints only)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Connect to a live TLS endpoint given as host:port and return the certificate chain the server presents, one row per certificate (seq, subject, issuer, validity window, CA flag, SHA-256 fingerprint). Defensive inspection only: it opens a network connection, so use AUTHORIZED endpoints only. insecure defaults to true so it inspects whatever is presented (expired / self-signed included); the dial and handshake are bounded by timeout_ms.

functions.name: cert_signature_algorithm
functions.comment: Certificate signature algorithm (Go crypto/x509 canonical name, e.g. ECDSA-SHA256)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Return the algorithm the issuing CA used to sign this certificate, as a `VARCHAR`. The value is Go crypto/x509's canonical name for the algorithm and is drawn from a fixed vocabulary: for RSA PKCS#1 v1.5, `SHA256-RSA`, `SHA384-RSA`, `SHA512-RSA` (and the legacy `SHA1-RSA`, `MD5-RSA`, `MD2-RSA`); for RSA-PSS, `SHA256-RSAPSS`, `SHA384-RSAPSS`, `SHA512-RSAPSS`; for ECDSA, `ECDSA-SHA256`, `ECDSA-SHA384`, `ECDSA-SHA512` (and legacy `ECDSA-SHA1`); for DSA, `DSA-SHA1`, `DSA-SHA256`; and the single-token `Ed25519`. An unrecognized OID yields `Unknown Signature Algorithm`. Note the ordering convention differs by family — RSA/DSA render as hash-then-key (`SHA256-RSA`) while ECDSA renders as key-then-hash (`ECDSA-SHA256`) — so match on the whole token, not a positional split. For a security audit, the SHA-1, MD5 and MD2 variants are considered weak/deprecated and are the ones worth flagging. Accepts PEM text (`VARCHAR`) or DER bytes (`BLOB`); NULL input yields NULL. Example: the committed fixture certificate is P-256 ECDSA and returns `ECDSA-SHA256`.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Read the certificate signature algorithm as Go crypto/x509's canonical name (e.g. `ECDSA-SHA256`, `SHA256-RSA`, `Ed25519`). The value comes from a fixed vocabulary; the SHA-1/MD5/MD2 variants are weak and worth flagging in an audit.

functions.name: cert_key_algorithm
functions.comment: Public-key algorithm with size/curve (e.g. RSA-2048, ECDSA-P256, Ed25519)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Return the certificate's subject public-key algorithm together with its key size or curve, as a `VARCHAR` built by this worker (not Go's bare algorithm name). The value follows a fixed convention: RSA keys render as `RSA-<bits>` where <bits> is the modulus size, typically `RSA-2048`, `RSA-3072` or `RSA-4096`; ECDSA keys render as `ECDSA-<curve>` with the curve name stripped of its hyphen, i.e. `ECDSA-P256`, `ECDSA-P384`, `ECDSA-P521`; Edwards keys render as the single token `Ed25519`. Any other key type falls back to Go's public-key algorithm name (e.g. `DSA`). For a security audit, RSA moduli below 2048 bits are considered weak. Accepts PEM text (`VARCHAR`) or DER bytes (`BLOB`); NULL input yields NULL. Example: the committed fixture certificate carries a P-256 ECDSA key and returns `ECDSA-P256`.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Read the public-key algorithm with its size or curve: `RSA-<bits>` (e.g. `RSA-2048`), `ECDSA-<curve>` (e.g. `ECDSA-P256`), or `Ed25519`. RSA moduli under 2048 bits are weak.

workers.title: XSLT, XQuery & XPath for XML
workers.tagline: XSLT 3.0 / XQuery 3.1 / XPath 3.1 over XML for DuckDB (Python, SaxonC-HE)
workers.summary: XSLT 3.0 / XQuery 3.1 / XPath 3.1 over XML for SQL (SaxonC-HE).
workers.doc_md:
# XSLT, XQuery & XPath for XML in SQL

![Saxonica SaxonC-HE logo](https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/3630933?s=240&v=4)

Transform, query, and shred XML directly in DuckDB SQL with full **XSLT 3.0**, **XQuery 3.1**, and **XPath 3.1** support, powered by the production-grade Saxon processor.

This extension turns DuckDB into an XML processing engine. Instead of exporting data to a separate XSLT/XQuery toolchain, you can apply stylesheets, evaluate XPath expressions, run XQuery FLWOR programs, and explode XML documents into relational rows without ever leaving SQL. It is built for data engineers and analysts who land XML in columns -- SOAP/EDI payloads, RSS/Atom feeds, OOXML and SVG fragments, scientific and financial document formats -- and need to extract, reshape, or validate that markup at query time, row by row, with NULLs passed through cleanly.

## Key concepts

- **Per-row scalars vs. set-returning table functions.** Scalars compute one value per row (a string, boolean, number, or list); table functions and the array-plus-UNNEST pattern explode a single document into many rows -- the natural way to *shred* XML into a relational result.
- **Transform, query, and validate.** XSLT reshapes documents, XPath and XQuery pull values out of them, and a well-formedness check lets you filter malformed rows before processing.
- **NULL / invalid / error.** A NULL input yields NULL output (or no rows); malformed XML or a bad stylesheet/expression raises a clean DuckDB error, so bad data never crashes the worker.

## When to use it

Reach for this worker whenever XML lands in a DuckDB column and you need to read a value out of it, transform it into another shape, or normalize its repeated structure into rows for downstream SQL.

## Under the hood

The worker is backed by [SaxonC-HE](https://www.saxonica.com/), the free Home Edition of [Saxonica](https://www.saxonica.com/)'s Saxon processor -- the reference implementation for XSLT 3.0 / XQuery 3.1 / XPath 3.1 -- via the [saxonche](https://pypi.org/project/saxonche/) Python bindings. A single native Saxon processor is booted once per worker and reused; compiled stylesheets and queries are cached on their source text, so a constant stylesheet applied down a column compiles once and transforms many rows. Note that SaxonC-HE is not schema-aware, so there is no XSD validation; the well-formedness check provides the strongest guarantee the free edition offers.

## Learn more

- [Saxonica homepage](https://www.saxonica.com/)
- [Saxon documentation](https://www.saxonica.com/documentation/index.html)
- [Saxon-HE source on GitHub](https://github.com/Saxonica/Saxon-HE)
- [`saxonche` on PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/saxonche/)
- W3C specs: [XSLT 3.0](https://www.w3.org/TR/xslt-30/), [XPath 3.1](https://www.w3.org/TR/xpath-31/), [XQuery 3.1](https://www.w3.org/TR/xquery-31/)
workers.readme_sql: INSTALL vgi FROM community; LOAD vgi; ATTACH 'xslt' (TYPE vgi, LOCATION 'uv run xslt_worker.py'); SELECT xslt.xpath_string('x', '//a'); -- 'x' SELECT xslt.xpath_boolean('', 'count(//a) = 1'); -- true SELECT xslt.xpath_number('42', 'number(//n)'); -- 42.0 SELECT UNNEST(xslt.xpath_array('ab', '//i')); -- 'a','b' ← shred! SELECT xslt.xquery('ab', 'string-join(//i, ",")'); -- 'a,b' SELECT xslt.is_well_formed(''); -- true SELECT * FROM xslt.xpath_nodes('ab', '//i'); -- (seq, value) rows SELECT version, schema_aware FROM xslt.saxon_info; -- engine capabilities

example_queries.description: Pull the string value of an XPath match out of a document.
example_queries.sql: SELECT xslt.main.xpath_string('x', '//a')

example_queries.description: Test an XPath count predicate as a boolean.
example_queries.sql: SELECT xslt.main.xpath_boolean('<r><a/></r>', 'count(//a) = 1')

example_queries.description: Read a numeric value out of a document via XPath.
example_queries.sql: SELECT xslt.main.xpath_number('<r><n>42</n></r>', 'number(//n)')

example_queries.description: Shred every XPath match into rows with UNNEST.
example_queries.sql: SELECT UNNEST(xslt.main.xpath_array('ab', '//i')) AS item

example_queries.description: Join matched values into one string with an XQuery string-join.
example_queries.sql: SELECT xslt.main.xquery('ab', 'string-join(//i, ",")')

example_queries.description: Filter to only well-formed candidate documents.
example_queries.sql: SELECT xslt.main.is_well_formed('') AS well_formed

example_queries.description: Explode a document into numbered (seq, value) rows in document order.
example_queries.sql: SELECT seq, value FROM xslt.main.xpath_nodes('ab', '//i') ORDER BY seq

example_queries.description: Read the engine version and whether XSD validation is available.
example_queries.sql: SELECT version, schema_aware FROM xslt.main.saxon_info

example_queries.description: Confirm the XSLT and XQuery language levels the engine implements.
example_queries.sql: SELECT xslt_version, xquery_version FROM xslt.main.saxon_info

example_queries.description: Explode an XQuery FLWOR result into numbered rows.
example_queries.sql: SELECT seq, value FROM xslt.main.xquery_rows('12', 'for $x in //i return $x*2') ORDER BY seq

example_queries.description: Apply an XSLT 3.0 stylesheet, lifting an inner element value into a new wrapper element.
example_queries.sql: SELECT xslt.main.xslt('<doc><n>hi</n></doc>', '<xsl:stylesheet version="3.0" xmlns:xsl="http://www.w3.org/1999/XSL/Transform"><xsl:template match="/"><out><xsl:value-of select="//n"/></out></xsl:template></xsl:stylesheet>')

tags.vgi.doc_md:
# main

XSLT 3.0 / XQuery 3.1 / XPath 3.1 processing over XML, backed by SaxonC-HE.

The functions in this schema group into four capabilities:

- **Transform** an XML document with an XSLT 3.0 stylesheet.
- **Query** a document with XPath or XQuery to pull out a string, boolean, or numeric value.
- **Shred** a document into relational rows -- per row via an array you UNNEST, or via a set-returning table function.
- **Validate** that text is well-formed XML before you process it.

## saxon_info (table)

A single-row, directly-browsable table describing the SaxonC engine bundled with this worker — its version and edition, the XSLT/XQuery/XPath language levels it implements, and whether it is schema-aware.

**When to use:** learn the engine's capabilities before relying on them. The `schema_aware` column is the key signal: it is always false on the Home Edition, so there is no XSD validation. The table has no arguments and a single row of engine facts, so it is directly browsable.

**Columns:** `version`, `edition`, `xslt_version`, `xquery_version`, `xpath_version` (all `VARCHAR`) and `schema_aware` (`BOOLEAN`).

functions.name: xquery_rows

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## xquery_rows

Run an **XQuery 3.1** query against one document and emit **one `(seq, value)` row per item** of the result sequence, in sequence order.

**When to use:** when the query yields a sequence (e.g. a FLWOR `for $x in //i return $x*2`) and you want each item as its own row to join, filter, or aggregate in SQL. Use the `xquery` scalar instead when you want the whole result serialized into one value.

**Inputs:** `xml` (the document, bound as the context item) and `expr` (the XQuery 3.1 source). Both `VARCHAR`; named-argument syntax supported.

**Output columns:** `seq` (`BIGINT`, 1-based position) and `value` (`VARCHAR`, the item's string value).

**Behavior & edge cases:** an empty result sequence -> zero rows. Malformed XML or a malformed query raises a clean DuckDB error.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# xquery_rows

Table function: one `(seq, value)` row per item in an XQuery 3.1 result sequence.

## Usage

Call `xslt.main.xquery_rows(xml, expr)` in a `FROM` clause to expand each item of the result sequence into a numbered `(seq, value)` row.

## Notes

- One row per sequence item; `seq` is the 1-based position.
- Use the `xquery` scalar for a single serialized result.
- Invalid XML/query raises an error.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT seq, value FROM xslt.main.xquery_rows('12', 'for $x in //i return $x*2') ORDER BY seq

## xpath_nodes

Explode a single XML document into rows: emit **one `(seq, value)` row per XPath 3.1 match**, in document order.

**When to use:** shred one constant document into a relational result — turn `//item` matches into a numbered table you can join, filter, and aggregate. For shredding a *column* of documents instead, use the `xpath_array` scalar with `UNNEST`.

**Inputs:** `xml` (the document) and `expr` (an XPath 3.1 expression). Both `VARCHAR`; table-function named-argument syntax (`name := value`) is supported.

**Output columns:** `seq` (`BIGINT`, 1-based position) and `value` (`VARCHAR`, the match's string value).

**Behavior & edge cases:** no matches -> zero rows. Malformed XML or XPath raises a clean DuckDB error.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# xpath_nodes

## Notes

- Binds a single constant document; use `xpath_array` + `UNNEST` per row.
- `seq` is the 1-based document-order position of each match.
- Invalid XML/XPath raises an error.

functions.name: xslt
functions.comment: Transform an XML document with an XSLT 3.0 stylesheet; returns the serialized result

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## xslt

Apply an **XSLT 3.0** stylesheet to an XML document and return the serialized transformation result as text.

**When to use:** reshape, rename, filter, or compute over XML — the full power of XSLT 3.0 (templates, `xsl:value-of`, `xsl:for-each`, modes, functions) — directly in SQL.

**Inputs:** `xml` (the source document) and `stylesheet` (the XSLT 3.0 source). Both are `VARCHAR`.

**Output:** `VARCHAR` — the serialized result tree (often XML, but the stylesheet's `xsl:output` may select text/HTML/JSON).

**Behavior & edge cases:** a NULL in either argument yields NULL for that row. Malformed XML or a malformed stylesheet raises a clean DuckDB error. A constant stylesheet down a column compiles once and is reused. SaxonC-HE is not schema-aware, so schema-aware (validating) XSLT is unavailable.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# xslt

Transform an XML document with an XSLT 3.0 stylesheet, returning the serialized result.

## Usage

Call `xslt.main.xslt(xml, stylesheet)` in any projection to transform a document column against a stylesheet.

## Notes

- Powered by SaxonC-HE (XSLT 3.0).
- NULL input -> NULL output.
- Invalid XML or stylesheet raises a DuckDB error.
- A constant stylesheet is compiled once and reused across rows.

functions.name: xpath_number
functions.comment: Numeric (`DOUBLE`) value of the first XPath 3.1 match (NULL if non-numeric)

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## xpath_number

Evaluate an **XPath 3.1** expression against an XML document and return its **numeric value** as a `DOUBLE`.

**When to use:** extract a number from XML and use it in SQL arithmetic — a measurement, a count (`count(//item)`), a sum (`sum(//price)`), or any numeric XPath computation.

**Inputs:** `xml` (the document) and `expr` (an XPath 3.1 expression). Both `VARCHAR`.

**Output:** `DOUBLE` — the numeric value of the first match, or NULL when the value is non-numeric (XPath NaN) or nothing matches.

**Behavior & edge cases:** NULL in either argument yields NULL. Wrap a path in `number(...)` to coerce a text node. Malformed XML or XPath raises a clean DuckDB error.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# xpath_number

Return the numeric (`DOUBLE`) value of the first XPath 3.1 match, or NULL.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT xslt.main.xpath_number('<r><n>42</n></r>', 'number(//n)');  -- 42.0
```

## Notes

- Non-numeric results (XPath NaN) come back as NULL.
- Use XPath aggregates like `count(...)` / `sum(...)` directly.
- NULL input -> NULL output; invalid XML/XPath raises an error.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT xslt.main.xpath_number('<r><n>42</n></r>', 'number(//n)')

functions.name: xquery
functions.comment: Run an XQuery 3.1 query with the document as context item; returns the serialized result

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## xquery

Run an **XQuery 3.1** query against an XML document (bound as the context item) and return the serialized result.

**When to use:** richer querying than a single XPath — FLWOR expressions (`for`/`let`/`where`/`order by`/`return`), constructed elements, joins across parts of the document, and string/sequence functions like `string-join(//i, ',')`.

**Inputs:** `xml` (the document, available as `.` and `/`) and `query` (the XQuery 3.1 source). Both `VARCHAR`.

**Output:** `VARCHAR` — the serialized query result (atomic text, or constructed XML, depending on the query).

**Behavior & edge cases:** NULL in either argument yields NULL. Use `xquery_rows` instead when you want one row per item of the result sequence. Malformed XML or a malformed query raises a clean DuckDB error.
tags.vgi.doc_md: # xquery Run an XQuery 3.1 query with the document as the context item; returns the serialized result. ## Usage ```sql SELECT xslt.main.xquery('ab', 'string-join(//i, ",")'); ``` ## Notes - The document is the context item (`.` / `/`). - For a result sequence, `xquery_rows` returns one row per item. - NULL input -> NULL output; invalid XML/query raises an error.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT xslt.main.xquery('ab', 'string-join(//i, ",")')

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## xpath_string

Evaluate an **XPath 3.1** expression against an XML document and return the **string value of the first match** (or NULL when nothing matches).

**When to use:** pull a single text value out of XML — an element's text, an attribute, or any atomic computed by XPath (`string(...)`, `concat(...)`, etc.).

**Inputs:** `xml` (the document) and `expr` (an XPath 3.1 expression). Both `VARCHAR`.

**Output:** `VARCHAR` — the string value of the first node/atomic in document order, or NULL if the expression selects nothing.

**Behavior & edge cases:** NULL in either argument yields NULL. A malformed document or a malformed XPath raises a clean DuckDB error. Namespaces follow the document's in-scope bindings; use `//*:name` or `local-name()` predicates for namespace-agnostic matching.
tags.vgi.doc_md: # xpath_string Return the string value of the first XPath 3.1 match in a document, or NULL. ## Usage ```sql SELECT xslt.main.xpath_string('x', '//a'); -- 'x' ``` ## Notes - Returns the FIRST match only; use `xpath_array` to collect all matches. - NULL input -> NULL output; invalid XML/XPath raises an error. - Namespace-agnostic matching: `//*:tag` or `local-name() = 'tag'`.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT xslt.main.xpath_string('xy', '//a')

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## xpath_boolean

Evaluate an **XPath 3.1** expression against an XML document and return its **effective boolean value** (EBV).

**When to use:** test a condition over XML inside a SQL `WHERE`/`CASE` — does a node exist (`boolean(//x)`), does a count match (`count(//a) = 1`), or any predicate that XPath can express.

**Inputs:** `xml` (the document) and `expr` (an XPath 3.1 expression). Both `VARCHAR`.

**Output:** `BOOLEAN` — the EBV of the expression (a non-empty node-set is true, an empty one is false; numeric/string EBV rules apply for atomics).

**Behavior & edge cases:** NULL in either argument yields NULL. Malformed XML or XPath raises a clean DuckDB error.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# xpath_boolean

Return the effective boolean value of an XPath 3.1 expression over a document.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT xslt.main.xpath_boolean('<r><a/></r>', 'count(//a) = 1');  -- true
```

## Notes

- Follows XPath effective-boolean-value rules (existence, numbers, strings).
- NULL input -> NULL output; invalid XML/XPath raises an error.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## xpath_array

Evaluate an **XPath 3.1** expression against an XML document and return the string values of **all matches** as a `VARCHAR[]` list.

**When to use:** shred XML into rows. Apply this to a column of documents and `UNNEST(...)` the result to turn one document into many rows — the per-row counterpart to the `xpath_nodes` table function (which binds one constant document).

**Inputs:** `xml` (the document) and `expr` (an XPath 3.1 expression selecting many items). Both `VARCHAR`.

**Output:** `VARCHAR[]` — the string value of every match, in document order; an empty list when nothing matches.

**Behavior & edge cases:** NULL in either argument yields NULL (not an empty list). Malformed XML or XPath raises a clean DuckDB error.
tags.vgi.doc_md: # xpath_array Return the string values of ALL XPath 3.1 matches as a `VARCHAR[]` list. ## Usage ```sql SELECT UNNEST(xslt.main.xpath_array('ab', '//i')); ``` ## Notes - `UNNEST` the list to shred a column of documents into rows. - For a single constant document, the `xpath_nodes` table function is handier. - NULL input -> NULL output; invalid XML/XPath raises an error.

functions.name: is_well_formed
functions.comment: True if the text is well-formed XML; false if malformed (never an error)

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## is_well_formed

Test whether a string is **well-formed XML** — returns `true` if it parses, `false` if it is malformed. **Never raises** (unlike the other functions).

**When to use:** validate or filter a column of candidate XML before transforming or querying it, e.g. `WHERE xslt.main.is_well_formed(doc)`, so malformed rows do not abort the scan.

**Inputs:** `xml` (the candidate text). `VARCHAR`.

**Output:** `BOOLEAN` — `true` for well-formed XML, `false` for malformed text; NULL input yields NULL.

**Behavior & edge cases:** this checks *well-formedness* (does it parse), not schema validity — SaxonC-HE is not schema-aware, so there is no XSD validation. Well-formedness is the strongest XML check the HE edition offers.
tags.vgi.doc_md: # is_well_formed Return `true` if the text is well-formed XML, `false` if malformed (never errors). ## Usage ```sql SELECT xslt.main.is_well_formed(''); -- true SELECT xslt.main.is_well_formed(''); -- false ``` ## Notes - Checks well-formedness only; there is no XSD/schema validation (HE limitation). - Safe to use in `WHERE` to filter out malformed rows. - NULL input -> NULL output.

vgi.example_queries.description: Check whether a string is well-formed XML.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT xslt.main.is_well_formed('')

tags.vgi.title: Check XML Well-Formedness

workers.title: YARA Malware Scanning
workers.tagline: Scan data/files against YARA rules in DuckDB (Rust, yara-x)
workers.summary: Defensive YARA-X malware scanning: compile YARA rules and scan blobs/text for matches, all in SQL over Apache Arrow.
workers.doc_md:
# YARA Malware Scanning in SQL

![YARA-X logo](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/VirusTotal/yara-x/main/ls/editors/code/images/icon.png)

Scan blobs, files, and text columns for malware and indicators of compromise (IOCs) straight from DuckDB SQL by compiling and matching **YARA rules** — no external scanner, no native `libyara`, just functions you can call in a query.

This extension brings defensive YARA rule matching to the database, so security engineers, threat hunters, and data teams can triage suspicious files, hunt for signatures, and enforce detection rules over data they already have in DuckDB. Instead of exporting samples to a standalone tool, you write a YARA ruleset (or load one from a column) and let SQL fan it across millions of rows: filter a table of email attachments, label artifacts in an object store, or join scan verdicts back onto your metadata — all in one place.

Matching is powered by [YARA-X](https://github.com/VirusTotal/yara-x), VirusTotal's pure-Rust rewrite of the classic YARA engine, embedded directly in the worker so there is no C dependency to install or keep patched. Rules are compiled once per batch and reused, and scanning is *total*: untrusted, garbage, empty, or deliberately hostile data simply yields no matches rather than crashing the worker, so you can point it at live malware safely. The full YARA syntax — string, hex, and regex patterns, conditions, namespaces, tags, and the standard `pe`/`elf`/`hash`/`math` modules — is supported.

Two shapes of access are offered. Per-row scalar functions test a whole column of blobs or text against a ruleset, giving you a filter predicate, a match count, or the name of the rule that fired — ideal for triaging a table of samples or labelling artifacts in place. Table functions instead expand a single scan into detail rows, one per matching rule or per individual pattern hit (with byte offsets and the matched bytes), for forensics and drill-down. There is also a validation helper for checking that a ruleset compiles before you scan with it, and a `yara_modules` reference table listing the YARA-X modules (`pe`, `elf`, `hash`, `math`, …) a rule may import.

For rule-writing syntax and module reference see the official [YARA-X documentation](https://virustotal.github.io/yara-x/) and the [yara-x crate docs](https://docs.rs/yara-x).

example_queries.description: Validate that a YARA ruleset compiles before scanning with it.
example_queries.sql: SELECT yara.main.yara_check('rule demo { strings: $a = "malware" condition: $a }') AS compiles;

example_queries.description: Predicate: does the text match any rule in a ruleset?
example_queries.sql: SELECT yara.main.yara_matches('this file contains malware', 'rule demo { strings: $a = "malware" condition: $a }') AS hit;

example_queries.description: Name the first rule that matches the data.

tags.vgi.doc_md:
# YARA — `main` schema

The single schema holding this worker's YARA rule-compilation and malware-scanning functions over Apache Arrow. The functions fall into a few groups:

- **Scanning** — per-row scalars that test a column of blobs or text against a ruleset (match predicate, matching-rule count, first matching rule).
- **Match Details** — table functions that expand a single scan into detail rows: one per matching rule, or one per individual pattern hit with byte offsets.
- **Rule Validation** — check that a ruleset compiles before you scan with it.
- **Reference** — the `yara_modules` table lists the YARA-X modules (`pe`, `elf`, `hash`, `math`, …) compiled into this worker that a rule may import.

Scanning is *total*: untrusted or hostile data yields no matches rather than crashing the worker; only an invalid rule source raises an error.

workers.doc_md:
## Yahoo Finance

Market data from Yahoo Finance, exposed as three keyless DuckDB table functions.

- **`history`** — OHLCV candles for one ticker over a named range or explicit date range.
- **`quote`** — a current-price snapshot (price, change, day & 52-week range, volume) for a list of tickers.
- **`search`** — resolve a company name or partial symbol to candidate tickers.

No secret or API key is required. Prices are delayed and provided for informational use only; review Yahoo's terms before redistribution. Intraday candles are only available for recent ranges.

LOAD vgi;
ATTACH 'yfinance' AS yf (TYPE vgi, LOCATION '/path/to/vgi-yfinance-worker');

example_queries.description: Find a ticker by company name
example_queries.sql: SELECT symbol, long_name FROM yfinance.main.search('vanguard')

example_queries.description: List the reference tickers for a given asset type
example_queries.sql: SELECT symbol, name, exchange FROM yfinance.main.symbol_reference WHERE asset_type = 'ETF' ORDER BY symbol

Pick a named window (range := '1y') plus a candle width (bar := '1wk'), or an explicit start_date/end_date range. The symbol may be a column, so LATERAL history(t.sym) fetches candles for every row. Returns columns symbol, timestamp (UTC), open, high, low, close, adjclose, and volume.

tags.vgi.doc_md:
## history

Historical OHLCV candles for one ticker from Yahoo's chart feed. Choose a named `range` (e.g. `'6mo'`, `'1y'`, `'max'`) plus a `bar` candle width (`'1d'`, `'1wk'`, `'1mo'`, or an intraday width like `'5m'` on recent ranges), or pass an explicit `start_date`/`end_date` pair to override `range`. Emits one row per candle, ordered oldest-first; thin or halted candles come back with NULL price cells rather than failing the scan. Intraday bars are only retained by Yahoo for recent windows, so an intraday `bar` on a long `range` yields fewer rows than the range implies. `adjclose` falls back to `close` when Yahoo omits it.

arguments.name: symbol
arguments.description: The ticker to fetch, written the way Yahoo lists it — equities, class shares, crypto pairs, and caret-prefixed indices are all accepted. Passed as the first positional argument (not symbol := ...); a literal or a column (LATERAL history(t.sym)). A NULL or empty symbol yields no rows.

arguments.name: bar
arguments.description: Candle width — how much time each bar spans. Intraday widths only work on recent ranges. Default '1d'.

arguments.name: end_date
arguments.description: Exclusive end date 'YYYY-MM-DD'. Defaults to now when start_date is set.

arguments.name: prepost
arguments.description: Include pre-market and post-market candles. Default false.

arguments.name: range
arguments.description: Named lookback window over which to fetch candles. Ignored when start_date is set. Default '1mo'.

arguments.name: start_date
arguments.description: Inclusive start date 'YYYY-MM-DD'. When set, [start_date, end_date) overrides range. Empty = use range.

examples: SELECT timestamp, close, volume FROM yfinance.main.history('AAPL', range := '1mo') ORDER BY timestamp DESC LIMIT 5
SELECT timestamp, close, volume FROM yfinance.main.history('MSFT', range := '1y', bar := '1wk')
SELECT max(high) AS high_52w, min(low) AS low_52w FROM yfinance.main.history('SPY', range := '1y')
SELECT w.sym, max(h.close) AS high_close FROM (VALUES ('AAPL'), ('MSFT')) w(sym), LATERAL yfinance.main.history(w.sym, range := '1mo') h GROUP BY w.sym

functions.name: quote
functions.comment: Current market snapshot for one or more symbols (keyless, from the chart meta plane): price, change vs previous close, day range, 52-week range, volume. Pass a comma-separated symbol list, or a column (LATERAL quote(t.sym)) for one quote per row.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: A current market snapshot for one or more tickers: last price, change vs the previous close, day high/low, 52-week high/low, and volume. Keyless — one lightweight request per symbol. Use it for watchlists and dashboards; use `history` for a time series.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## quote

Current-price snapshot for a comma-separated list of tickers, one row per symbol. Backed by Yahoo's keyless chart-metadata plane, so `regular_market_change` and `regular_market_change_percent` are derived from the previous close, and market cap is not available. An unresolvable ticker is dropped rather than failing the batch, so the result may have fewer rows than symbols requested. Each symbol is fetched with its own lightweight request, in parallel, so a long watchlist stays responsive.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT symbol, regular_market_price, regular_market_change_percent FROM yfinance.main.quote('AAPL')
vgi.example_queries.description: Snapshot quote for Apple

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT symbol, regular_market_price FROM yfinance.main.quote('AAPL,MSFT,GOOG')
vgi.example_queries.description: Latest price for several symbols at once

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT w.sym, q.regular_market_price FROM (VALUES ('AAPL'), ('MSFT')) w(sym), LATERAL yfinance.main.quote(w.sym) q
vgi.example_queries.description: Latest price for every ticker in a table, via LATERAL

arguments.name: symbols

One request is made per distinct symbol; an unresolvable ticker is dropped rather than failing the batch. functions.name: search
functions.comment: Look up ticker symbols by name or partial symbol (v1 search API). Returns candidate symbols with exchange and instrument type, best matches first. The query may be a column, so LATERAL search(t.name) resolves every row.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Resolve a company name or partial symbol to candidate ticker symbols, best matches first. Use it when you only know a name — take the resulting `symbol` and pass it to `history` or `quote`. Returns equities, ETFs, indices, and other instruments with their exchange and type.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## search

Ticker lookup over Yahoo's search endpoint. Returns up to `count` candidate symbols (news results are dropped), ranked by Yahoo's relevance score, best matches first. Take the resulting `symbol` and feed it into `history` or `quote`. The `count` argument caps how many candidates come back and is clamped to 1..50 (default 8).

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT symbol, short_name, exchange FROM yfinance.main.search('apple')
vgi.example_queries.description: Find symbols matching 'apple'

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT symbol, long_name, exchange FROM yfinance.main.search('vanguard', count := 20)
vgi.example_queries.description: Up to 20 candidate symbols for a query

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT c.name, s.symbol FROM (VALUES ('apple'), ('microsoft')) c(name), LATERAL yfinance.main.search(c.name, count := 1) s
vgi.example_queries.description: Best-matching ticker for every company name in a table, via LATERAL

arguments.name: query
arguments.description: Free-text company name or partial ticker symbol to look up. Passed as the first positional argument (not query := ...); a literal or a column (LATERAL search(t.name)). A NULL or empty query yields no rows.

examples: SELECT symbol, short_name, exchange FROM yfinance.main.search('apple')
